title: Feature request: CLI flags to handle super-hub-driven low-cohesion communities
body:
Thanks for graphify — I've been using it on a React/Firebase PWA codebase and it's been really useful for surfacing structural patterns I wouldn't have caught manually.

Related: #830 — god-node transit in BFS/DFS. The two issues address the same underlying phenomenon (high-degree hubs degrading downstream analysis), applied here to clustering rather than path-finding.

## Context

Running graphify on a ~1500-node React/TypeScript graph, the output flagged Community 0 (86 nodes) with cohesion 0.05. Manual inspection showed the community is not a semantic neighborhood: it bundles six distinct sub-families (UI primitives, page roots, modal family, layout/nav, PWA bootstrap, RBAC) that have been aggregated together by the clustering algorithm rather than by topology that reflects the actual codebase structure.

The aggregation traces to two "super-hub" nodes:

| Node | Degree | Breakdown |
|---|---|---|
| `src/components/ui/index.tsx` | 44 | 14 external imports + 30 contained symbols (barrel re-export module) |
| `useRBAC()` hook | 32 | 13 imports + 18 call sites across consumer modules |

Both hubs are adjacent to nodes from every sub-family at once, which forces Leiden to attract them all into the same basin under uniform edge weights.

## Why the existing second-pass mitigation doesn't catch this

I noticed the comment at `cluster.py:124-125` showing that you've already addressed a related class of cluster bloating (doc-hub bridging, e.g. `CLAUDE.md` connected to everything) with the cohesion-based second-pass split. Two reasons it doesn't cover the case described here:

1. **The cohesion threshold doesn't trigger.** The actual cohesion of Community 0 is `178 / 3655 = 0.0487`. `cohesion_score()` at `cluster.py:166` returns `round(actual / possible, 2)`, producing `0.05`. The threshold check at `cluster.py:128` (`cohesion_score(G, nodes) < _COHESION_SPLIT_THRESHOLD`) becomes `0.05 < 0.05 → False`, so the community falls through unchanged. (See *Additional context* below — this looks like a small latent bug worth a separate one-line fix.)

2. **Even if it triggered, the second pass would not separate this case.** `_split_community()` re-runs `_partition()` on the same subgraph with the same Leiden invocation (uniform edge weights, no resolution control). The super-hubs are still in the subgraph and would re-attract the same neighbors, producing the same partition. The safety net at `cluster.py:151-152` (`if len(sub_communities) <= 1: return [sorted(nodes)]`) would then return the community unchanged.

So the second-pass mitigation is sound for *doc-hub bridging* but doesn't cover *gravitational super-hub attraction*. They look similar from the cohesion metric, but the underlying mechanism differs.

## Proposed solution

A CLI option (or three) to give users levers when the structural assumptions of plain Leiden don't fit their codebase. Ranked from smallest delta to most ambitious:

1. **`--exclude-hubs <degree-percentile>`** (e.g. `p99`) — exclude nodes whose degree is above the given percentile of the graph's degree distribution from the partitioning pass, then re-attach them post-clustering by majority neighbor community. Direct fix for the super-hub case. Minimal implementation: a thin wrapper around `_partition()` in `cluster.py`. Percentile is preferred over an absolute degree threshold because hub degree scales with corpus size.

2. **`--algorithm <leiden|louvain>` plus `--resolution <N>`** — expose parameters that `graspologic.partition.leiden()` already supports natively (`resolution`, `randomness`, `use_modularity`). Pure wire-up, no algorithmic work. Useful when the graph is genuinely modular but the default Leiden resolution isn't sharp enough.

3. **`--edge-weight-mode <uniform|inverse-degree|inverse-log-degree>`** — assign edge weights inversely proportional to endpoint degree, so edges incident to super-hubs are down-weighted automatically. The most principled fix; it solves the root cause without requiring the user to pick a threshold.

For the case described here, option 1 alone would be sufficient. Option 3 is the cleanest architecturally if you'd prefer a single configurable knob.

## Alternatives considered

- **Pre-processing `graph.json` to delete high-degree nodes before `--cluster-only`**: workable as a user-side workaround, but loses information and isn't reproducible across runs.
- **Raising `_COHESION_SPLIT_THRESHOLD`**: would force more splits but risks over-splitting healthy communities. The threshold isn't the right knob — the underlying partitioning is.
- **Manual annotation in `GRAPH_REPORT.md`**: not scalable and defeats the point of automated detection.

## Additional context — side observation

While tracing the threshold behavior I noticed that `cohesion_score()` at `cluster.py:166` rounds to 2 decimals before returning, and the same function is used both for display and for the threshold comparison at line 128. This makes the threshold effectively unreachable for boundary cases — any community with raw cohesion in `[0.045, 0.05)` rounds to `0.05` and fails the strict `< 0.05` check.

Minimal fix would be returning the unrounded value and rounding only at display sites, or using `<=` in the threshold comparison. Happy to send a one-line PR for this independently if useful.

## Environment

- `graphifyy` 0.8.8 (installed via pipx)
- Python 3.12, Linux Mint
- Codebase under analysis: React 18 + TypeScript + Vite + Firebase v12 PWA, ~1500-node graph

Happy to provide more details, additional repro data, or contribute a PR for `--exclude-hubs` if there's interest in this direction.

title: Sensitive filename detection misses underscore-separated names (\b boundary)
body:
## Issue

`_SENSITIVE_PATTERNS` in `graphify/detect.py` uses `\b` word boundaries. Python's `\b` treats `_` as a word character (per `[A-Za-z0-9_]`), so the regex `\b(credential|secret|passwd|password|token|private_key)s?\b` does **not** match common secret filenames that use underscores:

- `api_token.txt`
- `session_token.txt`
- `secret_access_key.txt`
- `aws_credentials.txt`
- `private_key.pem` _(saved by `.pem` extension regex, but the wordboundary one misses it)_

## Reproduction

```python
import re
p = re.compile(r'\b(credential|secret|passwd|password|token|private_key)s?\b', re.IGNORECASE)
print(p.search('api_token.txt'))         # None — should match
print(p.search('session_token.txt'))     # None
print(p.search('secret_access_key.txt')) # None
```

## Real-world impact

In a 1100-file repo audit, `_is_sensitive` caught **0/101** files with token/key/secret patterns in their name. Most were legitimate code files (`iam_token_exchange.py`, `update_api_token.py`), but 5 were actual credentials under `.secrets/` directories that slipped through `detect()` filtering and would have been read by semantic extraction subagents.

Local mitigation via `.graphifyignore` works but requires every user to know about this gap.

## Proposed fix

Two-part:

**1. Replace `\b` with lookarounds that treat `_` as a separator:**

```python
re.compile(
    r'(?<![A-Za-z0-9])(credential|secret|passwd|password|token|private_key)s?(?![A-Za-z0-9])',
    re.IGNORECASE,
)
```

This still allows letter/digit boundaries (so `MyToken.java` matches) but also catches `_token_`, `.token.`, `-token-`, etc.

**2. Add directory-level filter (covers the credentials-by-location case):**

```python
_SENSITIVE_DIRS = {".secrets", "secrets", ".aws", ".gnupg", ".ssh"}

def _is_sensitive(path: Path) -> bool:
    if any(part in _SENSITIVE_DIRS for part in path.parts):
        return True
    return any(p.search(path.name) for p in _SENSITIVE_PATTERNS)
```

## Side-effect to consider

The stricter regex would now flag legitimate code files like `iam_token_exchange.py` as sensitive. Two options:

- Restrict filename-based filter to explicit credential file extensions only (`.pem`, `.key`, `.txt` under a sensitive dir)
- Keep current behaviour and rely on the directory filter for actual credentials, leaving filename heuristics as a soft check

Happy to send a PR if helpful.

title: fix: guard against empty choices and None message in LLM responses
body:
## What

Add guards before accessing `resp.choices[0].message` in `_call_openai_compat` and `_call_llm`.

## Why

The OpenAI-compatible API spec allows HTTP 200 responses with an empty `choices` list or with `choices[0].message = None`. Both occur in production:

- **Empty `choices`**: content-filtered responses on some providers (e.g. Gemini returns `choices=[]` on `PROHIBITED_CONTENT` with HTTP 200)
- **`message = None`**: documented in the OpenAI spec as possible when the response is filtered

Without a guard, both cases raise an unhandled `IndexError` or `AttributeError` that crashes the caller.

`_call_openai_compat` already contains a comment documenting exactly this hazard:

```python
# An overwhelmed local model (typically Ollama) can return HTTP 200 with
# empty / null content or unparseable half-generated JSON.
```

The `_response_is_hollow` check that follows is the right recovery path — but it's unreachable when `choices` is empty. The two-line guard closes that gap.

## Change

```python
# before
resp = client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)
raw_content = resp.choices[0].message.content  # IndexError if choices=[]

# after
resp = client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)
if not resp.choices or resp.choices[0].message is None:
    raise ValueError("LLM returned empty or filtered response")
raw_content = resp.choices[0].message.content
```

Same fix applied to `_call_llm` (line 1041).

## Proof

This crash vector is confirmed by Gemini's own documentation and by [a live test](https://github.com/qizwiz/pact/blob/main/proof/gemini_live_proof.md) that reproduces the `choices[0].message = None` case with an actual API call to `gemini-2.5-flash-preview`.

title: to_wiki: per-community Relationships always empty — _cross_community_links reads an un-annotated graph
body:
**Summary**

`wiki.py:_cross_community_links()` renders "No strong cross-community connections detected" for **100% of communities** whenever `to_wiki()` is called with a graph produced by `build_from_json()`, even though the graph has abundant cross-community edges and `GRAPH_REPORT.md` (same run) correctly enumerates them.

**Root cause**

`_cross_community_links` derives a neighbour's community from the in-memory node attribute `G.nodes[neighbor].get("community")`. `build_from_json(extraction)` (`build.py:56`) copies only the extraction's own node attributes, and a pre-clustering extraction has no `community` key. So `ncid` is `None` for every node, the `if ncid is not None and ncid != own_cid` guard never passes, and the empty-state branch (`wiki.py:72`) always fires. `to_wiki()` already receives the authoritative `communities` dict (`wiki.py:170`) but `_cross_community_links` ignores it. Every other consumer is correct because it derives community from that dict via `_node_community_map(communities)` — `analyze.py:_cross_community_surprises` (feeds the working GRAPH_REPORT bridges), `export.py:289` (`to_json`), `export.py:943` (`to_obsidian`/graphml).

**Reproduction**

```python
from graphify.build import build_from_json
from graphify.wiki import to_wiki
G = build_from_json(extraction)          # extraction = pre-cluster, no node 'community'
communities = cluster(G)                  # {cid: [node_ids]}
to_wiki(G, communities, "out")            # every community: "No strong cross-community connections detected"
```

Confirmed across 4 independent codebases (1.6k–large graphs): raw graphs held 325 / 886 / 2590 / 4253 cross-community edges respectively; `to_wiki` rendered zero in all. Annotating `G.nodes[*]['community']` from the `communities` dict before `to_wiki()` (mirroring `export.py:943`) yields correct output (e.g. 0 → 31 populated communities on one graph), consistent with the bridges `GRAPH_REPORT.md` independently computes.

**Proposed fix** (mirrors the pattern every other exporter already uses)

Make `_cross_community_links` derive community from the `communities` dict instead of the node attribute. Thread a `node_community` map (built once in `to_wiki`/`_community_article` via the existing `_node_community_map`) into `_cross_community_links`, replacing `G.nodes[neighbor].get("community")` with `node_community.get(neighbor)`. This makes `to_wiki` consistent with `to_json`/`to_obsidian`/`analyze` and removes the dependence on a graph-shape contract `build_from_json` does not guarantee.

Happy to open a PR.

title: fix(extract): resolve TypeScript wildcard path aliases (@*, @*/foo)
body:
v7's tsconfig path-alias resolution drops the substitution wildcard, so paths like `"@*": ["features/*/src/"]` or `"@*/interfaces": ["features/*/src/interfaces.ts"]` never resolve to a real file. Common pattern on Nx/Angular monorepos that use a generic catch-all alongside specific aliases — `_load_tsconfig_aliases` and `_resolve_js_import_target` need to preserve and substitute the `*`.

## What was broken

`_read_tsconfig_aliases` strips trailing `/*` from both the alias key and the target, so:

```json
"@*": ["features/*/src/"]
"@*/interfaces": ["features/*/src/interfaces.ts"]
```

become `{ "@": "<repo>/features", "@*/interfaces": "<repo>/features/*/src/interfaces.ts" }` — the substitution group is lost for `@*`, and the resolver has no concept of wildcards anyway, so the second entry is dead code.

`_resolve_js_import_target` then matches by literal prefix only. `@communicate/documentv2` matches the bare `@` prefix, joins the rest, and produces `<repo>/features/communicate/documentv2`. No file there, falls through to basename `documentv2`. Every import that goes through a wildcard alias becomes a stub.

## Fix

1. **Preserve wildcards.** `_read_tsconfig_aliases` keeps both the alias key and the target verbatim when either contains `*`. Non-wildcard aliases still get the trailing-`/` strip.

2. **Wildcard substitution in the resolver.** `_resolve_js_import_target` splits a wildcard alias on the `*` into `(prefix, suffix)`, matches the import as `raw.startswith(prefix) and raw.endswith(suffix)` with at least one captured char, then substitutes the captured segment into the target's `*`.

3. **Specificity sorting.** Aliases are sorted before matching per the TypeScript path-mapping spec: exact (non-wildcard) entries win over wildcard entries; among wildcards, the longer non-wildcard prefix wins. `@common/integration/*` beats `@*` when both could match.

## Sub-bug fixed too: phantom-node ids on alias resolution

Even when alias resolution found the right file, `_make_id(str(resolved))` was computing a node id from the absolute path (`/Users/.../features/foo/bar.ts`) while the file extractor uses `_make_id(str(path))` against the project-relative path it was given. The two ids never matched, so every alias-resolved import pointed at a phantom node.

New `_resolved_path_to_nid` helper relativizes the resolved Path to `Path.cwd()` before computing the node id, falling back to the absolute form only for paths outside cwd.

## Measured impact

Same Nx/Angular monorepo (7,759 TS files, ~50 tsconfig path entries including a `@*` catch-all and three `@*/foo` patterns):

| | edges (AST) | edges (final graph after dedup) |
|---|---|---|
| v7 baseline | 164,041 | 99,871 |
| with this fix | **193,970** (+30K) | **107,369** (+7.5K) |

Specific failing case from triage on the source repo:

```typescript
// features/cross/agent/src/context/context-providers.ts
import { FileChipComponent, FilesComboListFormComponent } from '@communicate/documentv2';
```

The repo's tsconfig.base.json defines `@communicate/chat/*`, `@communicate/document/*`, `@communicate/feed/*`, plus a catch-all `@*: features/*/src/`. The `documentv2` import has no specific alias and relies on the wildcard.

- Before: importing file had **zero** `imports_from` edges, only internal `contains` edges. The `@communicate/documentv2` import collapsed to a bare `documentv2` basename node disconnected from the real file.
- After: 1 `imports_from` edge to `features_communicate_documentv2_src_index_ts` at L5, plus a symbol-level `imports` edge to `FileChipComponent`. 29 total edges now target the documentv2 index node.

Bare/scoped imports (npm packages, unmatched aliases) keep the existing basename fallback unchanged.

## Test plan

I didn't add tests in this PR — the existing `tests/` directory has no coverage for `_read_tsconfig_aliases` or `_resolve_js_import_target` that I could extend. Happy to add a fixture + tests as a follow-up if you'd like, or attach them to this PR before merge.

The three behaviours that need tests:
- Wildcard alias substitution: `@*` → `features/*/src/` resolves `@foo/bar` to `features/foo/bar/src/`
- Specificity ordering: `@common/integration/*` beats `@*` for `@common/integration/foo`
- Non-wildcard aliases keep working unchanged

The fix is also straightforward to verify against the spec at https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/module-resolution.html#path-mapping.

title: watch.py bypasses .graphifyignore; recursive watch on busy volumes causes CPU saturation from FSEvents firehose
body:
## Body

### Summary

`graphify watch <path>` schedules a recursive `watchdog.observers.Observer()` watcher and then filters events in the Python handler using **only** three hardcoded rules:

1. `path.suffix.lower() in _WATCHED_EXTENSIONS` (code/doc/paper/image)
2. `not any(part.startswith(".") for part in path.parts)`
3. `"graphify-out" not in path.parts`

The handler does **not** consult `.graphifyignore`, even though the project has a working `_load_graphifyignore()` + `_is_ignored()` pair in `detect.py` that is used by `update`, `extract`, and the post-commit hook path.

This means: when `graphify watch` is pointed at a directory that lives on a high-FS-event-volume root (Time Machine snapshot volume, Spotlight-indexed volume, Docker/Colima-shared mount, sync staging directory), the Python event handler is woken for every file event in the tree before discarding it. On a quiescent project tree this is fine. On a busy shared mount, this saturates a CPU core.

I have hit this pattern twice on the same host roughly a month apart:
- First occurrence: `graphify watch` over a project tree that shared an APFS volume with a Colima virtio mount; sustained 1-min load avg in the low 20s while the watcher was active.
- Second occurrence: several `graphify watch` instances over different subdirectories of the same APFS volume; sustained load avg 25+ for several days until the watchers were disabled.

The workaround is "don't run graphify watch on shared/busy volumes at all," which is unsatisfying because the watcher would be useful on the *project subdirectories* — it's the recursive enumeration of every event in a shared root that's the problem.

### Why filing this as a bug rather than an enhancement

Two reasons:
- `.graphifyignore` is a documented and supported mechanism (see issues #861, #882, #870, #869, all of which treat it as the canonical filter). Users reasonably expect it to be honored everywhere the tool walks the filesystem, including the watcher.
- The fix is small (~10 lines in `watch.py`) and uses code that already ships in the package.

Happy to relabel as an enhancement if maintainer prefers.

### Affected version

- pipx package `graphifyy` 0.4.1
- CLI reports `graphify 0.7.15`
- Python 3.14.3

### Environment

- macOS, Apple Silicon
- File systems involved: APFS with Time Machine local snapshots enabled, Spotlight-indexed; Colima virtio-shared mount over the same volume root.
- The pattern should reproduce on any `recursive=True` watch over a tree that has a steady background rate of FS events from external sources.

### Reproduction

1. On macOS, install `graphifyy` via pipx.
2. Create a `.graphifyignore` in a project root with broad patterns:
   ```
   *
   !src/**
   ```
   (i.e. ignore everything except `src/`)
3. Run `graphify watch <project_root>`.
4. In a separate terminal, generate FS events outside `src/` at a steady rate. Easiest reproducer: run a TM local snapshot (`tmutil localsnapshot`), or `touch` 1000 files in a subdir not under `src/`, or rsync into a sibling directory.
5. Observe `python3` CPU consumption in `top`. It will spike well past what `.graphifyignore` would suggest is necessary.

Expected: handler skips events under ignored paths, CPU near zero.
Actual: handler wakes for every event, only filters at the suffix / `.`-prefix / `graphify-out` stage.

### Code citation

`src/graphify/watch.py` (current `main` as of v0.7.15):

```python
class Handler(FileSystemEventHandler):
    def on_any_event(self, event):
        nonlocal last_trigger, pending
        if event.is_directory:
            return
        path = Path(event.src_path)
        if path.suffix.lower() not in _WATCHED_EXTENSIONS:
            return
        if any(part.startswith(".") for part in path.parts):
            return
        if "graphify-out" in path.parts:
            return
        last_trigger = time.monotonic()
        pending = True
        changed.add(path)
```

vs. `detect.py:288` (the existing infrastructure that's not being used here):

```python
def _is_ignored(path: Path, root: Path, patterns: list[str]) -> bool:
    """Return True if path matches any .graphifyignore pattern."""
    ...
```

### Suggested fix

Two-line change in `watch.py`, leveraging existing `detect` helpers. Load patterns once at `watch()` startup; check in the event handler. Sketch:

```python
def watch(watch_path: Path, debounce: float = 3.0) -> None:
    from graphify.detect import _load_graphifyignore, _is_ignored
    ignore_patterns = _load_graphifyignore(watch_path)
    ...
    class Handler(FileSystemEventHandler):
        def on_any_event(self, event):
            ...
            if ignore_patterns and _is_ignored(path, watch_path, ignore_patterns):
                return
            ...
```

(Caveat: this loads `.graphifyignore` once at startup, so adding patterns mid-session requires a watcher restart. That seems acceptable; if not, a stat-based reload check is a one-liner.)

### Adjacent enhancements that would also help

If you're already in this code path, two small additions would unblock most "watcher unsafe on this volume" scenarios:

1. **Expose `watchdog.observers.polling.PollingObserver` via a `--poll` flag.** The default `Observer()` resolves to FSEvents on macOS, which delivers events for the whole tree regardless of where the consumer is interested. `PollingObserver(timeout=<interval>)` walks the tree on a schedule instead, trading I/O for predictable cost. Useful escape hatch for volumes where FSEvents delivery is itself the cost driver. ~3 lines.
2. **Allow multiple `watch_path` arguments** (e.g. `graphify watch src/ tests/ docs/`) so users can avoid `recursive=True` on a root containing busy siblings. Currently the only way to scope is run multiple graphify processes. ~5 lines.

Either of those would also resolve the use case, but the `.graphifyignore` fix is the most principled because it uses an already-supported mechanism.

### Workaround in use

Disabled the affected `graphify watch` instances. Still using `graphify update <path>` on a daily schedule — that gives ~90% of the watcher's value at zero background cost. Probably worth a note in README under "macOS / shared volumes" until a release lands.

### Willingness to PR

Happy to send a PR for the `.graphifyignore`-honoring change if useful (~10 lines + test). Less sure about the polling/multi-path additions since those are more API-surface decisions.

title: Semantic extractors emit mixed absolute/relative source_file paths
body:
## Symptom

After running graphify on a docs corpus from the repo root with no explicit path argument (so graphify defaults to `.`), the resulting `graph.json` contains a roughly 50/50 mix of absolute and relative `source_file` values on nodes, links, and hyperedges.

Concrete numbers from one of our runs (2,587-node graph over a markdown/docs corpus):

| Element     | Absolute | Relative |
|-------------|---------:|---------:|
| nodes       |    1,292 |    1,295 |
| links       |    1,479 |        — |
| hyperedges  |       55 |        — |

Absolute samples (note: these are not paths we passed in — graphify was invoked from the repo root with no path arg, so the cwd is the only thing it knew about):

```
/Users/dennis/Documents/projects/documents/document-linking-investigation.md
/Users/dennis/Documents/projects/documents/CLAUDE.md
```

All affected nodes are `file_type: document` (`.md` files) — i.e., they go through the semantic-extraction subagent path, not the AST path. AST-extracted nodes appear to be consistently relative.

## Impact

Downstream consumers that key off `source_file` for exact-string matching break silently. For us, the MCP traversal seeder matches chunk paths (which are always relative) against `source_file`, so every absolute-path node/link/hyperedge becomes invisible to graph traversal — roughly half the graph in our case.

## Likely cause

The subagent prompt in the SKILL/README instructs each chunk worker to emit `\"source_file\":\"relative/path\"`, but with no enforcement the LLM is free to echo whatever it received in `FILE_LIST`. In practice ~half the time it does. The fix probably belongs in the extractor write path — normalize `source_file` to be relative to the corpus root before serializing into `graph.json` — rather than relying on the subagent to obey the instruction.

## Workaround we're using

A post-processing script that rewrites `graph.json` after every build, stripping the docs-root prefix. Effective but obviously a band-aid — happy to upstream if useful, but a guarantee at write time would be the right fix.

Let me know if a repro corpus would help.

title: Files in failed semantic chunks are permanently skipped on re-run
body:
### Description

When a semantic extraction chunk fails (e.g. 429 rate limit), graphify marks
the files in that chunk as processed in `manifest.json` anyway. On the next run,
incremental mode reports "0 files changed" and skips them permanently — those
files never make it into the graph.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run `graphify extract` with Gemini free tier (TPM=250K/min):
   `graphify extract . --backend gemini --token-budget 100000 --max-concurrency 1`
2. Chunks 1 and 2 succeed (~100K tokens each, 200K total within the minute window)
3. Chunk 3 hits 429 — cumulative 300K tokens exceeds TPM=250K limit
4. Re-run the same command
5. Output: incremental mode, 0 files to re-extract
6. Files from chunk 3 onwards are absent from the graph — silently

### Expected behavior

Files whose chunk failed should remain `pending` in manifest.
Re-running should build new chunks only from pending files.

### Root cause

`manifest.json` records file state (mtime/hash) per file, not chunk-level
success/failure. There is no way to distinguish "file was successfully
semantically extracted" from "file was grouped into a chunk that later failed".

### Environment

- graphify 0.8.8
- Backend: `gemini` (gemini-3-flash), `--max-concurrency 1`, `--token-budget 100000`
- Some chunks succeeded, others failed with 429 (TPM=250K/min limit exceeded)

### Suggested fix

Write chunk results to manifest only after the chunk completes successfully.
Files whose chunk failed keep their previous manifest state and are included
in the next run's chunk planning.

title: cluster-only crashes with FileNotFoundError if graphify-out/ doesn't exist before invocation
body:
Surfaced while testing v0.8.11 on #919. One-line fix; opening as a standalone issue rather than commenting on the closed #919 thread.

## Reproducer

```
$ rm -rf graphify-out
$ graphify cluster-only . --graph some/other/path/graph.json --exclude-hubs 99
Loading existing graph...
Graph: 1501 nodes, 2200 edges
Re-clustering...
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../graphify/__main__.py", line 1827, in main
    (out / "GRAPH_REPORT.md").write_text(report, encoding="utf-8")
  ...
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md'
```

## Root cause

On `v8` HEAD (`__main__.py` SHA `895f626`, line 1827):

```python
(out / "GRAPH_REPORT.md").write_text(report, encoding="utf-8")
```

`out` is dereferenced without first being ensured to exist. The pattern `out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` is used correctly elsewhere in the same file at 20 different sites — including `__main__.py:2935` where the very same identifier `out` is created before being written to. So this looks like an asymmetry between the `extract` codepath (creates `out` first) and the `cluster-only` codepath (assumes `out` already exists), rather than a design choice.

The crash is reachable any time a user renames or deletes `graphify-out/` before re-running `cluster-only` — a natural workflow for archiving a previous run before re-clustering with new flags (the scenario that surfaced it). Related precedent: #422 (`cluster-only` skipping detect-phase setup) showed the same general pattern.

## Suggested fix

One line, right before the first write into `out`:

```python
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
(out / "GRAPH_REPORT.md").write_text(report, encoding="utf-8")
```

## Workaround in the meantime

```
mkdir -p graphify-out && graphify cluster-only ...
```

## Environment

- `graphifyy` 0.8.11 (installed via pipx); line still present on `v8` HEAD (v0.8.13, same SHA `895f626`)
- Python 3.12, Linux Mint
- Reproduced on the same React/Firebase PWA codebase as #919

Happy to send a PR if useful.

title: wiki.to_wiki() crashes with TypeError when communities contain stale node IDs
body:
### Summary

`graphify.wiki.to_wiki()` raises `TypeError` inside `_community_article` whenever any community in the input dict contains a node ID that isn't present in the graph `G`. This is reproducible on a real-world graph after a `graphify update .` where some nodes were extracted in a prior run but no longer exist (renamed files, deleted modules, etc.) while the analysis JSON still references them.

### Environment

- **graphifyy:** 0.6.1 (`pip install graphifyy`)
- **Python:** 3.14.0 (Windows 11)
- **NetworkX:** whatever 0.6.1 pulls (3.x — relevant because `DegreeView` is the 3.x type)
- **Graph size at repro:** 9163 nodes, 26434 edges, 117 communities

### Reproducer

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path
import networkx as nx
from graphify.wiki import to_wiki

out_root = Path("graphify-out")
data = json.loads((out_root / "graph.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
if "edges" in data and "links" not in data:
    data = dict(data, links=data["edges"])
G = nx.node_link_graph(data, directed=False, multigraph=False, edges="links")

analysis = json.loads((out_root / ".graphify_analysis.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
communities = {int(k): list(v) for k, v in analysis["communities"].items()}

labels = json.loads((out_root / ".graphify_labels.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
labels = {int(k): v for k, v in labels.items()}

# Crashes if any community contains node IDs no longer in G:
to_wiki(G, communities, "graphify-out/wiki", community_labels=labels)
```

### Stack trace

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../site-packages/graphify/wiki.py", line 207, in to_wiki
    article = _community_article(G, cid, nodes, label, labels, cohesion.get(cid))
  File ".../site-packages/graphify/wiki.py", line 33, in _community_article
    top_nodes = sorted(nodes, key=lambda n: G.degree(n), reverse=True)[:25]
TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'DegreeView' and 'int'
```

### Root cause

`graphify/wiki.py:33`:

```python
top_nodes = sorted(nodes, key=lambda n: G.degree(n), reverse=True)[:25]
```

In NetworkX 3.x, `G.degree(n)` returns an `int` when `n in G`, but returns a `DegreeView` object (the "all-nodes" view) when `n not in G` — apparently because `.degree(missing)` falls back to the no-argument call rather than raising. Mixing ints and `DegreeView` in `sorted()`'s comparator triggers the `TypeError`.

In my repo, this happened because `.graphify_analysis.json` listed 13 node IDs across various communities that were not present in `graph.json` after the latest `update`. The communities dict is therefore stale relative to the graph.

### Suggested fix

One-line: filter `nodes` to graph members before sorting.

```python
# graphify/wiki.py:33
top_nodes = sorted([n for n in nodes if n in G], key=lambda n: G.degree(n), reverse=True)[:25]
```

The same defensive filter should arguably be applied to `_cross_community_links` (line 13) — it iterates `nodes` and calls `G.neighbors(nid)`, which would also break on missing nodes (raises `NetworkXError` rather than silently returning a weird view, but still a crash).

A more invasive fix would be to filter at the `to_wiki` entry point so all downstream helpers can assume `nodes ⊆ G.nodes`. I'd lean toward that — fixes the symptom in one place and protects future helpers.

### Workaround currently in use

Filter `communities` at the call site before invoking `to_wiki`:

```python
node_set = set(G.nodes)
communities = {cid: [n for n in nodes if n in node_set] for cid, nodes in communities.items()}
communities = {cid: nodes for cid, nodes in communities.items() if nodes}
```

### Bonus context (related but separate concern)

`to_wiki` is exposed as a module-level API in `graphify/__init__.py` but isn't reachable through the `graphify` CLI — neither `graphify update .` nor any other subcommand triggers it. To regenerate the wiki I had to write a small wrapper script that loads the artefacts and calls `to_wiki` directly. If the wiki is meant to be a first-class output of `update`, it would be useful to wire it in (perhaps behind a `--wiki` flag for users who don't want it). Happy to file this as a separate feature request if you'd prefer.

Happy to send a PR for the crash fix if the suggested approach looks right.

title: fix: CJK/Unicode labels silently skipped in _norm/_norm_label dedup (follow-up to #811)
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to **#811**: the original fix correctly changed `_make_id()` and `_normalize_id()` to use `[^\w]+` with `re.UNICODE`, but **two more functions** still use ASCII-only regex patterns, causing CJK/Unicode labels to be silently stripped:

### Affected functions

| Function | Before (broken) | After (fixed) |
|----------|-----------------|---------------|
| `dedup.py` `_norm()` | `[^a-z0-9]+` | `[^\w]+` + `re.UNICODE` + `casefold()` |
| `build.py` `_norm_label()` | `[^a-z0-9 ]` | `[^\w ]` + `re.UNICODE` + `casefold()` |

### Impact

When processing repos with Chinese/Japanese/Korean identifiers, these two functions strip all Unicode characters from labels before dedup comparison. This causes:
- **False dedup merges**: different Chinese labels like `道具处理类_初始化` and `道具处理类_数据处理` both normalize to empty strings, getting merged into a single node
- **Silent data loss**: CJK nodes that should be distinct entities are collapsed into one

### What changed

- `dedup.py:17` — `lower()` → `casefold()`, `[^a-z0-9]+` → `[^\w]+` with `flag=re.UNICODE`
- `build.py:230` — `lower()` → `casefold()`, `[^a-z0-9 ]` → `[^\w ]` with `flag=re.UNICODE`

Using `casefold()` instead of `lower()` for better Unicode case folding (e.g. German ß → ss).

### References

- Original issue: #811
- The upstream fixed `extract.py:_make_id()` and `build.py:_normalize_id()` but missed these two dedup functions.

title: Enhancement: Agent-driven semantic refinement of graph during file reads
body:
# Problem
The knowledge graph is static — it reflects the state of files at extraction time and never improves through use. When an AI agent reads a file in full during a session, any new semantic connections it discovers are lost after the session ends.
This is related to #874 (MCP server caches graph.json at startup with no hot-reload), but goes a step further: rather than just reloading a manually-updated graph, the agent itself could contribute new knowledge back to it.

# Proposed feature
When an agent reads a file in full, allow it to write back inferred relationships to graph.json with a new provenance tag, e.g. AGENT_INFERRED, alongside a confidence score and timestamp. This would make the graph progressively richer through use, without requiring a full re-run.

# Why it matters
Personal knowledge vaults (like Obsidian) contain heavy implicit context that static extraction misses. A graph that learns from agent sessions would stay aligned with how the user actually thinks and works — not just what they explicitly wrote.

# Possible concerns
Quality control: agent-inferred edges could pollute the graph. A confidence threshold or human review flag could mitigate this.
Scope: this moves Graphify closer to a persistent memory system, which may be out of scope. An opt-in flag like --agent-refinement could keep it optional.

#enhancement

title: BrokenProcessPool kills the whole extraction when any single worker dies
body:
**Summary**

`graphify.extract`'s parallel-extraction path (`_extract_parallel` at `extract.py:3732`) crashes the entire pool with `concurrent.futures.process.BrokenProcessPool` when one worker dies (e.g. tree-sitter segfault, OOM, or any uncaught error inside `_extract_single_file`). All in-flight work is lost; the overall `extract()` call then raises and no partial result is returned.

I hit this reliably on a fresh clone of `openai/tiktoken` (it's a Rust + Python codebase — likely tree-sitter is the trigger), running on macOS 26.5 / arm64 / Python 3.11.15 / graphifyy 0.7.0.

**Environment**

- graphifyy: 0.7.0
- Python: 3.11.15
- OS: macOS 26.5 (Darwin arm64)
- Install method: `uv tool install graphifyy`

**Reproducer**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openai/tiktoken /tmp/tk
rm -rf /tmp/tk/graphify-out
cd /tmp/tk
graphify  # or the equivalent skill invocation
```

When the bug fires, the build crashes mid-way through "AST extraction"; the traceback ends in `concurrent.futures.process.BrokenProcessPool: A process in the process pool was terminated abruptly while the future was running or pending.`

The crash is intermittent — on a repeat run against the already-clean clone it sometimes completes successfully (the worker that crashed previously may have been picking on a specific file order, or there's a transient resource pressure). But it reproduces often enough on a first-time clone that I had to add a fallback to my own wrapper.

**Suspect code**

`graphify/extract.py:3750-3757`:

```python
with concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool:
    futures = {
        pool.submit(_extract_single_file, item): item[0] for item in work_items
    }
    for future in concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures):
        idx, result = future.result()  # <-- raises BrokenProcessPool, kills the run
        per_file[idx] = result
```

When any worker dies (segfault, hard kill, uncaught exception that crashes the interpreter, etc.) the entire pool enters a broken state and every remaining `future.result()` raises `BrokenProcessPool`. There's no per-future try/except, so one bad file kills the whole extraction.

**Expected behavior**

A single bad file should not lose all the extraction work. Two options that would help:

1. **Wrap `future.result()` in try/except**, treat the bad future as `None`/missing, and continue with the rest of the pool. The user gets a partial graph with a count of skipped files at the end.

2. **Detect `BrokenProcessPool` and rebuild the pool** to recover the unfinished work. More engineering, but recovers more.

Option 1 is the minimal fix and matches what the comparable code in many other AST-parallel tools does.

**My current workaround**

I wrote a wrapper script (`graphify-build`) that catches the build crash and falls back to `graphify update` (which uses the sequential `_extract_sequential` path, so it works even when parallel breaks). It emits a machine-readable `GRAPHIFY_BUILD_DEGRADED=1` line so downstream tooling knows the result is degraded. This is fine for me but obviously not a real fix — the parallel path should be robust to single-worker failures.

**Happy to test a patch** if you'd like — I have a reliable-ish reproducer with `openai/tiktoken`.

title: Feature: fall back to .gitignore when .graphifyignore is absent
body:
## Proposal

When a project has no `.graphifyignore`, fall back to reading `.gitignore` automatically. Keep current behavior when `.graphifyignore` exists (explicit always wins).

## Why

Most projects already maintain `.gitignore` for the same directories that pollute graphify scans (logs, build artifacts, caches). Without a fallback, first-time users hit a wall on real codebases.

Related: #303 — an author there suggests copying `.gitignore` to `.graphifyignore` as a workaround, which confirms the equivalence is intuitive to users.

## Real-world example

Firefox extension repo. `.gitignore` already covers `logs/`, `tmp/`, `telegram-export/`.

| Run | total_files | total_words |
|---|---|---|
| Out of the box | 10,239 | 72,882,253 |
| After copying ignore rules to `.graphifyignore` | 163 | 308,159 |

Reduction: -98.4% files, -99.6% words. The `.graphifyignore` I had to create is a near-duplicate of `.gitignore`.

## Design notes

- Behavior: if `.graphifyignore` exists → use it (current behavior). Else if `.gitignore` exists → use it.
- Backward compatible.
- Opt-out: `--no-gitignore-fallback` flag or env var.
- Detection point: `_load_graphifyignore()` in `detect.py` (~line 464).

## Alternative

A note in the README's "Ignoring files" section recommending users start from `.gitignore`. Lower effort, partial fix.

title: Feature request: --exclude flag and .gitignore honoring for monorepo scans
body:
## Summary

`graphify .` in v0.8.13 scans everything under the target directory, including paths listed in `.gitignore`. For monorepos that contain large generated or vendored content (especially git worktrees under `.worktrees/`), this produces a `graph.json` that exceeds GitHub's 100MB per-file limit and blocks the documented "commit graph.json to the repo" workflow.

## Repro

- Run `graphify .` at the root of a monorepo that has multiple sibling service directories plus git worktrees in `.worktrees/`.
- `.worktrees/` is in `.gitignore` but graphify scans it anyway.
- Result: `graphify-out/graph.json` is ~558 MB.
- `git add graphify-out/graph.json` then `git push` is rejected by GitHub with the 100.00 MB file size limit error.

Single-service scans (run inside one service directory) work fine, ~1.68 MB graph.json. The blocker is specifically monorepo-root scans.

## Request

Any of the following would unblock the pilot. Ideally all three:

1. Honor `.gitignore` by default when scanning a directory that is a git repo (or has one).
2. Add a `--exclude <pattern>` flag accepting gitignore-style globs, repeatable, so users can exclude `.worktrees/`, `node_modules/`, `dist/`, etc. without relying on `.gitignore`.
3. Document the recommended pattern for monorepos in the README (per-service scans vs root scans, expected graph sizes, what to exclude).

## Context

Pilot setup: 4 monorepos across 3 businesses, 37 Railway services total, personal-account scale. The single-service flow is already useful. The monorepo-root flow is the one we cannot ship because of the 100 MB GitHub limit on `graph.json`.

Happy to test a pre-release build with either of these.

title: graphify update --no-cluster picks wrong import target on macOS for fully-qualified imports when two modules share a basename
body:
## Bug — `graphify update --no-cluster` resolves fully-qualified Python imports to the wrong target on macOS when two modules share a basename

### Observation

On a Python project with two `<name>.py` modules under different packages and a fully-qualified import of one of them, `graphify update . --no-cluster` produces different `graph.json` output on macOS vs Linux at the **same git SHA**, same graphifyy `0.8.13`, same Python 3.12.

Minimal layout (full repro below):

```
repro/
  pkg_a/__init__.py
  pkg_a/settings.py        # class Settings
  pkg_b/__init__.py
  pkg_b/settings.py        # class Settings
  main.py                  # from pkg_a.settings import Settings
```

The import `from pkg_a.settings import Settings` is unambiguous: it refers to `pkg_a/settings.py`. After v0.8.13's directory-qualified stem fix, both files become distinct nodes (`pkg_a_settings_settings` and `pkg_b_settings_settings`) — no node-ID collision.

When the same SHA is rebuilt on a Linux GitHub Actions runner and diffed against a macOS-built `graph.json` committed by a developer, edges originating in `pkg_a/*` flip their `target` between the two same-basename nodes:

```diff
 {
   "source": "main_f",
-  "target": "pkg_b_settings_settings",
+  "target": "pkg_a_settings_settings",
   "relation": "uses",
   "source_file": "main.py",
   ...
 },
```

The `+` (Linux) target is correct. The `−` (macOS) target is wrong — `pkg_a.settings.Settings` and `pkg_b.settings.Settings` are different symbols.

The pattern repeats for every edge that touches one of these same-basename modules: the resolver lands on whichever `<basename>.py` came first in the filesystem walk, ignoring the import's package prefix.

### Why this is unexpected after v0.8.13

The "Node ID collisions across same-named files in different directories" fix in 0.8.13 makes both files distinct nodes, but the import-target lookup appears to still match candidates by bare `<basename>` and pick the first hit. The package prefix on the import (`pkg_a.` vs `pkg_b.`) is not used to disambiguate.

Hypothesis: filesystem walk order from `os.scandir()` differs between APFS (macOS) and ext4 (Linux). Either order is fine in isolation, but it shouldn't affect the picked target for a fully-qualified import.

### Practical impact

Teams that wire `graphify update . --no-cluster` into pre-commit + CI and commit `graph.json` to source control hit a noisy churn whenever a developer regenerates on macOS and CI (or another developer) regenerates on Linux at the next commit. Edges flip `target` purely from the OS-dependent resolver pick, drowning out the real change in the diff.

A `git diff --exit-code` gate against the committed graph isn't workable in this state, so we're falling back to graphify's own topology fast-path (`No code-graph topology changes detected`). That keeps CI green but means we ship a `graph.json` whose `links[].target` values are wrong on whichever OS lost the race.

### Questions

1. Is the resolver supposed to use the import's package prefix to disambiguate same-basename modules? If yes, this is a real bug and I'm happy to open a PR.
2. If the answer to (1) is "`--no-cluster` was scoped to cross-process determinism, not cross-OS resolver stability," is there a recommended way to pin the resolver's pick (e.g. sorting `scandir` results, or a hash-stable tiebreak) so committed `graph.json` files round-trip across CI?
3. Is there a documented pattern for teams that commit `graph.json` to source control? (e.g. "build only on Linux runners, devs query but don't regen") Happy to follow it instead of fighting the resolver.

### Reproduction

```bash
mkdir -p repro/{pkg_a,pkg_b}
touch repro/pkg_a/__init__.py repro/pkg_b/__init__.py
cat > repro/pkg_a/settings.py <<'PY'
class Settings: ...
PY
cat > repro/pkg_b/settings.py <<'PY'
class Settings: ...
PY
cat > repro/main.py <<'PY'
from pkg_a.settings import Settings  # fully-qualified, unambiguous
def f() -> Settings: ...
PY

cd repro
graphify update . --no-cluster
python -c "import json; g=json.load(open('graphify-out/graph.json')); \
  print([(l['source'], l['target']) for l in g['links'] \
         if 'main' in l['source'] and 'settings' in l['target']])"
```

Expected on every OS: target ends in `pkg_a_settings_settings`.
Observed on a real codebase: macOS picks `pkg_b_settings_settings` for some edges; Linux picks `pkg_a_settings_settings` (correct).

(Disclaimer: I haven't run the 4-file repro above as a standalone repro yet — the diff observation comes from a larger codebase. Happy to bisect further if the minimal case doesn't reproduce out of the gate.)

### Environment

- graphifyy `0.8.13` (latest on PyPI as of 2026-05-20)
- Python 3.12.x on both sides
- macOS 14.x, APFS (case-insensitive)
- Ubuntu 24.04, GitHub Actions runner, ext4

title: Extract markdown links as first-class edges
body:
## Problem

When processing a corpus of interlinked markdown documents, Graphify's semantic extraction relies entirely on the LLM to infer relationships. However, markdown files often contain **explicit, human-authored links** (`[text](path.md)`) that represent high-confidence relationships between documents.

In our test with 1,256 Intercom help articles:
- 2,905 nodes extracted, but **1,636 (56%) are isolated** (≤1 connection)
- Many of these articles link to each other via standard markdown links
- The LLM-based extraction misses these because it focuses on conceptual entity extraction, not syntactic link parsing

These human-authored links are arguably the highest-quality relationship signal in a documentation corpus — someone deliberately said "this article relates to that article."

## Proposed Solution

Add a **deterministic pre-pass** that extracts markdown links as edges before/alongside LLM semantic extraction:

1. Regex/parser scan of all `.md` files for:
   - Standard links: `[link text](relative/path.md)`
   - Wikilinks: `[[page-name]]` (if applicable)
   - Relative URL references between files in the corpus

2. Emit edges with the existing schema:
   ```json
   {
     "source": "article_a_id",
     "target": "article_b_id",
     "relation": "links_to",
     "confidence": "EXTRACTED",
     "confidence_score": 1.0,
     "source_file": "path/to/a.md",
     "source_location": "line or section where link appears"
   }
   ```

3. Merge these edges into the graph in the same step where AST and semantic results are combined.

## Design Considerations

- **Link resolution**: Relative paths need to resolve to actual files in the corpus. Unresolvable links (external URLs, broken references) could either be skipped or emitted with a lower confidence score.
- **Link text as context**: The anchor text (`[this text here](...)`) often describes the relationship — could be stored as edge metadata.
- **Bidirectionality**: A link from A→B is directional, but you might optionally infer a `linked_from` back-edge.
- **Deduplication**: If the LLM also infers a relationship between the same two documents, the deterministic edge should take precedence (higher confidence).
- **New relation type**: `links_to` would join the existing set (`references`, `cites`, `conceptually_related_to`, etc.).

## Impact

For documentation-heavy corpora (help centers, wikis, technical docs), this could dramatically reduce isolated nodes and improve community detection quality — connecting clusters that the LLM extraction treats as separate because it processes files in batches without cross-file link awareness.

## Prior Art

This is analogous to how the AST extraction handles `imports` in code — deterministic, structural relationships that don't need an LLM to identify.

title: AST extractor produces ID collisions on identical filenames across folders, merging distinct functions into one node
body:
## Bug

`graphify.extract` (AST mode) generates node IDs from `{filename_stem}_{symbol}`. In monorepos where many folders contain a same-named file (e.g. Next.js App Router with one `action-bar/index.tsx` per feature, or one `lib/atom.ts` per feature), every function with the same name across those files collapses into a single graph node. The union of their edges then creates phantom cross-module "bridges" that don't exist in source.

## Repro

In a Next.js repo with structure:

    app/(innerPages)/<feature>/action-bar/index.tsx   # each exports `function ActionBar()`
    app/(innerPages)/<feature>/lib/atom.ts            # each exports `useFeatureAtom`

Run `graphify .` on a code-only corpus.

Result: a single node `action_bar_index_actionbar` accumulates `contains` edges from ~16 distinct files and `calls` edges to atoms from ~10 unrelated features. `god_nodes()` reports it as the most connected abstraction. `surprising_connections()` flags fake cross-feature bridges.

## Expected

IDs should be unique per source file, e.g. derived from the full relative path (`innerpages_<feature>_action_bar_index_actionbar`) or filepath hash, so functions with identical names in different folders remain distinct nodes.

## Evidence

In one 552-file scan, 16 `action-bar/index.tsx` files merged into 1 node showing 30 edges and 0.167 betweenness — entirely an artifact.

## Suggested fix

Change ID generation in the AST extractor to use the relative source path (slashes → underscores) instead of just `Path(...).stem`. This is also what the Step 3 prompt instructs semantic subagents to do, so the AST extractor would just be matching its sibling.

## Version

graphifyy from PyPI, Python 3.x via pipx.

title: Add v8 affected-symbol resolution for imports, aliases, and re-exports
body:
## Summary

  Adds graph-level affected-symbol resolution for imports, aliases, and re-exports on top of `v8`.

  This lets graphify answer “what is affected if this symbol changes?” across common indirection patterns instead of only direct declarations/usages.

  ## Why

  Large JS/TS and Python projects often route symbols through barrels, aliases, and re-export layers. Without resolving those relationships, affected analysis misses real downstream impact.

  This improves practical query precision for monorepos and framework-heavy codebases where the changed symbol is rarely consumed directly from its defining file.

  ## What changed

  - Added `graphify affected`.
  - Added generic affected-symbol support for import, alias, and re-export relationships.
  - Added JS/TS coverage for:
    - `export *`
    - `export { X as Y }`
    - inline import aliases
    - type/interface/abstract class/value exports
    - const aliases
    - imported symbol usage affecting local callers
  - Added Python import-resolution coverage.
  - Kept SQL tests optional when `tree_sitter_sql` is not installed.
 
 ## Related

  Related to https://github.com/safishamsi/graphify/issues/569 and the broader
  source-resolution/import-noise issues around large workspaces and ambiguous traversal.

  - #949: import target ambiguity when multiple modules share the same basename.
  - #952: AST node identity collisions for identical filenames across folders.
  - #462: resolving workspace/package imports in JS/TS monorepos.
  - #147: TypeScript path alias resolution.
  - #572: context-aware graph queries; this PR improves the source/import relationship data
  that query filtering can build on.

title: feat: add generic .tab structured extraction
body:
## Summary

Adds generic structured extraction for `.tab` files and wires the new file type through graphify's detect -> extract -> watch -> build flow.

## Why

Some projects use tab-delimited configuration files as code-adjacent artifacts rather than plain documents. These files often define entities, columns, row identities, enum-like values, and references to scripts such as Lua AI behavior files. Treating `.tab` files as unsupported input misses important graph edges between configuration and executable code.

The implementation intentionally does not require schema-specific headers such as `AIType` or `ScriptFile`, because real `.tab` files can use many different schemas. Instead, it extracts generic table structure and path-like references while keeping false positives bounded.

## How

- Classifies `.tab`/`.TAB` as code and includes them in collection and watch rebuilds.
- Adds `extract_tab()` to parse tab-delimited files with UTF-8 BOM, UTF-8, and GB18030 decoding.
- Emits file, column, row, low-cardinality value, and path reference nodes/edges.
- Avoids treating URL values as local path references.
- Keeps direct `.tab` extraction references as tab-owned stubs so incremental rebuilds cannot overwrite richer scanned file nodes.
- Redirects `.tab` reference edges to real scanned file nodes during aggregate extraction and after watch incremental preserved-node merging.
- Rejects absolute and parent-traversal path resolution as real local targets to avoid out-of-corpus node pollution.

## Review Notes

The main subtlety is path references. A `.tab` cell may point at `scripts/ai/StandardAI.lua`. If that Lua file is scanned in the same graph, the final `references` edge should point to the Lua file node. If only the `.tab` file is rebuilt incrementally, the temporary tab-owned stub must not replace the preserved Lua node. This PR handles both cases with a two-stage redirect:

- `extract_tab()` emits a tab-owned reference stub plus temporary `target_ref` metadata.
- `extract()` and `watch._rebuild_code()` redirect the edge to a real scanned/preserved file node when available, then drop the temporary stub/metadata.

## Validation

- `uv run pytest tests/test_detect.py tests/test_watch.py tests/test_tab.py -q`
  - `146 passed, 2 skipped`
- `uv run python -m compileall graphify tests -q`
  - passed
- `uv run pytest tests/ -q`
  - `1285 passed, 7 failed`
  - The remaining failures are all in `tests/test_security.py`; in this local environment, `example.com` and `arxiv.org` resolve to `198.18.x.x`, so the existing SSRF protection rejects them as private/internal IPs before mocked fetch behavior is reached.

title: feat: detect circular import dependencies at file level
body:
## Summary

Adds file-level circular import cycle detection on top of v8.

This surfaces dependency loops that are hard to spot in symbol-level graphs and helps identify refactor blockers for tree-shaking and modularization.

## Why

Import cycles in JS/TS and mixed-language projects can:

- make dependency flow harder to reason about
- increase coupling between modules
- block or reduce bundler/tree-shaking optimizations
- create fragile refactor paths

A built-in cycle detector makes these risks visible and actionable in graph analysis.

## What changed

- Added find_import_cycles(G) in analyze.py.
- Collapses symbol-level graph relationships into a file-level directed import graph.
- Uses directed-cycle detection to find import loops.
- Normalizes and deduplicates cycle results so equivalent rotations are not repeated.
- Returns cycles in a stable, readable order to support reporting and downstream tooling.
- Added test coverage for:
  - simple 2-node cycles
  - longer multi-node cycles
  - no-cycle graphs
  - deduplication/normalization behavior
  - mixed edge scenarios around import relationships

## Related

- Related to refactor-report goals around identifying high-impact structural problems.
- Complements barrel re-export resolution by improving dependency analysis accuracy at file level.

## Test Plan

title: Feature request: support local file:// paths and --allow-local flag for `graphify add` (WSL2 environments blocked)
body:
## Environment

- graphify version: 0.7.16
- - OS: WSL2 (Ubuntu 24) on Windows 11
- - - Network: WSL2 NAT networking (standard configuration)
## Problem

`graphify add` is completely unusable in WSL2 environments due to the IP safety filter blocking all reachable addresses:

**Attempt 1 -- External URL:**
```
graphify add "https://listings.pcisecuritystandards.org/documents/PCI_DSS-QRG-v4_0.pdf" --backend ollama
error: ingest: Blocked private/internal IP 64:ff9b::36cc:3134 (resolved from 'listings.pcisecuritystandards.org')
```
WSL2 translates external IPv4 addresses to NAT64 (64:ff9b:: prefix, RFC 6052), which graphify classifies as private/internal.

**Attempt 2 -- Local file path:**
```
graphify add /mnt/c/Users/user/Downloads/document.pdf --backend ollama
error: ingest: Blocked URL scheme '' - only http and https are allowed.
```
Local file paths are rejected outright.

**Attempt 3 -- Localhost HTTP server:**
```
graphify add "http://localhost:8899/document.pdf" --backend ollama
error: ingest: Blocked private/internal IP 127.0.0.1 (resolved from 'localhost')
```
127.0.0.1 is classified as private/internal.

There is no bypass flag -- `graphify --help` confirms no `--allow-local` or `--allow-private` option exists.

## Feature Request

One or more of the following would resolve this:

1. **`file://` scheme support** -- allow `graphify add file:///path/to/document.pdf` for local file ingestion
2. 2. **`--allow-local` flag** -- bypass the private IP check for explicit local use cases
3. 3. **Treat NAT64 addresses as external** -- 64:ff9b::/96 is the RFC 6052 IPv4-mapped range used by WSL2 NAT; these are not truly private addresses
## Use Case

Ingesting regulatory documents (PCI DSS, ISO 27001, NIST CSF) as build-time operations to enable cross-graph queries against a codebase graph. This is a powerful capability that is entirely blocked in WSL2 without one of the above fixes.

## Workaround

Currently none available in WSL2.  Direct database queries against pre-seeded regulatory tables serve as a partial alternative.

title: god_nodes fails with relative import error when serve.py run as script
body:
## Bug

The `god_nodes` MCP tool fails with:
```
Error executing god_nodes: attempted relative import with no known parent package
```

## Root Cause

`serve.py` line 633 uses a lazy relative import:
```python
def _tool_god_nodes(arguments: dict) -> str:
    from .analyze import god_nodes as _god_nodes  # <-- fails
```

When `serve.py` is run directly as a script (`python3 /path/to/serve.py graph.json`), `__package__` is `None`, so relative imports (`from .`) are illegal.

This is the **only** relative import inside a tool handler in `serve.py`. All other tools work fine.

## Reproduction

```bash
# Start MCP server (this is how .mcp.json configures it)
python3 /path/to/graphify/serve.py /path/to/graph.json

# Call god_nodes tool → fails with relative import error
# All other tools (get_community, get_node, query_graph, etc.) work fine
```

Tested with graphify 0.8.14 across 3 different graph files (154–1,860 nodes). Consistent failure.

## Fix

Either:
- **One-line fix:** Change `from .analyze import god_nodes` → `from graphify.analyze import god_nodes` (line 633)
- **Invocation fix:** Users can work around by launching with `python3 -m graphify.serve` instead of `python3 serve.py` (sets `__package__` correctly)

I'm using the `-m` workaround, but the one-line fix would help everyone.

## Environment

- graphify 0.8.14
- Python 3.12
- macOS (installed via `uv tool install graphifyy`)

title: serve.py ImportError recommends `pip install mcp` — wrong env, ignores the documented `graphifyy[mcp]` extra
body:
## Summary

When `graphify.serve` is invoked without the `mcp` SDK available, it raises:

```python
raise ImportError("mcp not installed. Run: pip install mcp") from e
```

— `serve.py:391` ([v0.8.14](https://github.com/safishamsi/graphify/blob/main/graphify/serve.py#L391)).

The hint is misleading in two ways:

1. **Wrong package.** graphifyy already declares `mcp` as the `[mcp]` extra in `pyproject.toml` and the README lists it: `pip install "graphifyy[mcp]"`. The error message bypasses the project's own packaging story and tells users to install `mcp` standalone.
2. **Wrong env in the common case.** Users who installed graphifyy via `uv tool install graphifyy` or `pipx install graphifyy` (both recommended in the README) live in an *isolated* tool venv. Running `pip install mcp` afterwards installs `mcp` into whatever Python happens to be on `$PATH` — typically a different env than the tool venv — so the next `graphify.serve` invocation hits the exact same ImportError and the user has no idea why their "fix" did nothing.

## Reproduction

```sh
uv tool install graphifyy        # bare install, no [mcp] extra
python -m graphify.serve graphify-out/graph.json
# ImportError: mcp not installed. Run: pip install mcp

pip install mcp                  # follow the hint
python -m graphify.serve graphify-out/graph.json
# ImportError: mcp not installed. Run: pip install mcp   (still fails — wrong env)
```

The fix is `uv tool install --with mcp graphifyy --reinstall` (or `uv tool install "graphifyy[mcp]"`), but the user can't discover that from the error message.

## Proposed fix

Change the ImportError hint to recommend the declared extra:

```python
raise ImportError(
    'mcp not installed. Run: pip install "graphifyy[mcp]" '
    '(or `uv tool install "graphifyy[mcp]"` / `pipx install "graphifyy[mcp]"` '
    'if you installed graphifyy as a tool — installing `mcp` separately '
    'lands in the wrong env).'
) from e
```

Optional follow-up: detect `sys.executable` living under `~/.local/share/uv/tools/` or `~/.local/pipx/venvs/` and tailor the hint to that specific tool's reinstall command, but the generic message above already routes users to the right install command in the vast majority of cases.

## Why it matters

For agent integrations (Claude Code `.mcp.json`, etc.), the MCP server failing to register is a *silent* failure — the agent simply loses a category of tools, and the only diagnostic is whatever the server printed to stderr before exiting. Making that one line actionable saves a non-trivial debugging session per onboarded teammate.

title: feat(multigraph): add schema-aware graph loader and stable edge identity
body:
## Summary

Schema-aware graph loader and stable edge identity module — PR 2 of the MultiDiGraph rollout.

This is stacked on #958 (projections) which is itself stacked on #956 (capability probe). Until those land this PR will include their commits; the diff that is purely PR 2 is the top commit `429ac1e`.

### New files

**`graphify/edge_identity.py`**
- `SCHEMA_KEY_FIELD = "key"` — reserves the node-link `"key"` field as schema, never a regular edge attribute
- `make_stable_key(relation, source_file, source_location) -> str` — SHA-256 over a canonical JSON payload; versioned `edge:v1:<hex>` format; delimiter-injection-safe (raw `:` joining was collision-prone)
- `strip_schema_key(attrs) -> (key_value, cleaned_attrs)` — separates `"key"` before `G.add_edge(u, v, key=k, **attrs)` to avoid passing the kwarg twice

**`graphify/graph_loader.py`**
- `load_graph(data, *, require_capabilities=True)` — detects graph type from `multigraph`/`directed` flags and returns `nx.Graph`, `nx.DiGraph`, or `nx.MultiDiGraph` accordingly
- `load_graph_file(path)` — size-capped file loader
- `G.graph["graphify_profile"]` with `{"graph_type": "simple" | "digraph" | "multidigraph"}` on all paths
- Missing-key repair: generates a full-payload SHA-256 key so distinct parallel edges with identical identity fields but different metadata both survive
- Non-string key guard: raises `TypeError` before NetworkX sees `list`/`dict`/`int` keys
- Input robustness: non-list `edges`/`links` raises `TypeError`; non-dict edge entries are skipped; non-dict `graphify_profile` falls back to `{}`

### Patch

**`graphify/build.py`** — strips `SCHEMA_KEY_FIELD` from edge attrs in `build_from_json`, reserving `"key"` as schema in extraction dicts too

### Tests

31 TDD tests in `tests/test_edge_identity.py` and `tests/test_graph_loader.py` covering all seven Wave 3 / PR 2 required scenarios, delimiter-collision safety, missing-key repair for parallel edges, `directed: true` preservation, malformed input policies, and non-string key rejection.

title: Merge cross-file Swift extension nodes into the canonical type
body:
## Summary

- tree-sitter-swift parses both `class Foo` and `extension Foo` as `class_declaration`, and node ids carry the file stem (`_make_id(stem, name)`). Same-file extensions dedupe via `seen_ids`, but cross-file ones leak — each file extending `Foo` produces its own `Foo` node, which inflates god-node rankings, drags down community cohesion, and prevents the generic cross-file call resolver from attaching call edges to a single target.
- Per-file `_extract_generic` now tags Swift `class_declaration` nodes whose children include the `extension` keyword and stashes them in `result["swift_extensions"]`. Corpus-level `extract()` runs a new `_merge_swift_extensions()` pass: when exactly one non-extension declaration shares the label, the extension nodes redirect onto it and their edges are rewritten (self-loops dropped, duplicates collapsed). Extensions of types outside the corpus (no canonical found) and ambiguous label matches (multiple canonicals) are left untouched — picking arbitrarily would invent edges.
- The existing in-file extension tests (`test_swift_extension_methods_attach_to_type`, `test_swift_extension_does_not_duplicate_type_node`) keep their behavior; same-file dedup still flows through `seen_ids` and never reaches the new pass.

## Real-world impact

On a 25-file Swift project I extracted before and after the fix:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Parser` god-node entries (top 10) | 4 split entries (44 + 38 + 25 + …) | 1 entry, 131 edges |
| `Lexer` top-10 entries | 1 entry, 24 edges | 1 entry, 48 edges |
| `TokenKind` | not in top 10 | rank 2 (85 edges) |
| Total edges | 1551 | 1644 |

Edge count goes up rather than down because consolidating the type lets graphify's generic cross-file call resolver pick unambiguous targets where multiple stem-qualified candidates previously forced it to skip — strictly more accurate, not noisier.

## Test plan

- [x] New regression test `test_swift_extension_across_files_merges_into_canonical_type` (with two fixture files in `tests/fixtures/swift_cross_file/`) extracts via the top-level `extract()` entry point and asserts a single `Foo` node plus both methods attaching to it. Goes through the per-file + corpus seam since the bug lives there.
- [x] All 23 Swift tests pass.
- [x] Full test suite: 911 pass, no regressions. The 8 unrelated SQL failures (`test_sql_finds_tables` etc.) reproduce on stock 0.8.14 without this patch.

title: fix(llm): honor GRAPHIFY_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS for OpenAI-compatible back…
body:
…ends

Backends routed through _call_openai_compat (gemini, openai, kimi, deepseek, ollama) silently ignored the documented env override when their backend config dict carried a hardcoded max_completion_tokens. The dispatcher used:

    cfg.get("max_completion_tokens", max_out)

which always returned the config-dict value when the key was present, shadowing the env-var-resolved max_out.

For gemini specifically, the hardcoded cap of 16384 truncated extracted-graph JSON mid-response on multi-document chunks (~17 specs of 100-1500 lines each pushing the output past 16k tokens). Symptom: cascading 'LLM returned invalid JSON, skipping chunk: Unterminated string at column 4XXXX' followed by bisect-retry storms that bill input tokens without producing graph nodes.

Fix: route the same _resolve_max_tokens(...) call that the Claude and Bedrock paths already use, so the override applies uniformly across backends.

Verified with gemini-2.5-pro over a 20-doc / 76k-input-token chunk: output of 36008 tokens emitted without truncation, producing 193 nodes / 223 edges / 23 communities in a single chunk.

title: Feature: Add Vertex AI backend for semantic extraction
body:
## Feature idea

Add Google Vertex AI as a backend for `graphify extract`. Vertex AI is the enterprise-managed route to Gemini models for teams that don't use (or can't use) a direct `GEMINI_API_KEY`.

## Why this helps

- Enterprise/GCP teams already govern model access through Vertex AI — they may not have a standalone Gemini API key at all.
- Vertex AI exposes an [OpenAI-compatible endpoint](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/multimodal/call-gemini-using-openai-library), so the implementation can reuse `_call_openai_compat()` from `llm.py`.
- Enables headless CI extraction in GCP-native pipelines (Cloud Build, GitHub Actions with Workload Identity Federation) using Application Default Credentials or a service account token.

## Authentication: Application Default Credentials (ADC) support

Many enterprise organizations restrict or prohibit creating service account key files (JSON key export). The backend should support [Google Application Default Credentials (ADC)](https://cloud.google.com/docs/authentication/application-default-credentials) as the primary auth method, not just explicit API keys/tokens.

ADC automatically resolves credentials from (in order):
1. `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` env var (service account key file, where allowed)
2. User credentials from `gcloud auth application-default login`
3. Attached service account (GCE, Cloud Run, GKE Workload Identity)
4. Workload Identity Federation (GitHub Actions OIDC → GCP, no keys at all)

This can be implemented using the `google-auth` Python library to obtain a bearer token, then passing it to the OpenAI-compatible endpoint:

```python
import google.auth
import google.auth.transport.requests

def _get_vertex_token() -> str:
    """Get access token via Application Default Credentials."""
    credentials, project = google.auth.default(
        scopes=["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    )
    credentials.refresh(google.auth.transport.requests.Request())
    return credentials.token
```

This is critical for CI/CD environments where:
- Org policy blocks service account key creation (`constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`)
- Workload Identity Federation provides keyless auth (e.g., GitHub Actions OIDC → GCP)
- Users authenticate via `gcloud auth application-default login` locally

## Proposed implementation

Add a `"vertex"` entry to the `BACKENDS` dict in `graphify/llm.py`:

```python
"vertex": {
    "base_url": os.environ.get(
        "GRAPHIFY_VERTEX_BASE_URL",
        "https://us-central1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/openai/"
    ),
    "default_model": "gemini-2.5-flash",
    "env_keys": ["GRAPHIFY_VERTEX_API_KEY", "GOOGLE_ACCESS_TOKEN"],
    "model_env_key": "GRAPHIFY_VERTEX_MODEL",
    "pricing": {"input": 0.50, "output": 3.00},
    "temperature": 0,
    "max_completion_tokens": 16384,
}
```

Auth resolution order:
1. `GRAPHIFY_VERTEX_API_KEY` — explicit token (e.g., from `gcloud auth print-access-token`)
2. `GOOGLE_ACCESS_TOKEN` — explicit token via env var
3. **Application Default Credentials** — automatic via `google-auth` library (fallback when no explicit key is set)

Usage:

```bash
# With ADC (preferred — no explicit token management)
gcloud auth application-default login  # one-time setup
graphify extract . --backend vertex

# With explicit token
export GRAPHIFY_VERTEX_API_KEY=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
graphify extract . --backend vertex

# In GitHub Actions with Workload Identity Federation (keyless)
# ADC is automatically configured by google-github-actions/auth
graphify extract . --backend vertex

# With a custom regional endpoint
export GRAPHIFY_VERTEX_BASE_URL=https://europe-west1-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1beta1/openai/
graphify extract . --backend vertex
```

The base_url needs to be configurable via env var since it includes the GCP region.

## Related

- #959 — requests `OPENAI_BASE_URL` override for the `openai` backend (similar pattern)
- #723 — PR adding a generic `custom` backend with configurable base_url (would also solve this, but a named `vertex` backend is more discoverable)
- #757 / Bedrock backend — precedent for adding cloud-provider-specific backends (Bedrock similarly uses SDK-based auth rather than a simple API key)

title: Feature: Add GitHub Models backend for semantic extraction
body:
## Feature idea

Add [GitHub Models](https://docs.github.com/en/github-models) as a backend for `graphify extract`. GitHub Models exposes an OpenAI-compatible inference API at `https://models.inference.ai.azure.com`.

## Why this helps

- **CI/CD environments already have the token.** In GitHub Agentic Workflows (gh-aw), the agent environment has a `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` (a fine-grained PAT with Copilot Requests permission) that can authenticate against GitHub Models. No additional secret setup is needed — the token is already there, graphify just can't use it.
- **Zero extra cost** for users with GitHub Copilot Pro/Business/Enterprise — model access is included in the subscription.
- **OpenAI-compatible** — the implementation can reuse `_call_openai_compat()` from `llm.py`, making this a small addition to the `BACKENDS` dict.

## Important: token requirements

Not all GitHub tokens can access GitHub Models. The required token is a **fine-grained Personal Access Token** with **Account permissions > Copilot Requests = Read**. This is distinct from:

- `GITHUB_TOKEN` (auto-generated in Actions) — repo-scoped, does **not** have Copilot/model access
- `GH_TOKEN` (from `gh auth login`) — may or may not have model access depending on scopes

The correct env var to check is one explicitly configured for model inference. Auto-detecting from `GITHUB_TOKEN` would silently fail in most CI environments.

## Proposed implementation

Add a `"github-models"` entry to the `BACKENDS` dict in `graphify/llm.py`:

```python
"github-models": {
    "base_url": "https://models.inference.ai.azure.com",
    "default_model": "gpt-4.1-mini",
    "env_keys": ["GRAPHIFY_GITHUB_MODELS_TOKEN", "COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN"],
    "model_env_key": "GRAPHIFY_GITHUB_MODEL",
    "pricing": {"input": 0.0, "output": 0.0},  # included in Copilot subscription
    "temperature": 0,
    "max_tokens": 16384,
}
```

Note: `GRAPHIFY_GITHUB_MODELS_TOKEN` as the primary env key avoids clashing with or accidentally consuming the general-purpose `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Users explicitly opt in to GitHub Models by setting this variable.

## Usage

```bash
# In gh-aw (COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN is already injected by the runtime)
graphify extract . --backend github-models

# Locally — use a fine-grained PAT with Copilot Requests (read) permission
export GRAPHIFY_GITHUB_MODELS_TOKEN="ghp_..."
graphify extract . --backend github-models

# Override model (default: gpt-4.1-mini)
GRAPHIFY_GITHUB_MODEL=gpt-4.1 graphify extract . --backend github-models
```

To create the required PAT: [github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) → Resource owner = your user account → Account permissions → Copilot Requests = Read.

## Concrete use case

I run a [gh-aw agentic workflow](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/) that builds a unified knowledge graph across ~40 OADP ecosystem repos. The workflow installs graphify via `pipx install graphifyy` and runs `graphify extract` on each repo. The gh-aw runtime already injects `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` for the Copilot agent engine, but graphify has no backend that recognizes it. The agent had to discover at runtime that `extract` failed (no LLM backend available) and fall back to `graphify update` (AST-only), losing all semantic enrichment.

If graphify recognized `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` via a `github-models` backend, semantic extraction would work out of the box in any gh-aw workflow.

## Related

- #959 — requests `OPENAI_BASE_URL` override (similar need for flexible endpoints)
- #723 — PR adding a generic `custom` backend (would work but a named `github-models` backend is more discoverable and enables detection from `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`)
- #134 / PR #145 — Copilot CLI support (skill installation, not LLM backend)
- #757 / Bedrock backend — precedent for cloud-provider backends
