title: Silent data loss: env/*_env directories pruned as false-positive venvs, with zero trace in any report bucket
body:
## Summary

`detect.py`'s directory-noise heuristic (`_SKIP_DIRS` / `_is_noise_dir`) treats any directory literally named `env` (or ending in `_env`) as a Python virtualenv and silently prunes it during the walk — with **zero trace** in any reportable bucket (`ignored`, `unclassified`, or any warning). This causes large, silent, undetectable data loss for any codebase that uses `env`/`*_env` as a real source directory name — a naming convention common in hardware/ASIC verification environments (UVM testbenches), and plausibly in other domains too.

## Root cause

```python
# graphify/detect.py
_SKIP_DIRS = {
    "venv", ".venv", "env", ".env",
    ...
}

def _is_noise_dir(part: str, parent: "Path | None" = None) -> bool:
    if part in _SKIP_DIRS:
        return True
    ...
    if part.endswith("_venv") or part.endswith("_env"):
        return True
    ...
```

This check is applied unconditionally to every subdirectory encountered during the `os.walk` traversal (`detect()`, around the `kept_dirs`/`dirnames[:]` pruning loop), **before** the `_is_ignored()` / `.graphifyignore` negation logic runs. Because of this ordering:

1. A `.graphifyignore` negation (`!env/`) **cannot** rescue the directory — pruning happens earlier and unconditionally.
2. Pruned directories are never added to `ignored`, `unclassified`, or any other bucket in the `detect()` return value — there is no way to detect the loss from the tool's own output. The only symptom is a lower file/node count than expected, with nothing pointing at why.
3. The exact-name check (`env`) applies to *every* subdirectory the walker descends into, not just files reached directly — so even pointing `detect()`/`extract` directly at a parent directory (e.g. `src_env/`) does not protect a nested `env/` subdirectory from being pruned.
4. The suffix check (`_env`) additionally prunes any directory whose *own* name ends in `_env` (e.g. `src_env/`) the moment it's reached as a subdirectory from a parent scan — even though it's not literally named `env`.

## Reproduction

Any repo with this structure:
```
repo/
  src_env/          # <- pruned entirely when scanned from repo root (matches *_env)
    env/            # <- pruned even if src_env/ itself is the scan root (exact match)
      my_class.py
    other_dir/
      also_real.py  # <- also lost, since the whole src_env/ subtree is pruned from the root scan
```

```python
from graphify.detect import detect
from pathlib import Path
detect(Path("repo"))          # my_class.py and also_real.py: silently absent
detect(Path("repo/src_env"))  # my_class.py: still silently absent (env/ pruned as subdir)
                               # also_real.py: found (not under the env/ subdir)
```

## Measured real-world impact

On a live Sandisk/WDC Gen-II UVM verification repo (`ip-ctrl_mem_verif`) that follows the extremely common convention of naming the top-level environment directory `src_env/` and the user-owned environment-logic subdirectory `env/` (e.g. `verif_sv/src_env/env/ctrl_mem_env.sv`):

- **93 of 109 `.sv` source files (705 KB)** were completely absent from the graph — including the core environment class, config, scoreboard, coverage collectors, and every sequence file.
- The build reported success with no errors or warnings, and produced a plausible-looking (but badly incomplete) community/report structure — nothing in the tool's own output indicated anything was wrong.
- Verification required manually diffing `find . -iname "*.ext" | wc -l` against `detect()`'s reported count per extension to even notice the gap.

This will reproduce on **every** repo following this convention — which is the default directory-naming convention for an entire class of hardware verification methodology (Sandisk/WDC "Gen-II" UVM environments), not a one-off.

## Suggested fixes (any of these would help; happy to discuss/PR)

1. **Report pruned noise-dirs.** Add pruned directories to a new bucket (e.g. `pruned_as_noise_dir`) in `detect()`'s return value, the same way `ignored`/`unclassified` already work — so at minimum the loss is visible and diffable.
2. **Let `.graphifyignore` negation override `_is_noise_dir`,** not just `_is_ignored`, so `!env/` in a `.graphifyignore` can rescue a real source directory the same way it already rescues gitignored-but-wanted paths.
3. **Narrow the heuristic with context**, similar to the existing `snapshots` special-case (`_JS_SNAPSHOT_TEST_ROOTS` / checking for `*.snap` files before pruning a bare `snapshots` dir) — e.g. only treat `env`/`venv` as a Python virtualenv if it actually contains venv markers (`pyvenv.cfg`, `bin/activate` or `Scripts/activate.bat`, `lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages`), rather than pruning on bare name alone.

Happy to provide the exact repo structure / a minimal repro directory tree if useful.

## Environment
- graphify version: 0.9.20
- Installed via: `pip install graphifyy` (python 3.11.1)
- OS: Linux (RHEL-based, dspg CAD infra)

title: Office sidecar name is keyed on the absolute source path, so every checkout of the same repo emits a duplicate converted/*.md
body:
## Summary

`convert_office_file` names Office sidecars `<stem>_<sha256(resolved absolute path)[:8]>.md`. The suffix is salted with the *checkout location* rather than the content, so the same `.xlsx` in two clones of one repo produces two differently-named, byte-identical sidecars.

## Why it matters

Committing `graphify-out/` is a supported workflow: the installed post-commit hook explicitly handles it, with a branch commented "Skip when only graphify-out/ artifacts changed (avoids rebuild loop when graph outputs are tracked in git)".

Under that workflow the duplicates are unbounded. Every additional clone or `git worktree` that runs the hook adds another permanent copy. In our monorepo four had accumulated for a single spreadsheet, all byte-identical (`md5 13a827e5c5971cc895cd1d5419ff4d73`), one per checkout path. Worse, `graph.json` ingested each as a *distinct source document*, so the same content was triple-counted in the graph.

## Reproduction

```
git clone <repo-with-a-tracked-.xlsx> /path/to/checkout-a
git clone <same-repo>                 /path/to/checkout-b
# run graphify in each
ls */graphify-out/converted/
#   checkout-a: report_b8dd23a5.md
#   checkout-b: report_350564c8.md   <- identical content, different name
```

## Root cause

`graphify/detect.py`, in `convert_office_file`:

```python
normalized_path = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", str(path.resolve()))
name_hash = hashlib.sha256(normalized_path.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
```

## Related issues

This shares a root cause with two already-fixed issues, but has a different trigger:

* **#1226**, NFC/NFD normalization producing duplicate sidecars for one file.
* **#1649**, "sidecar keyed on path hash", where modified sources never re-entered `--update`.

Both fixed a *consequence* of hashing the absolute path. This report covers the remaining consequence: the name is not portable across checkouts.

## Suggested fix

Hash the path **relative to the scan root** instead of the absolute path. That preserves the stated purpose of the hash (disambiguating same-stem files in different directories) while making the output stable across checkouts. `root` is derivable from the existing `out_dir` argument as `out_dir.parent.parent`, so the function signature does not need to change.

I would avoid content-hashing: the sidecar name would then change on every edit, which churns filenames and interacts badly with the mtime-comparison logic added for #1649.

## Environment

Found on `graphifyy` 0.8.28. Behaviour verified as still present in the v0.9.20 source.

title: post-checkout hook rebuilds on branch creation even when PREV_HEAD == NEW_HEAD
body:
The post-checkout hook installed by `graphify hook install` triggers a full
background rebuild on any branch switch (`$3 == 1`), including
`git checkout -b <new-branch>`. In that case `$1` (PREV_HEAD) and `$2`
(NEW_HEAD) are identical — no file in the tree actually changed — yet the
hook still launches `_rebuild_code`, which then produces reordering/community
churn in graph.json unrelated to any real code change.

In a shared repo this generates recurring, purely cosmetic diffs on
graphify-out/* every time someone starts a new branch, which teams end up
discarding via `git stash` rather than committing.

Suggested fix: early-exit when `$1 = $2`, e.g. right after the existing
`BRANCH_SWITCH != 1` check in the generated hook template:

    if [ "$PREV_HEAD" = "$NEW_HEAD" ]; then
        exit 0
    fi

Version: graphifyy 0.9.16 (hook template written by `graphify hook install`)

title: fix(hooks): skip post-checkout rebuild when HEAD doesn't move
body:
## Summary
- `git checkout -b <new-branch>` off the current HEAD sets `BRANCH_SWITCH=1` even though `PREV_HEAD`/`NEW_HEAD` are identical, so the post-checkout hook launched a full graph rebuild for a switch with no underlying code change.
- Since community detection isn't fully deterministic across runs, that produced pure reordering churn in `graphify-out/graph.json`, which teams ended up discarding via `git stash`.
- Added an early-exit guard right after the existing `BRANCH_SWITCH != 1` check: skip the rebuild when `PREV_HEAD` equals `NEW_HEAD`.

Fixes #2060

## Test plan
- [x] `uv run pytest tests/test_hooks.py -q` — 61 passed (3 new tests covering the guard, static + end-to-end)
- [x] `uv run ruff check graphify/hooks.py tests/test_hooks.py`
- [x] `uv run python -m tools.skillgen --check`

title: graphify uninstall deletes user-written content
body:
the section-strip regex matches ### graphify as well as ## graphify

The issue follows the conventions of the repo's existing reports (Summary / Why it matters / Reproduction / Root cause / Suggested fix / Environment), and I tightened a few things while writing it:

- Repro runs through the real CLI, install claude --project → uninstall claude --project, not internal function calls — so nobody can dismiss it as unreachable.
- The blast radius is five files, not one. I mapped each duplicated site to the file it rewrites: GEMINI.md (:726), .github/copilot-instructions.md (:817), AGENTS.md (:1553), CLAUDE.md (:1773), CODEBUDDY.md (:1863).
- The framing is asymmetry with #1688, which hardened the install side against this exact bug via line.strip() == marker. That makes it a known-class regression rather than a novel report, which usually lands better.
- The guards don't save you either — _CLAUDE_MD_MARKER not in content is itself a substring test, so a file whose only match is a user's H3 still passes the guard and proceeds to strip. I nearly missed this: my first verification script used the same substring check and gave a false negative, which is a decent illustration of how easy the mistake is.
- The fix is validated, not proposed blind — I ran the line-anchored regex against a real post-install CLAUDE.md and confirmed graphify's own section is removed while both user H3 sections survive.

title: fix(kotlin): emit references edges for primary-constructor class_parameters
body:
## Title
Kotlin extractor drops constructor-injected fields (`primary_constructor`/`class_parameters` never walked)

## Summary
`extract_kotlin` never emits `references` edges for dependencies declared in a
class's **primary constructor** (`class Foo(private val x: Bar)`) — the
idiomatic Kotlin/Hilt/Dagger DI pattern. Only two Kotlin-specific code paths
exist in `graphify/extractors/engine.py`:

1. `delegation_specifiers` → `inherits`/`implements` edges for supertypes.
2. `property_declaration` → `references` edges for **body-level** `val`/`var`.

Neither walks `primary_constructor → class_parameters → class_parameter`, so
every constructor-injected field is invisible to the graph. Scala already has
the equivalent handling for its structurally identical `class_parameters` node
(same file, ~30 lines below the Kotlin block) — Kotlin never got the same
treatment.

## Reproduction
Using the project's own fixture, `tests/fixtures/sample.kt`:

```kotlin
class HttpClient(private val config: Config) {
    ...
}
```

```python
from graphify.extract import extract_kotlin
r = extract_kotlin(Path("tests/fixtures/sample.kt"))
refs = [(e["source"], e["target"]) for e in r["edges"] if e["relation"] == "references"]
assert ("HttpClient", "Config") in refs  # currently FAILS
```

No edge from `HttpClient` to `Config` is ever emitted, despite `Config` being
a required, explicit, statically-typed constructor dependency. Existing tests
(`test_kotlin_parameter_return_generic_and_field_contexts`,
`test_kotlin_user_types_still_emit_references`) already assert `references`
edges for a **body-level** `val` on `DataProcessor`, so the gap was masked —
nobody had asserted the primary-constructor case.

## Why this matters (real-world impact)
Found while running `/graphify` on a ~600-file, multi-module Kotlin/Android
app that uses constructor-injection (Hilt) everywhere — the standard pattern
for every ViewModel and Repository. Before the fix:

- A `MealDraftStore` class injected into **5 production ViewModels** via
  `private val mealDraftStore: MealDraftStore` showed **zero** incoming edges
  from any of them in the graph — only from test classes that instantiate it
  directly (`MealDraftStore()` in a test's `.setUp()`, captured via the
  `calls` path, which *is* handled).
- A `FirestoreSyncService` injected into 3 repositories was equally invisible.
- Applying the fix and re-running extraction (AST-only, no LLM cost) on the
  same corpus: **+292 edges** (5,452 → 5,744), and the top god-nodes' degree
  jumped accordingly (`GlucoseSettingsRepository` 58→68, `HistoryViewModel`
  41→53, `Food` 63→72) — all constructor-injection edges that were silently
  dropped before.

For any Kotlin codebase using DI via primary-constructor (which is close to
all idiomatic modern Kotlin), this means the dependency graph systematically
undercounts how classes actually depend on each other, skewing god-node
rankings, community detection, and "who uses X" queries.

## Fix
Mirror the existing Scala `class_parameters` handling
(`graphify/extractors/engine.py`, Scala block a few lines below the Kotlin
`delegation_specifiers` block) for Kotlin's `primary_constructor →
class_parameters → class_parameter` nodes. Patch attached (`kotlin-primary-
constructor-fix.diff`, applies cleanly to `v8` HEAD as of `abff1b1`):

- `graphify/extractors/engine.py`: +33 lines, new Kotlin-specific block
  right after the existing `delegation_specifiers` block.
- `tests/test_languages.py`: +14 lines, one new regression test
  (`test_kotlin_primary_constructor_val_emits_references`) using the
  existing `sample.kt` fixture — no fixture changes needed, the reproducing
  case (`HttpClient(private val config: Config)`) was already there.

Verified:
- `pytest tests/test_languages.py` — 318 passed, 13 skipped (unrelated
  optional deps), **0 failures**, including the 13 Kotlin tests (12 existing
  + 1 new).
- `pytest tests/test_extract.py tests/test_multilang.py
  tests/test_cross_language_call_resolution.py` — 174 passed, 12 skipped,
  0 failures.
- Manually confirmed on the real-world corpus described above that the fix
  produces exactly the expected new edges (constructor-injected ViewModels →
  their injected repositories/stores) and nothing spurious.

## Scope note
This fixes constructor-parameter type references only. It does **not**
address a related but separate gap: `when (result) { is Result.Success ->
... }` pattern-matching inside function bodies also isn't walked for type
references anywhere in the extractor (any language) — that's a broader,
more expensive change (walking arbitrary expression bodies) and out of scope
here.

title: feat(extract): add R language extractor (regex, no tree-sitter grammar exists)
body:
## Summary

- `.r`/`.R` is in `CODE_EXTENSIONS` but has no AST extractor, so R files silently contribute nothing and trip the #1689 warning on every run. `tree-sitter-r` isn't published on PyPI, so this follows `apex.py`'s precedent: a regex extractor over a comment/string-masked copy of the source, brace-matched so nested closures scope correctly.
- `extract_r` (`graphify/extractors/r.py`) emits function definitions (including backtick-quoted infix operators like `` `%||%` ``), calls, `library()`/`require()`/`pkg::` imports, and `source()` edges — including unrolling the common `for (mod in files) source(paste0(mod, ".R"))` bootstrap loop into individual per-file edges, which a literal-string `source()` regex alone would miss.
- R has one flat namespace once every file is `source()`'d into `.GlobalEnv`, so a single-file extractor can't tell a cross-file call from a typo. `extract_r` resolves same-file calls and stashes a bare-name hint on the rest; `_resolve_r_bare_calls` (`graphify/extractors/resolution.py`), wired into `extract()` the same way `_resolve_cross_file_imports` is for Python, does the corpus-wide lookup afterward and leaves ambiguous (>1 candidate) names dangling rather than guessing — never inventing an edge.
- `_symbol_safe_name` moves to `base.py` (shared, not R-specific) because an all-symbol identifier normalizes to the empty string in `make_id`, which silently collapsed a `%op%` operator node onto its own file's node id and produced a self-loop `contains` edge. Fixed at the shared layer since any future backtick-identifier language hits the same bug.

## Validation

Ran against a real 15-file, ~150-function R analysis pipeline (not a synthetic fixture):
- 97% symbol recall (138/142) against a prior LLM-extracted graph of the same codebase, 0 false-positive nodes
- 0 self-loops, 0 dangling `sources` edges — all 13 edges of a dynamic `source()` loop recovered correctly
- Every remaining dangling `calls` edge audited by hand: genuine external package calls (`Biobase::`, `ggplot2::`, base-R `strrep`/`setNames`/etc.), zero false negatives

Two existing tests pinned `.r`/`.R` as "no extractor exists" as their fixture (`test_extract_warns_on_code_files_with_no_ast_extractor`, `test_extract_progress_final_line_uses_consistent_denominator`) — closing the gap makes both fail by design. Repointed both at a synthetic `.zzznolang` extension so they keep testing the *general* no-extractor warning path without pinning it to a specific language, and added `test_extract_r_extracts_functions_calls_and_sources` to lock in the new behavior (functions, cross-file call resolution, imports, sources).

Full suite, this branch vs. clean HEAD: identical 54 pre-existing failures on both (`tree-sitter-hcl` unavailable, Windows watch/repo-root path handling, a shallow-clone git-log fixture — none R-related). Net +1 passing test, 0 regressions.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/test_extract.py -k "no_ast_extractor or extract_r_extracts or no_warning_when_all_code or progress_final_line"` — all pass
- [x] Full suite diffed against clean HEAD — same failure set, +1 net pass
- [x] Manual validation against a real-world R corpus (see above)
- [ ] Maintainer: confirm `.r` dispatch placement/`_DISPATCH` ordering convention is acceptable (placed next to `.jl`, the closest thematic neighbor — bespoke single-extension scripting extractor, no interop family)

title: fix(scala): walk type_definition right-hand sides for type references
body:
Fixes #2049

`type_definition` nodes (plain aliases, `opaque type`, match types) sit at the exact same `template_body` sibling level as `val_definition`/`var_definition`, but the Scala-specific dispatch in `_extract_generic` only fired for the latter — so alias right-hand sides produced zero `references` edges of any kind, as reported.

## Changes

Two small edits in `graphify/extractors/engine.py`:

1. **Widen the dispatch** to include `type_definition`. Verified against tree-sitter-scala that the RHS lives under the same `type` field a val/var annotation uses (for plain aliases, `opaque type`, and match types alike), so the existing walk is reused verbatim — exactly the one-line widening the issue suggested.
2. **Teach `_scala_collect_type_refs` about `match_type` / `type_case_clause`**. As the issue predicted, the dispatch alone isn't enough for match types: the walker's recursion whitelist didn't know these node types, so a correctly-dispatched match-type RHS still resolved nothing. Adding them to the existing recursion tuple lets case patterns and results resolve.

## Before / after

```scala
class Repo {
  type Alias = List[Int]
  opaque type Id = Long
  type Elem[X] = X match { case String => Char; case Array[t] => t }
}
```

Before: `Repo` has no outgoing `references` edges.
After: `references` edges to `List`, `Int`, `Long`, `String`, `Char`, `Array`, `t`, `X` — matching what an equivalent `val` annotation already produced.

## Tests

Extended `tests/fixtures/sample.scala` with a `TypeAliases` class covering all three shapes, plus four new tests asserting the alias (`Map`/`HttpClient`), opaque (`Long`), and match-type case (`Option`/`ListBuffer`) references. Full run: `tests/test_languages.py` + `tests/test_builtin_global_type_refs.py` → **324 passed, 13 skipped**.

Out of scope (kept separate deliberately): file-scope/trait containers (#2042, #2054) and qualified `stable_type_identifier` names (#2055) — this PR only closes the `type_definition` dispatch gap so it composes cleanly with fixes for those.

title: --update silently deletes freshly extracted nodes for every changed file (prune_sources applied after build)
body:
## Summary

`--update` silently discards the freshly extracted nodes of every **changed** file. The graph is left containing the *old* nodes of unchanged files only — the update is a net deletion. There is no error, and the `#479` anti-shrink guard is bypassed by construction.

Version: `graphifyy 0.9.12`.

## Root cause

`references/update.md` (the `--update` runbook) builds the prune list from **deleted + changed** files:

```python
deleted = list(incremental.get('deleted_files', []))
changed = [f for files in incremental.get('new_files', {}).values() for f in files]
prune = list(dict.fromkeys(deleted + changed)) or None   # <-- changed files go into prune_sources

G = build_merge([new_extraction], graph_path='graphify-out/graph.json', prune_sources=prune)
```

But `build_merge()` applies `prune_sources` **after** `build()`, matching on `source_file` of the *merged* graph:

```python
all_chunks = base + list(new_chunks)
G = build(all_chunks, ...)          # fresh nodes for changed files are now IN G
...
if prune_sources:
    to_remove = [n for n, d in G.nodes(data=True) if d.get("source_file") in prune_set]
    G.remove_nodes_from(to_remove)  # ...and are removed again here
```

So a changed file's nodes are added by `build()` and then deleted by the prune pass, because the prune set contains that file's `source_file`.

This also contradicts the function's own docstring, which scopes `prune_sources` to deletions:

> Re-extracted files REPLACE their prior contribution: any `source_file` present in `new_chunks` is dropped from the loaded graph before merging […] **deleted files are removed via `prune_sources`.**

The stale-node problem the runbook comment cites (`#1178`) is already handled by the `new_sources` replace-pass earlier in `build_merge`, so adding changed files to `prune_sources` is not just harmful — it's redundant.

Two things make it silent:

1. The anti-shrink guard is explicitly skipped when pruning: `if graph_path.exists() and not dedup and not prune_sources:` — and `--update` always passes `dedup=True` *and* a non-empty `prune_sources`, so it can never fire.
2. The log line reads `Pruned 220 node(s) from 7 deleted source file(s)` — it says *deleted*, and the count is the **new** chunk's node count, which reads like healthy churn.

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.build import build_merge

Path('graphify-out').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
base = {'nodes': [{'id': 'A', 'label': 'A', 'source_file': 'f.md'},
                  {'id': 'B', 'label': 'B', 'source_file': 'f.md'}],
        'links': [{'source': 'A', 'target': 'B', 'relation': 'x', 'source_file': 'f.md'}]}

# f.md changed; re-extraction now yields a third node C
new = {'nodes': [{'id': 'A', 'label': 'A', 'source_file': 'f.md'},
                 {'id': 'B', 'label': 'B', 'source_file': 'f.md'},
                 {'id': 'C', 'label': 'C NEW', 'source_file': 'f.md'}],
       'edges': [{'source': 'A', 'target': 'C', 'relation': 'x', 'source_file': 'f.md'}]}

Path('graphify-out/graph.json').write_text(json.dumps(base))
G = build_merge([new], graph_path='graphify-out/graph.json', prune_sources=['f.md'])
print(G.number_of_nodes(), sorted(G.nodes()))   # 0 []          <-- as the runbook calls it

Path('graphify-out/graph.json').write_text(json.dumps(base))
G = build_merge([new], graph_path='graphify-out/graph.json', prune_sources=None)
print(G.number_of_nodes(), sorted(G.nodes()))   # 3 ['A','B','C'] <-- as documented
```

**Expected:** `3 ['A', 'B', 'C']` in both cases.
**Actual:** `0 []` in the first — the entire file's contribution vanishes.

## Real-world impact

On a 119-file corpus (~1600 nodes), an `--update` touching 7 changed files:

- baseline: 1606 nodes / 1829 edges
- new chunk: 220 nodes / 301 edges extracted correctly
- after `build_merge`: **1399 nodes** — i.e. `1606 − 220 + ~13`, the fresh extraction gone

The LLM extraction cost is paid and then thrown away. Worse, it compounds: an earlier `--update` on the same corpus had already wiped ~112 nodes' worth of converted PDF/DOCX sidecars, and that loss was invisible until the graph was audited by hand.

## Suggested fix

In `references/update.md`, scope the prune list to deletions only:

```python
prune = list(dict.fromkeys(deleted)) or None
```

Optionally, harden `build_merge` so misuse can't be silent — either drop `new_sources` from `prune_set` defensively:

```python
prune_set -= new_sources
```

…or let the anti-shrink guard run when `prune_sources` contains files that are also present in `new_chunks`, since that combination is never a legitimate deletion.

title: build_from_json's ghost-duplicate merge keys on bare filename, silently collapses unrelated same-named docs across corpora
body:
## Summary

`build_from_json`'s "ghost-duplicate merge" pass (referenced in the code as issue #1145) keys its AST/LLM duplicate-detection on `(Path(source_file).name, label)` - the bare filename, discarding the directory. On a multi-corpus documentation graph, this causes it to silently merge/delete unrelated nodes from *different* files that happen to share a common basename (`index.md`, `overview.md`, `quickstart.md`, `README.md`, `mcp.md`, etc.) and a similarly generic label (a page's own title), rewiring their edges onto the wrong survivor.

## Where

`graphify/build.py`, `build_from_json()`, the two-pass block right after node insertion (search for `#1145 (extended)`):

```python
_loc_nodes: dict[tuple[str, str], str] = {}
...
for nid in node_set:
    attrs = G.nodes[nid]
    label = str(attrs.get("label", "")).strip()
    sf = str(attrs.get("source_file", ""))
    basename = Path(sf).name if sf else ""
    ...
    if attrs.get("source_location") or is_ast:
        key = (basename, label)
        ...
```

## Why this is a false match for documents (not code)

The design intent (per the surrounding comments) is: an AST extractor produces a parent-qualified ID for a code symbol (`mingpt_bpe_get_pairs`), an LLM/semantic pass produces a bare-stem ID for the *same* symbol (`bpe_get_pairs`) - different IDs, same entity, same file. Keying on bare basename makes sense there because both extractions are of the *same file*.

For a documentation corpus, this assumption breaks: totally unrelated files across different products/sections legitimately share a generic basename, and their extracted "title" labels are often identical or near-identical strings (e.g., every course's own `README.md` gets labeled `"README.md"` or `"About this course"`; every product's own onboarding page gets labeled `"Quickstart"`). Two unrelated documents can collide on `(basename, label)` even though they have nothing to do with each other.

The pass is also unconditional - it is not gated on `file_type == "code"`, and it runs regardless of the public `dedup=False` parameter passed to `build()`/`build_merge()` (that flag only controls a separate, later dedup step in `build()`; this pass is inline inside `build_from_json` and always runs).

## Reproduction (real data, not synthetic)

Against our own multi-corpus doc mirror (~25,300 nodes across 8 separately-sourced documentation sets: GitHub docs, Intune docs, Claude Code docs, Anthropic Skilljar courses, a Canva API mirror, etc.), we found:

- **653** distinct `(basename, label)` key collisions across genuinely different files.
- **529** of those have at least one member eligible to become "canonical" (truthy `source_location` or `_origin == "ast"`).
- Concrete examples of what collides:
  - `(README.md, "README.md")` → all 18 of our mirrored Anthropic Skilljar course READMEs (18 different courses, 18 different files) collapse onto one key.
  - `(overview.md, "overview.md")` → 18 unrelated pages across two different products (Microsoft Intune docs + Claude Code docs).
  - `(quickstart.md, "quickstart.md")` → 5 unrelated products' quickstart pages (GitHub CLI, GitHub Actions, Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, GitHub Apps).
  - `(mcp.md, "mcp.md")`, `(plugins.md, "plugins.md")`, `(skills.md, "skills.md")` → each collides between two different sections of the *same* product's docs (Claude Code's own "Build" section vs. its "Agent SDK" section) - so this isn't even limited to cross-product cases.

We triggered a real merge (`build_merge`) with 178 legitimately new/updated nodes and watched **462 pre-existing, entirely unrelated nodes disappear** from corpora we hadn't touched in that run (GitHub Actions docs, Intune MDM security-baseline settings, Skilljar course readmes) - `build_merge`'s own shrink-guard (`ValueError: would shrink graph from X → Y nodes`) is what caught it before any write happened, which is how we found this. The shrinkage is order-dependent (`for nid in node_set:` iterates a Python `set`, whose de-facto iteration order shifts as the node count changes), so the *same* pre-existing collisions had apparently been silently sitting unresolved for a while, and a routine merge is what happened to tip several of them into an actual deletion.

## Suggested fix

Include the full (normalized) `source_file` in the key instead of just the basename - i.e. `key = (source_file, label)` rather than `key = (Path(source_file).name, label)`. This still correctly catches the original #1145 case (AST node and LLM ghost node extracted from the *same* file) while no longer matching unrelated files that happen to share a name. Alternatively/additionally, gate the whole pass on `file_type == "code"` (or on both nodes actually being code-flavored), since the underlying assumption (distinct-ID, same-symbol duplication) is a code-extraction concern, not a documents/concepts one.

Happy to provide the (basename,label) collision dump we generated, or test a candidate fix against our corpus if useful.

title: feat(serve): honor a token_budget on get_neighbors/get_community
body:
## Problem

`get_neighbors` and `get_community` render every edge/member line unbounded. On a god node or a large community, one tool call floods an MCP client's context window with 100KB+ of text — the exact problem `query_graph` already solves with the ~3-chars/token cut in `_subgraph_to_text`.

## Change

- New `_cut_lines_to_budget(lines, token_budget, narrow_hint)` helper applying the same budget rule to pre-built line lists: cut at a line boundary, report how many lines were dropped, and point at the narrowing path.
- `token_budget` (integer, default 2000 — same as `query_graph`) added to both tools' input schemas.
- `get_neighbors` hints `relation_filter` / `get_node`; `get_community` hints raising the budget / `get_node`.

## Behavior

- Output **under budget is byte-identical to today** — no change for small results.
- Over budget: truncated at a line boundary with `... (truncated — N more lines cut by ~2000-token budget. <hint>)`, matching the existing `_subgraph_to_text` message shape.

Motivation context: we run graphify-mcp as a read-only code-structure organ for LLM sessions; unbounded neighbor/community dumps were the last two tools that could blow a session's context in one call. Happy to adjust naming/defaults to taste.

title: --code-only is missing from --help and the README
body:
`--code-only` is a genuinely useful flag and it is currently discoverable only by triggering an error. It appears in neither the README nor `graphify --help`.

I evaluated graphify for a documentation-heavy repository where the docs contain infrastructure hostnames that must not leave the machine, so "can this run without any network call" was the deciding question. The README says code is parsed locally with tree-sitter and that docs go through an LLM, but it does not say whether the LLM path can be turned off. `graphify --help` lists `--watch`, `--wiki`, `--no-label`, `--no-viz` and others, and no code-only option. On that evidence I concluded no such flag existed and was about to drop the tool.

It exists. I found it by running with no API key set:

```
error: no LLM API key found (2 doc/paper/image file(s) need semantic extraction).
Set GEMINI_API_KEY or ... or pass --backend. A code-only corpus needs no key.
Or pass --code-only to index just the code (local AST, no key) and skip the non-code files.
```

That error message is excellent. It names the file count, lists the options, and gives the escape hatch. The problem is that you only see it if you run without a key, and someone evaluating the tool on a privacy constraint will often decide before that point.

`--code-only` worked exactly as described. 34 Python files, no key set, no network, 927 nodes and 2,016 edges.

Two suggestions, both small:

1. Add `--code-only` to `graphify --help`, alongside `--no-label` and `--no-viz`.
2. Add one line to the README's docs table, something like "pass `--code-only` to skip all non-code files and run with no API key and no network calls".

Worth saying that the underlying behaviour is already right. Refusing to run rather than silently falling back to a remote call is the correct default, and grepping the source turned up no telemetry endpoint. This is a documentation gap in front of a good design, not a design problem.

title: Scan root silently changes the graph: src-layout project loses most 'imports' edges, same node count, no warning
body:
The same files produce a different graph depending on which directory you point `graphify` at. Node count is identical, so nothing looks wrong, and no warning is printed.

For a src-layout project, scanning the repository root instead of the package root silently drops most `imports` edges. In my real case that was 219 edges out of 2,236, about 10%.

## Minimal reproduction

Four files in a package `mypkg`, using absolute imports (`from mypkg.core import Engine`), which is what a src-layout project looks like on disk.

```
mre/
  direct/            <- scan THIS: package root
    mypkg/
      __init__.py    from mypkg.core import Engine
      core.py        class Engine
      app.py         from mypkg.core import Engine; import mypkg.helpers as helpers
      helpers.py     from mypkg.core import Engine
  nested/
    src/             <- identical bytes, one level deeper
      mypkg/ ...
```

`nested/src/` is a byte-identical copy of `direct/`, verified with `diff -rq`.

Run the same command in each directory, graphify 0.9.22, no API key set:

```
graphify . --code-only --no-label --no-viz
```

Result:

```
direct   ->  8 nodes, 14 edges, 3 communities
nested   ->  8 nodes, 10 edges, 4 communities
```

Edge relations:

| relation | direct | nested | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| imports | 4 | 1 | **-3** |
| re_exports | 1 | 0 | **-1** |
| calls | 3 | 2 | -1 |
| imports_from | 2 | 3 | +1 |
| contains | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| method | 1 | 1 | 0 |

Same signature at real-project scale: 34 files, 927 nodes in both cases, 2,236 edges vs 2,016, with the gap being 197 `imports`, 17 `imports_from` and 5 `re_exports`. Every other relation matched exactly, and `calls` differed by one.

## Why this is easy to hit and hard to notice

1. Pointing at a repository root is the natural first thing to do, and it's what the README's `graphify .` implies.
2. The node count is unchanged, so the graph looks complete.
3. No warning is emitted. I grepped the degraded run's output for `warn`, `unresolved`, `could not` and `skip` and got zero lines.
4. **The ranking changes.** In my real project, `god-nodes` on the correct graph reports `A` (40), `B` (39), `C` (38). On the degraded graph it reports `C` (37), `B` (33), `A` (31). The top three are the same three nodes in a different order, so a reader draws a different conclusion about which component is most central, from a graph that gives no sign of being incomplete.

Point 4 is the reason I'm filing this rather than just changing my command. A silently incomplete graph that still answers questions is worse than one that fails.

## Suggestions

Any one of these would have saved me the investigation:

- When a module-level import target can't be resolved to a node in the corpus, count them and print a summary line, e.g. `197 import edge(s) unresolved — is the scan root the package root?`
- Detect a single `src/` (or `lib/`) directory at the scan root containing the package and either descend or warn.
- Document in the README that the scan root should be the directory imports resolve against, not necessarily the repository root.

Happy to test a patch against the real 34-file project if useful.

Environment: graphifyy 0.9.22, Python 3.14, macOS.

title: --no-label persists placeholder names into .graphify_labels.json, permanently suppressing the free hub labeler
body:
Running `cluster-only --no-label` once writes the `Community N` placeholders into `graphify-out/.graphify_labels.json` as if they were real labels. Every later run then preserves them, so the free hub labeler never gets a chance to run and the graph reads `Community 0` permanently.

The same command produces different output depending on whether that cache file exists, and nothing tells you it's there.

## Reproduction

A four-file package, graphify 0.9.22, no API key set in the environment.

```
mypkg/
  __init__.py   from mypkg.core import Engine
  core.py       class Engine: run(), stop()
  app.py        from mypkg.core import Engine; import mypkg.helpers
  helpers.py    from mypkg.core import Engine
```

```
$ graphify . --code-only --no-label
   -> 11 nodes, 19 edges, 4 communities

$ graphify cluster-only . --no-label
   names:  ['Community 0', 'Community 1', 'Community 2', 'Community 3']
   .graphify_labels.json now contains those four strings

$ graphify cluster-only .            # no --no-label, still no API key
   names:  ['Community 0', 'Community 1', 'Community 2', 'Community 3']    # <-- expected hub names
   ("Labeling communities..." never prints)

$ rm graphify-out/.graphify_labels.json graphify-out/.graphify_labels.json.sig
$ graphify cluster-only .            # byte-identical command to the one above
   Labeling communities...
   names:  ['Engine', 'app.py', 'core.py', 'helpers.py']                   # <-- correct
```

The last two invocations are the same command. The only difference is a dotfile the user never asked for and is unlikely to know about.

## Why I think this is a bug rather than intended caching

`label_communities_by_hub` in `cluster.py` describes itself as "Used as the default (no-backend) labeler", and it works exactly as documented once the cache is out of the way. The caching logic is also clearly deliberate and well-reasoned. The docstring on `community_member_sigs` explains that it exists to avoid reusing a stale LLM label on a community whose membership changed, which is a real problem worth solving.

The gap is that a placeholder is stored in the same place as an earned label and is then treated as one. A placeholder is precisely the thing that should always be recomputed.

I hit this on a 927-node project. 40 of 42 communities stayed as `Community N` through repeated runs, and I had assumed naming simply required an API key I did not want to configure. It does not. It was one stale dotfile.

## Suggestions

Any one of these fixes it:

- Don't persist labels at all when `--no-label` is passed. The placeholders carry no information, so there is nothing worth caching.
- Or treat a label matching `^Community \d+$` as absent when deciding what to re-label.
- Or have `--no-label` skip only the LLM naming pass and still apply the free hub labeler, which is what the flag's help text ("skip LLM community naming") already implies it does.

The third reads closest to the documented intent. `--no-label` is described as skipping *LLM* naming, and a user passing it to avoid a network call is unlikely to intend giving up the local labeler too.

Environment: graphifyy 0.9.22, Python 3.14, macOS.

title: graphify path: non-deterministic shortest-path route + calls label not backed by any stored edge
body:
**Summary**

`graphify path "<A>" "<B>"` returns a different shortest path on repeated, identical invocations against the same unmodified `graph.json` — and one of the observed paths displayed a `--calls-->` edge label that does not correspond to any stored edge with `relation: "calls"` in the graph data (there were zero `calls`-relation edges in the entire graph).

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Build a graph with `/graphify` (code + docs + papers corpus, ~490 nodes / ~1300 edges after build).
2. Run: `graphify path "<node_id_A>" "<node_id_B>"` where the shortest path is 4 hops with more than one route of equal length available.
3. Run the exact same command again (no changes to `graph.json` in between).

**Observed**

Run 1:
```
Shortest path (4 hops):
  <A> --rationale_for [EXTRACTED]--> ProductArgument <--references [EXTRACTED]-- ShuffleArgument --calls [EXTRACTED]--> ShuffleConsistencyArgument <--rationale_for [EXTRACTED]-- <B>
```

Run 2 (same command, same graph.json, no edits in between):
```
Shortest path (4 hops):
  <A> --rationale_for [EXTRACTED]--> ProductArgument --shares_data_with [EXTRACTED]--> VectorCommitment <--references [EXTRACTED]-- MultiExpArgumentSqrt <--rationale_for [EXTRACTED]-- <B>
```

Two different routes, both length 4, returned on identical repeated calls.

Additionally, when I went looking in `graph.json` for the edge that produced the `--calls-->` label from Run 1 (to fix what I initially assumed was a bad EXTRACTED edge), I found:
- Zero edges anywhere in the graph with `"relation": "calls"`.
- Zero direct edges of *any* relation between the two class-level nodes (`ShuffleArgument`, `ShuffleConsistencyArgument`) shown adjacent in that path.

So the `--calls-->` shown in the CLI path output does not appear to come verbatim from a stored edge's `relation` field — it looks like either a display-layer synthesized/fallback label, or the path traversal is silently passing through an intermediate node (e.g. a shared/ambiguous generic node like `.prove()` or `.verify()` that appears at multiple source locations) whose real relation got mislabeled or collapsed in the printed output.

**Why this matters**

Users (and the agent driving `/graphify`) reasonably treat `EXTRACTED`-confidence output as ground truth per the skill's own Honesty Rules ("never invent an edge"). A shortest-path command that (a) isn't deterministic between identical calls, and (b) can print a relation label that doesn't trace back to any real stored edge, undermines that guarantee specifically for the `path` command's output — someone could act on `--calls-->` as fact when no such edge exists.

**Environment**
- graphifyy 0.9.21
- Windows 11, Git Bash, Python via `uv tool`
- Graph: ~490 nodes, ~1300 edges, 21 communities, undirected

**Suggested fix directions**
- Make `path`'s tie-breaking among equal-length shortest paths deterministic (e.g. stable sort by node id).
- When printing an edge in the path, read the relation directly from the stored edge object rather than any synthesized/fallback label, and if multiple parallel edges exist between the same two nodes, either print all relations or pick deterministically (not silently pick one that doesn't match what's stored).

title: docs(cli): surface --code-only in the extract usage and README (#2071)
body:
Fixes #2071.

`--code-only` has been in the top-level `graphify --help` since #1734, but two other surfaces still never mention it:

- The `graphify extract` usage string (printed on an empty/bad invocation) lists `--no-cluster`, `--no-gitignore`, `--postgres`, `--cargo`… but **not** `--code-only`.
- The README documents the *concept* ("a code-only corpus requires no API key") but never the actual **flag**.

Someone evaluating graphify under a "can this run with no network call?" constraint reads the extract usage / README first, so they can reasonably conclude the flag doesn't exist — which is exactly what the reporter almost did before finding it by triggering the no-key error.
