title: fix(extract): resolve Python cross-file type references instead of ghosting them (#2363)
body:
Closes #2363

## What I found

The reported duplication is one defect with two id shapes, plus a second, separate defect that the issue title also names. Both are Python-only gaps against behavior other languages already have.

I first measured the reporter's layout with a single definition of `PricePoint` and four referring files: that comes out clean on `v8` head, one node and four correct edges. The missing ingredient for the ghosts is a **second same-named definition** elsewhere in the corpus. With that, both reported shapes reproduce, and which one you get depends only on how many files refer to it:

```
ambiguous + 1 referring file
   pricepoint                                                     <- bare ghost

ambiguous + 4 referring files
   signal_intelligence_connections_prices_py_pricepoint           <- path-qualified ghosts
   signal_intelligence_fronts_agri_deviation_py_pricepoint
   signal_intelligence_fronts_upstream_watch_signals_py_pricepoint
   signal_intelligence_signal_resolution_py_pricepoint
```

Those are the four ids from the issue, character for character. The mechanism: each referring file mints its own sourceless stub with the bare id `pricepoint`; when there are several, they collide on that id but carry different `origin_file`s, so `_disambiguate_colliding_node_ids` salts each into a path-qualified id **before** `_rewire_unique_stub_nodes` runs. So the "two different ID-generation schemes colliding" the issue describes is really one scheme observed at two corpus sizes.

**1. Class-body field annotations were never collected.** `_python_collect_type_refs` had exactly two call sites, function parameters and return types. Nothing walked a `class_definition` body, so the dataclass shape named in the issue title emitted no edge at all — a dropped edge, not a ghost:

```python
@dataclass
class Quote:
    point: PricePoint    # before: no edge, no node
```

Java and TS both handle their equivalent today. Measured on identical corpora:

```
JAVA  b_quote_quote -> a_pricepoint_pricepoint  references field
TS    b_quote_quote -> a_base_pricepoint        references field
PY    (nothing)
```

**2. An ambiguous class name leaves the reference stuck on a shadow stub.** `_rewire_unique_stub_nodes` bails when the label is not globally unique, so with two modules defining `PricePoint` the sourceless stub survives and the edge stays on it — which is exactly the bare-lowercase ghost variant the reporter hit 7 times:

```
3 PricePoint nodes:
  pkg_a_base_pricepoint   src=base.py
  pkg_z_other_pricepoint  src=other.py
  pricepoint              src=''        <- ghost
  pkg_b_c_f -> pricepoint  references parameter_type
```

`from pkg.a.base import PricePoint` names the defining module exactly. Java resolves this with `_resolve_java_type_references`, PHP and C# with their own resolvers. Python had none — `_collect_python_symbol_resolution_facts` collects `imports` and `calls`, never type references. Java on the identical corpus gets it right:

```
2 PricePoint nodes, no ghost
  b_svc_svc_take -> a_pricepoint_pricepoint  references parameter_type
```

## The fix

Both changes follow existing precedent rather than introducing anything new — no new edge type, no schema, exporter or `affected` changes.

- `engine.py`: a Python class-body walk emitting `references` with context `field` / `generic_arg`, mirroring the Java record-component branch, through the same `_semantic_reference_edge` emitter the parameter/return path already uses (it validates the context against `REFERENCE_CONTEXTS`).
- `resolution.py` + `extract.py`: `_resolve_python_type_references`, mirroring `_resolve_java_type_references`, keyed on the local binding so `import X as Y` resolves. Runs after `_rewire_unique_stub_nodes`, so it only handles the ambiguous remainder.

Two deliberate narrowings, both measured rather than assumed:

- The repoint set omits `imports`, which Java and C# both carry. A Python file-level import edge is resolved upstream and never lands on a bare-name stub — verified against ambiguous, aliased and unresolvable-module corpora — so including it would have been an untested no-op.
- The resolver early-returns unless shadow stubs exist, so its parse pass is only paid on a corpus that actually has unresolved references.

## Before / after, real CLI

`graphify extract . --code-only` on one definition of `PricePoint` in `pkg/a/base.py`, a second in `pkg/z/other.py`, and a `Quote` dataclass importing the first:

Before — the field reference is absent entirely, and `Quote` is isolated:
```
E pkg_a_base -> pkg_a_base_pricepoint contains
E pkg_b_quote -> pkg_a_base_pricepoint imports
E pkg_b_quote -> pkg_b_quote_quote contains
E pkg_z_other -> pkg_z_other_pricepoint contains
```

After — the edge exists and binds to the imported definition, not the other same-named one:
```
E pkg_b_quote_quote -> pkg_a_base_pricepoint uses field
```

## Verification

- 11 tests in `tests/test_python_type_references.py`. Checked out against base, 8 fail and 3 pass — the 3 are the pins and negative controls (the no-import bail-out, the plain `x = 1` attribute, the already-working unambiguous case), which are supposed to be green both sides.
- One of them drives the real CLI and asserts on the written `graph.json`, since a unit test on `extract()` can pass while the shipped pipeline drops the result.
- The fix was staged in halves to confirm each test is load-bearing: the engine change alone flips the field tests, the resolver flips the ambiguity tests.
- Full suite: 4 failed / 3906 passed / 3 skipped. All 4 reproduce with the change reverted (`test_ollama.py` x3 and `test_llm_backends.py`, all reading real env vars), so the failure-set diff is empty.
- `ruff` clean. `python -m tools.skillgen --check` → `check OK: 134 artifact(s)`.

## Known limitations

- A reference whose name is ambiguous and which has **no** import naming its definition is still left on the stub. Guessing one of two equally-plausible classes would invent an edge; there is a test pinning this.
- Star imports (`from pkg.a.base import *`) are not used for disambiguation.
- Wide-corpus perf: the resolver re-parses Python files, like the Java and C# resolvers do. Gated on stubs existing, so a clean corpus pays nothing.

## Relationship to #1231

#1231 targets this same area and has been conflicting since June. I did not build on it — it routes annotations through `_SymbolUseFact`, which is a larger redesign of which layer owns Python type references, and it emits `context="annotation"`, which is not a member of `REFERENCE_CONTEXTS`. Happy to close this if you would rather revive that one.

title: Markdown skips extract_markdown in the Claude Code skill pipeline: docs go to the LLM instead of the structural extractor
body:
# Markdown never reaches `extract_markdown` in the skill pipeline: docs are sent to the LLM instead of the structural extractor

**Repo:** `safishamsi/graphify` · **Version:** graphifyy 0.9.32 (uv tool) · **Backend:** `gemini-3-flash-preview`

---

## Summary

`graphify/extractors/markdown.py` is a deterministic, zero-token markdown extractor. It emits heading nodes, `contains` edges for heading nesting, and `references` edges for inline links, reference-style links, and `[[wikilinks]]` — all at `confidence: EXTRACTED`, with no LLM.

In the `/graphify` skill pipeline it never runs on `.md` files.

Step 3 Part A passes only `detect['files']['code']` into `extract()`. `detect` classifies `.md` as `document`. Documents route to Part B (semantic/LLM extraction). So markdown files are sent to a model to have their structure inferred, while the exact structural parser for them sits unused.

Code does not have this problem: it gets the AST baseline *and* a semantic layer. `references/extraction-spec.md` even tells the model so:

> Code files: focus on semantic edges AST cannot find (call relationships, shared data, arch patterns). **Do not re-extract imports - AST already has those.**

There is no equivalent instruction for documents, because no structural pass ran to make one true.

## Relation to #2014

This is the complementary direction of #2014 ("Possible silent downgrade of semantic Markdown nodes during AST-only rebuild", fixed in v0.9.21, verified present in 0.9.32).

- **#2014:** the CLI `graphify update` path *does* run `extract_markdown` on `.md`, and it replaced the semantic layer with heading nodes. Fixed by making the semantic layer survive an AST-only rebuild.
- **This issue:** the Claude Code `/graphify` skill pipeline never runs `extract_markdown` on `.md` at all, so the structural layer is never added in the first place.

Same two layers, opposite failure. #2014 stopped structural from clobbering semantic; this asks for structural to actually run alongside semantic — which is what the code path already does with AST.

## Evidence

Same four markdown files, two paths.

**Path A — what the pipeline actually did** (Part B, Gemini): tokens spent, structure inferred, heading tree absent from the graph.

**Path B — calling the structural extractor directly:**

```python
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.extract import extract
files = [Path('nlm/SPEC-governed-docs-corpus.md'), Path('nlm/nlm-corpus-spec.md'),
         Path('CONTRACT-technical-implementation-handback.md'), Path('prompts/fable5-prompting.md')]
r = extract(files, cache_root=Path('.'))
```

```
nodes: 48  edges: 49
relations: [('contains', 44), ('references', 5)]
input_tokens: 0  output_tokens: 0
```

Nodes carry real heading structure and `source_location`:

```
nlm_spec_governed_docs_corpus                              SPEC-governed-docs-corpus.md
nlm_spec_governed_docs_corpus_spec_governed_docs_corpus    SPEC: Governed Docs Corpus
nlm_spec_governed_docs_corpus_0_prior_art_read_before_...  0. Prior art — read before building anyt…
nlm_spec_governed_docs_corpus_1_why                        1. Why
nlm_spec_governed_docs_corpus_2_what_it_is                 2. What it is
```

48 nodes and 49 edges, deterministic, for zero tokens — from four files that the pipeline instead sent to an LLM.

### Effect on a full run

Input: 28 files (26 documents/images, 2 code), 726k words, at `~/projects/meta-tools` (files enumerated in `graphify-out/manifest.json`; greppable with `rg <pattern> ~/projects/meta-tools/`). Result: 491 nodes, 388 edges, 177 communities, 1,945,808 input / 64,399 output tokens.

Relation distribution in the resulting `graph.json`:

| relation | edges |
|---|---:|
| `references` | 131 |
| `calls` | 105 |
| `inherits` | 67 |
| `implements` | 50 |
| `imports` | 10 |
| `contains` | 8 |
| `rationale_for` | 7 |
| `conceptually_related_to` | 7 |
| `cites` | 2 |
| `semantically_similar_to` | 1 |

Only 8 `contains` edges across the whole graph, from 26 document files that collectively hold hundreds of headings — because the heading-structure pass never ran on them. In the four-file structural test above, those same four files alone produce 44.

Downstream, the `graphify export wiki` audit trail on document communities reports:

```
## Audit Trail
- EXTRACTED: 4 (50%)
- INFERRED: 4 (50%)
```

Half of a document community's relationships are model-reasoned, in a graph where a deterministic extractor for those same files was available and unused. 340 of 491 nodes finished with ≤1 connection.

## Proposed fix

Run the structural pass on document-classified files before semantic extraction, mirroring the code path:

1. Part A feeds structural extraction with `.md`/`.mdx`/`.markdown`/`.rst` files from `detect['files']['document']`, not just `files['code']`. `_MD_LINKABLE_EXTS` in `extractors/markdown.py` already enumerates the extensions.
2. Part C merges structural + semantic for documents exactly as it does for code.
3. `references/extraction-spec.md` gains the document analogue of the existing code instruction: *"Do not re-extract headings or markdown links — the structural pass already has those. Focus on named concepts and relationships the parser cannot see."*

This costs no new architecture — it reuses the AST/semantic split already proven on the code path — and it moves document structure from `INFERRED` to `EXTRACTED` while reducing token spend.

### Measured effect of the fix

I applied it: ran `extract()` over the 24 document-classified `.md` files plus the 2 code files, merged the result into the existing semantic graph, and rebuilt. Structural extraction returned **367 nodes and 362 edges for 0 tokens**.

| | nodes | edges | `contains` | deg-0 | components | largest component |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| before | 491 | 388 | 8 | 121 | 171 | 157 |
| after | 832 | 715 | 335 | 122 | 185 | 157 |

What the fix does deliver: +341 nodes, +327 edges, all `EXTRACTED` at zero token cost, and heading hierarchy going from 8 `contains` edges to 335.

**What it does not deliver, stated plainly:** connectivity is unchanged. The largest connected component stays at 157 nodes, fully-disconnected nodes go 121 → 122, and component count rises as each document grows its own heading tree. The structural pass recovers *intra*-document structure only. In this input the documents contain 2 cross-document markdown links in total, so there was nothing for the link extractor to connect.

I checked that this is not an ID-merge defect: taking one document (`nlm/SPEC-governed-docs-corpus.md`, 19 nodes in the rebuilt graph) and mapping its nodes to connected components puts 18 of 19 in a single component. The structural heading tree does attach to that document's semantic nodes. The disconnection is genuinely *between* documents.

That is worth stating because it separates the two problems cleanly. Routing markdown to the structural extractor is a correctness and cost fix, not a connectivity fix. Inter-document connectivity is a genuinely separate gap — see the frontmatter section below.

One incidental finding while testing: `graphify.extract` uses a process pool, and on macOS (spawn start method) a caller whose module-level code is not under an `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard causes every worker to abort with "A process in the process pool was terminated abruptly," silently dropping those files with only a per-file warning. The library recovers and reports `21 source file(s) produced zero nodes`, which reads like an extraction failure rather than a caller-side spawn problem. A clearer diagnostic here would save debugging time.

## Secondary: `relation` values are not validated against the declared enum

Possibly a separate issue.

The enum in `references/extraction-spec.md` is:

```
calls|implements|references|cites|conceptually_related_to|
shares_data_with|semantically_similar_to|rationale_for
```

**85 of 388 edges (21.9%)** in the run above carried values outside it — `inherits` (67), `imports` (10), `contains` (8).

These have two distinct origins, and the distinction matters:

- **`contains` (8)** traced entirely to `analysis/wall-of-text-analysis.py` — emitted by the **Python AST extractor**, not the LLM. `extractors/markdown.py` emits it too. This is a legitimate structural relation that the documented enum simply omits.
- **`inherits` (67)** came from document-classified `.txt` files, i.e. the LLM path inventing a relation the prompt never offered it.

So the enum is both incomplete (it omits relations graphify's own structural extractors legitimately emit) and unenforced (the LLM path adds more on top).

The adjacent field is validated strictly (`file_type` "MUST be one of exactly these six values... Any other value is invalid and will be rejected"), but `relation` appears unvalidated. Either enforce the enum, or widen it to include what extractors actually emit — `manifest_ingest.py` emits `depends_on`, `cargo_introspect.py` emits `crate_depends_on`, and `extractors/markdown.py` emits `contains`, none of which are in the documented enum. As it stands the documented schema and the produced graph disagree on roughly a fifth of edges, which makes `graph.json` unreliable for programmatic consumers.

## Optional, lower priority: declarative relations in frontmatter

Independent of the above. Markdown's structural extractor recovers *hierarchy* (`contains`) and *linkage* (`references`), but not the kind of relationship — whether doc A supersedes, constrains, corrects, or merely mentions doc B. `references/extraction-spec.md` contains no lifecycle relation terms (`supersedes`, `depends_on`, `constrains`, `corrects`, `derived_from`, `replaces`, `refines` — all zero occurrences).

Frontmatter is already parsed for provenance (spec line 44: `source_url`, `captured_at`, `author`, `contributor`). A `relations:` block would let an author declare relation kind deterministically:

```yaml
---
relations:
  supersedes: archive/historical/SPEC-old-playbook.md
  rationale_for: specs/indexing-plan.md
  cites: [specs/governed-docs.md]
---
```

Worth noting for scoping: the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2 spec — `GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog`, `okf/SPEC.md`, §6.1 — deliberately declines to type links ("the specific kind... is conveyed by the surrounding prose, not by the link itself"), so this is not something an emerging standard will supply. It would be graphify's own extension.

The measurement above is the argument for it. Once markdown is routed through the structural extractor, the remaining disconnection is not a pipeline defect — it is the absence of any declarable inter-document relationship. Headings and links are recoverable from the file; "this spec supersedes that one" is not, because nothing in the format lets an author write it down.

## Reproduction

```bash
uv tool install "graphifyy[gemini]" --force
cd <a directory of markdown docs>
python - <<'EOF'
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.extract import extract
import collections, glob
files = [Path(p) for p in glob.glob('**/*.md', recursive=True)][:5]
r = extract(files, cache_root=Path('.'))
print(len(r['nodes']), 'nodes', len(r['edges']), 'edges', r.get('input_tokens'), 'tokens')
print(collections.Counter(e.get('relation') for e in r['edges']).most_common())
EOF
```

Structural extraction returns nodes and edges at zero token cost. Then run the full `/graphify` pipeline on the same directory and compare `contains` edge counts in `graphify-out/graph.json` — the pipeline's count will be far lower, because Part A never received those files.

## Environment

- graphifyy 0.9.32 via `uv tool`, Python 3.13
- macOS (Darwin 25.6.0), Apple Silicon
- Backend: Gemini `gemini-3-flash-preview`, 28 chunks, `max_concurrency=6`, 0 failed chunks

## Minor: `openai` missing from the base install

`uv tool install graphifyy` does not pull `openai`, which the Gemini backend requires for its OpenAI-compatible endpoint. With `GEMINI_API_KEY` set, all 33 chunks of a first run failed in under a second. The error message named the exact fix (`uv tool install "graphifyy[gemini]" --force`), so impact is low — but installing the extra when a Gemini key is present would remove a guaranteed first-run failure. Happy to file separately.

title: Query ranking: local variables win seeds, answers tunnel into one community, and confidence/weight never affect retrieval
body:
**Version:** graphify 0.9.7 (pip `graphifyy`), macOS, Python 3.11

## Reproduction (real graph: 2,682 nodes / 3,218 links, code + docs corpus)

```
graphify query "how does reconcile decide contradictions"
```

Expected: the answer should reach `src/reconciliation.ts` (the module that
actually decides contradictions in this repo).

Actual: the top seed is a **local variable** literally named `reconcile`
inside a benchmark helper (`docs/research/context-benchmark/runner/
inject-stale.mjs`), and all 25 returned nodes come from that one file /
community. `src/reconciliation.ts` never appears. The whole answer is a
tunnel into a test utility.

Root causes, from reading `serve.py`:

1. Seed scoring has no notion of node kind — an exact-label match on a local
   variable outranks substring matches on files/classes, so any incidental
   local with a lucky name hijacks the query (`_score_nodes` tiers, tie-break
   by degree).
2. Seeds and expansion have no diversity constraint — when the top seeds land
   in one community, BFS depth-2 never escapes it, so one file supplies the
   entire budget.
3. Edge `confidence` (EXTRACTED/INFERRED/AMBIGUOUS) and the stored `weight`
   field are display-only: nothing in seeding, expansion, or output ordering
   consumes them, so an AMBIGUOUS edge ranks identically to an EXTRACTED one.

## Proposals (independent; any subset helps)

1. **Node-kind priors in seed selection.** Sort seeds by
   `(match_tier, kind_prior, degree)` with a prior like
   `file > class/function > variable`. A local variable is almost never the
   right entry point for a natural-language question.
2. **Community-diversity caps.** Require top-K seeds to span more than one
   community when matches exist elsewhere, and cap output nodes per
   file/community, so a single lucky file cannot consume the whole budget.
3. **Confidence/weight-aware ranking.** Use weighted degree in expansion and
   output ordering, with a factor per confidence class (e.g. EXTRACTED 1.0,
   INFERRED 0.5, AMBIGUOUS 0.25) multiplied by the existing `weight` field.
   This makes the audit-trail labels actually shape retrieval, and it gives
   external graph producers (we inject an intent layer from an architecture
   model, with evidence-verified links) a sanctioned way to mark
   higher-trust edges instead of relying on raw degree.

Happy to provide the full graph.json that reproduces this, or test a branch.

title: export wiki/html prefer a stale .graphify_analysis.json over the fresh per-node partition in graph.json — the existing fallback is gated on presence, not agreement
body:
**Version:** graphify 0.9.22 · macOS · repo: ~8.4k code files, 59,748 nodes / 175,324 edges

## Summary

`graphify export wiki` and `graphify export html` take their community partition from `.graphify_analysis.json`. That file is written only by `extract` (`cli.py:3396`) and `cluster-only` / `label` (`cli.py:1668`) — **never by `update` / the watch rebuild path** (`grep graphify_analysis watch.py` → no matches).

So after any number of `graphify update` runs, `graph.json` and `GRAPH_REPORT.md` advance while the analysis sidecar stays frozen at the last full `extract`. The exports keep reading the fossil, and the only signal is a `dropped N stale node ID(s)` line that reads like housekeeping.

In our repo the sidecar was **9 days and one re-partitioning era** behind:

| | value |
|---|---|
| `graph.json` | 59,748 nodes · **2,359** communities |
| `GRAPH_REPORT.md` | 2,359 communities (agrees with graph.json) |
| `.graphify_analysis.json` | **6,243** communities · 111,726 node ids · 9 days old |
| `graph.html` emitted | `aggregated: 6243 community nodes` ← the fossil partition |
| wiki emitted | 1,940 articles, `dropped 56369 stale node ID(s)` |

**Measured impact: 4,394 of 59,748 nodes (7.4%) were in no community of the sidecar, so they got no wiki article and were absent from the aggregated HTML.** `wiki.py:244` intersects the sidecar's communities with the live graph — it only ever subtracts, so that set grows with every commit and never recovers.

Nothing warns. The report says 2,359 communities, the HTML says 6,243, and both are written by the same tool in the same session.

## The fix is already in the code — gated on presence instead of agreement

`cli.py:2192-2211` already reconstructs communities from `graph.json`'s per-node `community` attribute, and the comment names this exact bug:

```python
# Fallback: graph.json carries the per-node community as a node attribute
# (`to_json` writes it on every node). The analysis sidecar is the
# canonical source — but the post-commit / watch rebuild path doesn't
# regenerate it, ...
if not communities:          # <-- fires only when the sidecar is MISSING
    reconstructed = ...      #     a sidecar that EXISTS but is stale wins
```

That fallback appears to come from #746 (`update` + `export wiki` wipes `wiki/` when the sidecar is **missing**) and #1610 (`cluster-only` not persisting it → `export html` reports "Single community"). Both are the *absent* case. The *stale* case looks identical from the outside — degraded artifacts, no error — but takes the other branch: when the sidecar exists and is wrong, the fresh data sitting in `graph.json`, already loaded into `G` two lines above, is ignored.

### Suggested fixes

**A. Minimal, at `cli.py:2201`.** Both datasets are already in memory, so the comparison is free: reconstruct unconditionally and prefer it (or at least warn) when the sidecar's node-id set disagrees with the graph's. This also repairs every graph already on disk, without a re-cluster.

⚠️ One caveat if you take A: the fallback reconstructs `communities` only. `cohesion` and `gods` are read from the same sidecar at `cli.py:2185-2187`, and in the `else` branch they become `{}` / `[]`. `gods_data` self-heals (`cli.py:2259-2260` recomputes via `_god_nodes(G)`), but `cohesion` does not — it flows into `wiki.py:90`, which prints `cohesion N.NN` in each community article's metadata, and into the HTML export at `cli.py:2242`. So "reconstruct and prefer" would swap one silent degradation for a smaller one unless it also recomputes cohesion; `score_all(G, communities)` at `cli.py:1521` is the same call the normal path already makes.

**B. Root cause, at `watch.py:1235/1263`.** `watch` already computes `communities = cluster(G)` and writes them into `graph.json` via `to_json(...)`. Writing `.graphify_analysis.json` from those same communities costs nothing extra and keeps the sidecar canonical.

Repairing it externally with `cluster-only` is *not* a good workaround, for two reasons already tracked here: clustering is not reproducible run-to-run (#1667 — we measured 2,363 vs 2,362 communities over a byte-identical `graph.json`), and re-clustering churns curated labels (#2298, #1653). In our repair run, 51% of 2,359 curated labels were renamed by hub.

A cheap consistency check is possible even outside the process: `GRAPH_REPORT.md` states the community count and `.graphify_analysis.json` holds the partition, so a wrapper can detect the desync **without loading the 101 MB `graph.json`** (we now do exactly this in our refresh script). Inside graphify it is cheaper still — zero I/O, since `G` and `communities` are both already loaded at `cli.py:2201`.

### Workaround, for anyone hitting this

Deleting `.graphify_analysis.json` and re-running the exports is enough to get a correct partition: it forces the `if not communities:` branch, so the partition is rebuilt from `graph.json`'s per-node attribute, labels are preserved and god-nodes are recomputed. The only loss is the cohesion metric in the wiki articles, until the next real `cluster-only` / `extract`.

Two things that are *not* obvious if you try to repair with `cluster-only` instead:

- The labels' `.sig` sidecar is also written only by `cluster-only` / `label`, so after a `watch` run the saved labels have no matching signature and every community is treated as changed and renamed by its hub.
- That degradation is invisible to a placeholder count: the no-LLM path renames by hub (`cli.py:1595-1597`), never to `Community N`, so `placeholders == 0` throughout. Weighted by nodes rather than by community count, ~110 renames covered **37.9% of the graph** — re-clustering perturbs the largest communities most, so 8 of the top 10 lost their prose name.

title: fix(cluster): honor --resolution on the community split passes
body:
`_split_community()` calls `_partition()` without forwarding `resolution`, so it always re-partitions at the default `1.0`. `cluster(resolution=...)` (the `--resolution` flag added in 2d783e5) therefore applies to the top-level partition but is silently dropped by **both** split passes:

- the oversized-community split (`cluster.py:214`)
- the cohesion re-split (`cluster.py:223`)

So `graphify build --resolution 0.5` partitions the graph at 0.5, then re-partitions its largest communities at 1.0 — the opposite granularity to the one requested.

### Change

Thread `cluster()`'s `resolution` through to both call sites and give `_split_community()` a `resolution: float = 1.0` parameter.

Default behaviour is unchanged — the default is 1.0 either way, which is what the split passes were already hardcoding. Only runs that pass an explicit `--resolution` change.

### Tests

Two tests in `tests/test_cluster.py`, both verified to fail without the fix:

- `test_split_community_forwards_resolution_to_partition` — asserts the kwarg reaches `_partition`
- `test_cluster_forwards_resolution_to_split_passes` — end-to-end through `cluster()` on a graph that trips the oversized-split path

Full suite: 3904 passed, 36 skipped. Two failures on this branch are pre-existing on a clean `v8` checkout and unrelated (`test_ollama_retry_cap.py` needs the `openai` extra; `test_labeling.py::test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size` asserts a batch completion order).

title: feat(llm): Entra ID auth for the Azure OpenAI backend
body:
The `azure` backend can only authenticate with `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`. Azure OpenAI resources provisioned with `disableLocalAuth: true` **cannot issue an API key at all**, so graphify currently has no way to talk to them — and key-based auth is the posture Azure recommends against generally.

### Precedent

`bedrock` already works exactly this way: `detect_backend()` routes to it on `AWS_PROFILE`/`AWS_REGION` alone with no API key, and `_call_bedrock` picks up whatever the ambient AWS credential chain provides. This PR gives `azure` the equivalent.

### Usage

```bash
export AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT=https://my-resource.openai.azure.com/
export AZURE_OPENAI_AUTH_MODE=entra   # 'aad' also accepted
graphify extract ./docs --backend azure
```

No key. `DefaultAzureCredential` resolves environment vars → workload identity → managed identity → Azure CLI → Azure PowerShell → azd, so the same code path covers a laptop running `az login` and a container using a managed identity. Token refresh is handled by `get_bearer_token_provider`.

### Changes

- `_azure_uses_entra()` — explicit opt-in, so nothing changes implicitly
- `_azure_client()` — passes `azure_ad_token_provider` instead of `api_key`
- the no-key dispatch guard now exempts `azure` under Entra, as it already does `bedrock` and `claude-cli`
- `detect_backend()` — endpoint + auth mode counts as a complete credential
- new `[azure]` extra pinning `azure-identity` (the backend previously had no extra of its own and pointed users at bare `pip install openai`); the import is deferred, so the key path is unaffected when it is absent
- README env-var table + backends table

**Default behaviour is unchanged** — without `AZURE_OPENAI_AUTH_MODE` the backend takes the same key path as before.

### Tests

Seven tests in `tests/test_llm_backends.py`, built on the existing `_install_fake_azure_openai` stub plus a matching `azure.identity` stub, so nothing needs the real SDKs. Five fail without this change; the other two are regression guards for the key path. They cover: token provider wired with the correct scope, no `api_key` sent on the Entra path, the `aad` spelling, key path unchanged by default, detection with and without the endpoint, the dispatcher guard, and the missing-`azure-identity` error message.

Full suite: 3909 passed, 36 skipped. Two failures on this branch are pre-existing on a clean `v8` checkout and unrelated (`test_ollama_retry_cap.py` needs the `openai` extra; `test_labeling.py::test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size` asserts a batch completion order).

### Possible follow-up

Treating "endpoint set, no key, no auth mode" as implicit Entra would match `bedrock` even more closely, but it converts today's clear "No API key" error into a connection attempt, so I left it explicit. Happy to add it if you'd prefer.

title: docs(readme): document libpq env vars for --postgres connections
body:
`introspect_postgres()` passes its DSN straight to `psycopg.connect()` (`pg_introspect.py:22`), so any connection field the DSN omits falls back to the standard libpq environment variables — `PGPASSWORD`, `PGSSLMODE`, `PGSSLROOTCERT`, `~/.pgpass`, and the rest.

That is already how you make a password-free `--postgres` connection, and it is what makes token-based auth work on managed PostgreSQL — on Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, for instance, Entra ID auth works by putting a short-lived access token in `PGPASSWORD`:

```bash
export PGPASSWORD=$(az account get-access-token \
  --resource https://ossrdbms-aad.database.windows.net --query accessToken -o tsv)
graphify extract --postgres "postgresql://me@my-server.postgres.database.azure.com/mydb?sslmode=require"
```

None of that is documented — the only `--postgres` example in the README embeds a plaintext password in the DSN, which also puts the credential in shell history and `ps` output.

**Docs only, no code change.** Adds the `PG*` row to the environment-variable table and a password-free `--postgres` example alongside the existing one.

title: feat(r): extract R with tree-sitter and resolve calls corpus-wide
body:
## What

Adds R as an extracted language. `.r`/`.R` were already in `CODE_EXTENSIONS`, so R files were counted as code and then contributed nothing — R is the language the #1689 no-AST-extractor warning uses as its example, and that comment is updated here.

## Why it is bespoke rather than a `LanguageConfig`

R has no named-function syntax. Every definition is an assignment whose right-hand side is an anonymous `function_definition`:

```r
compute_moments <- function(x) { ... }
rescale = function(x) { ... }
report <- \(x) { ... }
(function(x) x^2) -> square_it
```

`function_definition`'s only `name` field is the `function` keyword itself, so the config-driven walker labels all of them `function`. Right-assign needs care: `function(x) x^2 -> nm` binds `nm` *inside* the body (R deparses it as `function(x) nm <- x^2`), so only the parenthesised form is a function binding. The extractor and its fixture both follow R here.

## Why calls resolve corpus-wide

Within a package or an analysis directory, R has one shared namespace and no import statement binding a name to a file. `paste0(x)` and a sibling file's `compute_moments(x)` are the same syntax, and nothing in the file distinguishes them — so a per-file extractor that emits both produces either a base-R god node or a flood of dangling edges.

`extractors/r.py` therefore resolves only same-file callees (those are certain) and emits everything else as `raw_calls`. `r_resolution.resolve_r_calls`, registered through `resolver_registry`, links a callee only when the corpus defines it **exactly once** — the same god-node guard the Java and Objective-C resolvers use. Anything defined nowhere is base R or a third-party package and is dropped.

That keeps base R out of the graph with no hardcoded list of ~1,300 base names, and emits no dangling edges.

Sourced files resolve the same way. A bare `source("b.R")` becomes `imports`; an R path literal joined from string literals by a project helper — `source_once(paper_path("sub", "b.R"))`, the dominant shape in real analysis pipelines — becomes `references`. Both link only when the joined path matches exactly one corpus file, so a wrong separator guess cannot invent an edge.

## Also covered

`library`/`require`/`requireNamespace`/`loadNamespace` and `pkg::fn` imports, `obj$method()` calls, nested definitions scoped to their enclosing function, top-level statements attributed to the file node (most of an analysis script), and `Rscript` shebangs.

## Grammar dependency

The r-lib grammar has no standalone PyPI wheel, so it comes from `tree-sitter-language-pack` (~2 MB platform wheel) under a new optional `[r]` extra, hard-failing like `tree-sitter-sql` rather than falling back. `get_language()` returns a ready `Language`, unlike the per-grammar modules whose `language()` returns a raw pointer — noted in the code since it is an easy mis-port.

## Measured

On a 541-file R corpus (an R package plus a 400-file analysis pipeline): **2,171 nodes, 7,434 edges, 0 dangling, 2.2 s.** Relations: 4,312 `calls`, 1,393 `defines`, 927 `references`, 802 `imports`. Highest-degree targets are all real project functions — no base-R hub. Of 30,804 cross-file call sites, 6,466 resolve, 24,127 are dropped as undefined (base R, `test_that`, package calls), and 211 (0.7%) are dropped as ambiguous across 25 names.

## Tests

`tests/test_r.py` — 14 tests covering every binding form, nested definitions, same-file calls, the absence of base-R nodes, imports, the no-dangling-edges invariant, and the four resolver paths (cross-file call, ambiguity guard, sourced file, wrapper-joined path, out-of-corpus path).

Two tests in `tests/test_extract.py` used `.r` as their example of a code extension with **no** extractor. They move to `.ets`, which is now one of the two that remain (`.ejs`, `.ets`). The subjects of those tests (#1689's warning and #1693's progress denominator) are unchanged.

Full suite: same 15 failures as the base commit `00efd6e` (11 `test_skillgen`, 4 `test_ollama_retry_cap` — all pre-existing and unrelated), 3,906 passed.

`.Rmd` and `.Rd` are deliberately out of scope — they are in no extension set today, and each is a different format.

title: feat(r): extract roxygen cross-references and S3 dispatch
body:
> **Stacked on #2393** (R language support). That PR is the first commit here; review/merge it first, and this diff reduces to the single `feat(r): extract roxygen cross-references and S3 dispatch` commit.

## Roxygen

Roxygen lives in `#'` comments, so the AST cannot see it — tree-sitter reports a block as a run of `comment` nodes with no link to the binding below. The tags carry relationships nothing else in R does:

- **`@seealso` / `@inheritParams`** name functions the documented one never calls, which is exactly what a call graph structurally cannot find.
- **`@template`** names a file under `man-roxygen/` that nothing sources — roxygen splices it at document time — so those files were corpus orphans.
- **`@export`** is the only thing separating the public API from an internal helper; it is recorded on the node, as is `@family`.

Blocks are matched to code by line, because roxygen requires the block to sit directly above its object. Parsing is line-oriented for the same reason: it is how roxygen itself reads them.

## S3

S3 dispatch leaves no syntax behind. `print.hetid_moments` is a method only because `print` is a generic and `hetid_moments` is a class, and **neither fact is in the file that defines the method**. So the extractor emits every dot position as a candidate generic/class split and `r_resolution` keeps only what the corpus evidences:

1. a `UseMethod` generic of that name — the definitive marker, preferred; or
2. a site assigning that class (`structure(..., class = "x")`, `class(x) <- "x"`).

Neither present ⇒ nothing emitted, so `is.null`, `as.matrix` and `compute.stuff` fabricate no method edges. A class is often re-attached after a transformation, leaving several sites that assign it; R's `new_<class>` constructor convention breaks that tie.

## The bug this surfaced

The shared cross-file pass turns **any** raw_call carrying a `callee` into a `calls` edge by name. A `@seealso` record therefore shipped as a phantom `calls` edge *and* then blocked the real `references` edge as a duplicate — the same trap Ruby's mixin markers hit in #1668, which that code comments on directly.

Fixed by naming the field `ref_name` on non-call records, so they are invisible to that pass (`if not callee: continue`) and only `r_resolution` reads them. No shared code changed. On a 550-file R corpus this moved **18 edges out of `calls` and into `references`**, where they belong. A test pins it.

## Measured

Same 550-file R corpus (an R package plus a 400-file analysis pipeline):

| | |
|---|---|
| `@template` edges | 74 |
| `@seealso` / `@inheritParams` edges | 18 |
| S3 method edges | 2 |
| functions marked `exported` | 35 |
| dangling edges | 0 |

Worth stating plainly: on this corpus every `@seealso` target is a function the documenting function *already calls*, so those 18 are reclassifications rather than new pairs. The value shows up on codebases where `@seealso` points somewhere the call graph does not reach.

## Tests

Nine added to `tests/test_r.py` (23 total): every binding form still passes, plus `@export` marking, `@family`, seealso/template emission, cross-file `@seealso` resolution, `@template` → `man-roxygen/` resolution, S3 via class constructor, S3 preferring a `UseMethod` generic, an ordinary dotted name producing nothing, and the no-`callee`-on-non-call-records invariant.

Full suite: same 15 failures as base commit `00efd6e` (11 `test_skillgen`, 4 `test_ollama_retry_cap` — pre-existing, unrelated), 3,915 passed.

title: load_cached() silently swallows corrupt cache entries (55% of a real-world cache was dead, no diagnostics)
body:
While auditing a knowledge graph built from a personal Markdown vault (~230 files, Windows 11), I found that 138 of 249 entries in `graphify-out/cache/` were invalid JSON. Every incremental run had been re-extracting more than half the corpus, paying that LLM work again each time, and nothing in the output suggested it.

The cause is in `graphify/cache.py`:

```python
try:
    result = json.loads(entry.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError):
    return None
```

`load_cached()` treats a corrupt entry exactly like a missing one, so the corruption never surfaces and the file stays in place, failing again on every future run. I checked the current `v8` HEAD and the behavior is still there.

How my entries got corrupted is a separate story: they came from an old install (graphifyy 0.3.4) that wrote Windows paths with unescaped backslashes into `source_file` (`"C:\Users\..."`). That producer side looks covered by #2380 and #2197. This issue is only about the consumer side: whatever the origin, corrupt entries deserve a signal.

Repro on HEAD: drop any invalid-JSON file into `graphify-out/cache/` and run an incremental update. The entry is re-extracted, nothing is logged, and the file remains for the next run.

Two small changes would cover it:

1. Count decode failures in `load_cached()` / `check_semantic_cache()` and print one warning per run, e.g. `warning: 138 corrupt cache entries ignored (will re-extract)`.
2. Optionally rename bad entries to `.corrupt` so they stop being re-parsed every run.

Happy to send a PR for either if that helps.

Environment: Windows 11, Python 3.14; corruption produced under graphifyy 0.3.4; silent behavior verified in `v8` HEAD `graphify/cache.py`.

title: Incremental update loses cross-file edges from changed→unchanged files (batch-scoped import resolution + replace-on-re-extract)
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.19 · Windows 11 · Python 3.14 · TS/TSX corpus (~540 code files)

## Symptom

After an incremental update (re-extracting only changed files, then `build_merge`), the graph silently loses every cross-file edge from a **changed** file to an **unchanged** file. In our repo a utility imported by ~every component (`v2/src/lib/cn.ts`, byte-identical `import { cn } from "@/lib/cn"` across files) dropped from ~100 edges to 4, and its neighborhood became a disconnected island. ~610 edges were lost in one update.

The failure signature is exact and makes the cause easy to confirm:

| edge | outcome |
|---|---|
| changed → changed (`case-detail.tsx → text.ts`) | survives |
| unchanged → unchanged (`Kbd.tsx → cn.ts`) | survives |
| **changed → unchanged** (`case-detail.tsx → cn.ts`) | **deleted** |

## Root cause

1. `extract()` resolves cross-file imports only against the batch it is given (`_augment_symbol_resolution_edges(paths, ...)`). When the update batch contains only changed files, imports of unchanged files resolve to nothing — those edges are simply never produced.
2. `build_merge`'s replace-on-re-extract then drops the changed file's **old** (complete) edge set and replaces it with the new (gutted) one.

Each behavior is individually reasonable; combined they guarantee edge loss on every incremental update of a codebase.

## Minimal repro

```python
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.extract import extract
from graphify.build import build_merge
# A.ts imports { b } from "./B"
r_full = extract([Path("A.ts"), Path("B.ts")], cache_root=None)   # A→B edge present
r_incr = extract([Path("A.ts")], cache_root=None)                 # A→B edge absent (B not in batch)
# build_merge([r_incr], graph_path=...) replaces A's edges → A→B edge deleted from graph.json
```

## Suggested fix

Since AST extraction is deterministic and cheap (~30 s for 500 files, no LLM), the update path could always run structural extraction over the **full corpus** and be incremental only for semantic (LLM) extraction. Alternatively, `_augment_symbol_resolution_edges` could resolve against the existing `graph.json` node index in addition to the batch.

## Secondary finding: dangling edges to never-created node ids

In a full, clean extraction of the same corpus, ~356 edge endpoints reference node ids that no node pass ever creates:

- **Barrel re-exports:** imports of `Button`/`Surface`/`Input` through `v2/src/design/primitives/index.ts` emit edges to e.g. `..._primitives_index_button`, but no such node exists (the components live in `Button.tsx` as `..._primitives_button_button`).
- **Wrapper consts:** re-exported consts like `const Dialog = DialogPrimitive.Root` get edges (`..._ui_dialog_dialog`) but no node.
- Some of these ids also carry an **absolute-path prefix** (`c_users_<user>_dev_<repo>_v2_src_...`) that escaped the relativization/id-remap pass, so they can't even be suffix-matched to real nodes.

Happy to provide the full dangling-id list or run diagnostics against a branch.

title: feat(extract): add dbt model .sql extractor for ref()/source() lineage
body:
## Summary

dbt models wrap SQL in Jinja (`{{ config(...) }}`, `{{ ref('model') }}`,
`{{ source('schema','table') }}`), so the existing `tree-sitter-sql`
extractor can't parse them — `ref()`/`source()` dependencies stay
invisible in the graph. This adds a dedicated extractor that parses
the Jinja AST directly (no rendering, no dbt project context needed)
and resolves `ref()` as `depends_on` edges and `source()` as
`reads_from` edges.

## Design

- **Detection is content-sniffed, not path-based.** `_get_extractor()`
  already content-sniffs ambiguous suffixes (e.g. `.h` for ObjC vs
  C++). Same precedent here: a `.sql` file routes to `extract_dbt_sql`
  if it contains any `{{`/`{%` in its first 4KB, otherwise falls
  through to the generic SQL extractor.
- **No dependency on dbt's manifest.json.** dbt already produces a
  `manifest.json` with a fully resolved DAG, but consuming it directly
  would mean tracking a schema that changes across dbt-core versions
  (the `manifest_schema_version` has bumped repeatedly, and fields like
  `depends_on`/`sources` aren't guaranteed stable), and dbt Fusion has
  moved to a Parquet manifest instead of JSON — a second format to
  support. It's also only produced by actually running `dbt parse` (or
  `compile`/`run`), which requires a working dbt environment: a
  `profiles.yml`, valid warehouse credentials, installed packages, and
  a successful connection. Parsing the `.sql` source directly needs
  none of that — just the file on disk.
- **File node label uses `path.stem`, not `path.name`**, and stub
  target nodes carry no `origin_file` — both are required for a model
  referenced by multiple callers, or one nested in a subdirectory, to
  resolve onto a single node instead of a dangling duplicate.

## extract.py changes

Two small additions to `_get_extractor()`/`extract()`, both required:

- A dispatch check routes a Jinja-templated `.sql` file to
  `extract_dbt_sql`; without it the new extractor is never reached
  through the normal `extract()` path.
- `.sql` can now hard-fail on two different missing deps
  (`tree-sitter-sql` or `jinja2`) depending on content.
  `_EXTRA_FOR_EXTENSION`'s existing flat per-extension lookup only
  knows one extra per extension, so without a separate
  `_EXTRA_FOR_MISSING_PACKAGE` check, a dbt model missing `jinja2`
  gets told to `pip install "graphifyy[sql]"` — the wrong extra,
  verified by reverting the check locally and reproducing the
  incorrect hint.

## Optional dependency

`pip install jinja2` (or `pip install 'graphifyy[dbt]'`). If not
installed, `extract_dbt_sql` returns `{"nodes": [], "edges": [],
"error": ...}` and the rest of the pipeline is unaffected.

title: Markdown [[wikilinks]] resolve sibling-only, dropping every cross-folder link in note-type vaults
body:
### Summary

`[[wikilinks]]` between Markdown docs are resolved **sibling-only**, so in a vault
that organizes notes into folders (Concepts/, Entities/, Guides/, Maps/ ...) every
cross-folder link is dropped from the graph. Obsidian resolves `[[name]]` against
the whole vault by filename, not relative to the linking note's directory.

On a real 499-file Obsidian vault this dropped **1,030 of 2,323 authored links (44%)**.

### Where

`graphify/extractors/markdown.py` → `_resolve_markdown_link()`:

```python
candidate = Path(target)
if not candidate.is_absolute():
    candidate = source_dir / candidate     # sibling-only
return Path(os.path.normpath(str(candidate)))
```

`add_link()` then existence-gates the `target_file` stamp:

```python
target_file = None
try:
    if resolved.is_file():
        target_file = str(resolved)
except OSError:
    pass
```

So when the sibling guess misses, no stamp is written, the #2169 remap pass has
nothing to canonicalize, and the edge keeps an absolute-path-derived id that
matches no node — `build_from_json` drops it. This is the same failure shape as
#2211 (fixed in v0.9.28 for the incremental case), but here the target is not in
the sibling directory at all, so the stamp is never produced in the first place.

### Reproduce

```
vault/
  Concepts/alpha.md      # contains: [[beta]]
  Entities/beta.md
```

```python
from graphify.extract import extract
res = extract([src, tgt], cache_root=root, root=root, parallel=False)
node_ids = {n["id"] for n in res["nodes"]}
refs = [e for e in res["edges"] if e["relation"] == "references"]
[e for e in refs if e["target"] in node_ids]     # -> []  (expected: 1 edge)
```

Observed target id: `..._entities_beta_md` built from the *sibling* guess
`Concepts/beta.md`, which does not exist.

### Measured impact (real vault, 499 notes, v0.9.32)

| | before | after fix | authored baseline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| valid `references` | 1,293 | 2,323 | 2,339 |
| recall | 55.3% | **99.3%** | 100% |
| graph edges | 7,623 | 8,470 | — |

The residual 16 are links to files that genuinely do not exist in the vault, and
correctly stay dangling.

### Why this matters beyond one vault

Note-type folders are the default layout for several popular Obsidian setups
(PARA, Zettelkasten with type folders, LYT/MOC). For those vaults the wikilinks
*are* the curated ground-truth relationships — the point raised in #295 — so
losing half of them silently makes the graph substantially sparser than what the
author already encoded, with no warning.

### Proposed fix

Keep sibling resolution first (it is correct for path-qualified links and cheap),
and add a corpus-level fallback for wikilinks only:

1. `markdown.py` — when the sibling guess missed *and* the link came from
   `_MD_WIKILINK_RE`, stamp the bare name (`wikilink_name`) on the edge.
   Path-qualified `[text](./other.md)` links never get the stamp, so relative-link
   semantics are unchanged.
2. `extract()` — in the existing post-pass (the first point that knows every
   in-root file), build a `stem -> [rel path]` index and repoint stamped edges.
   Ambiguity resolves deterministically: same folder as the linking note first
   (mirrors Obsidian), then shallowest path, then lexicographic.

The stamp is transient and popped in the same pass, so `graph.json` is unchanged
in shape. No public interface changes.

Happy to send a PR — I have the patch and tests ready (59 lines across the two
files, 4 new tests, full suite green against the same baseline as `v8` HEAD).

title: fix(markdown): resolve [[wikilinks]] vault-wide, not sibling-only
body:
Fixes #2413.

## Problem

`[[wikilinks]]` were resolved sibling-only. Obsidian resolves `[[name]]` against
the whole vault by filename, so in a vault organized by note type (`Concepts/`,
`Entities/`, `Guides/`, `Maps/`) every cross-folder link missed: no `target_file`
stamp was written, the #2169 remap pass had nothing to canonicalize, and
`build_from_json` dropped the edge.

Same failure shape as #2211 (fixed in v0.9.28 for the incremental case), but here
the target is not in the sibling directory at all, so the stamp is never produced
in the first place.

## Approach

Sibling resolution still runs first and still wins. Only a wikilink whose sibling
guess **missed** is stamped with its bare name; `extract()`'s post-pass — the
first point that knows every in-root file — builds a `stem -> [rel path]` index
and repoints those edges.

- **Path-qualified links are untouched.** `[text](./other.md)` is relative by
  spec, never gets the stamp, and never enters the new code path. Covered by a
  dedicated non-regression test.
- **Deterministic ambiguity resolution**: the linking note's own folder first
  (mirrors Obsidian), then shallowest path, then lexicographic.
- **Transient stamp**: `wikilink_name` is popped in the same pass, so `graph.json`
  shape is unchanged.
- **Broken links still dangle**: a `[[name]]` pointing at a file that exists
  nowhere behaves exactly as before.
- No public interface changes.

## Measured impact

Real Obsidian vault, 499 notes, against `v8` HEAD (0.9.32):

| | before | after | authored baseline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| valid `references` | 1,293 | **2,323** | 2,339 |
| recall | 55.3% | **99.3%** | 100% |
| graph edges | 7,623 | 8,470 | — |

The residual 16 are links to files that genuinely do not exist in the vault.

## Tests

4 new cases in `tests/test_languages.py`:

- `test_markdown_wikilink_stamps_name_when_sibling_missing` — stamp appears only
  for the non-sibling target; the sibling one resolves normally
- `test_markdown_path_qualified_link_is_not_stamped` — relative-link
  non-regression
- `test_extract_resolves_wikilinks_across_folders` — cross-folder link resolves,
  a genuinely missing target still dangles, no stamp leaks to the caller
- `test_extract_wikilink_prefers_same_folder_on_ambiguity` — same-stem tie-break

Full suite is green against the same baseline as `v8` HEAD: `3,891 passed` with
the identical 16 pre-existing `test_skillgen.py` failures present before and after
this change (they come from a shallow clone lacking the skill sources, unrelated
to this patch).

title: Post-merge phantom nodes are never healed: union merge-driver resurrects deleted symbols, and the scoped post-commit rebuild cannot prune them
body:
# Post-merge phantom nodes are never healed: union merge-driver resurrects deleted symbols, and the scoped post-commit rebuild cannot prune them

**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.30 (installed from the `v8` checkout) · macOS 15.6 (darwin 24.6) · Python 3.14.6

## Summary

The `graphify merge-driver` union-merges `graph.json`, which by design discards
deletions made on either side of a merge. That is a reasonable trade to avoid
conflict markers, and a full `graphify update .` does correctly clean the
resurrected nodes.

The problem is that **nothing in the installed hook set ever runs that full
update**. The post-commit hook rebuilds only the files listed in
`GRAPHIFY_CHANGED`, so a symbol resurrected by a merge inside a file that is not
touched again persists in `graph.json` indefinitely — long after the code is
gone. The graph reports it with an `EXTRACTED` confidence tag and a real
`file:line`, so there is no signal that it is stale.

This is distinct from #2406 (which is about *losing* real edges on the
incremental path). This one is the opposite direction: *retaining* nodes that no
longer exist.

## Reproduction

Minimal synthetic repo, all commands verbatim:

```bash
mkdir proj && cd proj && git init -q .
mkdir -p src
cat > src/util.py <<'EOF'
def helper_alpha():
    return 1

def helper_doomed():
    return helper_alpha()
EOF
cat > src/main.py <<'EOF'
from src.util import helper_alpha, helper_doomed

def run():
    return helper_alpha() + helper_doomed()
EOF
git add -A && git commit -qm base

graphify update .            # baseline: contains src_util_helper_doomed
cp graphify-out/graph.json ../graph_BASE.json

# branch deletes helper_doomed
git checkout -qb branch-a
cat > src/util.py <<'EOF'
def helper_alpha():
    return 1
EOF
cat > src/main.py <<'EOF'
from src.util import helper_alpha

def run():
    return helper_alpha()
EOF
git add -A && git commit -qm "delete helper_doomed"
graphify update .            # correctly pruned -> node is gone
cp graphify-out/graph.json ../graph_A_deleted.json

# simulate the merge git would perform on graph.json
cp ../graph_BASE.json ../graph_CURRENT.json
graphify merge-driver ../graph_BASE.json ../graph_CURRENT.json ../graph_A_deleted.json
```

**Step 1 — the merge resurrects the deleted node:**

```
$ python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('../graph_CURRENT.json'));
print([n['id'] for n in d['nodes'] if 'doomed' in n['id'].lower()])"
['src_util_helper_doomed']
```

**Step 2 — the *scoped* rebuild the post-commit hook performs does not clean it.**
Put the merged graph back, commit a change to an unrelated file, and run exactly
what `_REBUILD_BODY_COMMIT` runs:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.watch import _rebuild_code
_rebuild_code(Path('.'), changed_paths=[Path('src/unrelated.py')], force=False)
```

```
[graphify watch] Rebuilt: 8 nodes, 7 edges, 3 communities
helper_doomed still present: True      # <-- phantom survives
```

**Step 3 — only an unscoped rebuild heals it:**

```
$ graphify update .
[graphify watch] Rebuilt: 7 nodes, 7 edges, 2 communities
helper_doomed present: False           # <-- cleaned
```

## Expected vs actual

**Expected:** after a merge, the graph converges back to the code within a
commit or two of normal hook-driven activity.

**Actual:** it never converges. `src/util.py` is never in `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED`
again unless someone happens to edit it, so the phantom node is permanent for
practical purposes. It is indistinguishable from a real node in
`graphify explain` / `query` / `affected` output.

## Root cause

Three behaviours that are each individually reasonable compose into the bug:

1. `graphify/cli.py:2047` — the merge driver is `_nx.compose(G_cur, G_oth)`, a
   pure union. `%O` (the merge base) is accepted as an argument but never
   loaded, so there is no way to distinguish "deleted on one side" from "added
   on the other".
2. `graphify/hooks.py:110` and `graphify/hooks.py:141`
   (`_REBUILD_BODY_COMMIT`) — the post-commit hook reads `GRAPHIFY_CHANGED` and
   passes `changed_paths=changed` into `_rebuild_code`, scoping re-extraction to
   the commit's files.
3. `graphify/hooks.py:298-300` — the post-commit hook deliberately exits early
   during merge/rebase/cherry-pick states, so the merge itself never triggers a
   rebuild either.

The prune path (`_stale_graph_sources` / `_prune_graph_json_sources`) only drops
nodes whose `source_file` is gone or newly excluded. Here the file still exists;
only a symbol inside it was deleted. That is repaired by re-extraction replacing
the file's nodes — which the scoped rebuild never performs for that file.

## Suggested fix

Any one of these would close it:

1. **Install a `post-merge` hook** that runs an unscoped `_rebuild_code(root)`
   (no `changed_paths`). This is the smallest change and matches the existing
   `post-commit` / `post-checkout` pattern in `graphify/hooks.py`. `post-merge`
   fires after a successful merge, which is exactly when the union damage lands.
2. **Have the merge driver mark the graph dirty** — write a
   `graphify-out/.needs_full_rebuild` stamp when it runs, and have the next
   post-commit rebuild honour it by dropping `changed_paths` for that one run.
3. **Use `%O` in the merge driver** to compute a real three-way merge: a node
   present in base and in one side but absent from the other was *deleted*, not
   *added*, and should not be resurrected. Most correct, most work.

(1) and (2) are complementary and both cheap; (3) is the principled fix.

## Documentation gap

Independently of the code fix, `README.md`'s Team setup section says
`graphify hook install` "also sets up a git merge driver so `graph.json` is never
left with conflict markers — two devs committing in parallel get their graphs
union-merged automatically." That is accurate but reads as though the merge case
is fully handled. It would help to state that a merge inflates the graph and that
an unscoped `graphify update .` is needed afterwards, until the above is fixed.

title: explain silently caps connections at 20 and never points to affected, which returns the complete set
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.32 (pip), Windows 11, Python 3.12.9
**Graph:** 8,988 nodes / 21,571 edges, code-only corpus (JS/JSX + SQL), built with `graphify update .`

## Summary

`explain` prints at most 20 connections. The cap is hardcoded and no flag lifts it. That alone would be fine — the header does say `Connections (159)` and a `... and 139 more` line is printed — but in practice agents read the visible list as the answer and conclude "nothing else imports this". On a real service that is a 20-of-159 view.

The fix that already exists in the tool is `affected`, which has no cap and returns the complete set. Nothing in `--help`, the README, or the `explain` output points from one to the other, so it is only found by reading `cli.py`.

## Reproduction

```console
$ graphify explain "payroll.service.js" | grep -E "^Connections|and .* more"
Connections (159):
  ... and 139 more

$ graphify explain "payroll.service.js" | grep -cE "^  (-->|<--)"
20

$ graphify explain "payroll.service.js" --top-k-edges 200 | grep -cE "^  (-->|<--)"
20
```

`--top-k-edges` is accepted without error but changes nothing — it is parsed for `serve`/inspector (`cli.py:1995`), not for `explain`.

The `Grouped by file` section has the same cap:

```console
$ graphify explain "payroll.service.js" | grep -A25 "Grouped by file" | grep -c connection
20
```

Source, `cli.py:1394`:

```python
if connections:
    print(f"\nConnections ({len(connections)}):")
    connections.sort(key=lambda c: G.degree(c[1]), reverse=True)
    for direction, nb, edata in connections[:20]:
```

Note the sort key: `G.degree(neighbor)` — incoming and outgoing edges are pooled into one list and then cut. Because a busy service imports far more than imports it, the outgoing side dominates the surviving 20 and the incoming side is what gets dropped.

Concretely, `payroll.service.js` has 5 production consumers. Exactly one of them (`payroll-closure.service.js`) survives the cap; `payroll.controller.js`, `payslip.service.js`, `profitability.service.js` and `mobile.service.js` are all cut, while outgoing imports like `settings.service.js` and `leave-balances.service.js` are kept. For a "who depends on this" question that is the wrong half of the list.

## `affected` returns the complete set

```console
$ graphify affected "payroll.service.js" --relation imports_from --depth 1 | grep -c "^- "
21

$ grep -rlE "from ['\"].*payroll\.service" apps/api --include=*.js | wc -l
21
```

Exact match with grep — paths and line numbers included, no truncation.

## Why this bites agents specifically

The Claude Code hook installed by `graphify claude install` pushes `query` as the mandatory first step, and the read-guard text tells the model to propagate the rule to subagents. So the agent path is: hook fires → `query` or `explain` → agent reads 20 lines → answers. Nothing in that chain surfaces `affected`.

I hit this with a real subagent on a 56-consumer service. It ran `explain`, saw 20 entries, and under-reported dependants by roughly half. Only after being told about `affected` did it get the complete list. Same task, same graph — the difference was entirely which command it knew about.

## Suggestions (independent, any subset helps)

1. **Point at `affected` from the truncation line.** Cheapest fix, no behaviour change:
   `... and 139 more — run 'graphify affected "payroll.service.js" --relation imports_from --depth 1' for the full list`
2. **Honour a limit flag on `explain`** (`--limit N` / `--all`). `--top-k-edges` is currently accepted-but-ignored here, which reads as a bug on its own; either wire it up or reject it for this subcommand.
3. **Cap each direction separately.** Pooling in- and out-edges before `[:20]` lets the outgoing side crowd out the incoming one, which is the half that answers "who uses this". Something like 10 in / 10 out — or truncating per direction — would keep the visible slice representative.
4. **Mention `affected` in the agent-facing guidance** (`hook-guard` text / skill SKILL.md), since that is where the command choice actually gets made.

Happy to send a PR for (1) if the wording is agreed — it is a one-line change and would have saved this entire investigation.

## Related

- #2384 — query ranking; same underlying theme of agents getting a confidently-wrong subset

title: fix(cli): point explain truncation at affected for full blast-radius (#2420)
body:
Fixes #2420

## Problem

`graphify explain` prints at most 20 connections. On high-degree nodes the header correctly reports `Connections (N)` and `... and M more`, but nothing in that truncation line points at `affected`, which returns the **uncapped** reverse blast-radius.

Agents often read the visible 20 as the complete answer and under-report dependants. Issue suggestion **(1)** is the cheapest fix with no behavior change to the cap.

## Fix

Extend the truncation line only:

```text
... and 139 more — run 'graphify affected "payroll.service.js" --depth 1' for the full reverse blast-radius
```

- Cap remains 20; sort key unchanged
- No skillgen / hook-guard edits in this PR
- Suggestions (2)/(3)/(4) (`--limit`, per-direction caps, skill text) left for follow-ups

## Evidence

Synthetic 25-edge hub:

```text
Node: payroll.service.js
Connections (25):
  ...
  ... and 5 more — run 'graphify affected "payroll.service.js" --depth 1' for the full reverse blast-radius
  Grouped by file:
```

## Testing

- Added `test_explain_truncation_points_to_affected`
- Existing #2009 high-degree / grouping tests still pass
- `python -m tools.skillgen --check` → OK

## Notes

Intentionally small (suggestion 1 only) so it can be cherry-picked cleanly.
