title: On Windows, gemini and agents share one global skill path (~/.agents/skills/graphify), so installing or uninstalling either one clobbers the other
body:
## Summary

On Windows, `gemini`'s user-global skill destination is `~/.agents/skills/graphify/SKILL.md` — byte-identical to the `agents` platform's destination on every OS. Two platforms that install *different* skill files share one path, so installing one silently replaces the other, and uninstalling one deletes the other's install along with its `references/` and version stamp.

`graphify/install.py::_platform_skill_destination`:

```python
if platform_name == "gemini":
    if project:
        return (project_dir or Path(".")) / ".gemini" / "skills" / "graphify" / "SKILL.md"
    if platform.system() == "Windows":
        return Path.home() / ".agents" / "skills" / "graphify" / "SKILL.md"   # <-- line 74
    return Path.home() / ".gemini" / "skills" / "graphify" / "SKILL.md"

...

if platform_name == "agents":
    # The generic Agent-Skills target: project ./.agents/skills, global the
    # spec's user-global ~/.agents/skills (read by `npx skills` and compliant
    # frameworks), NOT amp's ~/.config/agents/skills.
    if project:
        return (project_dir or Path(".")) / ".agents" / "skills" / "graphify" / "SKILL.md"
    return Path.home() / ".agents" / "skills" / "graphify" / "SKILL.md"       # <-- line 108
```

They are not merely similar paths: the two install different content. `_copy_skill_file` special-cases gemini to ship `skill.md`, while `agents` ships its own `skill-agents.md` bundle:

```python
skill_file = "skill.md" if platform_name == "gemini" else _PLATFORM_CONFIG[platform_name]["skill_file"]
```

## Consequences on Windows

- `graphify install --platform gemini` then `--platform agents` (or the reverse) leaves one SKILL.md; the second install silently overwrites the first, and the shared `.graphify_version` stamp then describes whichever ran last.
- `graphify uninstall --platform gemini` removes `~/.agents/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`, its `references/`, and its stamp — i.e. the `agents` installation — and then `_remove_skill_file` walks the emptied parents away with `rmdir`.
- The reverse holds too: uninstalling `agents` removes the gemini user-global skill.

Neither command warns, and neither is scoped to the platform the user named.

This looks like the same class #2694 and #2777 are about (installs and version stamps leaking across platform boundaries), just reached through a shared destination rather than a shared stamp.

## Every gemini/agents install-scope test on Windows shows it

These are currently failing on `v8` @ `4fca621`, all for this one reason — the tests assert the POSIX layout (`~/.gemini/skills/graphify`) while the install lands in `~/.agents/`:

```
FAILED tests/test_install_references.py::test_gemini_install_references_all_resolve
FAILED tests/test_uninstall_scope.py::test_bare_call_still_removes_global[gemini]
FAILED tests/test_uninstall_scope.py::test_remove_user_skill_opt_in_with_project_dir[gemini]
```

with the install itself reporting the shared path:

```
  references       ->  ...\test_gemini_install_references0\.agents\skills\graphify\references
  skill installed  ->  ...\test_gemini_install_references0\.agents\skills\graphify\SKILL.md
graphify section written to ...\test_gemini_install_references0\GEMINI.md
```

The test job runs `ubuntu-latest` only, where line 74 is unreachable, so none of this is visible in CI.

## What I am unsure about

I could not find the rationale for line 74 in the history — it arrived with `cc2d3c1` (the `install.py` extraction) already in this form, and unlike the neighbouring hermes branch, which cites #1403 for using `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, it carries no comment or issue reference.

So I do not know which of these you intend:

1. **Gemini CLI on Windows really does read `~/.agents/skills`.** Then the destination is right and the collision is the bug: `_remove_skill_file` needs to not delete a directory another platform owns, and install should warn (or refuse) when the target already holds a different platform's skill. The three tests above are then also wrong to hardcode `.gemini` and should ask `_platform_skill_destination`.
2. **It is a leftover** and gemini should use `~/.gemini/skills/graphify` on Windows like everywhere else. Then the fix is deleting those two lines, and the tests are already correct.

Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer — say which and I will open it. I did not guess, because (1) and (2) produce opposite changes to the same tests, and picking wrong would bake the wrong layout into the suite.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| graphify | `v8` @ `4fca621` (0.9.44) |
| Python | 3.12, Windows 11 |

title: JS/TS/Python: distinct same-file symbols still collapse after ID normalization in v0.9.45
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.45 · macOS arm64 · Python 3.14.7
**Follow-up to:** #2779 / #2780 (Go, fixed) — same invariant, different extractors
**Related but distinct:** #2774 (Rust, bare-name trigger), #438 / #952 (cross-*file* id collision; this is within a single file, which `_disambiguate_colliding_node_ids` skips via its `len(source_keys) < 2` guard)

## Summary

#2780 correctly fixes the Go case it scoped itself to, and says so explicitly:

> Scope: Go extractor only. The same first-wins `add_node` pattern exists in the other extractors

This issue tracks that remaining scope. The same post-normalization same-file collision is
still live in the JS, TS and Python paths on v0.9.45: two distinct sibling declarations
normalize to one node id, `add_node` drops the second on `if nid in seen_ids: return`, and the
lost declaration's body edges are re-attributed to the survivor.

`ids.py` is byte-identical between v0.9.44 and v0.9.45, so nothing about the shared
normalization changed — which is expected given the PR's stated scope, and is why the other
languages are unaffected by the fix.

## v0.9.44 → v0.9.45

One file, two sibling declarations. "one node" means the second declaration produced no node
at all.

| language | source | v0.9.44 | v0.9.45 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Go** | `func Run()` + `func run()` | one node | **two nodes — FIXED by #2780** |
| JS | `class R { _onBegin(a){} onBegin(b){} }` | one node | one node |
| JS | `class W { #close(a){} close(b){} }` | one node | one node |
| TS | `declare class Q { $set(a); set(b); }` | one node | one node |
| JS | `function parseURL(a){}` + `function parseUrl(b){}` | one node | one node |
| Python | `def _run(a)` + `def run(b)` | one node | one node |
| Python | `def a_(p)` + `def a(q)` | one node | one node |
| *control* | `def alpha(p)` + `def beta(q)` | two nodes | two nodes |

The `parseURL` / `parseUrl` row is the direct one: that is the **same case-folding axis as
#2779**, and outside Go it still collapses on v0.9.45.

The others are separate axes of the same recipe — `normalize_id` casefolds, maps `[^\w]+` to
`_`, collapses repeated `_`, and strips leading/trailing `_`, so `_x`/`x`, `$x`/`x`, `#x`/`x`
and `x_`/`x` all land together too. (There is an NFKC axis as well; I worked through each stage
in detail in
[a comment on #2779](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/issues/2779#issuecomment-5308526393)
rather than repeat it here.)

## Confirmed on real files — v0.9.45

Each run through `extract()`, one file at a time, from `node_modules`:

| file | pair | result |
|---|---|---|
| happy-dom `websocket/WebSocket.js` | `#close` / `close` | `close` only — `#close` lost |
| happy-dom `xml-serializer/XMLSerializer.js` | `#serializeToString` / `serializeToString` | public only — private lost |
| happy-dom `nodes/html-form-element/HTMLFormElement.js` | `#submit` / `submit` | public only — private lost |
| mongoose `document.d.ts` | `$set` / `set` | `$set` only — `set` lost |
| playwright `lib/runner/index.js` | `_onBegin` / `onBegin` | `_onBegin` only — `onBegin` lost |

Which member survives is declaration order (first-wins), not visibility — the private half
survives in some files and the public half in others.

Two of these are worth separating out:

**`#close` is a private class method**, a distinct language-level member that can coexist with
`close` by design. That is not a naming convention an extractor could reasonably fold.

**The playwright row has a second ingredient** and should not be read as a pure normalization
collision. Its two methods live in *different* classes, but both owners are class expressions:

```js
var TeleReporterReceiver = class { … _onBegin() … }    // L104
var TerminalReporter     = class { … onBegin(suite) … } // L1113
```

JS `class_types` is `frozenset({"class_declaration"})` (the TS set adds only
`abstract_class_declaration` / `interface_declaration` / `enum_declaration` /
`type_alias_declaration`), so neither expression mints an owner node, and their methods fall
back to file-level ids instead of class-qualified ones. Normalization collision and lost
ownership qualifier compound there. The rename control still isolates the collision as the
trigger:

```
original                      nodes=408   _onBegin=1  onBegin=0
rename _onBegin -> _zzBegin   nodes=409   _zzBegin=1  onBegin=1
```

The public method reappears and the node count rises by exactly one, so this is not one of the
"methods not extracted" gaps (#2419 / #2110 / #2524).

## Impact

Four consequences of the same collision mechanism reproduce outside Go:

1. **The second declaration vanishes** — no node for it anywhere in the graph.
2. **Its body edges are misattributed** to the surviving sibling.
3. **`local_bound_names` is overwritten** for the shared id.
4. **A fabricated `indirect_call` follows from (3).** Minimal Python repro:

```python
# vendor.py
def helper(a):
    return a

# b.py
from vendor import helper

class B:
    def _run(self, helper, p):
        return p.submit(helper)

    def run(self, x, p):
        return p.submit(x)
```

```
_run alone            nodes=['._run()', 'helper()']   indirect_call: none
_run + run            nodes=['._run()', 'helper()']   indirect_call: ._run() -> helper()
```

The collision is required — delete `run` and the phantom goes away. `run`'s shadow set (`{x}`)
lands on the surviving `_run` entry, so `_run`'s own `helper` parameter stops shadowing and the
argument resolves by name to the imported `helper`.

## Constraints on a fix

Not proposing a patch — raising what any fix has to satisfy, since the two obvious shapes both
have a catch.

**Changing `normalize_id` has a wide blast radius.** Its module docstring sets out that the
recipe is shared by three producers (AST extractor, LLM subagents, graph builder) and that
divergence between them is a recurring bug class (#811, #550, #1033, #1104).

**Salting inside `add_node` is not sufficient on its own.** `add_node` returns `None` and the
caller owns the id, continuing to use its own copy afterwards — e.g. `engine.py` at the
function-def site:

```python
func_nid = _make_id(parent_class_nid, func_name)
add_node(func_nid, f".{func_name}()", line)
add_edge(parent_class_nid, func_nid, "method", line)
...
callable_def_nids.add(func_nid)
local_bound_names[func_nid] = _python_local_bound_names(node, source)
```

`add_edge`, `callable_def_nids`, `local_bound_names`, `function_bodies` and the per-language
tables all key off the caller's `func_nid`. A collision-aware registration layer near the
`seen_ids` check would have to **return** the resolved id and propagate it through all of them;
moving the node alone would leave every consumer pointing at the old id.

Doing this per-language, as #2780 did for Go, is a reasonable increment — but the JS, TS and
Python paths are the ones still open, and #2774 has the Rust flavor.

## Repro

```python
from graphify.extract import extract
from pathlib import Path
# src/a.js:  export class W { #close(a){ return a; } close(b){ return this.#close(b); } }
r = extract([Path('src/a.js')], cache_root=Path('.c'), parallel=False)
print([n['label'] for n in r['nodes']])   # ['a.js', 'W', '.#close()']  — no `close`
```

Happy to hand over the per-package candidate lists or the scanner I used to find these sites;
the claims above are limited to the five confirmed through `extract()`.

title: cluster() community-splitting pass is nondeterministic across PYTHONHASHSEED (_partition itself is not; edge-count loss appears fixed since 0.9.6)
body:
## Localised: `_partition` is deterministic, `cluster()` post-processing is not

Same graph object, graphifyy 0.9.42, 4 unpinned runs + 2 with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`:

```
_partition(G)   61 communities, identical partition hash in all 6 runs
cluster(G)      345 / 342 / 346 / 350 unpinned
                344 / 344 with PYTHONHASHSEED=0
```

`_partition`'s sorted node/edge construction and hardcoded `seed=42` work
correctly - it never varies, pinned or not. The variance is introduced
downstream, in `cluster()`'s community-splitting pass
(`_MAX_COMMUNITY_FRACTION` / `_MIN_SPLIT_SIZE` / `_COHESION_SPLIT_THRESHOLD` /
`_COHESION_SPLIT_MIN_SIZE`), which expands 61 communities to ~345 - about 85%
of the final structure - without inheriting `_partition`'s ordering
guarantees.

**Caveat on the numbers above:** measured on a synthetic 4,000-node /
9,000-edge fixture, on Linux / Python 3.11 - not the ORE corpus this issue
was originally opened against.

Re-ran the same `_partition`-vs-`cluster` comparison on our frozen ORE
extraction to check it holds there too (graphifyy 0.9.42, Windows, Python
3.12.4, same `.graphify_extract.json` as every measurement in this issue), 4
unpinned runs + 2 pinned:

```
_partition(G)   83 communities, identical hash all 6 runs (eaaaf43442be)
cluster(G)      230 / 230 / 231 / 229 unpinned
                231 / 231 with PYTHONHASHSEED=0
```

Same shape on a completely different, real-world input: `_partition` never
moves, `cluster()` does, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` fixes it. This localises the bug
inside `cluster()`'s splitting/re-splitting passes rather than in
`_partition`, `build_from_json`, or Leiden/Louvain itself.

**Suggested direction:** apply the same normalisation `_partition` already
does - iterate communities and their members in a sorted, deterministic
order when deciding what to split and how, in `_split_community` and the
cohesion-based second pass in `cluster()`.

**Correction to the hypothesis in the previous update:** the `json.dumps`
list-ordering theory is refuted - `G.edges()` yield order and edge
orientation were byte-stable across hash seeds, so the sort key passed into
`_partition` was never the variable. Posting as a correction rather than
editing the earlier text away.

---

## Update: edge loss looks fixed since 0.9.6; clustering nondeterminism remains on 0.9.42

Re-ran the same frozen-input repro below against **graphifyy 0.9.42** in a
clean venv (0.9.6 left untouched). On our real extraction input:

| | edges (3 unpinned runs) | communities (3 unpinned runs) | pinned (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`, 3 runs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0.9.6**  | 7513 / 7518 / 7519 (varies) | 212 / 208 / 210 (varies) | 7522 edges, 209 communities — identical all 3 |
| **0.9.42** | 7095 / 7095 / 7095 (**stable**) | 230 / 230 / 231 (varies) | 7095 edges, 231 communities — identical all 3 |

Edge count is no longer a source of nondeterminism in 0.9.42 on this input —
only the Louvain partition still is, and by a much narrower margin than 0.9.6
(1 community of drift here vs. up to 4). Retitled this issue to lead with the
clustering nondeterminism, since that's the part still open; the edge-loss
numbers below are kept for the record and to show the delta between
versions. `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` still fully fixes it on 0.9.42 (3/3 identical
runs) — required, not just historically.

**One correction to the original report below:** it claimed `cluster()` is
"deterministic on its own" without a test that actually isolates hash-seed
effects (the in-process check described doesn't - the seed is fixed for the
lifetime of a process either way, so running it multiple times in one process
proves nothing about hash-seed sensitivity specifically; sorry for the
imprecision). Looking at the source instead: `cluster.py`'s `_partition()`
already rebuilds the input into a `stable` graph with nodes and edges sorted
by `str()` / `json.dumps(attrs, sort_keys=True)` before calling Louvain with
a hardcoded `seed=42` - so given an identical `networkx.Graph` object, that
function should already be order-independent. If that's right, the residual
0.9.42 variance is more likely upstream of `_partition`: an edge attribute
holding a *list* (e.g. a relation-type list collapsed from a set somewhere in
`build_from_json`) would still sort inconsistently under
`json.dumps(..., sort_keys=True)`, since that only orders dict keys, not list
contents - which would perturb `_partition`'s edge sort order even though the
edge *set* is now stable. Haven't traced this to a specific line, but it
would explain why edges converged in 0.9.42 while communities didn't.

---

## Original report (graphifyy 0.9.6)

## Summary

Given byte-identical extraction input, `graphify.build.build_from_json()` followed by `graphify.cluster.cluster()` produces a different graph (edge count) and a different Louvain partition (community count and membership) on every process run, unless `PYTHONHASHSEED` is pinned. This makes any pipeline built on graphify's public API non-reproducible by default: two people building from the same commit get different community structure, and any downstream artifact keyed by community id (labels, anchors, reports) silently drifts.

## Environment

- graphifyy 0.9.6 (PyPI)
- Python 3.12.4, Windows
- networkx 3.6.1
- Reproduces with default `bufsize`/no other flags; not specific to our extraction pipeline (see minimal repro below, which calls only stock graphify functions on a frozen input file).

## Minimal reproduction

`extract.json` below is a `.graphify_extract.json` produced once by `graphify.extract.extract()` and then frozen to disk, so every run reads the exact same bytes as input — no re-extraction, no filesystem variance, no code from our project.

```python
import json
from graphify.build import build_from_json
from graphify.cluster import cluster

ex = json.load(open("extract.json", encoding="utf-8"))
G = build_from_json(ex, root="/path/to/repo", directed=False)
comm = cluster(G)
print(G.number_of_nodes(), G.number_of_edges(), len(comm))
```

Run three times **without** `PYTHONHASHSEED` set:

```
4047 nodes  7513 edges  212 communities
4047 nodes  7518 edges  208 communities
4047 nodes  7519 edges  210 communities
```

Run three times **with** `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`:

```
4047 nodes  7522 edges  209 communities   (identical all three times)
```

Node count is stable across all six runs (4047) — only edges and the resulting partition vary. The edge-count delta (7513–7519, up to 6 edges short relative to the pinned run) and the community-count delta (208–212) are both consistent with iteration over an unordered/hash-ordered collection (a `set` or `dict` keyed by node/edge identity strings) somewhere in edge construction or deduplication inside `build_from_json`, before the graph is handed to `cluster()`.

We separately confirmed `cluster()` is deterministic on its own: clustering one already-built, byte-identical `networkx.Graph` object in-process three times gave identical results each time. The drift enters earlier, while `build_from_json` is still constructing the graph.

## Impact

Any project that clusters a `build_from_json` graph and treats community ids or edge sets as stable — labelling, diffing, caching, reporting — gets silent drift instead of a reproducibility guarantee. We worked around it downstream by relaunching under `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` for any command that builds or clusters, but that's a workaround at the call site, not a fix — anyone calling these functions without knowing to pin the seed will hit this with no warning.

At full pipeline scale (90k nodes, our real corpus) the same pattern held: unpinned runs varied between 190,503 and roughly 190,550 edges with correspondingly different community counts; three pinned full builds were byte-identical.

## Suggested fix direction

Somewhere in the edge construction/dedup path of `build_from_json`, an unordered `set`/`dict` keyed by node-id strings appears to be iterated to decide edge order or dedup precedence. Sorting that iteration (or using an insertion-ordered structure keyed consistently) before building the edge list should make the output invariant to `PYTHONHASHSEED`, without needing every caller to pin it.

Happy to share the exact repro script and the frozen `.graphify_extract.json` input if useful.

title: JS/TS: block-scoped let/const bindings suppress genuine indirect_call edges outside their scope
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.45 · macOS arm64 · Python 3.14.7
**Related:** #2241 / #2517 / #2569 / #2606 — the same shadow set, but those were all cases of a binding *missing* from it. This is the opposite direction: bindings applied more widely than their real scope.

## Summary

`_js_local_bound_names` collects `let` / `const` bindings into one **function-wide** set, but
both are block-scoped in JS. A reference to a same-named module callable made *outside* the
block that binds the name has its genuine `indirect_call` edge suppressed.

Two shapes reach it, and they are the same defect in the same walk:

- a `const` / `let` declared inside any block (`if`, `try`, a bare `{}`)
- a `for...of` / `for...in` head, added in v0.9.42 for #2606

I am **not** proposing a patch. I prototyped the obvious change, but it was not safe; details in
[Why no patch](#why-no-patch) below.

## Repro — v0.9.45

Each case emits the edge when the inner binding is removed, so the binding is what suppresses it.

```js
// (1) block-scoped const, reference OUTSIDE the block
function k(x){ return x; }
export function run(flag, p){
  if (flag) { const k = 1; void k; }
  return p.submit(k);          // <- module `k`. Edge suppressed.
}

// (2) for-of, reference AFTER the loop
function k(x){ return x; }
export function run(p){ for (const k of [1]) void k; p.submit(k); }

// (3) reference from a closure that outlives the loop
function k(x){ return x; }
export function run(p){ for (const k of [1]) void k; return () => p.submit(k); }
```

| case | expected | v0.9.45 |
|---|---|---|
| (1) block-scoped `const`, ref outside the block | edge | **none** |
| (2) `for (const k of …)`, ref after the loop | edge | **none** |
| (2′) same with `let` | edge | **none** |
| (3) ref from a closure after the loop | edge | **none** |
| *control:* loop variable used **inside** the loop (#2606) | none | none ✓ |
| *control:* case (1) with the inner `const` deleted | edge | edge ✓ |

The last two rows matter: the #2606 behaviour this would interact with is correct and must stay
correct, and the control shows the inner binding is the trigger.

## Mechanism

`engine.py`, `_js_local_bound_names`. Its own docstring scopes the intent to function and class
boundaries:

> Nested function and class scopes are not descended into.

and `_JS_SCOPE_BOUNDARY` is exactly that — function and class node types, no block statement:

```python
_JS_SCOPE_BOUNDARY = frozenset({
    "function_declaration", "function_expression", "function", "arrow_function",
    "method_definition", "class_declaration", "class", "generator_function",
    "generator_function_declaration",
})
```

So `walk` descends through every block in the body and both branches feed the one function-wide
`bound` set:

```python
def walk(n) -> None:
    for c in n.children:
        if c.type in _JS_SCOPE_BOUNDARY:
            continue
        if c.type == "variable_declarator":
            ...                     # case (1): a `const` inside any block
        elif c.type == "for_in_statement":
            left = c.child_by_field_name("left")
            ...                     # cases (2)-(3), added for #2606
        walk(c)
```

That was accurate for `var` (function-scoped, hoisted) and has been over-broad for `let` /
`const` since ES6.

The repository already has the channel for a correctly-scoped binding — `extra_locals`, threaded
through `walk_calls` by #2241 and used by the `catch_clause` fold from #2517, which applies a
binding to its own subtree only. `var` heads would still belong in the function-wide set.

## Why no patch

I previously prototyped the obvious `extra_locals` routing, but it exposed other inaccuracies in
the shadow collector and was not safe. I have not revalidated that prototype on v0.9.45, so I am
not presenting its old measurements as evidence or proposing it here.

A correct fix has to preserve function-scoped `var`, keep suppressing a loop binding *inside* its
own loop (#2606), and not open a path for unrelated by-name references.

## Field frequency of the for-of arm on v0.9.45

Diffing `indirect_call` edge sets between v0.9.45 and v0.9.45 with the for-of hunk reverted
(one file differs), over 920 non-minified JS/TS files — minified bundles excluded because a
judgment about `j() -> b()` inside a one-line bundle is not worth much:

```
corpus                          files   without hunk   with hunk   suppressed
dfs-crawler/src                    51             31          31            0
mongoose                          295             68          47           21
handlebars                        106             56          56            0
puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth     54              7           7            0
eslint                            414            360         359            1
                                  920                                      22   (0 gained)
```

I classified all 22 with the parser — whether the reference site lies inside the body of a
for-in/of that binds that name — and got **22/22 CORRECT**, no regressions and nothing
unclassified.

Scope of that result: no out-of-loop suppression from the for-of arm appeared in this sample.
This A/B says nothing about ordinary block-scoped declarators — case (1) — because that
collector path is identical in both builds, so the diff cannot see it. I have no field
measurement for case (1).

So: reproducible in isolation, with the one arm I could A/B showing no field occurrences.
Filing anyway because the scoping rule is wrong independently of how often it is hit, and
because someone writing `for (const x of …)` or an `if`-block `const` followed by a same-named
module helper loses a real edge with no signal. Weight it accordingly.

## Note on the interaction with #2606

#2606 is still open and reports the opposite direction — a loop binding *not* shadowing inside
its own loop. The v0.9.42 hunk addresses that; this issue is the scope regression that hunk
introduced on the other side of the same collector.

Fixing this must not regress #2606 — a loop variable used *inside* its loop still has to shadow.
The control row above is that case, and any candidate fix should keep it. The distinction is
where the reference sits relative to the binding's real scope, which is what `extra_locals`
already expresses for `catch`.

title: normalize_id disagrees with its own caseless form when a combining mark casefolds into a base letter (U+0345), inserting a spurious separator
body:
## Summary

`tests/test_id_normalization_contract.py::test_property_normalize_id_agrees_with_its_own_caseless_form` asserts

```python
assert normalize_id(s) == normalize_id(s.casefold())
```

and it does not hold. A combining mark that casefolds into a **base letter** changes how the mark after it is treated, so the casefolded form gains a `_` separator the original does not have.

Found by the existing Hypothesis property test — it surfaced a new counterexample on an unrelated branch of mine, and reproduces on a clean `v8` @ `4fca621`.

## Reproduce

```python
from graphify.ids import normalize_id

s = "߫ͅİ"          # COMBINING GREEK YPOGEGRAMMENI + NKO mark + LATIN CAPITAL I WITH DOT ABOVE
normalize_id(s)              # 'ιi'
normalize_id(s.casefold())   # 'ι_i'      <-- extra separator
```

Hypothesis reports it as:

```
E   AssertionError: assert 'ιi' == 'ι_i'
E   Falsifying example: test_property_normalize_id_agrees_with_its_own_caseless_form(
E       s='߫ͅİ',
E   )
```

## It is a class, not one string

Brute-forcing all 2-to-4 character strings over just `{U+0345, U+07EB, U+0130, U+0307, i}` gives **96** mismatching inputs. Two of them:

```
codepoints ['0x345', '0x7eb', '0x130']  ->  'ιi'  vs  'ι_i'
codepoints ['0x345', '0x7eb', '0x69']   ->  'ιi'  vs  'ι_i'
```

The second is the smaller shape: the trailing `İ` is not required, an ordinary ASCII `i` triggers it too. So the trigger is the **leading pair** — U+0345 followed by a combining mark — rather than anything about the dotted capital I.

U+0345 is the interesting one: it is categorised as a combining mark but casefolds to `ι`, a base letter. Before casefolding, the NKO mark that follows it is a mark trailing a mark; afterwards it is a mark trailing a letter, and the normaliser evidently treats those two situations differently.

## Why it matters

`normalize_id` decides node identity, so anything that makes it disagree with its own caseless form is in the same family as the case-only collisions in #2779 / #2810 — two spellings of one symbol either collapsing when they should not, or failing to collapse when they should. The blast radius is small in practice (it needs U+0345 or a similar mark in an identifier), but the property test exists precisely because identity bugs here are expensive and quiet.

The test is currently a latent failure: it passes on most runs and fails once Hypothesis wanders into this corner, at which point it is cached in `.hypothesis/` and fails every run on that machine. That makes it look like a regression from whatever branch happened to be checked out — it cost me a detour on an unrelated PR before I confirmed it reproduces on a clean tree.

## Not a regression

Verified by stashing all working-tree changes and replaying the stored example on `v8` @ `4fca621`: identical failure. `ids.py` is untouched by anything I have open.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| graphify | `v8` @ `4fca621` (0.9.44) |
| Python | 3.12, Windows 11 |
| Found via | the repo's own `test_property_normalize_id_agrees_with_its_own_caseless_form` |

title: fix: render rationale in graph read surfaces
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2821.

Rationale is already persisted as a node attribute during semantic cleanup, but the existing read surfaces never rendered it. This made the rationale effectively write-only: query could identify the correct node, but the explanation for why that node was relevant was unavailable to the caller.

This PR adds opt-in rationale rendering to the CLI and MCP read surfaces.

## Changes

- Add `--rationale` to:
  - `graphify query`
  - `graphify explain`
- Add `include_rationale` to:
  - MCP `query_graph`
  - MCP `get_node`
- Render rationale inline as `WHY ...` for query/query_graph.
- Render rationale as a dedicated `Rationale:` field for get_node/explain.
- Add shared rationale sanitization and truncation.
- Cap query rationale at 512 characters per node.
- Cap detail rationale at 2048 characters.
- Include query rationale in the existing token budget.
- Preserve the existing output and behavior when rationale is not requested.

## Backward compatibility

Rationale is opt-in and defaults to disabled.

Existing CLI invocations and MCP callers that do not request rationale retain the existing output format.

## Tests

Added coverage for:

- rationale sanitization and whitespace handling
- rationale truncation
- query/query_graph rendering
- existing token-budget behavior
- `get_node` and `explain` rendering
- CLI `--rationale`
- MCP `include_rationale`
- missing/empty rationale
- backward compatibility when `include_rationale` is omitted

Focused test suites:

- **237 passed**

The full suite also passes all tests relevant to this change; the remaining failures are pre-existing Windows/POSIX-specific tests unrelated to this PR.

title: feat(extract): recognize .zsh and add SAS (.sas) extraction
body:
## Summary

`.zsh` scripts are now recognized as shell code and routed through the existing Bash AST extractor, so zsh files contribute functions, calls, and source edges instead of being silently skipped. `.sas` files get first-class structural extraction: `data`/`proc` steps and `%macro` definitions become nodes, and `%macro` call sites resolve to their definitions — including macros invoked inside steps and case-variant names, which SAS treats as equivalent.

SAS extraction is deterministic and local (tree-sitter, no LLM), matching the pattern used by the other niche-language extractors. It ships behind a `sas` optional extra so default installs are unaffected.

Fixes #2825, Fixes #2681.

## Validation

- 4,637 tests pass (full suite minus pre-existing `test_skillgen` failures that require full git history unavailable in a shallow clone).
- New coverage: `.zsh` classification + dispatch + extraction; `.sas` classification + dispatch, step/macro nodes, defines and calls edges, multi-step files, same-line steps, case-insensitive macro resolution, duplicate-macro dedup, and the missing-dependency error path.
- `ruff` and `pyright` clean on all changed files.
- Node/edge behavior verified against the real `tree-sitter-sas` 0.4.2 grammar, including the nested in-step macro call case.

title: Question: is there a path on which the JS/TS import gate (`extract.py:6514`) does not apply?
body:
## What was observed

On a TypeScript corpus extracted with graphifyy **0.9.45** — cold full extract, no cache, `graphify extract . --code-only`, pure AST path — the graph contained 6 edges tagged `INFERRED`. Five of the six shared one shape:

- an unresolved short identifier bound cross-file to a same-named symbol,
- with no import statement between the two files,
- and in 3 of those 5 the target was a non-callable string constant.

I am not asserting a defect. I could not reproduce this on 0.9.46, and both halves of the shape appear to be already fixed. This is a mapped negative result and one question.

## Could not reproduce on 0.9.46

`repro/fileA.ts`:

```ts
export const B = "some-string";

export function makeLabel(suffix: string): string {
  return B + "-" + suffix;
}
```

`repro/fileB.ts`:

```ts
export function run(value: string): string {
  return B(value);
}
```

`B` is called in `fileB.ts`, defined nowhere in it, imported nowhere in it.

```bash
graphify extract ./repro --code-only
```

Result: 5 nodes, 3 edges — all `EXTRACTED`, all `contains`. No `calls` or `indirect_call` edge from `fileb_run` to `filea_b`. The target node exists and carries no `_callable` marker, while `filea_makelabel` and `fileb_run` both carry `"_callable": true`.

Variants tried, all negative:

1. Non-exported `const B` — produces no node at all, so there is no candidate to bind to; exporting it is what puts a target in the graph.
2. Target is a real exported function called cross-file with no import — still no edge, so the absence is not specific to non-callable targets.
3. Call outside return position (`const out = B(value);`).
4. Lowercase and multi-letter identifiers, ruling out a single-uppercase-letter heuristic.
5. Identifier referenced by name rather than called (`sink.add(B)`), exercising the `indirect_call` path.
6. Multi-file layout: three single-letter string constants exported from one file, called without import from a second file that carries a real decoy import from a third. 11 nodes, 10 edges, zero `INFERRED`; the only cross-file edge is the genuinely imported call, promoted to `EXTRACTED`/1.0.
7. C, Ruby, Rust, Python — in each, scalar constants do not become nodes, so no candidate exists and the case does not arise.

Reproduction environment: graphifyy 0.9.46 via `uv tool install`, macOS, Python 3.13, source read at branch `v8` @ `558df6d`.

## Both halves appear already fixed

- [#1659](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/issues/1659) — JS/TS cross-file calls gated on import evidence. Landed in **0.9.7**.
- [#2241](https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/issues/2241) — false `indirect_call` at INFERRED/0.8 binding to an unrelated single-letter helper. Fixed in **0.9.29**.

Both predate 0.9.45, which is what makes the observation puzzling rather than actionable.

## Resolver map

Live cross-file raw-call pass, inside `extract()`:

| What | Location |
|---|---|
| Raw-call loop | `extract.py:6346` |
| Candidate lookup by bare callee label | `extract.py:6380` onward |
| Ambiguous-candidate tie-breakers | `extract.py:6440`–`6476` |
| `callable_nids` / `class_nids` construction | `extract.py:6265` / `6269` |
| Import-evidence index (`imports` / `imports_from`) | `extract.py:6288`–`6296` |
| Per-call import sets, `_has_import_evidence()` | `extract.py:6427`–`6428`, `6430` |
| `indirect_call` emission (callable-gated) | `extract.py:6488`–`6500` |
| JS/TS no-import gate | `extract.py:6514` |
| Direct `calls` emission | `extract.py:6516`–`6537` |

The gate:

```python
if not has_import_evidence and str(rc.get("source_file", "")).endswith(_JS_TS_CALL_SUFFIXES):
    continue
```

The caller's import list is available at bind time via `imported_symbols` / `imported_modules`. Both raw-call emitters in `extractors/engine.py` (lines 4662 and 5223) always populate `source_file`, so the `endswith` check does not appear to fail open. Existing no-import coverage: `tests/test_phantom_cross_package_call.py:36/46/59/80` and `tests/test_extract.py:1124`.

For reference when reading edge scores: `0.8` is a hard-coded literal at both no-import emitters (`extract.py:6497` and `6526`), while `0.5` is the `INFERRED` default backfilled by `_CONFIDENCE_SCORE_DEFAULTS` in `export.py:160` for edges carrying no explicit score — so those two values come from different producers rather than from one scale.

## The question

Is there a path on which the gate at `extract.py:6514` does not apply, or on which a JS/TS cross-file call is emitted without passing through it?

One candidate I could not test: the incremental path noted at `extract.py:6265` (#2438), where `callable_nids` is built by reading the `_callable` marker from persisted nodes rather than from a fresh parse. The observed run was a cold full extract with no cache, so that path was not exercised there and I have not exercised it here either.

`symbol_resolution.py:307` (`resolve_cross_file_raw_calls`) emits INFERRED/0.8, takes no import information, and gates its label index on `file_type == "code"` rather than `_callable` — but `git log -S` finds no commit wiring it into `extract.py`, and `tests/test_symbol_resolution.py` is its only caller, so it does not appear to be reachable in a real run.

Happy to run further fixtures against any shape that would be useful.

title: No detection of a stale or partially-built graphify-out/ for git-tracked corpora
body:
**Summary**

The skill's only existing-graph check (top of `SKILL.md`) is "does `graphify-out/graph.json` exist," used to decide whether to take the query-only fast path. For a git-tracked corpus, this has two blind spots:

1. **Staleness**: `graph.json` carries a `built_at_commit` field, but nothing compares it against the corpus's current `HEAD` before trusting an existing graph (fast path) or before starting a fresh build. A graph built at an old commit can be materially wrong — missing entire subsystems added since — while still passing every other health check.
2. **Interrupted runs**: if a prior invocation reached Step 4 (graph built, report generated) but stopped before Step 5/6/9 (labeling, HTML export, cleanup), the `graphify-out/` directory is left with orphaned `.graphify_chunk_*.json` / `.graphify_extract.json` / etc. temp files and a report full of generic `Community N` labels. Nothing in the skill detects or surfaces this state; a subsequent run (or a human) has to notice by inspection.

**What happened**

I found exactly this: an existing `graphify-out/` with a fully-formed `graph.json` and `GRAPH_REPORT.md`, generic community labels, no HTML, and five leftover `.graphify_*.json` temp files. `built_at_commit` pointed to a commit from before a significant amount of subsequently-merged work — the existing graph was silently missing an entire subsystem. Diagnosing this took several manual steps (checking `built_at_commit` against `git log`, checking for an active writer process via `lsof`/`ps`, inspecting the detect.json file-type breakdown) that the skill gave no guidance for.

I chose to discard the existing state and rebuild fresh in an isolated worktree rather than trust or resume it, given the ambiguity.

**Proposed fix**

- At the top of `SKILL.md`, before the fast-path check: if the corpus root is a git repository, compare `graph.json`'s `built_at_commit` against `git rev-parse HEAD` (or the working tree's dirty state). If they differ, do not silently take the fast path — surface the staleness and suggest `--update` or a rebuild.
- If `graphify-out/` contains leftover `.graphify_chunk_*.json` / `.graphify_extract.json` / `.graphify_ast.json` / `.graphify_semantic.json` / `.graphify_analysis.json` at the *start* of a new invocation (i.e. before this run created them), that's diagnostic of an interrupted prior run. Surface this explicitly rather than letting Step 1-3 silently overwrite or ignore them.
- This matters more than it might look: any workflow where multiple processes/sessions could plausibly invoke `/graphify` against a shared working directory (CI, multi-agent fleets, a team repo) will hit this.

title: Skill Part C never stamps _origin, so graphify update deletes the semantic layer of any doc without section numbers
body:
### Summary

After a semantic extraction via the skill's Part B/C (Agent-tool path, no API key), **the first `graphify update` deletes the entire semantic layer of any document whose extracted nodes carry a line-number `source_location`.** Measured on a 21-document run: **8 of 21 files lost, 133 nodes and 236 edges**, on a commit that touched only one of those files.

Version: graphify 0.9.46, `skill-windows.md` variant, Windows 11 / Python 3.10.

### Root cause

`build._is_ast_tier` decides a node's tier from `_origin` and **falls back to shape** when it is absent:

```python
def _is_ast_tier(item: dict) -> bool:
    o = item.get("_origin")
    if o is not None:
        return o == "ast"
    loc = item.get("source_location")
    return isinstance(loc, str) and bool(_AST_LOC_RE.match(loc))   # 'L<line>' -> AST
```

**`SKILL.md` Part C merges AST + semantic and never sets `_origin` on the semantic side.** So a semantic node's tier is decided by what its `source_location` happens to look like, which in turn is decided by whether the source document uses section numbers:

| document style | agent writes | `_is_ast_tier` | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| has section marks | `"§4"`, `"§5.2"` | False | recognised as semantic, preserved |
| no sections | `"L8-L12"`, `"L170-179"` | **True** | **treated as an AST heading node** |

In `watch._rebuild_code`, a file with no surviving semantic-tier node never enters `semantic_doc_identities`, so the #1915 guard does not apply to it, it is AST-quick-scanned, and its semantic nodes are evicted as AST-tier output of a re-extracted source.

Measured on our corpus: **135 of 409 semantic nodes** are misread by the shape fallback.

### Why nothing catches it

Three independent safety nets are all inapplicable on this exact path:

1. `_rebuild_code` calls `to_json(..., force=True)`, so the #479 shrink guard **cannot** refuse the smaller graph.
2. `graphify update` never consults `cache/semantic/`, so nothing re-derives the dropped nodes even though they are still on disk.
3. The manifest still reports the files as semantically extracted, so `detect_incremental` will not re-queue them either.

Net effect: nodes gone, cache intact, every surface green. It is only visible by counting `_origin: "semantic"` nodes **per file** — a corpus-wide total still looks healthy.

### Reproduce

1. Semantic-extract two markdown docs via the skill's Part B: one using section-numbered headings, one using none.
2. Complete Part C and Step 4 as written.
3. `graphify update .`
4. Count `_origin`-less nodes per source file. The unsectioned document's semantic nodes are gone; the sectioned one's survive.

### Fix

One line each in `SKILL.md` Part C:

```python
for n in sem['nodes']:
    n['_origin'] = 'semantic'          # add
    ...
for e in sem['edges']:                 # add
    e['_origin'] = 'semantic'
```

`_is_ast_tier` then short-circuits on the marker and never reaches the shape fallback. Verified across four subsequent commits: 21/21 files retained their layer, 385 nodes and 571 edges unchanged.

A defence-in-depth option worth considering separately: have `build_from_json` stamp tier at build time rather than relying on every producer to do it, since the shape fallback is load-bearing for legacy graphs and will keep catching new producers.

title: Python: no receiver-type inference for self.<attr>.<method>() — 33 live methods reported as dead code
body:
### Summary

Python has no receiver-type inference, so `self.<attr>.<method>()` calls produce no `calls` edge.
The practical effect is not just missing edges — it is **confidently wrong dead-code answers**:
on a 104-file / 23k-LOC Python repo, `graphify explain` reported **33 methods as having zero
callers when they demonstrably have callers**.

Every other receiver language already has this. Python is the gap:

| helper in `graphify/extractors/engine.py` | status |
|---|---|
| `_java_method_receiver_types` | present |
| `_csharp_method_receiver_types` | present |
| `_ts_receiver_type_table` | present |
| `_swift_receiver_name` | present |
| `_python_method_receiver_types` | **missing** |

I understand why: Java/C#/TS declare field types and Python does not. But in idiomatic Python the
binding is still recoverable from the constructor.

### Reproduction

```python
class AgentRunner:
    def bull_researcher(self, idea): ...

class Workflows:
    def __init__(self):
        self.agents = AgentRunner()          # <- the type is stated right here

    def deep_portfolio_review(self):
        return self.agents.bull_researcher(idea)   # <- no edge emitted
```

`graphify explain <AgentRunner.bull_researcher>` reports 0 incoming `calls` edges.

### Measured impact (graphify 0.9.46, `--code-only`, 114 files, 1848 nodes / 4647 edges)

- Recall on one representative method (`Workflows.deep_portfolio_review`): **11 of 19 real calls = 58%**.
  All 8 misses were attribute-mediated — and in that codebase they were every single agent invocation,
  i.e. the architecturally most important edges present.
- **33 methods reported as dead code that have callers**, including the entire public API surface of one
  class and the repository `add()` method at the centre of a production crash we were debugging.
- 36 methods had undercounted caller sets.
- 180 `self.X.y(...)` call sites in `src/` overall (70 distinct receivers).

Silent under-reporting is the dangerous failure mode here: the tool says "4 callers" with full
confidence when the answer is 12, and says "dead code" about live code.

### A working fix

I prototyped a ~200-line post-pass that builds an attr→class table per class from `self.x = C(...)`
assignments and PEP 526 `self.x: C` annotations, then re-walks method bodies and emits the missing
edges as INFERRED. Results on the same repo:

- recovered **61 edges**
- **61/61 precision** — every recovered edge verified twice: the call site exists at the reported
  line, and the target lands on the real `def`
- recall on the representative method **58% → 100%**
- **no over-correction** — a method that is genuinely dead still reports 0 callers
- only 2 unresolved receivers, both legitimately hard (a lazily-initialised attribute and a class constant)

Guarding on "only bind to class names that already exist as nodes" is what keeps precision at 100% —
it stops `self.rows = list()` from producing bogus bindings.

### Offer

Happy to port this into `_python_method_receiver_types` mirroring the Java/C# ones and send a PR
against `v8`, if that is a direction you want. Wanted to check before writing against a 5,772-line
`engine.py`. Also happy to just leave the analysis here if this is already on the roadmap.

title: docs: GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL is undocumented; claude-cli backend defaults to Opus for community naming
body:
## Summary

`GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL` is read by the claude-cli backend (`graphify/llm.py`, e.g. https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/blob/558df6d57d61cb6ef79c740ec7473c6d953d79a7/graphify/llm.py#L1546) but does not appear in the README's environment-variable list, nor in `graphify --help` for `label` / `cluster-only`. Since the backend defaults to **Opus** when the variable is unset, a user who follows the README and runs

```
graphify label . --backend=claude-cli
```

silently spends Opus quota on community naming — a job Haiku handles fine (I just named 97 communities of a 1.6k-node graph with `haiku`, results are good).

## Suggestion

1. Document `GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL` next to the other backend variables (`ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, `OPENAI_MODEL`, …), with a note that the default is Opus and that `haiku`/`sonnet` are usually enough for naming.
2. Mention it in the `--help` text of `label` / `cluster-only` (or make `--model` the documented way and print the effective model at the start of a labeling run so the cost surprise is visible).
3. Optional: consider defaulting the CLI backend to a cheaper model for labeling specifically, keeping Opus for the semantic extraction where it matters.

## Environment

graphifyy 0.9.46 (`uv tool install "graphifyy[terraform]"`), Windows 11, Claude Code CLI 2.1.229 on PATH.

title: detect_incremental reports live files as deleted when a file leaves the scan scope, and --update prunes them from the graph
body:
### Summary

`detect_incremental` derives its deleted set as "manifest key not in the scanned file set", while
`save_manifest` retains a manifest entry whenever "the file exists on disk". The two predicates
disagree. A file that leaves the scan scope — because `.graphifyignore` grew, for instance — but stays on
disk therefore satisfies the retain test and fails the deleted test, so it is reported deleted on every
subsequent run, permanently.

That set flows straight into `build_merge(prune_sources=...)`, so a completed `--update` evicts live
sources from the graph. The failure is silent and looks like a normal incremental.

### Mechanism

Two lines, in `graphify/detect.py` (0.8.33):

`save_manifest`, in the seed-from-existing block (`detect.py:1190-1205`) — retains on **existence**:

```python
for f, entry in existing.items():
    ...
    if Path(f).exists():
        manifest[f] = normalised
```

`detect_incremental` (`detect.py:1322`) — deletes on **scan membership**:

```python
current_files = {f for flist in full["files"].values() for f in flist}
deleted_files = [f for f in manifest if f not in current_files]
```

`detect()` honours `.graphifyignore` / `.gitignore` (`detect.py:707-711`), so scan membership can shrink
while the file is still on disk. Nothing ever removes the orphaned entry, because the only prune test is
existence.

The sink is `graphify/__main__.py:4183`:

```python
prune_sources=deleted_files or None,
```

and the same call appears in the `--update` skill flow
(`graphify/skills/*/references/update.md`, the `build_merge` step).

### Reproduction

1. Build a graph over a repo. The manifest now holds every scanned file.
2. Add a directory to `.graphifyignore` that the manifest already covers, and leave the files on disk.
3. Run the `--update` detect step.

`deleted_files` now holds every file under that prefix. Every one exists.

Observed on a repository where `.graphifyignore` gained three prefixes while their files stayed on disk.
The pre-run manifest held 3,808 entries; entries under the three newly-ignored prefixes numbered
620 + 612 + 6 = **1,238**, which is exactly the deleted count `--update` reported. After 1,220 of those
files were later deleted from disk, the count fell to **18** on its own, with no fix applied — which is
the mechanism confirming itself.

A useful diagnostic:

```python
from pathlib import Path
from graphify.detect import detect, load_manifest, _MANIFEST_PATH
cur = {f for v in detect(Path('.'))['files'].values() for f in v}
man = load_manifest(_MANIFEST_PATH, root=Path('.'))
d = [f for f in man if f not in cur]
print('deleted:', len(d), 'of which still on disk:', sum(1 for f in d if Path(f).exists()))
```

Any non-zero second number is a set of phantom deletions.

### Two things this is NOT

Both were proposed and both are wrong, so they may save you a wrong turn:

1. **Not a path-format mismatch between writers.** Every in-product `save_manifest` call passes `root=`
   (`watch.py:603/641/712`, `__main__.py:4152/4241`), so the on-disk manifest is uniformly relative, and
   `detect_incremental` re-anchors it on read at `detect.py:1268`. The key sets are format-compatible.
   The arithmetic also rules it out: zero key overlap would make **every** scanned file new, whereas the
   failing run reported 766 changed against a 3,808-entry manifest — 67 percent overlap.
2. **Not a missing relativize inside `detect_incremental`.** It already passes `root` to
   `load_manifest`.

### Suggested fix

Restrict the deleted set to entries whose file is actually gone:

```python
deleted_files = [
    f for f in manifest
    if f not in current_files and not Path(f).exists()
]
```

`prune_sources` exists to evict nodes for files that no longer exist. A file that exists but left the
scan scope has no nodes to evict, because the graph was never built from it.

Optionally, and separately: have `save_manifest` also drop entries outside the current scan scope, so the
manifest stops accumulating orphans. The reader change above is the safety half; that is the cleanup
half.

### Two lower-severity observations from the same investigation

1. **`--update`'s merge step calls `save_manifest(incremental['files'])` with no `root=`**
   (`graphify/skills/*/references/update.md`), so it writes the legacy absolute-keyed manifest while
   `watch.py` writes the relative form. It self-heals on the next `watch` run and it is **not** the cause
   of the bug above, but the two writers disagreeing on format is confusing to anyone debugging this
   area — it sent our first two analyses down the wrong path.
2. **The `to_json` node-count guard and `_check_shrink` both fired correctly** and are what prevented
   real damage here. Worth keeping. Neither sits inside `--update` itself, so a prune arriving through
   `build_merge` is not covered by them.

### Environment

- `graphifyy` 0.8.33, installed via `uv tool install`, Python 3.13.7
- Windows 11
- `.graphifyignore` present at the scan root

title: skill-windows.md declares name: graphify-windows while the installer places it in the graphify/ directory
body:
Hi! Small inconsistency in the bundled skill templates of `graphifyy` 0.8.22.

The package ships 14 variants of the skill file in `graphify/`: `skill.md`, `skill-windows.md`, `skill-codex.md`, `skill-opencode.md`, `skill-aider.md`, `skill-amp.md`, `skill-claw.md`, `skill-copilot.md`, `skill-devin.md`, `skill-droid.md`, `skill-kiro.md`, `skill-pi.md`, `skill-trae.md`, `skill-vscode.md`.

Thirteen of them declare `name: graphify` in the frontmatter. Only `skill-windows.md` declares `name: graphify-windows`.

Meanwhile `__main__.py` (`_PLATFORM_CONFIG["windows"]`, around lines 282-291) copies that file to `.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md` — the same directory name as every other variant:

```python
"windows": {
    "skill_file": "skill-windows.md",
    "skill_dst": Path(".claude") / "skills" / "graphify" / "SKILL.md",
    "claude_md": True,
},
```

So after `graphify install windows` the directory is `graphify` but the declared name is `graphify-windows`.

**Impact is mild but real:** the skill still resolves (agents key skills by directory name), yet the mismatch confuses readers and agents — we had an assistant session stall on whether `graphify-windows` was a separate command or just `graphify` run on Windows. There are no `graphify-linux` / `graphify-macos` variants, so the suffix does not distinguish platforms either — the variants differ by *agent*, not by OS.

**Suggested fix:** change line 2 of `skill-windows.md` to `name: graphify`, matching the other thirteen templates.

Thanks for the tool — the graph reports are genuinely useful.

title: [BUG] graph.json contains edges to undeclared nodes, so loaders materialise attribute-less phantom nodes (and merge-graphs fragments external modules per repo)
body:
### Summary

`graph.json` contains edges whose endpoints are not in the `nodes` array. Every consumer that builds a graph from the file, including networkx, materialises those endpoints as nodes with no attributes, so the node set the file declares and the node set the file produces disagree.

### Version

graphifyy 0.9.46, Python 3.13, `graphify update . --no-cluster`.

### Reproduction

Any Python source that imports from the standard library or an uninstalled package. Running against a small package (8 modules):

```python
import json, networkx as nx

g = json.load(open("graphify-out/graph.json"))
declared = {n["id"] for n in g["nodes"]}
G = nx.node_link_graph(g, edges="links")

print(len(g["nodes"]), G.number_of_nodes())
print(sorted(n for n in G.nodes if n not in declared))
```

### Actual

```
125 131
['dataclasses', 'mcp_server_fastmcp', 'pathlib', 'pyoxigraph', 're', 'typing']
```

Ten `imports` / `imports_from` edges point at module names that were never emitted as nodes. The file says 125 nodes; loading it yields 131.

This surfaces in graphify's own output too:

```
$ graphify explain "typing"
  Type:
  Community:
  Degree:    1
```

`Type` and `Community` are blank because there is no node record to read them from, and `graphify path` will route through these endpoints as though they were ordinary nodes.

### The cross-repo consequence

`merge-graphs` has to paper over this, and the way it does creates a second problem. Merging two repositories that both import `typing` and `pathlib`:

```
inputs: 5 + 6 nodes, 5 + 6 edges
merged: 15 nodes, 11 edges
```

The four extra nodes are the materialised endpoints, namespaced per repo:

```
id=repoA::typing    label=None  type=None
id=repoA::pathlib   label=None  type=None
id=repoB::typing    label=None  type=None
id=repoB::pathlib   label=None  type=None
```

So the same standard-library module becomes four distinct nodes across two repositories, and a merged graph cannot answer "which repos depend on `typing`", which is the question a cross-repo merge exists to answer. Namespacing is right for repo-local ids; these are not repo-local, they are external identifiers that happen to have arrived through a repo-local path.

### What I am not claiming

Not emitting nodes for external modules may well be deliberate, to keep the graph to code you own. If so, the issue is the edges rather than the missing nodes: an edge to a node that does not exist is not a neutral encoding of "this import goes outside the graph", because no consumer can distinguish it from a node the extractor forgot to write.

### Checked and clean, for what it is worth

Two things I expected to find and did not, both worth recording:

- **Builds are deterministic.** Two independent runs over the same tree produced identical node ids in identical order, identical edges in identical order, and identical top-level keys. The local-deterministic-parsing claim holds.
- **`merge-graphs` does not collide repo-local ids.** Two unrelated repositories that both contain `src/app/engine.py` produce the same bare id `src_app_engine`, and the merge correctly namespaces them to `repoA::` / `repoB::` while preserving `local_id` and `repo`. 7 nodes in, 7 nodes out, nothing silently unified.
- **`diagnose multigraph` works.** It found the same 8 same-endpoint edge pairs my own check did, including the `imports_from` / `re_exports` pairs on `__init__.py`.

title: test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size is flaky on v8 HEAD (order-dependent, full-suite only)
body:
## Summary
`tests/test_labeling.py::test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size`
fails intermittently when run as part of the full suite, but passes
consistently when run in isolation. Confirmed on a clean `v8` checkout with
no other changes applied.

## Version
v8 @ b14b52e (v0.9.47), Python 3.14.

## Reproduction

Isolated — passes every time:


uv run pytest tests/test_labeling.py::test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size -q

1 passed (repeated 6/6 runs)

Full suite — fails intermittently:

uv run pytest tests/ -q

FAILED tests/test_labeling.py::test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size
assert [100, 50, 100] == [100, 100, 50]

Reproduced this way twice on a clean tree (no local changes, verified via
`git stash` before each run).

## What the test asserts
The test dispatches 250 communities in batches of 100 and asserts the fake
LLM call receives them in submission order: `[100, 100, 50]`. Under the
full suite it sometimes observes `[100, 50, 100]` instead — same set of
batch sizes, different order.

## Suspected cause
Looks like `label_communities`'s batch dispatch doesn't guarantee
submission order is preserved on return — consistent with something like
`ThreadPoolExecutor` + `as_completed()` (completion order, not submission
order) rather than `executor.map()` (which preserves order). This would
only surface under contention, which lines up with it passing standalone
and failing under full-suite load.

Two possible fixes, not sure which is intended:
- `label_communities` switches to an order-preserving collection method, or
- the test sorts/normalizes `calls` before comparing, since exact dispatch
  order may not actually be a real invariant worth asserting

Haven't dug into `graphify/llm.py`'s batching implementation, so filing as
an observation rather than a proposed fix.

## Why filing this
CONTRIBUTING.md asks contributors to run the full suite and confirm it
passes before opening a PR. Flagging this since it currently blocks that
on a totally clean `v8` checkout, independent of any particular PR's
changes.

title: fix(#2873): stub-mint undeclared edge endpoints, prune manifest deps, fix merge repos-union clobbering
body:
Fixes #2873

## Summary

Two related problems from #2873, plus one bug found while fixing them.

### 1. Undeclared edge endpoints (the core report)
`graph.json` could contain edges pointing at node ids that were never
emitted — stdlib/third-party imports being the main case. Every consumer
that loads the file (networkx included) then materializes those endpoints
as attribute-less phantom nodes, so the declared node set and the produced
node set disagreed.

**Fix:** after every resolution/repoint/disambiguation pass runs, mint an
explicit, minimal stub node (`external: True`) for any edge endpoint still
not in the node set. This makes the "outside the graph" case *explicit*
instead of an implicit, per-consumer materialization.

Manifest/package-dependency edges (`depends_on`/`requires` relations, or
`pkg_*` ids) are excluded from stub-minting on purpose — the issue itself
noted that not emitting nodes for external packages may be deliberate, and
existing tests (`test_external_dependency_edge_pruned_not_orphaned`)
already encode prune-not-fabricate as the intended behavior for that case.
Kept it that way.

### 2. merge-graphs fragmenting external modules per repo
Since external stub nodes aren't repo-local, `merge-graphs` leaves them
unprefixed so `typing` unifies across repos instead of becoming
`repoA::typing` / `repoB::typing`.

While testing this, found a second bug: `nx.compose` merges shared-node
attributes with `dict.update`, so on a 3+ repo merge, each pass's `repos`
list on a shared external node overwrote the previous one instead of
unioning — only the last repo survived. `cli.py` now accumulates the
`repos` union itself and reattaches it after composing. Added
`test_merge_graphs_external_node_repos_union_not_clobbered` for this.

### 3. Stub-minting interaction with incremental rebuilds (found during testing)
Applying the stub-minting fix broke 4 previously-passing incremental
rebuild tests (cross-file `calls` edges to unchanged files silently
vanishing — surfacing as #2406/#2437/#2438 symptoms). Root cause: the
undeclared-endpoint check only looked at `all_nodes` (this run's freshly
extracted nodes), not at `resolution_context_nodes` — the read-only
persisted nodes from *unchanged* files that #2406's cross-file resolver
uses. So a real call target living in an unchanged file looked
"undeclared" during an incremental rebuild, got a stub minted over its
real id, and the real preserved node was reconciled away in favor of the
fabricated stub.

**Fix:** union `resolution_context_nodes` ids into the declared-id set
before deciding what's undeclared.

## Files changed
- `graphify/extract.py` — stub-minting, manifest-relation carve-out,
  `resolution_context_nodes` fix
- `graphify/build.py` — external items excluded from carry-forward-drop
  logic in the semantic/LLM merge path (defensive, same principle as the
  incremental fix above)
- `graphify/cli.py` — `repos` union fix for merge-graphs
- `tests/test_csharp_type_resolution.py` — assertions updated now that
  previously-`None` import targets resolve to real stub types
- `tests/test_merge_graphs_cli.py` — new coverage for the repos-union fix

## Test results
uv run pytest tests/ -q
4783 passed, 11 skipped


One unrelated, pre-existing flake:
`tests/test_labeling.py::test_label_communities_batches_when_over_batch_size`
fails intermittently in full-suite runs, passes 6/6 in isolation.
Reproduces identically on a clean `v8` HEAD (`b14b52e`, no changes applied)
— order-dependent, unrelated to anything touched here.  Filed separately as
#2877

title: --update leaves stale graph nodes when files leave scan scope
body:
## Summary

The `--update` skill flow can leave stale graph nodes behind when a file
remains on disk but leaves the active scan scope, for example after being
added to `.graphifyignore`.

`detect_incremental()` correctly classifies the file as `excluded_files`,
but the skill update flow only passes `deleted_files` to `build_merge()`.

At the end of the update, `save_manifest(..., scan_corpus=...)` removes the
excluded file from the manifest. This leaves the graph and manifest
inconsistent, and on subsequent runs the stale graph nodes are no longer
detectable through incremental manifest-based detection.

## Reproduction

1. Build a graph containing a file `A.py`.
2. Confirm that `A.py` is present in both the graph and manifest.
3. Add `A.py` to `.graphifyignore` while leaving the file on disk.
4. Run the `--update` skill flow.

Observed:

```text
deleted_files = []
excluded_files = [A.py]
````

The current skill flow passes only `deleted_files` to `build_merge()`:

```python
prune = list(deleted) or None

G = build_merge(
    [new_extraction],
    ...,
    prune_sources=prune,
)
```

As a result, `A.py`'s existing graph nodes remain.

The subsequent manifest save uses the current scan scope and removes
`A.py` from the manifest.

After the first update:

```text
graph.json:
    A.py nodes still present

manifest.json:
    A.py absent
```

Run `--update` again without changing anything else.

The second run reports:

```text
deleted_files = []
excluded_files = []
```

because `A.py` is no longer present in the manifest.

The stale `A.py` graph nodes therefore remain indefinitely.

## Expected behavior

When a previously indexed file leaves the scan scope, its graph
contribution should be removed during the same incremental update that
removes it from the manifest.

The expected transition is:

```text
included file
    ↓
file becomes excluded
    ↓
excluded_files = [A.py]
    ↓
prune A.py from graph
    ↓
remove A.py from manifest
    ↓
clean steady state
```

If the file is later brought back into the scan scope, it should be treated
as a new file and indexed again.

## CLI comparison

The CLI incremental path already includes both `deleted_files` and
`excluded_files` when constructing `prune_sources`:

```python
_prune_sources = list(deleted_files)

for _src in list(excluded_files) + graph_stale_sources:
    if _src not in _prune_sources:
        _prune_sources.append(_src)
```

Running the same scenario through the CLI correctly removes the graph
nodes for `A.py` while also removing its manifest entry.

The skill `--update` flow does not currently mirror this behavior.

## Root cause

`excluded_files` was introduced to distinguish files that are still alive
on disk but have left the scan scope from files that have actually been
deleted.

The manifest handling was subsequently updated to remove excluded files
from the manifest, but the skill `--update` merge step continued to pass
only `deleted_files` to `build_merge()`.

This creates an inconsistent transition:

```text
graph:
    A.py still present

manifest:
    A.py removed
```

Once the manifest entry is removed, subsequent incremental runs have no
manifest record from which to discover the stale graph contribution.

## Evidence

Reproduced on current `v8` with a minimal corpus containing:

```python
def hello():
    return "world"
```

Initial state:

* `A.py` exists on disk
* `A.py` is present in the manifest
* `A.py` contributes 2 nodes to the graph

After adding `A.py` to `.graphifyignore` and running the skill update:

* `deleted_files = []`
* `excluded_files = [A.py]`
* graph still contains 2 nodes sourced from `A.py`
* manifest no longer contains `A.py`

After a second unchanged update:

* `deleted_files = []`
* `excluded_files = []`
* graph still contains the 2 `A.py` nodes
* manifest remains empty

The equivalent CLI flow prunes the nodes correctly.

## Related

This was discovered while investigating #2870.

The original #2870 condition — incorrectly treating live files that leave
the scan scope as `deleted_files` — is already handled by the current
`detect_incremental()` implementation.

This issue concerns the downstream handling of those correctly identified
`excluded_files` in the skill `--update` flow.

title: TSX: bare & in JSX text node triggers partial extraction (tree-sitter-javascript rejects valid JSX)
body:
## Summary A bare `&` character in a JSX text node (e.g. `
VoIP & Chamadas
`) is rejected by the bundled tree-sitter-javascript grammar, causing the file to be **partially extracted** with a "syntax errors" warning. The file is valid TSX — esbuild, tsc, and React all accept it without complaint. On our 3 000-file TSX codebase, **31 files (1 %)** are affected, all because UI labels use `&` as a natural-language connector (e.g. `Conexões & Integrações`, `Configurações & Perfil`, `Privacidade & LGPD`). ## Reproduction — minimal ```tsx // with_amp.tsx — triggers "syntax errors" warning, first error at line 2 export function A() { return
VoIP & Chamadas
; } ``` ```tsx // no_amp.tsx — parses cleanly export function B() { return
VoIP e Chamadas
; } ``` Place both files in an empty directory and run: ```sh graphify update . --force ``` **Result:** ``` warning: 1 file(s) had syntax errors and may be partially extracted: with_amp.tsx (first error at line 2) (#2551) ``` `no_amp.tsx` extracts cleanly, confirming the trigger is the bare `&`. ## Why a workaround is impractical The obvious fix (`&` → `&` in a copy of the source before extraction) breaks TypeScript **intersection types** (`type X = A & B` → `A & B` is a TS parse error). Distinguishing JSX text `&` from intersection-type `&` requires exactly the parser that is failing. On our repo a blind replacement increased the warning count from 31 to 55. ## Behaviour compared to #2551 Same shape as #2551 (grammar-level, valid source, exit 0, silent partial extraction), different language/construct. Tree-sitter-javascript appears to expect `&` in JSX text nodes despite JSX/React explicitly allowing bare `&`. ## Environment - graphify `0.9.37` - Language: TSX (React + TypeScript) - Trigger construct: bare `&` in JSX text node - esbuild / tsc / React: all accept the file cleanly ## Expected behaviour Bare `&` in a JSX text node should parse without a syntax error, matching the behaviour of every other JSX toolchain.
