title: Code-only `_rebuild_code` unconditionally deletes the `needs_update` doc-staleness flag, silently cancelling every pending-docs signal
body:
## Summary

`graphify.watch._rebuild_code()` — the **code-only, no-LLM** rebuild that the installed `post-commit` hook, the `post-checkout` hook, `graphify update`, and the `graphify watch` loop all call — deletes `graphify-out/needs_update` on every exit path, with no check on whether the pass that ran was semantic.

`needs_update` is a **semantic-scope** flag. It is written only by `_notify_only()`, whose own message is *"Non-code files changed - semantic re-extraction requires LLM"*. It is read by `check_update()`, which tells the user *"Run `/graphify --update` to apply semantic re-extraction."* An AST-only rebuild cannot satisfy that condition, so clearing the flag asserts something the pass did not do.

The result is silent: the flag disappears, `graphify check-update` goes quiet, and the graph keeps answering from the **previous** version of those documents with a real-looking `source_location` citation attached.

**This is the half of #2015 that never shipped.** #2015 asked for exactly this change ("drop the `needs_update` unlink from `_rebuild_code`") and was closed as *"Fixed in v0.9.21"* with only the manifest half addressed. The unlink is still present, unchanged, in **0.9.53**.

**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.53 (`uv tool install`), Python 3.13.12, Windows 11.

---

## The code

All three sites are inside `_rebuild_code` (`def` at `watch.py:1305`; the next top-level `def` is `check_update` at `watch.py:2108`).

**Site 1 — `--no-cluster` path, `graphify/watch.py:1849-1852`:**

```python
            # clear stale needs_update flag if present
            flag = out / "needs_update"
            if flag.exists():
                flag.unlink()

            if same_graph:
                print("[graphify watch] No code-graph changes detected (--no-cluster); outputs left untouched.")
```

**Site 2 — unchanged-topology early return, `graphify/watch.py:1897-1899`:**

```python
                flag = out / "needs_update"
                if flag.exists():
                    flag.unlink()
                html_action = _reconcile_graph_html(out, existing_graph_data)
                ...
                else:
                    print("[graphify watch] No code-graph topology changes detected; outputs left untouched.")
                return True
```

**Site 3 — main clustered rebuild, `graphify/watch.py:2089-2092`:**

```python
        # clear stale needs_update flag if present
        flag = out / "needs_update"
        if flag.exists():
            flag.unlink()
```

Sites 1 and 2 are the sharp ones: they clear the flag on paths whose own log line is **"outputs left untouched."** graphify writes nothing, then declares the doc backlog resolved.

## The other side of the contract

```
graphify/watch.py:2123  def _notify_only(watch_path: Path) -> None:
                            """Write a flag file and print a notification ..."""
                            flag = watch_path / _GRAPHIFY_OUT / "needs_update"
                            ...
                            print("[graphify watch] Non-code files changed - semantic re-extraction requires LLM.")

graphify/watch.py:2108  def check_update(watch_path: Path) -> bool:
                            """Check for pending semantic update flag ...
                            Non-code file changes (docs, papers, images) require LLM-backed
                            re-extraction via `/graphify --update` ..."""
```

The only writer says *LLM required*. The only reader says *LLM required*. The clearer needs no LLM.

## Who triggers it

| Caller | Site |
|---|---|
| stock `post-commit` hook (detached rebuild) | `graphify/hooks.py:171` — `_rebuild_code(_root, changed_paths=changed, force=_force)` |
| stock `post-checkout` hook | `graphify/hooks.py:220` — `_rebuild_code(_root, force=_force)` |
| `graphify update` CLI | `graphify/cli.py:2427` — `_rebuild_code(watch_path, ..., block_on_lock=True)` |
| `graphify watch` loop | `graphify/watch.py:2261` — `_rebuild_code(watch_path)` |

**No git hook is needed to hit this.** The `watch` loop reaches it on its own (`graphify/watch.py:2260-2263`):

```python
                if _batch_triggers_rebuild(batch):
                    _rebuild_code(watch_path)
                if _batch_needs_llm_flag(batch):
                    _notify_only(watch_path)
```

Batch 1 is docs-only → `_batch_needs_llm_flag` is True → flag raised. Batch 2 is code-only → `_batch_triggers_rebuild` is True, `_batch_needs_llm_flag` is False → `_rebuild_code` deletes the flag raised by batch 1. The ordering inside a *single* batch happens to save the mixed case; it does nothing across batches.

The hook path is worse because the rebuild is **detached and asynchronous** — the flag vanishes seconds after the commit that raised it, with no output attached to the terminal that could tell anyone.

## Reproduction (verified on 0.9.53)

```
$ cd <repo with an existing graphify-out>
$ printf 'docs/PRD.md\n' > graphify-out/needs_update
$ graphify update .
Re-extracting code files in . (no LLM needed)...
  AST extraction: 7/7 uncached files (100%)
[graphify watch] No code-graph topology changes detected; outputs left untouched.
Code graph updated. For doc/paper/image changes run /graphify --update in your AI assistant.

$ ls graphify-out/needs_update
ls: cannot access 'graphify-out/needs_update': No such file or directory

$ graphify check-update .
$ echo $?
0
```

`check-update` prints **nothing** — no pending doc changes. Re-raising the flag proves the check itself is fine; only the clearing is wrong:

```
$ printf 'docs/PRD.md\n' > graphify-out/needs_update
$ graphify check-update .
[graphify check-update] Pending non-code changes in <repo>.
[graphify check-update] Run `/graphify --update` to apply semantic re-extraction.
```

And the pass that cleared the flag wrote nothing at all — mtimes are identical before and after the run:

```
-rw-r--r-- 102813 2026-09-02 11:56:40 graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md
-rw-r--r-- 7032843 2026-09-02 11:56:40 graphify-out/graph.json
-rw-r--r-- 52730 2026-09-02 11:56:40 graphify-out/manifest.json
```

(run performed at 12:06)

## Field observation

On a repo using the stock `post-commit` hook, a commit touching **five** documents raised the flag; the flag was gone before the next command ran, and the health check reported "no pending doc changes." The knowledge graph then described the pre-commit version of those five documents, and nothing announced it. The minimal repro above is the same mechanism with the asynchrony removed.

## Prior art in this tracker

- **#2015** (closed 2026-07-20, *"Fixed in v0.9.21"*) already documented this in its body, quoting the same three lines and asking to *"drop the `needs_update` unlink from `_rebuild_code` (a code-only rebuild hasn't cleared the doc backlog, so it shouldn't clear the flag)."* The fix that shipped addressed only the manifest-stamping half. **32 patch releases later the unlink is unchanged.** This issue exists to track the remaining half on its own so it does not get closed alongside a manifest fix again.
- **#2251** (closed) — `_rebuild_code` unconditionally overwrites `graph.json`, destroying semantic nodes. Same class: a code-only pass asserting semantic-scope state.
- **#2336** (closed) — `_rebuild_code` deletes document AST nodes without regenerating them.
- **#2440 / #2677 / #2782** (open) are the *opposite* concern — the skill's cleanup step targets `.needs_update` (dotted) and so never clears the real flag. Worth flagging for whoever picks those up: **#2440 currently cites this unlink as the correct behavior** (*"`graphify update` does clear it (`watch.py`), so the CLI path worked"*). If this issue is right, that premise is wrong, and "fixing" the skill's cleanup to also clear the flag after a code-only rebuild would widen the bug rather than close it.

## Proposed fix

Clear `needs_update` only when the pass that ran actually performed semantic extraction. Two workable shapes:

1. **Simplest — never clear it from the code-only path.** Delete the three unlink blocks from `_rebuild_code` and let the supervised `--update` / semantic flow own the flag's lifecycle. This is what #2015 asked for.

2. **Explicit contract.** Give `_rebuild_code` a `clears_doc_flag: bool = False` parameter (or gate on a `semantic=True` argument) and have exactly one caller — the LLM-backed update flow — pass it. Every hook and CLI caller keeps the default and leaves the flag alone.

Either way, the flag should be cleared by whatever *resolved* the condition, not by whatever ran next.

Worth auditing alongside: `_rebuild_code` also touches `manifest.json` on these same paths, and a stamped-but-never-extracted document is the failure mode #2015 was closed for.

## Workaround available today

Write a **second sentinel that graphify does not manage**, next to the flag graphify clears, and have your own tooling read yours:

```sh
# in post-commit, alongside whatever raises needs_update
printf '%s\n' "$_CHANGED_DOCS" >> graphify-out/needs_update        # graphify will delete this
printf '%s\n' "$_CHANGED_DOCS" >> graphify-out/.gfy_docs_stale     # nothing else clears this
```

Your health check reads `.gfy_docs_stale`; your semantic-extraction script truncates it on success. Confirmed working — the sentinel survived the repro above byte-for-byte while `needs_update` was deleted. It is a workaround, not a fix: it costs every downstream consumer a second file to know about, and users who rely on `graphify check-update` alone still get the wrong answer.

title: extract: "content is absent from the graph" has 14 different log wordings and no machine-readable status — post-flight tooling is confidently wrong
body:
## Summary `graphify extract` signals "some content did not make it into the graph" through **at least fourteen differently-worded log lines** spread across `llm.py`, `extract.py`, `cli.py` and `export.py`. There is no single machine-readable status for the run. Anything automating around graphify (a post-flight check, a CI gate, a wrapper script) has to scrape prose — and a scraper that matches the *documented* wording still misses real losses. The counts it would need **already exist in memory**; they are simply never written down. This is a persistence gap, not a measurement gap. Version: `graphifyy 0.9.53` (paths below are from the installed package). ## What actually happened A real run in my repo lost a whole chunk and 10 of 41 files: ``` [graphify] chunk of 17 timed out at depth 0 (TimeoutExpired); splitting in half and retrying [graphify] chunk 4/4 failed: claude -p exited 1: API Error: Unable to connect to API (ConnectionRefused) [graphify] WARNING: 1/4 semantic chunk(s) failed — see errors above. Partial results returned. [graphify] WARNING: dropped 31 out-of-scope node(s) attributed to file(s) not dispatched for extraction: ... [graphify] WARNING: 10/41 dispatched file(s) produced no nodes and are absent from the graph: ... (+5 more). [graphify extract] dropped 5 out-of-scope item(s) attributed to 5 file(s) not dispatched this run: ... [graphify extract] semantic extraction is incomplete: 10 dispatched file(s) produced no nodes and 0 came back truncated or hollow. ``` My post-flight matched the three "dropping"-style signatures I could find documented: ``` refusing to parse and dropping chunk | cannot be split further | — dropping ``` It reported **`dropped chunks : 0`**. Zero of those three patterns appear anywhere in that log. The check was confidently wrong about a run that lost a chunk and ten files. ## The full signature set (all verified in 0.9.53 source) | # | Wording | Source | Stream | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | `...bytes); refusing to parse and dropping chunk.` | `llm.py:1138-1139` | stderr | | 2 | `single-file chunk

{timed out\|exceeds model context} and cannot be split further: ` | `llm.py:2385-2386` | stderr | | 3 | `chunk of N {still times out\|still overflows context} at recursion depth D (max M) — dropping` | `llm.py:2393-2394` | stderr | | 4 | `chunk I/N failed: ` | `llm.py:2676`, `llm.py:2699-2701` | stderr | | 5 | `WARNING: K/N semantic chunk(s) failed — see errors above. Partial results returned.` | `llm.py:2717-2718` | stderr | | 6 | `WARNING: dropped N out-of-scope node(s) attributed to file(s) not dispatched for extraction: ...` | `llm.py:2788-2791` | stderr | | 7 | `WARNING: K/N dispatched file(s) produced no nodes and are absent from the graph: ...` | `llm.py:2809-2811` | stderr | | 8 | ` warning: N source file(s) produced zero nodes and are absent from the graph: ...` | `extract.py:6035-6038` | stderr | | 9 | `[graphify extract] dropped N out-of-scope item(s) attributed to M file(s) not dispatched this run: ...` | `cli.py:3943-3945` | **stdout** | | 10 | `[graphify extract] semantic extraction is incomplete: N dispatched file(s) produced no nodes and M came back truncated or hollow.` | `cli.py:3970-3974` | stderr | | 11 | `[graphify extract] semantic extraction is incomplete: unverified semantic shrink detected for ...` | `cli.py:211-213` | stderr | | 12 | `WARNING: new graph has N nodes but existing graph.json has M (net -K). Refusing to overwrite.` | `export.py:312-318` | stderr | | 13 | `WARNING: existing could not be read to verify the new graph is not smaller (). Refusing to overwrite` | `export.py:301-306` | stderr | | 14 | `error: extraction was incomplete (an AST/semantic pass failed) ... Refusing to overwrite a complete graph with a partial one.` | `cli.py:4254-4258`, `cli.py:4427-4433` | stderr | Specific traps a reasonable scraper falls into: - **#3 uses an em dash (U+2014), not a hyphen.** Confirmed: `[hex(ord(c)) for c in llm.py:2394 if ord(c)>127]` → `['0x2014']`. A pattern written with `--` never fires. - **#2 and #4 contain no form of the word "drop"** — the two most common real-world give-ups. - **#7 and #8 describe the same condition in different words** (`produced no nodes` vs `produced zero nodes`), and #8 has no `[graphify]` prefix at all — it is two spaces and a lowercase `warning:`. Anchoring on `^\[graphify` silently drops the whole AST path. - **#9 goes to stdout while every neighbouring give-up line goes to stderr** (`cli.py:3942-3946` — the `print()` has no `file=` kwarg). A wrapper that captures only stderr misses it. - **#7 truncates the file list to 5 basenames.** In the run above, 10 files were lost and only 5 basenames were printed, plus `(+5 more)` (`llm.py:2806-2807`; same at `extract.py:6032-6033`). Even a scraper that matches the line perfectly **cannot recover which files are missing** — the full list exists in `merged["uncovered_files"]` (`llm.py:2804`) and is thrown away. And two lines that look alarming but are **benign**, which a scraper widened to catch the real cases will false-positive on: - `partial result kept (not cached as complete)` — `llm.py:2456`, `llm.py:2472`. That content **is** in the graph; the marker only prevents caching it as authoritative. - `note: node 'X' was extracted twice from '' under different labels — keeping 'A', dropping 'B'` — `dedup.py:443`. A label choice, not content loss. In my log this accounts for **9 of the 9** lines containing the word "dropping" — so widening the pattern to bare `dropping` inverts the error: 9 false positives, 0 true positives. ## Exit code is not a fallback `llm.py:2712-2714`: ```python # Loud failure summary — surface chunk failures at end so they're never # buried mid-log. Exit 0 preserved for caller compatibility; the # summary block makes the problem visible. ``` A run that loses chunks exits 0. The only thing that turns loss into a non-zero exit is the shrink guard (`cli.py:4435` `sys.exit(1)`), and that guard is node-count-only and only applies when there is an existing `graph.json` to compare against (`export.py:280-320`). A first build, or a partial run that still nets more nodes than the previous graph, writes and exits 0 with content missing. ## What graphify already gets right This is not a "graphify hides failures" report — the opposite. Two things worked correctly and prevented real damage in the run above, and I want the ask read as *finish the job*, not *start it*: 1. **The shrink guard refused the write and saved the graph.** `export.py:311-320` prints `new graph has 5625 nodes but existing graph.json has 5651 (net -26). Refusing to overwrite.` and `return False`; `cli.py:4420-4435` then exits 1 rather than stamping the manifest. Verified: the guard's `return False` is reached on the `new_n < existing_n` branch. Without it the ConnectionRefused chunk would have silently clobbered a complete graph. This is exactly right. 2. **The "produced no nodes" warning names the affected files.** `llm.py:2800-2811` computes `uncovered` and prints the basenames. That is far better than a bare count, and it is what made the loss diagnosable at all. The only shortcoming is that it is prose, capped at 5 names, while the complete list sits unused in `merged["uncovered_files"]`. Likewise the design already treats incompleteness as first-class internally — `failed_chunks` (`llm.py:2594`, incremented at `2677`/`2702`), `uncovered_files` (`llm.py:2804`), `_partial_semantic_files` (`cli.py:3958`), the `partial: True` cache stamp. **Every field the ask below needs is already computed.** It just never reaches disk. ## Ask, in priority order **(1) Emit a machine-readable per-run status artefact.** Something like `graphify-out/last_run.json`, written unconditionally at the end of every `extract` (including the refused-write path, which is exactly when tooling most needs it): ```json { "ok": false, "schema_version": 1, "graphify_version": "0.9.53", "started": "2026-09-02T02:43:12Z", "finished": "2026-09-02T03:46:05Z", "wrote_graph": false, "refused_reason": "shrink_guard", "chunks_total": 4, "chunks_failed": 1, "chunk_errors": ["claude -p exited 1: API Error: Unable to connect to API (ConnectionRefused)"], "files_dispatched": 41, "files_with_no_nodes": ["docs/decisions/2026-08-27-openrouter-provider.md", "..."], "files_partial": [], "dropped": [], "nodes_written": 5625, "nodes_existing": 5651 } ``` Full paths, not truncated basenames — the truncation is the part that makes the existing warning undiagnosable. `ok` should be false whenever any content is missing, so the cheap check is one field. A `graphify status --json` subcommand reading the same struct would serve the same purpose; the artefact matters more than the surface. **(2) Failing that, document the complete set in one place and treat the wording as a compatibility surface.** A `docs/GIVE_UP_SIGNATURES.md` listing all fourteen with their stream (stdout vs stderr), plus the two benign look-alikes explicitly marked as benign, plus a stability commitment. Right now the only way to enumerate them is to grep the package source, which is what I had to do, and any release can change one without notice. A cheaper partial win either way: make the four "absent from the graph" wordings (#7, #8) identical, send #9 to stderr like its neighbours, and give every give-up line a stable machine-greppable token such as `[graphify:incomplete]`. ## Repro / verification Read-only; starts no extraction. Point `LOG` at an extract log from a run that lost content: ```python import io, re, pathlib log = io.open(pathlib.Path(LOG), encoding="utf-8").read() DOCUMENTED = r"refusing to parse and dropping chunk|cannot be split further|— dropping|-- dropping" print("documented-signature matches:", len(re.findall(DOCUMENTED, log))) print("chunk N/M failed :", len(re.findall(r"chunk \d+/\d+ failed:", log))) print("produced no nodes :", len(re.findall(r"produced no nodes and are absent from the graph", log))) print("lines containing 'dropping':", sum(1 for l in log.splitlines() if "dropping" in l)) print(" ...benign dedup notes :", sum(1 for l in log.splitlines() if "under different labels" in l and "dropping" in l)) ``` Output on my losing run: ``` documented-signature matches: 0 chunk N/M failed : 1 produced no nodes : 1 lines containing 'dropping': 9 ...benign dedup notes : 9 ``` Zero true positives from the documented patterns; nine false positives from the widened one. And `graphify-out/` after that run contains no run-status file of any kind — `manifest.json` is per-file hashes (`{mtime, seen, ast_hash, semantic_hash}`), not run state — while `grep -c "last_run\|run_status\|run\.json" *.py` across the package returns 0.

title: Resolve graph.json from an ancestor directory, plus two independent fixes
body:
In a multi-repo workspace the graph lives at a parent root — here `C:/Repositories/graphify-out/` covering 23 repos. Queries from a child repo or worktree failed with "graph file not found", because resolution only ever looked in cwd.

Five commits make ancestor resolution consistent: CLI, non-CLI callers, `hook-guard`, and the skill doc.

Two independent fixes:

- **extract** — `follow_symlinks=True` was overridden by a root-containment check, so linked trees were silently skipped rather than followed.
- **security** — the `graph.json` size cap rejected an 859 MB workspace graph. Raised to 2 GiB.

Verified on Windows against a 331k-node, 23-repo graph, resolving from the CLI, PowerShell, and the MCP server.

title: No persistence path enforces the 3-member hyperedge contract — pairs, dangling-member groups and un-folded alias groups reach graph.json and the semantic cache from twelve independent writers (0.9.53)
body:
Hyperedges are documented as group relationships — `build.py` states "a hyperedge is meaningful only with 3+ members" and routes pairwise relationships to the ordinary edge set. Nothing enforces that. A two-member group, a group whose members resolve to nothing, and a group whose member list is malformed all reach `graph.json` and the semantic cache, from a dozen independent write paths that share no code.

Reproduced on 0.9.53 (`v8` @ 33362d9):

```python
import json, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
import networkx as nx
from graphify.build import build_from_json
from graphify.export import to_json, attach_hyperedges

out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

G = build_from_json({
    "nodes": [{"id": n, "label": n, "file_type": "code", "source_file": "a.py"} for n in ("a", "b")],
    "edges": [],
    "hyperedges": [{"id": "pair", "nodes": ["a", "b"], "source_file": "a.py"}],
})
print("build_from_json  ->", G.graph.get("hyperedges"))

to_json(G, {0: ["a", "b"]}, str(out / "graph.json"))
print("graph.json       ->", json.loads((out / "graph.json").read_text())["hyperedges"])

H = nx.Graph(); H.add_nodes_from(["a", "b", "c"])
attach_hyperedges(H, [{"id": "pair2", "nodes": ["a", "b"]},
                      {"id": "alias", "members": ["a", "b", "c"]}])
print("attach_hyperedges->", H.graph["hyperedges"])
```

```
build_from_json  -> [{'id': 'pair', 'nodes': ['a', 'b'], 'source_file': 'a.py'}]
graph.json       -> [{'id': 'pair', 'nodes': ['a', 'b'], 'source_file': 'a.py'}]
attach_hyperedges-> [{'id': 'pair2', 'nodes': ['a', 'b']}, {'id': 'alias', 'members': ['a', 'b', 'c']}]
```

Three things in that output:

1. **The pair is persisted** at every boundary, including into `graph.json`.
2. **The alias-keyed group is persisted un-folded.** `members` is a supported spelling (#1561) that `build_from_json` folds onto `nodes` — but `attach_hyperedges` is reached by `merge-graphs` without passing through it, so the entry lands with no `nodes` key at all. Every consumer that reads `he["nodes"]` sees a group with no members.
3. `build_from_json`'s existing revalidation (#1916) only drops a hyperedge when **no** member resolves, so a 3+ group that degrades to a pair during member pruning survives as a pair.

## How groups degrade to pairs in practice

The invariant is easiest to violate through the existing remap machinery, none of which re-checks size afterwards:

- **#2805's dedup remap.** Two members that collapse onto one survivor legitimately shrink the group; nothing rechecks the total.
- **The semantic re-key** (`_semantic_id_remap`) is non-injective: `api_readme_foo` and `readme_foo` both map to `docs_api_readme_foo`, so two distinct members become one.
- **The doc-twin fold** maps `<slug>` onto `<slug>_doc`, so a group naming both twins is left with a duplicate.
- **`norm_to_id`** resolves a case variant onto the canonical id, so `Foo` and `foo` are one member.

In each case the member count is checked, if at all, on **list positions** rather than distinct resolved ids, so three positions naming two nodes passes.

## Write paths with no cardinality check

Auditing this turned up twelve places that persist hyperedges, sharing no common code path:

| Path | Note |
|---|---|
| `cache.save_semantic_cache` (×2 sites) | no node set available, so shape/cardinality only |
| `cli` pre-merge / pre-manifest-stamp | `_stamped_manifest_files` counts a hyperedge as output (#1920) |
| `build.build` → `dedup.deduplicate_entities` | three early returns skip the hyperedge pass entirely |
| `build.build_from_json` | positions, not distinct ids; malformed shapes appended verbatim |
| `build.build_merge` | carried groups revalidated only when `prune_sources` was passed |
| `export.to_json` | public API, takes `G.graph["hyperedges"]` verbatim |
| `export.attach_hyperedges` | reached by `merge-graphs` without `build_from_json` |
| `build.prefix_graph_for_global` | prefixes only a canonical `nodes` list |
| `cli` raw `--no-cluster` block | never builds a graph |
| `cli._prune_graph_json_sources` | exclusion-only prune, writes in place |
| `watch._rebuild_code` raw writer | `graphify update --no-cluster` |

## Consequences

- **Invalid data in `graph.json`.** A pair is not a group; queries and the report treat it as one.
- **Poisoned cache entries.** A group whose members resolve to nothing passes the cache gate (the cache has no node set), and the file is manifest-stamped from it (#1920). On replay `build_from_json` drops the group, so the run produces no semantic data for a file marked as extracted — and #2927's heal re-queues it straight back into the same cached content.
- **Silent loss of valid data.** The alias-keyed and object-member shapes above are *supported* spellings; at the `merge-graphs` boundary they are persisted unusable.

## Related, and distinct from

#2805 (dedup drops members instead of remapping), #3102 (carried hyperedges bypass the #2805 remap), #2484 / #2485 (the dual-slot and top-level-key problems) and #1916 (dangling members) each fixed one mechanism that can shrink or break a group. None of them established the size invariant itself, which is why the same class keeps recurring at each new boundary.

I have a fix ready that introduces one shared gate and applies it at all twelve paths, with regression coverage for each — PR to follow.

title: fix(watch): preserve pending semantic update flag
body:
Closes #3294.

## Problem

`_rebuild_code()` is an AST-only operation, but each of its three successful exit paths deleted `graphify-out/needs_update`. That flag records pending semantic re-extraction for changed documents, so a later code rebuild could silently mark unrelated document work as complete even though no LLM-backed extraction ran.

## Change

- Stop deleting `needs_update` from the no-cluster, unchanged-topology, and clustered rebuild paths.
- Add a parameterized regression test covering all three paths.
- Preserve the flag contents as well as its existence, so the code-only pass cannot rewrite pending semantic state.

The semantic workflow remains responsible for clearing the flag after it actually resolves the pending work.

## Verification

- Regression test before fix: 3 failed (flag deleted on all paths).
- `uv run --frozen pytest tests/test_watch.py -q --tb=short`: 145 passed, 3 skipped.
- `uv run --frozen pytest tests/ -q --tb=short`: 5302 passed, 11 skipped.
- All five `tools.skillgen` CI guards passed.
- `uv run --frozen ruff check graphify/watch.py tests/test_watch.py` passed.
- `uv run --frozen graphify update .` completed successfully.

title: detect_backend() silently routes extraction to Bedrock on the mere presence of AWS_PROFILE/AWS_REGION, with no env var or config key to override it
body:
# Summary

`detect_backend()` returns `"bedrock"` whenever `AWS_PROFILE`, `AWS_REGION`, or `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` is set in the environment — regardless of whether those credentials have Bedrock access, whether the profile even exists, or whether `boto3` is installed. Because these variables are routinely exported for completely unrelated AWS work (S3, ECS, Terraform, CI runners, `direnv`, a shell profile), a bare `graphify extract` on such a machine silently ships the corpus to Amazon Bedrock and bills the user's AWS account.

There is no way to prevent this by configuration. I grepped the installed package exhaustively: no `GRAPHIFY_BACKEND` (or equivalent) env var exists, and no config file participates in backend selection. The only escape hatch is passing `--backend` on every single invocation.

**Version:** `graphifyy` 0.9.41 (`uv tool install graphifyy`), Python 3.12, Linux.

# What happens

```
$ export AWS_REGION=us-east-1      # set hours earlier, for unrelated AWS work
$ graphify extract .               # corpus with docs/images -> needs an LLM
# -> silently selects the bedrock backend, calls bedrock-runtime:Converse,
#    bills the AWS account
```

# What was expected

Either:
- the backend stays unset and `extract` errors with the existing "no LLM API key found" message, telling me to pass `--backend`; or
- I can pin the backend once via an environment variable / config key and never think about it again.

Presence of AWS credentials in the environment is not consent to spend money on Bedrock. Every other cloud backend requires a **purpose-specific** secret (`GEMINI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, ...) whose presence really does signal "I intend to use this provider for LLM calls". `AWS_PROFILE` signals "I use AWS", which is a strictly weaker statement — AWS has ~200 other services.

# Minimal reproduction

No API key needed; `detect_backend()` is pure and can be called directly. Run each in an isolated environment so nothing else leaks in:

```bash
# 1. Region alone is enough.
env -i HOME=/tmp/probe PATH=/usr/bin:/bin AWS_REGION=us-east-1 \
  python -c "from graphify.llm import detect_backend; print(detect_backend())"
# -> bedrock

# 2. A profile that does not exist in ~/.aws/config is also enough.
env -i HOME=/tmp/probe PATH=/usr/bin:/bin AWS_PROFILE=definitely-does-not-exist-12345 \
  python -c "from graphify.llm import detect_backend; print(detect_backend())"
# -> bedrock          <-- not merely unvalidated for Bedrock access; not valid at all

# 3. An EXPLICIT local-backend opt-in loses to the incidental AWS var.
env -i HOME=/tmp/probe PATH=/usr/bin:/bin \
  AWS_PROFILE=bogus OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 \
  python -c "from graphify.llm import detect_backend; print(detect_backend())"
# -> bedrock          <-- expected: ollama

# 4. A custom provider from ~/.graphify/providers.json with its key set also loses.
#    (providers.json: {"myllm": {"base_url": "https://api.example.com/v1",
#                                "default_model": "m1", "env_key": "MYLLM_API_KEY"}})
env -i HOME=/tmp/probe PATH=/usr/bin:/bin AWS_PROFILE=bogus MYLLM_API_KEY=dummy \
  python -c "from graphify.llm import detect_backend; print(detect_backend())"
# -> bedrock          <-- expected: myllm

# 5. Control: nothing set.
env -i HOME=/tmp/probe PATH=/usr/bin:/bin \
  python -c "from graphify.llm import detect_backend; print(detect_backend())"
# -> None
```

Case 3 is the sharpest one. Setting `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` is a deliberate, unambiguous "send my corpus to this local model" — and it is silently overridden by a variable the user may not even remember exporting, in the direction of a *paid cloud* backend.

# Exact code path

`graphify/llm.py:2817-2847` — full function as installed:

```python
def detect_backend() -> str | None:
    """Return the name of whichever backend has an API key set, or None.

    Priority: gemini → kimi → claude → openai → deepseek → azure → bedrock → ollama (last, opt-in).

    Ollama is intentionally checked LAST so a paid API key (Anthropic/OpenAI/etc.)
    is never silently shadowed by an incidental OLLAMA_BASE_URL in the environment
    — see security finding F-002/F-029. Setting OLLAMA_BASE_URL alongside a paid
    key now keeps you on the paid backend; remove the paid key (or pass
    --backend ollama explicitly) to route to the local model.
    """
    for backend in ("gemini", "kimi", "claude", "openai", "deepseek"):
        if _get_backend_api_key(backend):
            return backend
    if _get_backend_api_key("azure") and os.environ.get("AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"):
        return "azure"
    if os.environ.get("AWS_PROFILE") or os.environ.get("AWS_REGION") or os.environ.get("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION"):
        return "bedrock"
    # Honor Ollama's own OLLAMA_HOST here too, not just OLLAMA_BASE_URL (#1940) —
    # otherwise a user who set the standard Ollama var but no --backend still
    # gets "no LLM API key found". Empty default -> falsy when neither is set,
    # so ollama stays opt-in and never shadows a paid key (checked first above).
    ollama_url = _resolve_ollama_base_url("")
    if ollama_url:
        _validate_ollama_base_url(ollama_url)
        return "ollama"
    for name in BACKENDS:
        if name not in ("gemini", "kimi", "claude", "openai", "deepseek", "azure", "bedrock", "ollama", "claude-cli"):
            if _get_backend_api_key(name):
                return name
    return None
```

The offending branch is **`llm.py:2833-2834`**. Note it sits *above* the ollama check (`llm.py:2839-2842`) and *above* the custom-provider loop (`llm.py:2843-2846`).

Call sites that hit it with no user opt-in:

- `graphify/cli.py:3216-3217`
  ```python
  needs_llm = bool(semantic_files) or dedup_llm
  if backend is None and needs_llm:
      backend = _detect_backend()
  ```
- `graphify/llm.py:1751` (`extract_corpus_parallel`, when `backend=None`)
- `graphify/llm.py:3140` (community labelling)

Three further observations:

1. **No probe of any kind.** Nothing between selection and the first billed call verifies Bedrock is reachable. The client is constructed lazily at `llm.py:1682-1684` and `llm.py:2653-2655` (`boto3.Session(profile_name=profile, region_name=region)`) — the first thing that touches AWS is `client.converse(...)`.
2. **`boto3` isn't even checked.** It ships only under the optional `bedrock` extra (`METADATA`: `Requires-Dist: boto3; extra == "bedrock"`). On a default `uv tool install graphifyy` it is absent, so auto-selecting bedrock guarantees a hard `ImportError` at the first LLM call (`llm.py:1675-1679`, `llm.py:2649-2652`) — after detection, chunking and cost estimation have already run — instead of falling through to a backend that actually works.
3. **`claude-cli` is unreachable by auto-detection.** It is excluded from the fallback loop at `llm.py:2844`, so a user whose only credential is an authenticated `claude` CLI gets bedrock rather than the backend they can actually use. (Related: #1404.)

# Why the current heuristic is wrong

- **Presence of a credential is not consent to spend it.** `AWS_PROFILE` is set by `aws configure`, `aws sso login`, `direnv`, CI task roles, and virtually every AWS tutorial. Reading it as "use Bedrock for LLM inference" infers a spending decision from an ambient fact.
- **It isn't even a validity check.** Repro #2 shows a profile name that exists nowhere on disk still selects bedrock. So the branch does not establish "Bedrock is usable" — only "the string is non-empty".
- **The guard is asymmetric, in the expensive direction.** The docstring correctly argues that an *incidental* `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` must never shadow a *deliberate* paid key. The exact inverse is what happens here: an incidental `AWS_PROFILE` shadows a deliberate `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` and routes to a paid cloud backend (repro #3). The design principle already stated in this function is not applied where the cost consequence is worse.
- **Silent.** No line is printed saying which backend was auto-selected or why, so the first signal is an AWS bill or a Bedrock `AccessDeniedException`.
- **Unfixable by configuration.** See below.

# There is no override

Grepping the installed 0.9.41 package for every `os.environ.get("*BACKEND*")` read yields exactly one hit:

- `graphify/prs.py:566` — `GRAPHIFY_TRIAGE_BACKEND`, scoped to PR triage (`_resolve_triage_backend`), not to `extract`.

There is no `GRAPHIFY_BACKEND`. There is no config file: `.graphify_build.json` (`watch.py:77-104`) stores only `excludes`/`gitignore`, and `~/.graphify/providers.json` (`llm.py:264-298`) can only *add* backends — `llm.py:289` (`if name in BACKENDS ... continue`) forbids redefining a built-in, and the custom-provider check runs *after* the bedrock branch anyway (repro #4). There is no `graphify config` subcommand.

So the only control available today is repeating `--backend X` on every invocation, which is exactly the thing an auto-detector is supposed to make unnecessary, and which fails open: forget it once and the run goes to Bedrock.

# Suggested fix

**1. Add an explicit override that takes precedence over all detection.** The project already has this pattern one file over, in `graphify/prs.py:562-572`:

```python
def _resolve_triage_backend() -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Return (backend, model) using GRAPHIFY_TRIAGE_BACKEND or first available key."""
    explicit = os.environ.get("GRAPHIFY_TRIAGE_BACKEND", "").strip()
    if explicit in BACKENDS:
        ...
        return explicit, model
    # ... auto-detect
```

Lift that to `detect_backend()`:

```python
def detect_backend() -> str | None:
    explicit = os.environ.get("GRAPHIFY_BACKEND", "").strip()
    if explicit:
        if explicit not in BACKENDS:
            raise ValueError(
                f"GRAPHIFY_BACKEND={explicit!r} is not a known backend. "
                f"Available: {', '.join(sorted(BACKENDS))}"
            )
        return explicit
    ...
```

This alone makes the behaviour fixable by configuration and is a small, backward-compatible change. Honouring `GRAPHIFY_BACKEND=none` (or similar) to mean "never auto-detect, require `--backend`" would additionally let a user fail closed.

**2. Make bedrock opt-in rather than inferred.** Drop `llm.py:2833-2834` from the detection chain, or gate it behind a purpose-specific signal that means "use Bedrock for LLM calls" — e.g. `GRAPHIFY_BEDROCK_MODEL` (already read at `llm.py:199`), an explicit `GRAPHIFY_ENABLE_BEDROCK=1`, or `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`. `--backend bedrock` continues to work either way: the presence allow-list at `cli.py:3271-3277` is the right check for an *explicit* request and should stay exactly where it is.

That distinction is the whole bug. #846 ("`--backend bedrock` rejects a valid AWS environment", closed) was correct: when the user has already named bedrock, "do you have AWS vars?" is a reasonable sanity check. The regression is that the same presence test was reused as an *inference* rule in `detect_backend()`, where the user has named nothing. An allow-list for an explicit opt-in is not a valid basis for an implicit one.

**3. Whatever the resolution, move bedrock below the explicit local/custom backends** so `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` and a configured custom provider both win over an ambient `AWS_PROFILE`, matching the principle the docstring already states.

**4. Announce the auto-selection.** One stderr line — `[graphify] no --backend given; auto-selected 'bedrock' (AWS_REGION is set). Override with --backend or GRAPHIFY_BACKEND.` — would have surfaced this immediately instead of at billing time. Naming the *triggering variable* is the important part.

**5. If bedrock is auto-selected, verify `boto3` imports at selection time** and fall through to the next candidate if it doesn't, rather than failing hard mid-extraction.

I'm happy to open a PR for (1) + (3) + (4) if that shape is agreeable.

title: save_query_result: memory docs sharing a second and a 50-char question prefix silently overwrite each other
body:
### Summary

`save_query_result` derives the memory-doc filename from a **one-second timestamp** plus the **first 50 characters** of the question, then writes with a plain `write_text`. Two saves that land in the same second and share a 50-character question prefix resolve to the same path, and the later one silently replaces the earlier one. No error is raised and both calls return normally.

The one-file-per-memory layout is what makes unrelated writes safe here — they touch different paths, so no lock is needed. The filename is the one place where that property does not hold.

### Where

`graphify/ingest.py` (v0.9.53):

```python
slug = re.sub(r"[^\w]", "_", question.lower())[:50].strip("_")
filename = f"query_{now.strftime('%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')}_{slug}.md"
...
out_path.write_text(content, encoding="utf-8")
```

Three properties combine:

- the timestamp has one-second granularity
- the slug is truncated at 50 characters
- the writer is not part of the name (`contributor` is hardcoded to `"graphify"` on this path)

### Reproduction

```python
"""Minimal reproduction: concurrent save_query_result calls silently overwrite."""
import shutil, tempfile
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from pathlib import Path

from graphify.ingest import save_query_result

def run(label, questions):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    try:
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(questions)) as ex:
            list(ex.map(lambda q: save_query_result(q, "an answer", Path(d)), questions))
        kept = len(list(Path(d).glob("*.md")))
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(d, ignore_errors=True)
    print(f"{label:52s} saved={len(questions):3d} kept={kept:3d} lost={len(questions)-kept:3d}")

PREFIX = "how does the authentication subsystem resolve tokens"
run("distinct questions", [f"how does module {i} work" for i in range(20)])
run("same question, same second", ["how does auth work"] * 20)
run("questions differing only after char 50", [f"{PREFIX} in module {i}" for i in range(20)])
```

Output on v0.9.53 (macOS, CPython 3.9, APFS):

```
distinct questions                                   saved= 20 kept= 20 lost=  0
same question, same second                           saved= 20 kept=  1 lost= 19
questions differing only after char 50               saved= 20 kept=  1 lost= 19
```

The first row is the design working: unrelated writes never collide. The other two are the filename.

Spacing the same question more than a second apart is enough to avoid it, which confirms the mechanism:

```
same question, 1.05s apart                           saved=  3 kept=  3 lost=  0
```

### Why it matters in practice

The third case is not contrived. When several agents sweep one subsystem in parallel, their questions share a long prefix:

```
"how does the authentication subsystem resolve tokens in module 1"
"how does the authentication subsystem resolve tokens in module 2"
```

Both truncate to `how_does_the_authentication_subsystem_resolve_toke`, so distinct findings collapse into one file. The symptom is only ever "the graph does not seem to know that", which is hard to distinguish from a retrieval miss — so it is unlikely to be reported as data loss.

### Suggested fix

Put something writer- or call-unique in the name, so distinct saves cannot resolve to one path — for example a short random suffix, or the contributor plus a counter:

```python
filename = f"query_{now.strftime('%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')}_{contributor}_{uuid4().hex[:8]}_{slug}.md"
```

An `open(..., "x")` retry loop would also close it without changing the naming scheme. Either keeps the existing layout and the `*.md` glob in `reflect.load_memory_docs` unchanged.

This is the same class as #2650 (`to_obsidian` case-only filename collisions silently overwriting node notes), on a different code path.

Happy to open a PR if a direction is preferred — I did not want to guess at the naming convention you would want in the filename.

title: Python: methods differing only by a leading underscore collide on node id — the public one is silently dropped from the graph
body:
**Version:** 0.9.53 (latest on PyPI at time of writing; also reproduced on 0.9.47)
**Platform:** Windows 11, Python 3.14.7, isolated venv (`pip install graphifyy==0.9.53`)
**Command:** `graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster`

> Note for maintainers: I first sent this through private vulnerability reporting
> (`GHSA-7hhr-924m-gwrf`) because SECURITY.md asks that security-relevant reports not be
> opened publicly. On reflection that was the wrong channel � this is a correctness bug, not
> a vulnerability in graphify � so I'm refiling it here. **Please close that private report as
> a duplicate of this issue**; I can't close it myself as the reporter.

## Summary

When a class defines two methods whose names differ only by a leading underscore (`_foo` and
`foo`), only one node reaches `graph.json`. Node ids appear to be slugified in a way that
strips the leading underscore, so both become `<module>_<class>_foo`, and the second
definition silently overwrites the first.

No warning is emitted, exit status is 0, and the file is not reported as partially extracted.
A public API method can therefore be **entirely absent** from the graph while its private
sibling occupies the public name.

## Reproduction

`mod.py` � three methods in, two nodes out:

```python
class Adapter:
    def _get_connection(self, url):     # L2
        return url

    def get_connection(self, url):      # L5
        return self._get_connection(url)

    def unrelated(self, x):             # L8   <- control
        return x
```

```console
$ graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster
[graphify extract] wrote graphify-out/graph.json - 4 nodes, 3 edges (no clustering)
```

Nodes for `mod.py`:

```
mod                         | mod.py             | L1
mod_adapter                 | Adapter            | L1
mod_adapter_get_connection  | ._get_connection() | L2
mod_adapter_unrelated       | .unrelated()       | L8
```

**Expected:** three method nodes. **Actual:** two. `Adapter.get_connection` (L5) is absent;
the id that would name it is held by `_get_connection` (L2).

The `unrelated` control extracts correctly, so this is specific to the underscore-differing
pair, not to methods generally.

## Real-world impact

Found while benchmarking context retrieval against `psf/requests` at `aa1461b6^`.
`src/requests/adapters.py` defines both `HTTPAdapter._get_connection` (L377) and
`HTTPAdapter.get_connection` (L406). The graph contains a single node
`src_requests_adapters_httpadapter_get_connection` pointing at **L377**; the public
`get_connection` at L406 has no node at all, only a stray docstring node at L407.

In a 25-symbol ground-truth set built from that repository's own fix commits, this defect
accounted for a measurable share of symbols that no graph query (`affected`, `explain`,
`query`, `path`) could reach. Anyone relying on graph completeness � for an API audit, a
refactor impact review, or a security pass � gets a quiet false negative.

## Root cause (hypothesis) and suggested fix

Id generation appears to normalise identifiers by stripping non-alphanumeric characters,
including the leading `_`, without disambiguating collisions.

1. Preserve the underscore in the id (e.g. `mod_adapter__get_connection`); or
2. Detect an id collision at insert time and disambiguate rather than overwrite.

(2) is more robust, since the same collapse likely affects other character-stripping cases
(`foo_bar` vs `fooBar` vs `foo-bar`, dunder names). A regression test asserting
**node count == definition count** for a file would catch the whole class.

## Related, but not duplicates

- **#387** (`.mjs` files produce 0 nodes, fixed v0.4.16) was an all-`.mjs` failure from a
  missing `_DISPATCH` entry. This is Python, the dispatch path plainly works (siblings in the
  same class extract fine), and the loss is per-symbol rather than per-file.
- **#2281** (JS/MJS ids minted from absolute paths) is a different cause but the same family:
  an id-shape defect that silently changes which node exists.

title: fix: prevent ambient AWS config from auto-selecting Bedrock
body:
Summary

Fixes #3300 by preventing ambient AWS environment variables from implicitly selecting the Bedrock LLM backend.

What changed

  • Remove automatic Bedrock detection from AWS_PROFILE, AWS_REGION, and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION.

  • Add GRAPHIFY_BACKEND as a global backend override.

  • Support none, off, and auto sentinel values.

  • Validate GRAPHIFY_BACKEND against registered backends.

  • Preserve explicit --backend bedrock / backend="bedrock" behavior.

  • Handle invalid GRAPHIFY_BACKEND values cleanly in the CLI.

  • Document GRAPHIFY_BACKEND in the README.

  • Add regression and integration tests for backend precedence and detection.

Why

Previously, a generic AWS environment variable such as AWS_REGION=us-east-1 could silently cause Graphify to select Bedrock, even when the user had not requested Bedrock.

This could result in:

  • boto3 import failures on default installations.

  • Unexpected AWS authentication/API errors.

  • Potential unintended Bedrock API usage.

  • Ambient AWS configuration overriding intentionally configured Ollama or custom providers.

Bedrock is now explicit-only for automatic backend resolution.

New behavior

Configuration | Result -- | -- AWS_REGION=us-east-1 | Does not select Bedrock AWS_PROFILE=default + Ollama | Ollama is detected AWS_PROFILE=default + custom provider | Custom provider is detected --backend bedrock | Bedrock is selected GRAPHIFY_BACKEND=bedrock | Bedrock is selected GRAPHIFY_BACKEND=none / off | Automatic detection disabled GRAPHIFY_BACKEND=auto | Normal automatic detection Invalid GRAPHIFY_BACKEND | Clear error + exit code 1

Explicit CLI/backend arguments continue to take precedence over GRAPHIFY_BACKEND.

Verification

  • 116 passed — tests/test_llm_backends.py

  • 4 passed — focused CLI regression tests

  • 21 passed — Ollama/provider registry tests

  • 78 passed, 2 skipped — Claude CLI/vision tests

  • python -m graphify update . — successful

  • git diff --check — clean

title: Extraction leaves source_location null on most edges — query results can't cite an exact line, forcing agents into a second file-read pass
body:
## Context

Ran a controlled benchmark: two fresh coding-agent instances studied the same repo from zero context, answering 5 identical cross-file questions — one agent using `graphify query` against a pre-built graph, one using only Read/Grep/Glob (forbidden from touching graphify at all). Repeated on two repos of different size/legibility.

## What happened

In both runs, the graphify-assisted agent's own self-report explained where its extra cost came from: it ran `graphify query "<question>"` first to locate the right file(s), then still had to `Read` those exact files afterward to pull verbatim detail — exact env var names, script line numbers, quoted wording — because the query results it got back didn't carry that detail at citable precision.

Checked this against the actual `graph.json` for both graphs used in the benchmark:

| Repo | edges w/ null `source_location` | nodes w/ null `source_location` | EXTRACTED-confidence edges w/ null `source_location` |
|---|---|---|---|
| small, self-describing repo (556 nodes / 757 edges) | 625/757 (82%) | 458/556 (82%) | 573/705 (81%) |
| larger, less self-describing repo (1,059 nodes / 1,204 edges) | 645/1204 (53%) | 674/1059 (63%) | 492/1002 (49%) |

So even edges marked `EXTRACTED` (relationship explicit in source, per the extraction spec) mostly carry no line reference back to where that was extracted — half to over 80% of the time depending on the corpus.

## Cost observed

| Repo | Nodes | With graphify | Without | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| small, self-describing | 556 | 79.6k tok / 71.9s | 53.1k tok / 58.8s | +50% tok / +22% time |
| larger, less self-describing | 1,059 | 83.5k tok / 66.8s | 62.1k tok / 61.8s | +35% tok / +8% time |

Both deltas track roughly with "go verify by reading the file anyway" as an extra pass on top of the query.

## Ask

Populate `source_location` (exact line or line range) during extraction wherever the source file structurally supports it — code already gets this for free from AST (line numbers are known at parse time), so the gap is concentrated in doc/YAML/markdown extraction, where a header, table row, or comment block still has an unambiguous position in the file that the semantic-extraction pass could capture and isn't currently asked to.

## Bonus motivation

This isn't only a cost problem. In the same benchmark, one graphify-assisted agent fabricated a specific line-number citation to support a claim — attributing a quote to a line that, when checked, was mid-paragraph of an unrelated principle that actually argued the opposite. Real `source_location` on `EXTRACTED` edges would let downstream tooling (or the querying agent itself) distinguish "this is a verified quote at line N" from "this is the graph's summarized rationale" before it gets asserted as a fact with an invented citation.

## Environment

graphifyy 0.9.53, Claude Code / Claude Sonnet 5 as both the extracting agent (built both graphs) and the querying/baseline agents in the benchmark.

title: graphify query returns a raw node/edge dump the caller must re-interpret — no synthesized-answer mode
body:
## Context

Same benchmark as the companion issue on `source_location` (#3307 — filed alongside this one): two fresh coding-agent instances answered 5 identical cross-file questions about the same repo, one via `graphify query` against a pre-built graph, one via plain Read/Grep/Glob with graphify forbidden. Repeated on two repos.

## What happened

`graphify query "<question>"` returns a BFS/DFS node-and-edge listing — in one run against a 556-node graph, the tool itself reported truncation: `[!] TRUNCATED: showing 41 of 73 nodes (~2000-token budget)`. There's no synthesized answer to the actual natural-language question in that output — the calling agent has to read the returned node labels/edges/community tags and construct the answer itself, then (see #3307) frequently re-read the underlying source files anyway because the returned node text is a paraphrase, not a citable quote.

In practice this turns one conceptual "ask the graph a question" into a 3-4 step chain: run query → parse/interpret the dump → re-derive an answer from it → verify against source files for exact wording. That's measurably more tool calls and tokens than answering the same question by direct `grep`/`Read` in both benchmark repos:

| Repo | Tool calls (graphify) | Tool calls (baseline) | Tokens (graphify) | Tokens (baseline) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| small, self-describing (556 nodes) | 13 | 10 | 79.6k | 53.1k |
| larger, less self-describing (1,059 nodes) | 14 | 12 | 83.5k | 62.1k |

## Ask

Add a mode to `graphify query` (or a separate command, e.g. `graphify ask`) that returns a direct, cited answer to the natural-language question — not just the traversal used internally to build that answer. The current BFS/DFS node dump is genuinely useful for open-ended exploration/debugging and shouldn't go away; this would be an additional output shape specifically for the common "answer this specific question" case, which is most of what an agent actually wants when it calls `graphify query` with a question string in the first place.

## Environment

graphifyy 0.9.53, Claude Code / Claude Sonnet 5 as the querying agent in the benchmark.

uv run --no-sync pytest -q tests/test_wheel_packaging.py -k leiden_extra
1 passed, 133 deselected
