- `kotlin` is absent from `_LANG_SUFFIXES` (`cross_repo_calls.py`, which lists only
  cpp/csharp/java/swift), so even a parked Kotlin call could not be matched after merge.
- The paired PR adds the park arm for the object-receiver case (declared nowhere in the
  build → `_park_unresolved_member_call(..., "kotlin", ...)`, builtin globals skipped) plus
  the `kotlin` suffix entry, so `merge-graphs` / `global add` bind it to the single
  declaration another repo owns.

### Expected

- `Registry.register()` on an object/class-qualified receiver declared in another repo is
  parked at build time and bound to its single out-of-repo declaration at merge time
  (INFERRED, context `cross_repo`), matching the Java/C++/C#/Swift/ObjC equivalents.
- A receiver name matching 2+ declared types, or a callee matching 2+ methods of the matched
  type, stays unresolved (the existing god-node guard).

### Out of scope

The lowercase **instance**-receiver shape
(`class App(private val greeter: Greeter) { fun run() { greeter.greet() } }`) is a separate
gap: the engine captures no `member_receiver` for it today, so neither v8 nor this PR
resolves it. That is tracked separately; this issue and its PR are strictly the
object/class-qualified cross-repo park.

A paired PR follows.

title: feat(kotlin): park object member calls for the cross-repo merge (#3388)
body:
### What

Park a Kotlin `Receiver.method()` call for the cross-repo merge when the object/class the receiver names is declared in another repository, so `merge-graphs` / `global add` can finish the edge (#3388).

### Rebased onto the landed cross-file resolver

When this PR was first opened it also added the in-repo cross-file resolver. That capability has since landed independently on `v8` as `_resolve_kotlin_member_calls` (#1698, cross-file object/class-qualified calls). This PR is now rebased to sit **on top of** that resolver and contribute only the missing piece: the cross-repo **parking**.

The landed resolver binds `Receiver.method()` only when the object is declared in the same build; a call into another repo was dropped with the receiver name already in hand, so nothing reached `graph.json` and no merge-time pass could recover it.

### Change (20 lines)

- `extract.py` — at the resolver's "declared nowhere here" bail-out, park the call by name via `_park_unresolved_member_call`, the same mechanism Java/C++/C#/Swift already use. Only when the object is declared nowhere (an ambiguous 2+ match still fabricates nothing); never for a builtin receiver.
- `cross_repo_calls.py` — add `kotlin: {.kt, .kts}` to `_LANG_SUFFIXES` so a parked Kotlin call is answered only by a Kotlin declaration, not a same-named type in another language.
- `tests/test_cross_repo_member_calls.py` — a `kotlin-object-receiver` case in the per-language end-to-end parametrize (real extraction → park → merge → edge).

### Verified

`tests/test_cross_repo_member_calls.py` green (20 passed, kotlin case runs), and the landed #1698 in-repo resolver tests stay green.

title: PHP: instance (`$g->m()`) member calls produce no edge across files, and nothing across repos
body:
## Net-new over v8 (verified against current v8 tip)

#3872 taught the PHP resolver to bind **scoped** calls — `Class::method()`,
`self::`, `static::`, `parent::` — to the actual method. Two gaps remain:

### 1. Instance calls stay unresolved

A call on a typed receiver is still dropped:

```php
// Greeter.php
class Greeter { public function greet(): void {} }

// App.php
class App {
    private Greeter $greeter;
    public function run(): void { $this->greeter->greet(); }   // no edge
}
```

`$this->greeter->greet()` / `$g->greet()` resolve to nothing — v8 routes a
`$var` receiver to its "dynamic scope" branch and gives up. The receiver's class
is written down (property, promoted ctor param, typed param, or `new`), so the
edge is recoverable. This is the PHP twin of the Swift gap in #1356.

### 2. Nothing crosses a repo boundary

Even once the receiver is typed, a class this build does not contain cannot be
resolved, and `php` is absent from `cross_repo_calls._LANG_SUFFIXES`, so the
parked entry (#3152) is never language-checked and the merge drops it.

## Scope

Resolution is by the receiver's declared type with the single-definition guard,
gated to the PHP interop family. An untyped, union, longer-chain or ambiguous
receiver produces no edge. The scoped `::` path from #3872 is unchanged.

PR: #3391

title: feat(php): resolve instance member calls through the receiver type and link them across repos
body:
## What

Extends the PHP member-call resolver that landed in #3872. That change made
`_resolve_php_member_calls` bind **scoped** `Class::method()` / `self::` /
`static::` / `parent::` calls to the actual method (EXTRACTED). This PR adds
the **instance** tier beside it and wires PHP into the cross-repo merge.

## Net-new over v8 (verified against current v8 tip)

v8 today:
- resolves scoped `::` calls (#3872);
- treats a `$var->method()` instance call as a dynamic scope and leaves it
  **unresolved** (its own test `test_instance_call_is_still_unresolved_no_regression`
  pins this as the deliberate scope boundary of #3872);
- does **not** list `php` in `cross_repo_calls._LANG_SUFFIXES`, so even a parked
  PHP entry is never language-checked and the cross-repo edge is dropped.

This PR:
1. **Instance receiver typing.** A per-file `_php_receiver_type_table` records
   `name -> TypeName` from typed properties (`private Greeter $g;`), promoted
   constructor params, typed parameters and `$g = new Greeter()`. The shared
   resolver looks the receiver up there, takes the single PHP declaration of
   that type, and emits the `calls` edge — **INFERRED** (0.85), since the type
   comes from the annotation, never the call site. The scoped `::` path is
   untouched and stays EXTRACTED.
2. **Interop-family gate.** The declaration index is corpus-wide, so a
   same-named class in another language would both answer the receiver and hide
   that no PHP file declares it. The index is gated to the PHP family.
3. **Cross-repo linking.** A receiver typed to a class declared nowhere in this
   build is parked (#3152); adding PHP's suffixes to `_LANG_SUFFIXES` lets the
   merge finish the call against the one declaration in another repo.

A receiver the table cannot type to exactly one class — untyped, union, longer
chain, two same-named classes — stays unresolved rather than guessing.

## Tests

- `tests/test_php_receiver_member_calls.py` — instance tier: property, promotion,
  typed param, `new` local, nullable; negatives for untyped / union / longer
  chain / ambiguous name; the cross-language parking case.
- `tests/test_php_static_call_resolution.py` — updated the #3872 boundary test to
  assert the instance call now resolves INFERRED (the limitation this PR lifts).
- `tests/test_cross_repo_member_calls.py` — a parked PHP call binds to the one PHP
  declaration in another repo, and not to a Java class of the same name.

title: Let builtin named member calls through to cross file resolution
body:
## What

`_LANGUAGE_BUILTIN_GLOBALS` is one union across every language, right for a bare call (`String(x)` really would become a god node) but wrong applied to a member call: `open` is a Python builtin and `Set` a JavaScript one, so `session.open()` in Swift or `_server.Set()` in C# was silently discarded outright — no same-file edge, but also no `raw_calls` entry, so cross-file resolution never got a chance to try it.

A member call carries a receiver, so it isn't the ambiguous case the union guards against. Lets it reach the existing `tgt_nid = None` deferral every receiver-typed resolver already uses for other cases, so it can only ever reach an edge through a guarded, receiver-typed resolver — never the unguarded bare-name path a real god node would need.

## Verified

- Python: `Session.open()` cross-file class-qualified call now resolves (EXTRACTED).
- Swift: reproduced the reporter's own real-world example directly — `AppleReadyStreamFinder.find -> RemuxPlayback.open` now resolves (INFERRED, via the field-typed receiver resolver).
- Same-file god-node guard still holds: `other.open()` does not bind to an unrelated same-file bare `open()` function, and a bare call to the actual builtin `open(...)` still produces no phantom edge.
- Full suite green, no regressions.

## Scope: `go.py`/`rust.py` intentionally not touched

The issue asks for the identical change in `extractors/go.py` (~L480) and `extractors/rust.py` (~L372) too. I traced where their `raw_calls` entries for member calls actually go: `extract.py`'s shared cross-file resolver skips **every** `is_member_call` entry unconditionally —

```python
# Skip member-call callees: obj.log() → "log" has no import evidence
# and collides with any top-level function named "log" in the corpus.
if rc.get("is_member_call"):
    continue
```

— regardless of builtin status, and neither Go nor Rust has a dedicated receiver-typed resolver the way Python (`_resolve_python_member_calls`), Java, C#, Swift, TypeScript, C++, and Objective-C do. Making the same edit there would be safe (it wouldn't reintroduce the god-node risk) but currently has **zero observable effect** on the final graph, since nothing downstream would ever consume the preserved `raw_calls` entry. Rather than ship an inert change, I left it out — worth revisiting once either language gets its own receiver-typed cross-file resolver.

Fixes #3381.

title: Go member calls resolve to nothing across files, and cannot cross a repo boundary at all
body:
## Net-new over v8 (verified @6478eb71, 0.9.80)

v8 today has no Go receiver typing at all: no `_resolve_go_member_calls` and no
`go_member_calls` registration in `graphify/extract.py`; `extractors/go.py` carries no
receiver name/type through `function_bodies` and stamps no `_callable`/`_callable_class`
on Go nodes; and `go` is absent from `_LANG_SUFFIXES` in `cross_repo_calls.py` (which
lists only cpp/csharp/java/swift). The recent member-call work on v8 is Python (#4198,
#2860), C# (#3797) and PowerShell (#4163) — none of it Go.

Still missing, and what the paired PR adds: resolve `recv.M()` through the receiver's
declared type to a method in another file, the `go.py` plumbing + `_callable_class`
markers that requires, and parking the call so a merged graph can finish it (#3152).
Fully net-new; nothing here is pre-empted.

---

## What happens

A Go method call on a receiver resolves only when the bare method name happens to
match a symbol declared in the caller's own file. Anything else produces no edge:

```go
// svc/greeter.go
package svc

type Greeter struct{}

func (g *Greeter) Greet() {}
```

```go
// svc/app.go
package svc

type App struct {
	greeter *Greeter
}

func (a *App) Run() { a.greeter.Greet() }   // no `calls` edge
```

`extract_go` reads the receiver's identifier and discards it unless it names an
imported package, so the shape Go dependency injection actually takes — a struct
field used from a method — contributes nothing to the call graph. The shared
cross-file pass then skips member callees outright (`obj.log()` → `"log"` has no
import evidence), and no `_resolve_go_*` resolver is registered to pick them up.
No test in the repo asserts that a cross-file Go receiver method call yields an
edge; `test_go_builtin_call_targets.py` states the omission explicitly.

Merging two repos loses the same edges for the same reason, plus one more: Go
nodes never carry the `_callable` / `_callable_class` markers (#2438), because
`extract_go` is the one extractor outside the tree-sitter engine and the engine is
the only place that stamps them. `link_cross_repo_member_calls` requires
`_callable_class` on the declaring type, so a Go type could not answer a parked
call even if one existed.

## What it should do

Bind the call through the receiver's declared type, as the Swift (#1356), C++
(#1547), ObjC (#1556) and C# (#1609) resolvers already do for their languages —
and when the type is declared nowhere in the build, park the call so a merged
graph can finish it (#3152).

Go writes the receiver's type down in four places, all of them cheap to read:

| shape | source |
|---|---|
| `type App struct { greeter *Greeter }` | struct field |
| `func (s *Server) M()` / `func f(g *Greeter)` | parameter |
| `var g Greeter` | var declaration |
| `g := Greeter{}` / `g := &Greeter{}` | composite literal |

The single-definition guard has to stay: a Go type node id folds in the package
directory, so two packages declaring `Greeter` are two nodes and without import
evidence neither one is the answer.

## Why it matters

Go is a backend language and services are split across repositories; the call
graph across that boundary is the reason to merge two graphs at all. Together with
the ObjC (#3384), TS/JS (#3386), Kotlin (#3388) and PHP (#3390) gaps, this covers
the languages a mobile-plus-backend org actually ships.

PR to follow.

title: Idea: token-budgeted connected subgraph retrieval for LLM context
body:
Hi! First of all, thanks for building Graphify! I came across the project recently and really like the idea of representing a codebase as an explicit knowledge graph rather than relying only on vector-based retrieval.

I maintain [SteinerPy](https://github.com/berendmarkhorst/SteinerPy), a Python package for Steiner tree problems and related graph optimization problems. Looking at Graphify's `graph.json` output made me wonder whether graph optimization could be useful for selecting the context that is eventually passed to an LLM.

### The idea

Suppose an agent asks a question about a large codebase. Graphify gives us a graph containing functions, classes, files, documentation, and their relations.

Each node could additionally be assigned:

* a **relevance score** for the current question;
* a **cost**, for example the number of tokens required to include the corresponding source fragment in the LLM context.

We could then select a connected subgraph that maximizes the relevance of the included information while respecting a fixed token budget.

In a simplified form:

$$
\max \sum_{v \in V} r_v x_v
$$

subject to

$$
\sum_{v \in V} c_v x_v \leq B,
$$

where $r_v$ is the relevance of node $v$, $c_v$ its token cost, and $B$ the available context budget, together with constraints requiring the selected nodes to form a connected subgraph.

This is closely related to the **budgeted maximum-weight connected subgraph problem**, for which SteinerPy already contains an implementation.

### Why connectivity might help

A simple alternative would of course be to take the $k$ most relevant nodes. The possible advantage of using the graph structure is that some information may not be particularly relevant on its own, but may be important for explaining how two highly relevant pieces of information are related.

For example:

```text
highly relevant function
        |
   helper function
        |
highly relevant test
```

The helper function may receive a relatively low relevance score and therefore be excluded by top-\(k\) retrieval. A connected-subgraph formulation can still include it if it is a useful and inexpensive connection between the other two nodes.

### Possible experiment

I think a small experiment could already show whether this is useful. For example, compare:

1. Graphify's current query/retrieval approach;
2. the top-\(k\) most relevant Graphify nodes;
3. a token-budgeted connected subgraph selected using SteinerPy.

All methods could receive exactly the same token budget, e.g. 4k, 8k, or 16k tokens. We could then compare both the number of tokens used and the quality of the resulting answer or coding task.

Importantly, I don't think this necessarily needs to become a dependency of Graphify. A first prototype could simply consume the existing `graph.json`, solve the selection problem externally, and map the selected nodes back to their source fragments.

Would you consider this useful for Graphify? If so, I would be happy to experiment with a small prototype. I am also curious whether you think this fits better as part of Graphify itself or as an external integration.

title: feat(go): resolve receiver-typed member calls, and park them across repos
body:
Fixes #3393. Follows the same two-commit shape as #3385 (ObjC), #3387 (TS/JS),
#3389 (Kotlin) and #3391 (PHP): the single-repo half first, then the park.

### Commit 1 — resolve Go member calls through the receiver's declared type

`extract_go` now exports a per-file `go_type_table` built from the four places a Go
receiver's type is written down: a struct field, a parameter (which covers the method
receiver `func (s *Server)`), `var x T`, and `x := T{}` / `x := &T{}`.
`_resolve_go_member_calls` looks the receiver up there, takes the single declaration of
that type, and emits the `calls` edge to its method.

It also stamps `_callable` / `_callable_class` on Go declarations. Go is the one
extractor outside the tree-sitter engine, so its nodes carried neither marker and were
invisible to every consumer that reads them off the node. Scoped check: the
indirect-call guard only consults them for `rc["indirect"]` entries, which Go never
produces, and `link_shared_type_declarations` additionally requires
`metadata.namespace`, which Go never sets — so nothing existing changes shape.

### Commit 2 — park the call when the type is in another repo

Parks the pair on the caller node and adds `"go": {".go"}` to the merge pass's
language guard.

### Design calls worth a look

- **The receiver travels as `member_receiver`, not `receiver`.** In this extractor
  `receiver` already means "imported package name", and — more importantly — the
  Swift/Python/Ruby member-call resolvers select on `is_member_call` plus `receiver`
  *without checking the language*. A Go name placed there would bind to their types in
  a mixed corpus. A key of its own is the precise fix; widening those three resolvers'
  gates is a separate change.
- **`s.logger.Log()` is read as a call on the `logger` field only when `s` is the
  enclosing method's own receiver.** This is the Go analogue of PHP's
  `$this->prop->method()`. The table is flat and file-scoped, so any other head could
  be a package or a variable whose type it cannot confirm; `p.greeter.Greet()` on a
  parameter stays unresolved on purpose.
- **Names are matched case-sensitively, unlike the sibling resolvers.** Go exports by
  capitalisation, so `Run` and `run` on one type are two different methods with two
  different visibilities. `cross_repo_calls._key` already preserves case and documents
  why, so both halves agree.
- **Go does not defer.** A member call reaches `raw_calls` only once the bare callee
  name misses in the caller's file, which is already the existing behaviour, so in-file
  resolution is byte-identical. `test_a_same_file_method_call_keeps_its_extracted_edge`
  pins that the pass neither downgrades nor doubles an in-file edge.
- **`confidence_score` is 0.85, not 0.8.** The rubric in `references/extraction-spec.md`
  is the discrete set {0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95}; same tier, a value the documented
  scale contains.
- **`.go` alone in the language guard.** Kotlin's set includes `.java` because the JVM
  classpath is one namespace; Go and Java share nothing, and a matching type name across
  a Go service and a Java service in one merge is a coincidence.
- **A single type name or nothing.** `Greeter` and `*Greeter` qualify; a slice, map or
  channel element is not the receiver of `x.M()`, and `pkg.Greeter` names a type no bare
  local name can stand for.

### Known costs

- `g := NewGreeter()` stays unresolved: typing it means reading the constructor's return
  type, which is a separate change.
- The type table is flat per file, so first binding wins across all four sources — a
  parameter named like a field in another function does not retype the field's calls.
  Pinned by `test_the_first_binding_of_a_name_wins`.
- Framework receivers on package-level values that no local table names remain
  unresolved, as before.

### Tests

`tests/test_go_receiver_member_calls.py`, 11 new cases — 5 positive shapes, 5 negatives
(constructor return, chain not rooted at the method's receiver, package-qualified type,
two packages declaring one name, first-binding-wins) and one that pins in-file
behaviour. 6 of them fail on `v8`. On the merge side, a `go-struct-field` arm in
`test_each_language_parks_the_call_and_the_merge_finishes_it`, plus a Go/Java negative
and a case-sensitivity negative.

Full suite: 5323 passed, 93 skipped, no regressions (`test_ollama_retry_cap.py`
deselected — it fails on `v8` too). `ruff` clean, no added line over 100 columns.

title: Rebuild watchdog's os._exit orphans a mid-task ProcessPoolExecutor worker
body:
## Summary

Filing separately from #3341, which is being closed as fixed by #3210. @Yo-TR's comment there (https://github.com/Graphify-Labs/graphify/issues/3341#issuecomment-5569597086) flagged a real, separate finding worth tracking on its own: when a git-hook rebuild watchdog fires while a ProcessPoolExecutor worker is still mid-task, os._exit(1) kills only the rebuild process itself. It skips every cleanup path, including the pool's own context-manager shutdown, so a worker that is still running becomes orphaned (reparented to PID 1 on POSIX) and keeps going unsupervised for as long as whatever it was doing takes. A worker stuck in catastrophic regex backtracking (the exact shape #3341 fixed) was observed surviving 2.5 days that way on macOS.

## Where

Both git-hook rebuild bodies in `graphify/hooks.py` (`_REBUILD_BODY_COMMIT`, `_REBUILD_BODY_CHECKOUT`) arm a `GRAPHIFY_REBUILD_TIMEOUT` watchdog. On platforms without `signal.SIGALRM`, the fallback is a `threading.Timer` whose callback calls `os._exit(1)` directly with no cleanup:

```python
def _bail():
    print(f'[graphify hook] graphify rebuild exceeded {_timeout}s', flush=True)
    os._exit(1)
```

`extract.py` already documents this exact risk for its own 1-worker special case (`# ...the parent's rebuild watchdog (os._exit) can orphan a worker that is mid-task`), but that only covers `max_workers == 1`; a real multi-worker pool spawned for a larger corpus is not covered.

## Suggested fix

Terminate any live worker processes before exiting, as @Yo-TR suggested. The watchdog fires on a separate timer thread with no reference to the pool object, but `multiprocessing.active_children()` enumerates every live worker process regardless of which thread asks. Kill (SIGKILL), not terminate (SIGTERM) — a worker stuck in a C-level call like regex backtracking never gets a chance to act on SIGTERM.

Environment (from the original report): graphifyy 0.9.53 → 0.9.55, CPython 3.14.7 (Homebrew), macOS 26 (Darwin 25.5.0).

title: Kill orphaned workers before the rebuild watchdog exits
body:
## What

`os._exit(1)`, used by the git-hook rebuild watchdog's SIGALRM-less fallback, terminates only the rebuild process itself — it skips every cleanup path, including a `ProcessPoolExecutor`'s own context-manager shutdown. A worker still running at the moment the watchdog fires is orphaned (reparented to PID 1 on POSIX) and keeps going unsupervised for as long as whatever it was doing takes.

`extract.py` already documents this exact risk for its own 1-worker special case (`max_workers == 1` deliberately falls back to sequential extraction in-process, specifically to avoid this), but that only covers that one case — a real multi-worker pool spawned for a larger corpus was not covered.

## Real-world trigger

Reported on #3341 (a ReDoS in the old TS import-type normalizer, since fixed by #3210): a worker stuck in catastrophic regex backtracking survived as an orphan pinning a CPU core for 2.5 days on macOS after the parent rebuild process exited.

## Fix

The watchdog fires on a separate timer thread with no reference to the pool object (it's a local variable deep in an unrelated call stack), but `multiprocessing.active_children()` enumerates every live worker process regardless of which thread asks. Kill them before exiting.

Verified `.kill()` (SIGKILL) actually terminates a worker stuck in exactly the reported failure mode — a process executing a long C-level `re.match()` call never returns control to the interpreter to check for a Python-level signal, so `.terminate()` (SIGTERM) would not have worked here; SIGKILL is enforced by the kernel unconditionally:

```
active children: [<SpawnProcess ... pid=97110 ...>]
killing (SIGKILL) 97110
97110 alive: False
```

Added an AST-based test (matching this file's existing convention for the embedded, shell-quoted hook bodies) verifying both rebuild bodies enumerate and kill live children in a statement that runs before `os._exit`, not after.

Fixes #3396.

title: OpenCode global install writes plugin and slash command to CWD instead of ~/.config/opencode/
body:
## Summary

Surfaced via automated review on #2727 (`_install_opencode_command`, adding the native `/graphify` slash command). A non-project (global, no `--project`) OpenCode install writes the plugin and the slash command to the current working directory's `.opencode/` instead of the documented `~/.config/opencode/`.

## Where

Both `_install_opencode_plugin` and `_install_opencode_command` in `graphify/install.py` document the intended global location in their own docstrings:

> OpenCode auto-loads every plugin file under .opencode/plugins/ (project) or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ (global) at startup

> Only a markdown file under .opencode/commands/ (or ~/.config/opencode/commands/ globally) becomes a /-menu entry

But every call site passes `Path(".")` for the non-project case instead of a `~/.config/opencode` base:

```python
_install_opencode_plugin(project_dir if project else Path("."))
_install_opencode_command(project_dir if project else Path("."))
```

`_OPENCODE_PLUGIN_PATH`/`_OPENCODE_COMMAND_PATH` also hardcode a leading `.opencode/` segment, which is right for a project-relative install (`<project_dir>/.opencode/plugins/graphify.js`) but wrong for the global case (should be `~/.config/opencode/plugins/graphify.js`, no extra `.opencode/` nesting) — so this needs more than just swapping the base path.

This predates #2709/#2727; the slash command PR just inherited the same pattern from its sibling function for consistency, since fixing it there would have meant reworking both functions across their several call sites in `install()`, `_agents_install`, `_agents_uninstall`, and `uninstall_all`.

## Fix

Likely needs `_install_opencode_plugin`/`_install_opencode_command` (and their uninstall counterparts) to take an explicit `project: bool` (or a pre-resolved base path) rather than always joining onto whatever `project_dir` they're handed, so the global case can correctly target `~/.config/opencode/` without the extra `.opencode/` segment, matching how `~/.config/opencode/skills/graphify/SKILL.md` is already resolved elsewhere in this file for the OpenCode skill itself.

title: Go: a package's type is fragmented into one node per file that declares a method on it
body:
## Net-new over v8 (verified @6478eb71, 0.9.80)

v8 has no Go decl/def fold: `graphify/extractors/resolution.py` has `_merge_decl_def_classes`
(C/C++/ObjC) but no `_merge_go_package_types`, and nothing collapses the per-file Go type
fragmentation before `_disambiguate_colliding_node_ids` salts the colliding ids by path.
The bug reproduces exactly as described below.

Still missing, and what the paired PR adds: `_merge_go_package_types`, invoked right after
`_merge_decl_def_classes` and before disambiguation, folding same-id bare-label `.go` type
nodes in one directory into a single node (declaration site wins; cross-directory
same-named packages and `_test.go` members excluded). Fully net-new.

---

## Summary

A Go type whose methods live in other files of the same package becomes **several nodes**, one
per file, each owning only the methods declared there. The declaring file's node owns none of
them. Every downstream single-definition guard then reads the set as an ambiguity and bails, so
an idiomatic multi-file package loses type-level resolution.

C/C++/ObjC hit the same id-collision between a header declaration and its impl and avoid this
through `_merge_decl_def_classes` (`graphify/extractors/resolution.py`), which folds the
collision *before* `_disambiguate_colliding_node_ids` splits it. Go has no equivalent.

## Reproducer

```
svc/a.go   package svc; type Server struct{}; func Run(srv *Server) { srv.Close() }
svc/b.go   package svc; func (s *Server) Close() {}
svc/c.go   package svc; func (s *Server) Save() {}
```

```
$ graphify extract svc/
```

Actual — three `Server` nodes, and the methods hang off two of them:

```
nodes labelled Server:
    ..._svc_a_go_svc_server | a.go
    ..._svc_b_go_svc_server | b.go
    ..._svc_c_go_svc_server | c.go
edges:
    a.go   -> Server    | contains
    Run()  -> Server    | references (parameter_type)
    Server -> .Close()  | method      <- the b.go node
    Server -> .Save()   | method      <- the c.go node
```

Expected — one `Server`, sourced at its declaration, owning both methods:

```
    svc_server | a.go
    a.go   -> Server   | contains
    Run()  -> Server   | references (parameter_type)
    Server -> .Close() | method
    Server -> .Save()  | method
```

## Why

`extract_go` mints the receiver's type node in **every** file that declares a method on it
(`graphify/extractors/go.py`, the `method_declaration` branch), keyed
`_make_id(pkg_scope, receiver_type)` where `pkg_scope` is the package directory's name. All those
nodes therefore share one id and differ only in `source_file` — which is exactly the input
`_disambiguate_colliding_node_ids` is built to split, so it salts each one with its own path.

## Impact

* `references` to the type land on whichever fragment the referring file produced, so a type's
  incoming uses and its methods are no longer reachable from one node.
* The id is salted with a file path, so it is neither the canonical `{pkg}_{type}` form nor
  stable across machines for the affected types.
* Every resolver that requires exactly one declaration of a name (member-call resolution, the
  Go type-reference rewire) bails, which is silent under-reporting rather than a visible error.

Splitting one Go type into two files is not an edge case; it is how any package larger than a
single file is written.

## Fix

Fold the id-collision before disambiguation, mirroring `_merge_decl_def_classes`. The nodes
already share an id, so no edge re-pointing is needed — only the redundant duplicates are
dropped and the declaring file's node survives.

Guards against a false merge: all members of the collision must be `.go` files in **one
directory** (the id folds in only the directory's *name*, so `a/svc` and `b/svc` collide while
being different packages), and a `_test.go` member stops the fold, since its package clause may
be the separate external `svc_test` package declaring a type of the same name — `extract_go`
does not parse the package clause, so same-directory is not evidence of same package there.

PR follows.

title: fix(go): fold a package's type into one node when its methods span files (#3399)
body:
Fixes #3399.

A Go type whose methods live in other files of the same package became several nodes, one per
file, each owning only the methods declared there — and the declaring file's node owning none of
them. `extract_go` mints the receiver's type in every file that declares a method on it, keyed
`_make_id(pkg_scope, receiver_type)`, so those nodes share one id and differ only in
`source_file`; `_disambiguate_colliding_node_ids` reads that as a collision between distinct
entities and salts each one with its own path.

## Change

One pass, `_merge_go_package_types`, run immediately after `_merge_decl_def_classes` and for the
same reason: before disambiguation, so it sees one `source_file` per id and leaves it alone. The
colliding nodes already share an id, so every edge already points at the survivor — only the
redundant duplicates are dropped, no edge moves.

The declaring file wins, identified as the only file with a `contains` edge to the type. When the
declaration lives outside the corpus the whole group is method-only; one node is still the
answer, so it folds on the lowest path.

## Guards against a false merge

* **One directory.** The id folds in only the directory's *name*, so `a/svc` and `b/svc` collide
  on id while being different packages. Those stay split, as today.
* **`_test.go` stops the fold.** Its package clause may be the separate external `svc_test`
  package declaring a type of the same name. `extract_go` derives `pkg_scope` from the directory
  and never parses the package clause, so same-directory is not evidence of same package there.
* **Bare type labels only.** A Go type name holds neither `.` nor `(`, while every other label
  the extractor mints does (`Run()`, `.Close()`, the file node's `a.go`), so a package whose
  helper function and a method share a name is untouched.

## Verification

Before, on the three-file package from the issue: three `Server` nodes, `.Close()` on the `b.go`
one and `.Save()` on the `c.go` one. After: one `svc_server` sourced at `a.go` owning both, with
the `parameter_type` reference from `Run()` pointing at it.

`tests/test_go_package_type_fold.py` — 6 tests: methods across files fold onto one owner; a
reference reaches the node that owns the methods; the declaring file survives a lower-sorting
method file; and the three guards above. The three positive tests fail on `v8` and pass here;
the guard tests pass both ways, pinning the no-regression half.

Full suite: 5315 passed, 93 skipped, `ruff check graphify tests` clean. The only failures in this
environment are the pre-existing `tests/test_ollama_retry_cap.py` ones (no `openai` module
installed), which fail identically on plain `v8`.

## Relation to #3395

Independent of it and based on `v8`. The Go member-call resolver added there needs exactly one
declaration of the receiver's type, so on a multi-file package it currently bails; this fold is
what lets it fire. Neither PR needs the other to land first.

title: CREATE POLICY is silently dropped from SQL graphs — grammar has no rule, and the ERROR fallback regex only covers FUNCTION/PROCEDURE
body:
### Summary

On a Postgres project that uses Row Level Security, **no policy ever becomes a
node**, and nothing warns you. On my repository that is 59 `create policy`
statements (45 distinct policy names) that exist in the source and are absent
from `graph.json`.

This matters more than a normal missing-node-type bug, because of *what*
policies are. In a Supabase/Postgres app the policy **is** the authorisation
rule — it is the answer to "who may read this row". A graph that silently omits
every policy will happily answer questions about access control, and it will
answer them wrong. A traversal that returns nothing reads as "no rule exists"
rather than "this tool cannot see rules".

Version: `graphify 0.9.48`, with `graphifyy[sql]` installed (`tree_sitter_sql`
importable).

### Root cause — two layers, and the first one is the real blocker

**1. The `tree-sitter-sql` grammar has no rule for `CREATE POLICY`.**

Parsing a migration containing seven policies produces no `create_policy` node
of any kind. The statements disintegrate into loose top-level tokens, plus an
`ERROR` node:

    L96    keyword_create
    L96    keyword_on
    L96    .
    L97    keyword_for      keyword_update      keyword_to
    L98    keyword_using    (  .  (  )  keyword_and  .  (  )  )
    L99    keyword_with     keyword_check  ( ... )
    L99    ;

So there is nothing for `walk()` in `extractors/sql.py` to dispatch on. Adding
an `elif t == "create_policy":` branch would not help — that node type is never
produced.

**2. The `ERROR` fallback in `extractors/sql.py` only rescues functions and
procedures.**

`sql.py` already knows the grammar gives up on PL/pgSQL and has a regex
recovery path for it:

    elif t == "ERROR":
        # tree-sitter-sql cannot parse PL/pgSQL CREATE FUNCTION/PROCEDURE
        # bodies (OUT/INOUT params, tagged dollar quotes, PERFORM, :=) and
        # emits an ERROR node instead, silently dropping the object.
        # Regex-scan the raw text as fallback ...
        for m in re.finditer(
            r"CREATE\s+(?:OR\s+REPLACE\s+)?(?:FUNCTION|PROCEDURE)\s+" ...

Policies land in exactly the same place — `ERROR` nodes and loose tokens — but
the alternation is `FUNCTION|PROCEDURE`, so they are dropped.

**3. `pg_introspect.py` (the `--postgres` path) does not cover it either.** It
queries `information_schema` tables/views/routines plus `pg_constraint`, and
never `pg_policy` — so live introspection has the same hole as static
extraction.

### Reproduce

```sql
-- policies.sql
create table public.employees (id uuid primary key, home_branch_id uuid);

create or replace function app.is_admin() returns boolean
  language sql stable as $$ select true $$;

create policy employees_select on public.employees
  for select to authenticated
  using (app.is_admin());

create policy employees_update on public.employees
  for update to authenticated
  using (app.is_admin()) with check (app.is_admin());

title: fix(extract): remove quadratic scan in TS import-type normalization (#3359)
body:
Fixes #3359.

## Root cause

Not a linearity-unsafe regex. Every `re.sub`/pattern in the extract path is linear — I benchmarked `textwrap.shorten`, `_TS_IMPORT_CALL_RE`, `_VUE_SCRIPT_RE` and the JS rescue patterns and none backtrack. The `_sre` frames in the reporter's `sample` output are the innermost frames of a quadratic **caller**.

`_normalize_ts_import_types` (the #3154 TypeScript `import(...)` normalizer) filters each regex match against every tree-sitter `type_arguments` byte range with a nested linear scan, in both passes:

```python
matches = [m for m in matches
           if not any(start <= m.start() < end for start, end in original_type_ranges)]
```

That is **O(matches × ranges)**, and `m.start()` is re-evaluated inside `any()` for every range — hence `re.Match.start` dominating profiles and `sample` appearing to indict a regex.

Both counts scale with file size in TypeScript that mixes generic calls (`fn<A, B>(x)` → one `type_arguments` range each) with `import(...)` types — the shape of generated and barrel modules in a large monorepo.

Measured on the filter alone:

| file | `import()` sites | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.8 MB | 10,000 | ~21 s | 0.003 s |
| 2.1 MB | 25,000 | ~2.6 min | 0.008 s |
| 4.2 MB | 50,000 | ~11.8 min | 0.019 s |

This accounts for every symptom in the report:

- **100% CPU with no open files** — all work is in-memory after the read.
- **Freeze point shifts with the file set** — content-triggered by a few large generated files, not by file count. Explains why `packages/` hangs while other top-level dirs and a 60-file repo finish.
- **`--max-workers 1` stalls *earlier*** (500/2469 vs ~2400/2470) — one worker reaches the pathological file sooner instead of ten racing past it first.
- **`--no-dedup`, 0.9.53 and 0.9.54 all reproduce** — the code is in the extract path and unchanged across those releases.

## Fix

Replace both scans with a binary search over start-sorted ranges plus a prefix-maximum of `end` values, so a lookup touches nesting depth instead of every range.

Type-argument ranges nest but never partially overlap, so the prefix maximum is a correct stop condition. The subtle part: a **closed inner sibling** must not terminate the leftward walk — a naive running-max break gets this wrong and silently drops enclosing ranges.

Normalization output is unchanged: byte-length and line-count preserving, identical masking decisions, and the runtime-vs-type disambiguation from 6baa5e0 still holds.

Also restores the emptiness guard in the second pass — the range list is now an index tuple, which is always truthy, so it checks the spans it holds rather than the container.

## Verification

- **500,000-case differential test** of the new lookup against the old predicate, including non-nested random ranges: zero mismatches.
- `_normalize_ts_import_types` scaling is now ~2× per doubling (was ~4×), linear out to 32k imports.
- Invariants re-checked: byte length, line count, TSX path, comparison-vs-generic ambiguity, comment/string literals untouched.
- New regression test asserts on **scaling** (2× input must not ~4× the time) rather than wall-clock, so it is not machine-dependent. It fails at ~3.4× before this change and passes after.

### Full-suite note

A whole-suite comparison against unmodified `c9f9901` shows 53 vs 61 failures, but the delta is environment flakiness on Windows, not this change:

- The diff lists 13 "new" failures **and 5 that disappeared** — a change confined to the TS normalizer cannot fix unrelated install tests.
- Every failure is in `serve_http` / `install*` / `hooks` / `watch`. None is in `extract`, `resolution`, or any TypeScript path, and no failing test references `_normalize_ts_import_types`, `_ts_ranges_containing`, `_ts_build_range_index`, or `_ts_type_argument_ranges`.
- The install tests are order- and state-dependent: the **same baseline code** produced 8 failures on one run then 3, 3, 3 on the next three, with no edits at all.
- Run head-to-head three times each on the same files, baseline and this branch are identical: 3 failed / 155 passed on every run.
- The 6 install/upgrade tests flagged as regressions all pass on this branch in isolation.

title: fix(sql): recover CREATE POLICY via regex fallback; add pg_policy introspection (#3401)
body:
Fixes #3401

## Problem
`CREATE POLICY` is silently dropped from SQL graphs. tree-sitter-sql's grammar
has no rule for it — policy statements disintegrate into loose tokens plus an
ERROR node, the same dead end CREATE FUNCTION/PROCEDURE bodies hit. The
existing ERROR-fallback regex in `extractors/sql.py` only covers
FUNCTION|PROCEDURE, so policies fall through with no node and no warning.
`pg_introspect.py`'s `--postgres` path has the same hole: it never queries
`pg_policy`.

## Fix
- **`graphify/extractors/sql.py`**: added `_POLICY_RECOVERY_RX`, a regex
  fallback (parallel to the existing routine-recovery regex) that runs inside
  the `root.has_error` path. Captures policy name, target table
  (schema-qualified), permissive/restrictive, command, roles, and the
  `USING`/`WITH CHECK` bodies. Each matched policy becomes a node with an
  `applies_to` edge to its table; function calls found in the USING/CHECK
  expressions become `references` edges.
- **`graphify/pg_introspect.py`**: added a `pg_catalog.pg_policy` query
  (joined to `pg_class`/`pg_namespace`, resolving `polqual`/`polwithcheck`
  via `pg_get_expr()` rather than regexing raw SQL) so live `--postgres`
  introspection reconstructs `CREATE POLICY` DDL and feeds it through the
  same pipeline as static extraction.
- **`tests/fixtures/policies.sql`**: repro fixture from the issue (one table,
  one function, two policies referencing it).
- **`tests/test_create_policy_snippet.py`**: asserts both policies land as
  nodes, each with an `applies_to` edge to `public.employees` and a
  `references` edge to `app.is_admin`.

## Review fixes
Addressed all three Copilot findings from initial review:
- Function nodes created by the routine-recovery fallback weren't registered
  in `table_nids`, so policy `references` edges always fell back to
  sourceless stub nodes instead of the real function node. Fixed by
  registering the function's id in `table_nids` at creation time.
- The `references`-edge loop could emit duplicate edges when the same
  function appeared in both `USING` and `WITH CHECK`. Fixed by deduping on
  normalized function name before emitting edges.
- `pg_introspect.py`'s DDL reconstruction quoted the `PUBLIC` pseudo-role as
  a literal identifier (`TO "public"`), which is invalid/incorrect DDL.
  Fixed to emit the bare `PUBLIC` keyword when the role is the default.

## Testing
uv sync --all-extras
uv run pytest tests/ -q -k "sql or policy" # 44 passed
uv run pytest tests/ -q # full suite; 1 known-flaky
# failure in test_labeling.py
# (unrelated to this PR —
# passes consistently in
# isolation, order-dependent
# under full-suite run)


## Notes
- Table/role names are schema-qualified where present (e.g. `public.employees`,
  `app.is_admin`) — matches how the extractor already treats other
  schema-qualified identifiers.
- No test added directly against `introspect_postgres`'s new policy-DDL
  generation (would need a live Postgres fixture); the static-extraction path
  is covered end-to-end via the shared DDL string.
- Branch was rebased onto current `upstream/v8` to drop unrelated Cursor
  install commits that were pulled in accidentally from the branch's original
  base.

title: fix(extract): emit imports edge for bare Lua require() statements (#3320)
body:
## Why

`graphify.extract._import_lua` only extracted an `imports` edge when a `require(...)` call appeared inside a `variable_declaration` (`local x = require("mod")`). The far more common Neovim/LazyVim idiom — a **bare** `require("mod")` statement with no assignment — produced **no edge at all**:

```lua
-- init.lua
require("config.lazy")
require("config.options")
require("config.keymaps")
```

A bare `require(...)` parses as a top-level `function_call`, which was not in `_LUA_CONFIG.import_types`, so the import handler never fired. Result: real Neovim configs graphed with almost no structure (e.g. a 14-file config produced 13 nodes but only 2 `contains` edges, zero imports).

## What changed

- Add `function_call` to `_LUA_CONFIG.import_types` so bare `require(...)` statements are dispatched to `_import_lua` (`graphify/extract.py`).
- Guard the new path in `_import_lua`: for a `function_call` node it only proceeds when the callee is the `require` global (AST `name` field), so `myrequire(...)`, a `require`-containing string literal (`print("require(x)")`), or a method call (`obj:require(...)`) do **not** mint a false import edge.
- The assigned form (`local x = require(...)`) is unchanged: it is a `variable_declaration`, and the engine returns after handling an import node, so its nested `function_call` is never re-dispatched — **no duplicate edge**.
- Call edges come from the separate `walk_calls` pass and are unaffected. The change is scoped to `_LUA_CONFIG` (Lua/`.luau`/`.toc` only).

## Why it's safe

Structure extraction in Lua only walks classes (none), `function_declaration` (a statement, never an expression argument), and imports — none of which live inside a `function_call`'s arguments. Verified empirically that base vs. branch output is byte-identical for `print(require("x"))`, `require("lazy").setup({})`, and callback-argument cases; the **only** behavioral difference is the intended bare-`require` import edge.

- `ruff check .` — clean
- `python -m tools.skillgen --check` — OK (no generated skill files touched)
- Full suite: **5479 passed, 14 skipped, 0 failed** (baseline v8 was 5475 passed, 0 failed; +4 new Lua tests)

## Test verification (RED → GREEN)

New test file `tests/test_lua_import_resolution.py`.

**RED** — on unmodified `v8` (fix reverted), the bare-require tests fail:

```
FAILED tests/test_lua_import_resolution.py::test_bare_require_statement_emits_import_edge
FAILED tests/test_lua_import_resolution.py::test_multiple_bare_requires_each_emit_an_edge
2 failed, 1 passed
```

**GREEN** — with the fix:

```
tests/test_lua_import_resolution.py ....                                 [100%]
4 passed in 0.29s
```

The `test_similarly_named_call_does_not_emit_import` and `test_assigned_require_still_emits_exactly_one_edge` cases lock in the no-false-positive and no-duplicate guarantees.

Fixes #3320

title: Python: module.attr() calls unresolved, and nested functions resolved to unrelated files as EXTRACTED/1.0
body:
Two Python call-resolution defects, found while indexing a 602-file polyglot monorepo with v0.9.56. They are separate bugs but share a root cause: call targets appear to be matched on bare name against a global symbol table, without consulting the importing module's namespace or the enclosing lexical scope.

The second is the more serious. It produces **wrong edges labelled `EXTRACTED` with `confidence_score: 1.0`**, which is worse than a missing edge, because nothing downstream can distinguish it from a real one.

Corpus: 602 code files → 3477 nodes, 6221 edges. `graphify extract . --code-only` (no LLM), Python 3.14, Windows. Paths below are anonymised; the shapes are verbatim.

---

## 1. `import module` + `module.func()` calls are never resolved

`from mod import func` → `func()` resolves correctly. `import mod` → `mod.func()` produces **no edge at all**.

```python
# pkg_a/collect.py
def q(conn, sql): ...      # returns tuples
def qd(conn, sql): ...     # returns dicts

# pkg_a/store.py
import collect
rows = collect.qd(conn, sql)          # line 119

# pkg_a/waker.py
import collect
rows = collect.q(conn, SIGNALS_SQL)   # line 103
```

`graphify explain` on `qd()` reports degree 2 — its `contains` edge and a docstring `rationale_for` edge. The call from `store.py` is absent. `q()` shows only its one same-file caller and misses both cross-module ones.

This is not a general cross-file failure: **331 of 2476 `calls` edges (13%) are cross-file and correct.** The split is exactly import style. In this corpus one package uses `from x import y` throughout and its call graph is good; a second uses `import x` + `x.y()` and its cross-module edges are essentially all missing.

Why it is easy to miss: "what calls this?" is the question the graph exists to answer, and a package where resolution fails returns *nothing* rather than an error. A function with no callers looks like a leaf, not like a gap.

## 2. Nested functions resolve to same-named module-level functions in unrelated files

This one manufactures edges that do not exist.

```python
# pkg_b/probe.py
def trace(...):
    def walk(n, d=0):     # line 53 — nested, local to trace()
        ...
    walk(root)
```

There is exactly one *module-level* `walk` in the corpus, in an unrelated tree:

```python
# pkg_c/overlay.py
def walk(node, path=""):   # line 74
```

GRAPH_REPORT.md promotes the collision into the **"Surprising Connections (you probably didn't know these)"** section:

```
- `trace()` --calls--> `walk()`  [INFERRED]
  pkg_b/probe.py → pkg_c/overlay.py
```

The two files share no import, no package and no call path. The nested `walk` shadows everything else; the local definition should win unconditionally.

A second entry in the same section is worse, because it is not even marked inferred:

```
- `parse_date()` --references--> `_date()`  [EXTRACTED]
  pkg_d/deadlines.py → pkg_b/grid.py
```

`pkg_d/deadlines.py` imports only stdlib, `requests`, and one local config module. `_date` is defined only in `pkg_b/grid.py`. There is no relationship of any kind. The edge carries `confidence: EXTRACTED`, `confidence_score: 1.0`.

**Of the five entries in "Surprising Connections" on this corpus, we could not verify a single one as real.** Because that section is framed as insight rather than as a guess, name collisions in a polyglot monorepo surface there as confident discoveries — and short generic names (`walk`, `main`, `trace`, `diff`, `esc`, `_date`) are exactly the ones that collide.

---

## Suggested fixes

1. **Resolve `module.attr()` through the import table.** The `imports` edges are already correct and 100% cross-file, so the alias→module binding is present — it just is not consulted when resolving a dotted call.
2. **Scope-check before falling back to global name matching.** If a name is bound by a `def`/`lambda`/assignment in an enclosing scope, resolve there and stop.
3. **Never emit a cross-file edge as `EXTRACTED` / 1.0 on a bare name match alone.** If resolution came from a global name table with no import path connecting the two files, it is by definition inferred, and low confidence. Gating "Surprising Connections" on the existence of an import path between the two files would have removed all five false positives here.

Reproduces every time on this corpus; happy to test a patch.

title: C#: an unqualified generic call (`Get<T>(...)`, `this.Get<T>(...)`) drops its `calls` edge
body:
## Summary

In C#, a call with an explicit type argument and **no receiver** never gets a `calls` edge, even
when the target method is declared on the caller's own class or on its base class. The
non-generic spelling of the same call resolves normally, so the type-argument list at the call
site is the whole trigger.

Measured on **v0.9.56**, the current release (published 2026-09-07). v0.9.55 behaves identically.

## Reproducer

Three files, no corpus, no build needed. `dotnet build` on net8.0: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

```csharp
// Settings.cs
namespace Demo
{
    public class Settings
    {
        public T Get<T>(string key) { return default(T); }   // target
        public string GetRaw(string key) { return key; }     // control target
    }
}

// Reader.cs
namespace Demo
{
    public class Reader : Settings
    {
        public int A() { return Get<int>("port"); }        // 1) no edge
        public int B() { return this.Get<int>("port"); }   // 2) no edge
        public string C() { return GetRaw("host"); }       // 3) edge
        public string D() { return this.GetRaw("host"); }  // 4) edge
    }
}

// Local.cs
namespace Demo
{
    public class Local
    {
        public T Make<T>() { return default(T); }
        public int E() { return Make<int>(); }             // 5) no edge, same class
    }
}
```

```
graphify extract src --code-only --no-cluster --out out
```

| # | Call site | v0.9.56 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Get<int>("port")` — unqualified, generic, target on base class | **no edge** |
| 2 | `this.Get<int>("port")` — same through `this` | **no edge** |
| 3 | `GetRaw("host")` — control, unqualified, non-generic | edge |
| 4 | `this.GetRaw("host")` — control, through `this` | edge |
| 5 | `Make<int>()` — unqualified, generic, target on the same class | **no edge** |

**2 of 5.** All five target member nodes exist in the graph, and `method`/`inherits` edges are
correct — only the call-site-to-member match fails. Case 5 shows inheritance is not involved.

## Expected

Cases 1, 2 and 5 should produce a `calls` edge to `.Get()` / `.Make()`, exactly as the
non-generic controls 3 and 4 do. The type-argument list is not part of the method's identity.

## Where it happens (v0.9.56, `graphify/extractors/engine.py`; identical in v0.9.55)

* **`:5389`** `elif fn_node is not None and fn_node.type == "identifier":` — for `Get<int>("port")`
  tree-sitter gives the `function` field as a `generic_name`, not an `identifier`, so this branch
  is skipped. Control flow falls into the generic fallback at **`:5391-5408`**, which takes the
  node text verbatim (`callee_name = raw` at **`:5407`**) and so assigns
  `callee_name = "Get<int>"`.
* **`:5365`** `callee_name = _read_text(mname, source)` — for `this.Get<int>("port")` the `name`
  field of the `member_access_expression` is a `generic_name`, so `callee_name` becomes
  `"Get<int>"`.
* In both cases the member index is keyed on the bare declared name, the lookup misses, and the
  edge is dropped silently.

**What makes this worth one small change:** a few lines further down, at **`:5409` and following**,
the very same call node is walked *structurally* to emit the `references[generic_arg]` edges added
in #2911 — the code descends into `generic_name` and reads its `type_argument_list` properly. So
v0.9.56 already recognises these call sites as generic and already records what they instantiate;
only the callee name a few lines above is still taken as raw text. The comment on that block says
so itself: "the fallback path uses raw text and never sees the structured type-arg list".

## Relation to existing reports — deliberately not a duplicate

#2624 (open) reports the **qualified** form, `Registry.Fetch<Payload>()` and
`Bag<Payload>.Make()`, and its reproducer contains only those. The unqualified forms appear nowhere in
that issue's reproducer; they were mentioned in passing in one comment on it, and demonstrated in
a comment on PR #2676. This report is about those forms only, with its own reproducer, its own
prevalence count, and — for the receiverless form — its own code path: `:5389` and the fallback,
which #2624's reproducer never reaches. (The `this.`-spelling shares `:5365` with it.)

PR #2676, open since 2026-08-12, strips the type-argument list from the call-site name; measured
locally against v0.9.56 it also resolves cases 1, 2 and 5 above. It is not part of any release,
so the behaviour described here is what v0.9.56 does today.

#2911 (type arguments at the call site) and #2913 (the same in field position) are closed and
their effect is in the release — the engine comment at `:5409` names both. The unqualified
`calls` edge is what is left.

## Scope

Counted on the syntax tree (not by regex) over a ~15,300-file C# estate, mixed .NET Framework and
net8: **2159** unqualified generic call sites and **628** spelled through `this`. Those are
occurrences of the shape, **not** confirmed lost edges — unlike the qualified form, whose targets
are frequently outside the corpus, these resolve against the caller's own class or a base class,
so their targets are in-corpus by construction. I am reporting the shape's prevalence, not
claiming a number of lost edges.

The three files above are the whole reproducer -- no corpus, no build step, and the
behaviour is reproducible from the PyPI release alone.

title: Symbol node IDs collide across directories; walk order decides the winner, so output is not reproducible across filesystems
body:
## Summary

Symbol node IDs are not path-qualified, so same-named symbols in different directories collapse into a single node. Which of the colliding definitions survives depends on filesystem walk order, because `detect()` never sorts its file list. The result is twofold:

1. **Silent data loss** — one of the definitions disappears from the graph entirely.
2. **Non-reproducible output** — the same commit produces a different `graph.json` on ext4 (Linux CI) than on APFS (macOS), so any workflow that hashes or commits Graphify artifacts can only pass on one platform at a time.

Verified on `graphifyy==0.5.6`.

## Reproduction

Two Next.js-style apps, each with the conventional `app/layout.tsx` exporting `RootLayout`:

```bash
mkdir -p demo/apps/admin/app demo/apps/reference-book/app && cd demo
for app in admin reference-book; do cat > apps/$app/app/layout.tsx <<'EOF'
export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return <html><body>{children}</body></html>;
}
EOF
done
graphify update .
python3 -c "
import json
g = json.load(open('graphify-out/graph.json'))
for n in g['nodes']: print(f\"{n['id']:32} {n.get('source_file')}\")
"
```

Actual — 3 nodes; `apps/admin`'s `RootLayout` is gone:

```
admin_app_layout_tsx             admin/app/layout.tsx
app_layout_rootlayout            reference-book/app/layout.tsx
reference_book_app_layout_tsx    reference-book/app/layout.tsx
```

Expected: 4 nodes, one `RootLayout` per file. Note the file-level IDs *are* path-derived and unique; only the symbol-level ID collides.

## Root cause

**Collision.** `extract._make_id` builds symbol IDs from `_file_stem(path)` plus the symbol name, and `_file_stem` qualifies only with the immediate parent directory:

```python
def _file_stem(path: Path) -> str:
    """Return a stem qualified with the parent directory name to avoid ID collisions
    when multiple files share the same filename in different directories (#550)."""
    parent = path.parent.name
```

So `apps/admin/app/layout.tsx` and `apps/reference-book/app/layout.tsx` both yield `app_layout_rootlayout`. One parent directory is not enough qualification for framework conventions that repeat the same path suffix per package — `app/layout.tsx`, `app/page.tsx`, `app/api/*/route.ts` in Next.js, and the equivalents in most monorepo layouts.

**Which one wins.** `graphify/build.py` documents that cross-file dedup is last-write-wins:

> Between files (build): NetworkX `G.add_node()` is idempotent — calling it twice with the same ID overwrites the attributes with the second call's values. Nodes are added in extraction order.

And extraction order is unsorted. `detect.detect()` (`detect.py:362`) accumulates `all_files` from a bare `os.walk` with no sort:

```python
for dirpath, dirnames, filenames in os.walk(scan_root, followlinks=follow_symlinks):
    ...
    for fname in filenames:
        p = dp / fname
        if p not in seen:
            seen.add(p)
            all_files.append(p)
```

`os.walk` yields raw directory order — ext4 htree hash order on Linux, b-tree order on APFS. (`extract._discover_files` *does* `sorted(results)`, which is why this is easy to miss.)

## Impact

Measured on `elnc-tech/logis`, a Next.js/Turborepo monorepo (~3,900 source files, 13,658 code nodes). The *identical* source tree, extracted on macOS/APFS and in a `node:20-bookworm` container/overlayfs:

| `source_file` prefix | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|
| `apps/admin` | 1795 | 1793 |
| `apps/webapp` | 5121 | 5088 |

Total node count matches; ~30 nodes are attributed to a different app depending on the filesystem. Sorting the walk changes the distribution again (admin 1699 / webapp 5182), which shows how many nodes are decided by ordering rather than by content.

## Suggested fix

Path-qualifying symbol IDs is the real fix — derive them from the full repo-relative path rather than just the parent directory, or fall back to a longer path prefix when a candidate ID is already taken. That removes both the silent loss and the ordering sensitivity at once.

Sorting the walk (`filenames.sort()` / `dirnames.sort()` in `detect.detect`, or `sorted(all_files)`) is worth doing regardless — it makes output reproducible and costs nothing — but on its own it only makes the loss *deterministic*, not absent.

## Workaround

For anyone hitting the reproducibility half of this before a fix lands: a `sitecustomize.py` on `PYTHONPATH` that wraps `os.walk` to sort in place is enough to make `graph.json` byte-identical across platforms. Sorting `dirnames`/`filenames` in place preserves `os.walk`'s contract that callers may prune `dirnames`.

```python
import os

_ORIGINAL_WALK = os.walk

def _sorted_walk(*args, **kwargs):
    for dirpath, dirnames, filenames in _ORIGINAL_WALK(*args, **kwargs):
        dirnames.sort()
        filenames.sort()
        yield dirpath, dirnames, filenames

os.walk = _sorted_walk
```

With that in place the same tree produced identical `graph.json`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md` and downstream artifact hashes on macOS (Python 3.13) and Linux (Python 3.11, container).

title: JS: `this.X = function` is extracted only inside a function *declaration* — every function-expression form drops it (incomplete fix of #1322)
body:
**Title:** JS: `this.X = function` is extracted only inside a function *declaration* — every function-expression form drops it (incomplete fix of #1322)

### Summary

#1322 listed `this.x = function(){}` "inside any function body" and was closed. In 0.9.56 only one enclosing form works: a named function **declaration**. If the enclosing function is an expression — assigned to a const, an arrow, an IIFE, or a callback argument — the member is silently dropped.

The callback-argument case is the AngularJS service pattern, so an AngularJS frontend extracts to file nodes only.

### Repro

```js
// p2.js
function DeclFn(){ this.inDecl = function(){ return 1; }; }
const AnonToConst = function(){ this.inAnonConst = function(){ return 2; }; };
const ArrowToConst = () => { this.inArrow = function(){ return 3; }; };
callIt(function(){ this.inCallbackArg = function(){ return 4; }; });
(function(){ this.inIIFE = function(){ return 5; }; })();
```

`graphify update .` produces:

```
.inDecl()        <-- only this one
AnonToConst()
ArrowToConst()
DeclFn()
p2.js
```

| enclosing function | result |
|---|---|
| `function DeclFn(){}` declaration | extracted |
| `const A = function(){}` | **missing** |
| `const A = () => {}` | **missing** |
| `callIt(function(){})` | **missing** |
| `(function(){})()` | **missing** |

### Framework form this hits

```js
angular.module('myApp').service('$thingService', function ($rootScope, $http) {
	this.loadThing = function (id) { /* ... */ };
	this.saveThing = function (thing) { /* ... */ };
});
```

A service file with 16 such members yields 0 nodes for them. A named `function foo(){}` declared inside the same callback **is** extracted, so the callback body is walked — only the `this.X` assignment is dropped.

### Expected

A node per member, contained by the enclosing function, in every enclosing form. Per #3338, `_js_member_assignment_target` materializes only `exports.X` and `Foo.prototype.X` and other receivers are dropped by the #1077 guard, so `this` inside a function expression may just need adding to that allowlist alongside the `window`/`globalThis` work.

### Impact

Measured on one private AngularJS + PHP codebase, 0.9.56, fully rebuilt:

| layer | files | nodes | avg/file | contributing only the file node |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PHP class layer | 844 | 7913 | 9.4 | 1 (0%) |
| AngularJS frontend | 661 | 1053 | 1.6 | **573 (87%)** |

The class layer extracts essentially completely. The frontend is opaque below file level, so the graph cannot answer "where is this behaviour implemented" for any of it.

### Related

#1322 (closed, declaration case only), #2419/#2433 (object-literal shorthand), #3337/#3338 (`window`/`globalThis` receiver). Same family, different receiver and enclosing form.

### Environment

graphify 0.9.56, macOS 15 (arm64), installed via `uv tool install graphifyy`.

title: PHP: closures produce no nodes in any position — assigned, arrow, or passed as an argument
body:
**Title:** PHP: closures produce no nodes in any position — assigned, arrow, or passed as an argument

### Summary

The PHP extractor nodes named functions and class methods, but no closure form produces a node. This differs from JS/TS, which nodes `const f = function(){}`. The practical effect is that closure-based routing layers (Slim, Laravel) are absent from the graph.

### Repro

```php
<?php
function namedFn() { return 1; }
$assigned = function () { return 2; };
$arrowAssigned = fn() => 3;
$app->get('/route-a', function ($req, $res) { return 4; });
$app->group('/g', function ($group) {
    $group->post('/route-b', function ($req, $res) { return 5; });
});
class C { public function method() { return 6; } }
```

`graphify update .` produces exactly:

```
.method()
C
namedFn()
p.php
```

**Missing:** `$assigned`, `$arrowAssigned`, and both route handlers.

### Observed vs expected

- **Observed:** no node for any closure, so nothing connects a route to the services its handler calls.
- **Expected:** at minimum, a node for a closure assigned to a variable, matching the JS `const f = function(){}` behaviour. For a closure passed as a call argument, a node contained by the file, ideally labelled from the call, would make route handlers addressable.

The constructs are `anonymous_function_creation_expression` and `arrow_function`, in both assignment and argument positions.

### Impact

Measured on one private Slim 4 codebase, 0.9.56, fully rebuilt:

| layer | files | nodes | avg/file | contributing only the file node |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PHP class layer | 844 | 7913 | 9.4 | 1 (0%) |
| Route files (closure handlers) | 219 | 240 | 1.1 | **207 (95%)** |

One route file with 17 registrations and 0 named functions yields 1 node. Classes extract completely, so no query can traverse from an HTTP endpoint into the service layer behind it.

### Related

The JS counterpart of the argument-position case is filed separately. No existing PHP issue covers closures — #1682 and #2615/#2617 concern member-call resolution, #3024 concerned interfaces/traits/enums.

### Environment

graphify 0.9.56, PHP 8.2 / Slim 4 codebase, macOS 15 (arm64), installed via `uv tool install graphifyy`.

title: Fix Python nested function call resolution
body:
## Summary

Fixes Python nested-function extraction and lexical call resolution for issue #3405.

### Changes

- Extract nested Python functions as proper Graphify function nodes.
- Add `contains` edges between parent and nested functions.
- Resolve unqualified calls using lexical scope.
- Correctly handle nested-function shadowing of module-level functions.
- Support nested sibling calls, recursion, async nested functions, and deeper nesting.
- Prevent local non-callable variables from being incorrectly emitted as unresolved calls.

### Tests

Added coverage for:

- Nested function extraction and node IDs
- Parent → nested `contains` relationships
- Outer → nested function calls
- Lexical shadowing
- Nested sibling calls
- Recursive nested functions
- Async nested functions
- Deeply nested functions
- Local non-callable suppression

Existing Python, confidence-rubric, and JavaScript nested-function tests also pass.

Issue: #3405

title: Incremental extract wipes PackageReference/TargetFramework nodes and edges of every .csproj referenced from a re-extracted .sln / .csproj (cross-file stub nodes pollute build_merge's replace-set)
body:
## Summary

On an incremental `graphify extract`, every `.csproj` that is merely *referenced* from a re-extracted `.sln` (or from a re-extracted `.csproj` via `ProjectReference`) is treated by `build_merge` as if it had been re-extracted itself. Its existing AST-tier nodes and edges (project node, `nuget_*` PackageReference nodes, `framework_*` TargetFramework nodes, their `imports`/`references` edges) are dropped, and only the bare cross-file stub node comes back. The manifest still stamps those `.csproj` files as unchanged, so the loss persists until a full `--force` rebuild.

## Environment

- graphifyy 0.9.56 (same code in 0.9.53 and 0.9.55), Linux, Python 3.13
- C# monorepo: 1 `.sln`, 416 `.csproj`, ~11 000 files
- nightly `graphify extract <repo> --backend foundry --no-viz --out <dir>` (incremental)

## Symptom

Counts taken from the dated `graphify-out/<date>/graph.json` backups of the same repo:

| graph.json | nodes | `nuget_*` nodes | `imports` edges whose `source_file` is a `*.csproj` |
|---|---|---|---|
| full rebuild (`--force --code-only`) | 105 775 | 129 | 2 121 |
| next incremental run (`PD3.sln` changed) | 105 598 | **1** | **33** |
| earlier full rebuild | 102 634 | 131 | 1 816 |
| +1 incremental (a few `.csproj` with `ProjectReference` changed) | 102 827 | 84 | 1 707 |
| +2 incremental (`PD3.sln` changed) | 104 184 | **4** | **77** |

Each such run also prints hundreds of

```
[graphify] note: node 'src_..._csproj' was extracted twice from 'src/.../X.csproj' under different labels — keeping 'X', dropping 'X.csproj'.
```

and `[graphify] Replaced 1650 node(s) from re-extracted source file(s).` although only ~100 files changed. In our case the resulting net shrink happened to coincide with an LLM omission in the semantic pass, so the #3203/#3105 shrink guard refused the write and the nightly job failed; on an ordinary night the wipe is written silently (`force=True` on the incremental path).

## Cause

1. `graphify/extractors/sln.py` (~L52–57) emits one node per solution project with `"source_file": abs_proj` — the absolute path of the **referenced** `.csproj`, not the `.sln` being extracted. The `ProjectReference` branch of the csproj extractor in `graphify/extract.py` (~L5005–5015) does the same (`"source_file": abs_ref`).
2. `build_merge` in `graphify/build.py` (~L1785–1800) derives the replace-set `new_ast_sources` from `n["source_file"]` of **every node** in `new_chunks` (raw and `_norm_source_file`-relativised).
3. Therefore every project referenced from the re-extracted `.sln` / `.csproj` becomes a "re-extracted AST source"; `_kept()` drops all of its existing AST-tier nodes and edges, and the chunk only re-adds the stub node (same id, label `X.csproj` → the "extracted twice" note). The manifest entry of the referenced `.csproj` is not touched, so nothing re-extracts it later.

## Minimal repro

```
repo/
  A.sln          # lists projects A and B
  A/A.csproj     # 2 PackageReference, 1 TargetFramework
  B/B.csproj     # ProjectReference ../A/A.csproj
```

1. `graphify extract . --no-viz` → `nuget_*` / `framework_*` nodes and `A.csproj → nuget` edges are present.
2. Edit `A.sln` only (reorder a line or add a comment) so that just the `.sln` is re-extracted.
3. `graphify extract . --no-viz` → `A.csproj`'s `nuget_*` / `framework_*` nodes and their edges are gone; `manifest.json` still lists `A/A.csproj` as unchanged.

The same happens when step 2 edits `B.csproj` instead of the `.sln` (the `ProjectReference` stub carries `source_file = A/A.csproj`).

## Suggested fix

- Derive the replace-set from the file each chunk was actually extracted from (the extractor's own `path`), not from per-node `source_file`; **or**
- mark cross-file stub nodes (e.g. `"_stub": True` / `"_origin": "ref"`) in `extract_sln` and the `ProjectReference` branch and skip them when building `new_ast_sources` — the AST-tier mirror of the #2926 scoping already applied to the semantic tier.

Either way a stub node must never make an un-dispatched file count as re-extracted.

## Workaround we use meanwhile

Before each incremental run we remove the `*.csproj` / `*.sln` entries from `manifest.json`, so every project file is re-parsed each run (cheap XML) and its fresh nodes are in the same chunks as the stubs. This restores the NuGet/project-dependency layer on every run, at the cost of the "extracted twice" / "minted by two different files" noise.

title: #3203 unverified-semantic-shrink guard has no verification path: a legitimately edited doc that yields fewer nodes fails every incremental run when the graph is net smaller (re-run reproduces it; only --allow-partial clears it)
body:
## Summary

The #3203 "unverified semantic shrink" guard arms `_extraction_incomplete` whenever a re-dispatched semantic source yields strictly fewer nodes than before. When the whole graph is also smaller (any legitimate deletion elsewhere), the write is refused (`force=False` path) and there is **no way to verify the shrink**: re-running reproduces it deterministically, so an unattended incremental pipeline fails night after night until a human passes `--allow-partial`. A doc that was *edited* (content hash changed) is expected to change its node count, so that case should not count as "unverified".

## Environment

graphifyy 0.9.56, Linux, Python 3.13, `graphify extract <repo> --backend foundry --no-viz --out <dir>` (incremental, nightly), C# monorepo ~11 000 files, ~106 000 nodes.

## What happened (real run, today)

1. A 4-line edit landed in `.agents/skills/pd-be-crw/feedback.md` (a 13 KB markdown ledger). The previous extraction of that file had produced 8 semantic nodes.
2. Incremental run: the model returned 1 node for the edited file →
   ```
   [graphify extract] semantic extraction is incomplete: unverified semantic shrink detected for '.agents/skills/pd-be-crw/feedback.md' (8 -> 1 nodes). The shrink guard stays armed for this write; pass --allow-partial to overwrite a larger existing graph anyway.
   [graphify] WARNING: new graph has 106216 nodes but existing graph.json has 106223 (net -7). Refusing to overwrite. ...
   [graphify extract] error: extraction was incomplete (an AST/semantic pass failed) and the resulting graph is smaller than the existing .../graph.json. Refusing to overwrite a complete graph with a partial one. Re-run after fixing the failures, or pass --allow-partial to overwrite anyway.
   ```
   Exit 1, manifest left unstamped (correct so far).
3. Immediate re-run (the "Re-run after fixing the failures" advice): the semantic cache for that file was cleared, the model was asked again and again returned 1 node → identical refusal. Nothing on the user side can "fix the failure": the file simply describes fewer entities now (or the model is consistently terser about it), and a net −7 on a 106 k graph is not a partial extraction.

The same guard class also fired last night from the sibling path (`1/29 dispatched file(s) produced no nodes` — model omission), where a re-run did help. The shrink variant is the problematic one because it is reproducible.

## Why this hurts

`_handle_unverified_semantic_shrink` (cli.py ~L182) offers only two outcomes: arm the guard, or `--allow-partial`. On an automated incremental pipeline `--allow-partial` is a blunt instrument (it also stamps genuinely omitted/failed files as done), so operators end up either failing nightly or always passing it — both defeat the purpose of the guard.

## Suggested fix

Treat a semantic shrink as **verified** (do not arm the guard) when any of these hold:

1. The source's content hash changed since the prior extraction (the file was edited → a different node count is expected). Only an *unchanged* file that suddenly yields fewer nodes is suspicious (pure model variance / hollow response).
2. The fresh extraction is a genuine model response (not hollow, not truncated, file present in `covered_files`) **and** the shrink is bounded, e.g. the file still yields ≥1 node — hollow/omitted files are already covered by `uncovered_files` and `_partial_source_files`.
3. Optionally: a second consecutive fresh extraction agrees (two independent responses with the same lower count = verified), so "re-run" actually becomes a fix path.

A narrower alternative: only arm the guard for the shrink when the *total* graph shrink exceeds the sum of the flagged files' own losses (i.e. something beyond those files was lost). In the run above the total shrink (−7) equals the file's own loss (8 → 1), so nothing else was lost and the write should proceed.

## Workaround we use

Our nightly wrapper retries `extract` once (helps the omission variant) and, if it fails again, runs it a third time with `--allow-partial`, relying on our own 90 % node-count floor and on the #2543/#2927 heal re-queues to recover omitted files later. We would much rather not need `--allow-partial` on an automated path.
