title: JS/TS: npm package subpath imports (next/image, next/link) produce no edge, while bare imports of the same package resolve
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.62 (PyPI) · Python 3.13.3 · macOS (darwin) · TypeScript extractor (tree-sitter)

## Summary

A static import of an npm package **subpath** (`next/image`, `next/link`) produces no edge at all, while a **bare** import of the same package (`next`) resolves correctly to the `package.json` node.

The importing file keeps its node, so nothing looks wrong — the file is simply disconnected from the framework it depends on. `graphify query "what uses next/image?"` returns nothing, with no warning.

This is a big blind spot for Next.js / React codebases, where `next/image`, `next/link` and `next/navigation` carry most of the framework coupling. In a real 327-node Next.js site I measured **21 dropped import edges** across 7 subpaths (`next/link` ×10, `next/navigation` ×3, `next/server` ×2, `next/image` ×2, `next/headers` ×2, `next/og` ×1, `next/font/google` ×1).

Note this is *not* the same as #3084, which reports that **bare** static imports also dangle — on 0.9.62 the bare case works (verified below), so that half appears to have been fixed since 0.9.39. The subpath case remains.

## Minimal reproduction

Three files in an empty directory:

`package.json`
```json
{
  "name": "mre-subpath-import",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "dependencies": { "next": "16.2.7", "react": "19.2.4" }
}
```

`bare.ts`
```ts
import type { Metadata } from "next";
import { useState } from "react";
export const meta: Metadata = {};
export const s = useState;
```

`subpath.ts`
```ts
import Image from "next/image";
import Link from "next/link";
export const i = Image;
export const l = Link;
```

Then:
```bash
graphify extract . --code-only
```

## Actual result

All four import edges should exist; only the two bare ones do.

```
NODES: ['bare.ts', 'dependencies', 'i', 'l', 'meta', 'name', 'next', 'next',
        'package.json', 'react', 'react', 's', 'subpath.ts', 'version']

IMPORT EDGES:
  package.json --imports--> next
  package.json --imports--> react
  bare.ts --imports_from--> next     <-- bare resolves
  bare.ts --imports_from--> react    <-- bare resolves
                                     <-- subpath.ts has NO import edges
```

`subpath.ts` is present as a node with zero outbound import edges.

## Expected result

A subpath specifier should resolve to its owning package node, so that
`subpath.ts --imports_from--> next` exists (ideally twice, or once with the
subpath retained as edge metadata).

Stripping the specifier to its package root before canonicalization would cover
the common cases: `next/image` -> `next`, `@scope/pkg/sub` -> `@scope/pkg`
(first *two* segments for scoped packages).

## Why it matters

Framework surface is exactly what an architecture graph should show. For a
Next.js project the questions you most want to ask — which routes use
`next/headers`, which pages client-navigate via `next/link`, which components
render `next/image` — all silently return nothing. An empty result is
indistinguishable from "no usages", so the gap is invisible unless you already
know the answer.

title: feat: add OrcaRouter as a first-class provider with API-key and OAuth 2.0 + PKCE sign-in
body:
# Add OrcaRouter as a first-class provider, with API-key and OAuth 2.0 + PKCE sign-in

## Summary

This adds [OrcaRouter](https://www.orcarouter.ai) to graphify as a first-class
`--backend orcarouter` provider, with **two explicit ways to authenticate** that
both end up holding the same ordinary `sk-orca-…` API key owned by the user.

OrcaRouter is an OpenAI-compatible AI gateway built for both models and agents,
with adaptive routing, automatic failover, zero-markup inference, observability,
guardrails, and agent-tool governance. It also runs gateway-level, zero-trust
security for AI agents on the same endpoint — screening every prompt/response
and governing every tool call on a default-deny basis, with no application code
changes.

```bash
# 1) Sign in with your OrcaRouter account (OAuth 2.0 + PKCE — no client secret)
graphify orcarouter login

# 2) …or paste an existing API key
graphify orcarouter key set          # prompts; or: export ORCAROUTER_API_KEY=sk-orca-…

graphify extract . --backend orcarouter
```

I'm an engineer on the OrcaRouter team.

- Discord: discord.gg/YEubt8enRA · X: <https://x.com/OrcaRouter>

## Why the CLI profile, not a GUI screenshot

Graphify is a Python CLI plus an MCP server; it has no GUI for adding a
provider. There is no `package.json` in the tree and `pyproject.toml` declares
none of the frameworks a rendered interface would need. The `.html` files under
`graphify/exporters/` and `worked/rsl-siege-manager/graph.html` are *generated
export artifacts*, not a settings surface. The two authentication choices
therefore appear where users actually configure a provider: as two discoverable
commands, plus `status`, in the `graphify orcarouter` group.

## Architecture

Every AI entry point that reaches a provider is wired — there are four:

| Entry point | Wiring |
|---|---|
| Semantic extraction (docs, papers, images) | `--backend orcarouter`; the model is resolved against the filtered catalog *before* dispatch |
| `--dedup-llm` tiebreaker | same backend registry, same credential seam |
| Community labelling | same backend registry |
| `graphify prs --triage` | `orcarouter` in both the auto-detect order and the OpenAI-compatible dispatch branch |

**Two origins, deliberately separate.** Authentication lives on
`https://www.orcarouter.ai` (`/auth`, `/api/v1/auth/keys`); inference and model
discovery live on `https://api.orcarouter.ai/v1`. Each is independently
overridable (`ORCA_AUTH_BASE_URL` / `ORCA_API_BASE_URL`), with `ORCA_BASE_URL`
as the shared single-origin fallback for self-hosted deployments; explicit
values win. Remote origins must be HTTPS — plaintext `http` is accepted only
for loopback. This matches the published discovery document
(`GET /.well-known/openid-configuration`, `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported:
["none"]`, `code_challenge_methods_supported: ["S256","plain"]`). Note that
`https://api.orcarouter.ai/v1/auth/keys` is a 404 — the relay is at `/v1`, the
auth endpoints are not — so the two origins are never derived from one another.

### Credential seam — one interface, two adapters

`graphify/orcarouter.py` defines `CredentialSource` with two implementations:

- **`ApiKeySource`** — `ORCAROUTER_API_KEY` (a deliberate per-invocation
  override) or a key stored by `graphify orcarouter key set`.
- **`PkceSource`** — `graphify orcarouter login`, OAuth 2.0 + PKCE (S256).

Both return the same `OrcaCredential` and persist through the same 0600 record
in `~/.graphify/orcarouter.json` — the project's existing trust anchor for
persisted provider config (`llm._custom_providers_path`), so no new secret store
is introduced. `resolve_credential_secret()` is the single downstream entry
point; `llm._get_backend_api_key("orcarouter")` calls it and nothing downstream
branches on which adapter produced the secret. Tests assert exactly that: both
adapters yield the same credential shape, and a downstream resolution test
proves the transport is source-agnostic.

The key is masked everywhere it is printed (`sk-orca-…02Vj`), and the store
tightens the file to `0600` after the atomic write.

### PKCE details

- **Flow A (loopback redirect) is the default** — graphify runs on the user's
  own machine, so a listener on `127.0.0.1` is reachable and `state` can be
  compared, in constant time, *before* the code is used.
- **Flow B (out-of-band code)** is selectable via `ORCAROUTER_OAUTH_FLOW=oob`
  for headless/SSH sessions where no browser can reach the loopback listener.
- **Flow C (device grant) is not implemented** — the spec allows it as an extra,
  but it cannot substitute for PKCE, so it was left out rather than half-built.
- Verifier and `state` are fresh from `secrets` on every attempt; the challenge
  is unpadded `base64url(sha256(verifier))`; `S256` is always sent, never
  `plain`, because the user can choose "Show me a code" on the consent screen.
  The verifier never leaves the process until the exchange — it is asserted
  absent from the authorize URL, from every raised message, and from the logs.
- A successful exchange yields a **durable key, not a refresh token**.
  OrcaRouter caps PKCE-issued keys at 10 per user per 24 hours, so graphify
  reuses the stored credential instead of re-authorizing on launch, never
  fabricates a refresh grant, and never deletes the old secret before a new
  login succeeds.
- `401` is terminal reauthentication: it marks the *exact* rejected credential
  generation (`key_id` + `generation`) as `needs_reauth`. A late failure from a
  superseded generation cannot poison a newer credential. A `403
  model_access_denied` is classified separately and does **not** mark the
  credential — the key is fine, the model scope is not.

### Model discovery and capability filtering

The single source of truth is the live `GET https://api.orcarouter.ai/v1/models`
with the user's key as a Bearer token, so the list reflects what that workspace
may actually call. Model IDs keep their `vendor/model` namespace verbatim, and
the response is bounded on every axis (timeout, bytes, item count, id length,
per-record shape).

Per-entry-point filtering — capabilities are **never** inferred from a model's
name:

| Capability | Rule |
|---|---|
| chat | `?capability=chat` **and** `supported_endpoint_types` intersects `openai` / `openai-response` / `anthropic` / `gemini`; image-generation, openai-video and jina-rerank models are excluded even when they also expose an OpenAI-shaped route |
| vision (multimodal) | chat **and** `architecture.input_modalities` must explicitly contain the modality actually being uploaded — undeclared means fail closed, never "sounds multimodal" |
| embedding / image / video / rerank | the matching endpoint type only (`embeddings`, `image-generation`, `openai-video`, `jina-rerank`) |

The CLI equivalent of a filtered dropdown is `orcarouter.resolve_model()`, and
`graphify/cli.py` calls it with `media=orcarouter.media_kinds(...)` computed from
the corpus about to be sent. The candidate list *is* the filtered catalog: an
incompatible explicit `--model` is **cleared** with the compatible options named
rather than silently kept, and a discovered outage falls back to last-known-good
and then to a small verified seed (`openai/gpt-5.5`, `anthropic/claude-opus-4.8`,
`google/gemini-3.5-flash`, `deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro`, `orcarouter/auto`) whose
reasoning-ladder and input-modality metadata is preserved. The seed is never
merged into a successful live result, and the degraded state is *reported*
(`catalog: seed [DEGRADED]`). `--model` is never free text against this
provider: an unknown id is refused with the catalog listed.

## Test evidence

Two suites, both committed:

**`tests/test_orcarouter_provider.py` — 67 tests, all offline.** Covers the
credential seam (save/read/mask/clear, env-over-store precedence, 0600
permissions, a corrupted key classified terminally), the PKCE flow against a
real local consent server over real HTTP (authorize URL shape and S256, Flow A
completion and state mismatch, Flow B `oob`, denial, timeout, exchange failure
classification, code reuse, scope downgrade refusal), origin independence,
catalog record validation and per-capability filters, the multimodal fail-closed
rule, seed/outage behaviour, and the 401 → exact-generation reauth path. Tests
assert the verifier and key never appear in any log or raised message. Every key
and code is a literal fake; the PKCE tests reach the fake consent server through
`ORCA_AUTH_BASE_URL`, the same override a self-hosted deployment would use.

**`tests/test_orcarouter_live.py` — 4 passed, 1 skipped, gated on
`ORCAROUTER_API_KEY`.** These run the implemented code against the real
gateway — `graphify.orcarouter` for the origins, credential seam and catalog,
`graphify.llm` for inference — so a pass means the wiring works, not merely that
the gateway is reachable. They assert the catalog comes from the API origin,
that chat options only contain declared chat routes, that every vision option
declares image input, that inference resolves its key through the credential
seam, and that an unusable selection is refused before it is sent. Because a
workspace catalog is scoped and an individual key can be narrowed further, the
callable model is discovered rather than assumed: a `model_access_denied`
refusal and an empty completion from a routing alias both just move to the next
candidate, and the final assertion is that some model from this workspace's own
catalog produced a real completion.

**Regression:** `tests/test_backend_extras.py`, `tests/test_provider_registry.py`,
`tests/test_llm_backends.py` and
`test_backend_env_isolation.py::test_env_list_covers_every_variable_detect_backend_reads`
— **122 passed**, confirming the new backend did not disturb the existing
registry or the detection env list.

**Full-suite honesty note.** `pytest tests/ -q` gives 161 failures on this
branch. I ran the same 23 files at the base commit in a clean worktree and got
the identical 161 failures — byte-for-byte the same test IDs. They are
pre-existing (they need `git` history for `git show`-based baselines, tree-sitter
grammars not present in this minimal environment, and a Python below CI's 3.10
floor for a few), and this change introduces none.

**Live end-to-end, through the provider path:**

```
$ graphify extract /tmp/orca-corpus --backend orcarouter --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash
[graphify extract] semantic extraction on 1 files via orcarouter...
[graphify extract] chunk 1/1 done
[graphify extract] wrote /tmp/orca-out4/graphify-out/graph.json: 6 nodes, 3 edges, 4 communities
[graphify extract] tokens: 946 in / 1,862 out, est. cost (~orcarouter): $0.0000

$ graphify extract /tmp/orca-multi --backend orcarouter --model deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp
[graphify extract] found 0 code, 1 docs, 0 papers, 1 images
[graphify extract] chunk 1/1 done      # the raster image was uploaded to a model that declares image input

$ graphify orcarouter models          # catalog: live, 16 models, vendor namespaces verbatim
$ graphify orcarouter models --capability vision   # 2 models, both in:text/image
```

The `model_access_denied` classification was exercised for real along the way:
this workspace's key may call the `deepseek/*` models but not the
`orcarouter/*` routing aliases, and graphify reported exactly that instead of a
credential error.

## Compliance self-check

- `git grep` shows no client secret, no fixed verifier, no real `sk-orca-` key in
  the implementation or config; only `sk-orca-…` (masked) and literal `fake`
  values in tests.
- The only occurrence of the string `/v1/auth/keys` is as the documented **404
  counter-example** in `graphify/orcarouter.py`, the README, and the tests that
  assert `EXCHANGE_PATH == "/api/v1/auth/keys"`.
- Auth requests go only to `www.orcarouter.ai` (or an explicit auth override);
  inference and discovery go only to `api.orcarouter.ai/v1` (or an explicit API
  override). Tests assert both directions independently, including that an
  exchange request is never sent to the inference origin.

## Primary sources

- Inference base and OpenAI compatibility: <https://docs.orcarouter.ai/getting-started/quickstart>
- API keys, `sk-orca-` prefix, Bearer auth, revocation via the console:
  <https://docs.orcarouter.ai/getting-started/get-api-key>
- OAuth 2.0 + PKCE sign-in (authorize URL, exchange endpoint, S256, single-use
  10-minute codes, 10 keys/user/24h, response fields):
  <https://docs.orcarouter.ai/getting-started/sign-in-with-orcarouter>
- Models list: <https://docs.orcarouter.ai/getting-started/models>
- Discovery document (verified this run): <https://www.orcarouter.ai/.well-known/openid-configuration>
- Key management and revocation: <https://www.orcarouter.ai/console/authorized-apps>
- Security model and trust center: <https://docs.orcarouter.ai/security/concepts/securing-ai-agents> · <https://www.orcarouter.ai/trust>
- Service status: <https://statuspage.incident.io/orca-router>

Maintenance owner for this integration: the OrcaRouter team (@OrcaRouter).
Evidence verification date: 2026-09-16.

title: TS: `export type *` namespace re-export triggers partial extraction (tree-sitter-typescript predates TS 5.0 syntax)
body:
## Summary

An `export type *` re-export (type-only namespace re-export, e.g. `export type * from "./dto";`) is rejected by the bundled tree-sitter-typescript grammar, causing the file to be **partially extracted** with a "syntax errors" warning and **no symbols extracted**. The file is valid TypeScript — `tsc` and esbuild accept `export type *` (added in TypeScript 5.0).

On a Drizzle/Fastify monorepo this hit **20 files**, every one a repository barrel whose second line is `export type * from "./dto";`. `export *` on the line above parses fine; the failure is specifically the `type` modifier on the wildcard.

## Reproduction — minimal

```ts
// with_typestar.ts — triggers "syntax errors" warning, first error at line 1, no symbols extracted
export type * from "./dto";
```

```ts
// without_typestar.ts — parses cleanly
export type { Foo } from "./dto";
```

```ts
// dto.ts
export type Foo = number;
```

Place all three in an empty directory and run:

```sh
graphify update . --force
```

**Result:**
```
warning: 1 file(s) had syntax errors and may be partially extracted: with_typestar.ts (first error at line 1, no symbols extracted)
```

`without_typestar.ts` extracts cleanly, confirming the trigger is the `type *` wildcard, not the type-only re-export syntax in general.

## Behaviour compared to #2922 / #3510

Same shape as #2922 (TSX bare `&`) and #3510 (C# 14 extension members): grammar-level rejection of valid source, exit 0, silent partial extraction, warning points at the recovery line. Different construct — here the bundled tree-sitter-typescript grammar predates `export type *` (TypeScript 5.0). `export type { … }` named re-exports parse, so only the namespace-wildcard form is missing.

## Environment

- graphify `0.9.61`
- Language: TypeScript (`.ts`)
- Trigger construct: `export type * from "…";`
- tsc / esbuild: accept the file cleanly (valid since TS 5.0)

## Expected behaviour

`export type * from "…";` should parse without a syntax error and extract the file's symbols, matching every other TypeScript toolchain. Barrels using it re-export only, so the lost symbols are pass-throughs indexed at their source, but the noisy warning and dropped file nodes obscure genuine extraction failures.

title: Resolve Kotlin object/class qualified member calls across files
body:
## Summary

Fixes #1698.

A Kotlin call on an object or class qualified receiver (`Config.load()`) only resolved when the receiver's declaration lived in the same file. The gap sits at the intersection of three existing pieces of behavior:

- The shared cross file call resolution pass in `extract.py` unconditionally skips every member call, by design (a bare method name colliding across the whole corpus would inflate god nodes, per #543/#1219). Member calls can only ever resolve cross file through a dedicated per language resolver.
- The engine deliberately does not capture a receiver for Kotlin's two segment `object.method()` navigation shape, specifically so it would not get deferred toward cross file resolution when no such resolver existed yet (deferring it with nothing to catch the deferred call would have broken the working same file case).
- No dedicated Kotlin member call cross file resolver had ever been written, unlike every other member call heavy language in the codebase (Swift, Python, TypeScript, C++, C#, Java, Objective C).

## Changes

- Capture the receiver for Kotlin's two segment qualified navigation shape and thread it into `raw_calls`.
- Add `_resolve_kotlin_member_calls`, mirroring the existing `_resolve_kotlin_qualified_calls` and the `type_by_name` / `methods_by_type` shape `_resolve_swift_member_calls` already uses: index Kotlin sourced classes and objects by bare name, resolve the receiver against that index, then look up the callee among that type's methods. Both steps bail on anything but exactly one candidate, the same god node guard every cross file resolver in this module already applies.
- Register the new resolver for `.kt` / `.kts` files.

## Test plan

- New regression tests in `tests/test_kotlin_grammar.py`:
  - the issue's own cross file case now produces an `EXTRACTED` `calls` edge
  - the pre existing same file case is unaffected (negative control)
  - a receiver defined identically in two packages correctly yields no edge (god node guard)
- Full suite: 5596 passed, 68 skipped, 2 deselected, no regressions.
- `python3 -m tools.skillgen --check`: OK.

title: Curated community labels are re-attached by community id, not membership — a reshuffle silently moves a label onto unrelated content (clean git diff, corrupt graph)
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.62 (PyPI) · Python 3.13.3 · macOS (darwin) · no LLM backend configured

## Summary

Curated community labels are re-attached by **community integer id**, not by membership. Community ids are positional and unstable across re-clustering, so any run that reshuffles communities silently moves a hand-written label onto unrelated content.

The label is not corrupted and nothing is dropped — which is what makes this bad. The file still contains exactly what the user wrote, so `git diff` on `.graphify_labels.json` is **clean**, while `graph.json`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md`, `graph.html` and `explain`/`query` output all now assert a confidently wrong grouping. There is no warning.

This is distinct from #3334, which measured the appending of filename placeholders for *unlabelled* communities and explicitly concluded "715 of 715 curated names were re-attached correctly by membership fingerprint ... this is a hygiene issue, not a data-loss issue". On 0.9.62 the reuse is not membership-based in this path, and the result is semantic corruption rather than hygiene.

## Minimal reproduction

Four files in an empty directory:

`package.json`
```json
{ "name": "mre-label-overwrite", "version": "1.0.0", "dependencies": { "react": "19.2.4" } }
```

`mailer.ts`
```ts
export type MailArgs = { to: string; body: string };
export type MailResult = { ok: boolean };
export function isMailConfigured(): boolean { return true; }
export function sendMail(a: MailArgs): MailResult { return { ok: isMailConfigured() }; }
```

`form.ts`
```ts
import { sendMail, type MailArgs } from "./mailer";
export type FormState = { error?: string };
export function validate(v: MailArgs): boolean { return v.to.length > 0; }
export function submit(v: MailArgs): FormState {
  if (!validate(v)) return { error: "bad" };
  sendMail(v); return {};
}
```

`README.md`
```markdown
# Demo Project
## Setup
Install things.
## Usage
Run things.
## Notes
Other things.
```

Then:

```bash
graphify extract . --code-only
graphify cluster-only . --no-label
```

giving three clean communities:

```
community 0: package.json, dependencies, react, name, version
community 1: FormState, MailArgs, submit(), validate(), form.ts
community 2: MailResult, isMailConfigured(), sendMail(), mailer.ts
```

Label them by hand, exactly as the workflow intends:

`graphify-out/.graphify_labels.json`
```json
{"0": "npm manifest", "1": "Form validation & submit", "2": "Mail delivery"}
```

Then run the documented maintenance command (the one `graphify install` writes into `CLAUDE.md`):

```bash
graphify update .
```

## Actual result

`update` widens the corpus to `README.md` (see note below), re-clusters, and reuses the labels by id:

```
[npm manifest]               <- package.json, dependencies, react, name, version
[Form validation & submit]   <- FormState, MailArgs, MailResult, submit(), validate(),
                                isMailConfigured(), sendMail(), form.ts, mailer.ts
[Mail delivery]              <- README.md, Demo Project, Notes, Setup, Usage
```

`Mail delivery` is now the name of the README. Community 1 silently absorbed the mailer code that the label described.

`git diff graphify-out/.graphify_labels.json` reports **no change**, so nothing in a normal review would catch this.

The corruption reaches every output surface:

```
$ graphify explain "Setup"
Node: Setup
  ID:        readme_setup
  Source:    README.md L2
  Type:      document
  Community: Mail delivery      <-- a markdown heading, in "Mail delivery"
```

## Expected result

A saved label should follow its community's **membership**, not its index. If a community's membership has changed beyond some threshold, the label should be dropped or flagged rather than silently re-bound to whatever inherited that id.

At minimum, `update` should report how many labels were re-attached to a community whose membership changed, and by how much.

## Also observed on a real repository

A 327-node Next.js site, 22 hand-labelled communities. `graphify update .` widened the corpus to markdown (22 -> 28 communities) and the run reported:

```
[graphify watch] community set changed since labeling (22 saved labels, 28 communities now;
                 renamed 3 community(ies) by their hub).
```

Here the three affected labels were replaced with hub names (`npm manifest & scripts` -> `package.json`, `Contact form, spam guard & email` -> `actions.ts`, `Middleware & session proxy` -> `proxy.ts`). So there appear to be two paths: one that renames by hub (detected, announced, destructive to the curated name) and one that re-binds by id (undetected, silent, destructive to the meaning). The MRE above exercises the silent one.

Restoring the corpus to its original code-only scope and re-running `extract --force` + `cluster-only` produced byte-identical community membership, and the curated labels were *still* replaced with hub names on that run — so the rename can fire even when nothing moved.

## Note on why `update` changes the corpus at all

`graphify update .` has no `--code-only` flag and does not inherit the one used to build the graph, so a graph built with `extract --code-only` gains doc nodes on the first `update`. That scope change is what triggers the re-clustering here. `.graphifyignore` is currently the only way to keep the two commands to the same corpus. #2053 covers the inverse direction (doc+code graph replaced by a code-only rebuild); this is the same missing-scope-persistence problem pointing the other way, and it is what makes the label misbinding easy to hit from the documented workflow.

title: Windows skill reference docs assume mktemp/POSIX paths despite shell = powershell
body:
Follow up from #3439 / PR #3442.

The Windows platform declares `shell = "powershell"` in `tools/skillgen/platforms.toml`, and the repo already has a dedicated, deliberately strict POSIX to PowerShell translator for the core skill body (`tools/skillgen/gen.py`, the `_PY_INVOKE_POSIX`/`_PY_INVOKE_PS_OPEN` etc. block). That translator only runs on the core monolith, not on the per-platform `references/*.md` files.

As a result, `graphify/skills/windows/references/add-watch.md` and `graphify/skills/windows/references/query.md` still contain literal `mktemp /tmp/graphify_*.XXXXXX` bash commands inside fenced code blocks, which don't exist on a native Windows shell. A Windows host following these reference docs (add, watch, query, path, explain) gets a command it can't run.

Fixing this properly needs a decision on approach, not a one line patch:

- Extend the existing strict translator to also run over `references/*.md`, adding a translation for `mktemp` (PowerShell equivalent is roughly `New-TemporaryFile` or `[System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName()`, but the "capture the printed path into a variable" idiom differs from bash's `$(mktemp ...)` and needs its own translation rule), or
- Give windows its own reference fragment variant for the handful of sections that use `mktemp`, or
- Some other approach the maintainers prefer.

Flagged by the graphify review bot on PR #3442 (`graphify/skills/windows/references/add-watch.md:15`, escalate/medium), confirmed real by grepping — the same pattern also appears in `references/query.md` (6 more occurrences), which the original finding didn't call out.

title: Resolve npm package subpath imports to the same node as a bare import
body:
## Summary

Fixes #3595.

A JS/TS import of an npm package subpath (`next/image`, `next/link`) produced no edge at all, while a bare import of the same package (`next`) resolved correctly to the `package.json` dependency node.

Root cause: once relative paths, tsconfig aliases, and workspace packages have all failed to resolve an import, `_resolve_js_import_target` falls back to an external reference namespaced on the whole raw specifier (`ref:<raw>`). A bare import of `next` produced `ref:next`, matching the dependency node `json_config.py` mints for `package.json`'s own `"next"` key — but a subpath import of `next/image` produced `ref:next/image`, a different id with no backing node, so `build.py` dropped the edge as dangling.

## Change

The external-import fallback now strips the specifier down to its package root before namespacing: the first segment for an ordinary package, the first two for a scoped one (`@scope/pkg/sub` → `@scope/pkg`), matching how the `package.json` dependency node is keyed. A subpath import now lands on exactly the same node as a bare import of that package.

## Test plan

- Two resolver unit tests: a plain subpath and a scoped-package subpath each resolve to the same target as their bare import, and a scoped subpath never folds onto a different package sharing the same scope.
- An end to end test using the issue's exact repro shape (`package.json` + a bare-import file + a subpath-import file): both files now resolve to the same target instead of the subpath file coming out disconnected.
- Existing `ref`-namespacing regression tests (`test_phantom_external_import.py`) still pass unchanged.
- Full suite: 5596 passed, 68 skipped, 2 deselected, no regressions.
- `python3 -m tools.skillgen --check`: OK.

title: Resolve Rust self.method() calls across files
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2234.

Rust receiver-method calls (`self.method()`, `receiver.method()`) never produced a cross-file `calls` edge. Rust is the only major supported language with no `_resolve_*_member_calls` pass, so its member calls were dropped by the shared "member calls have no import evidence" guard (#543/#1219) with nothing behind it to recover them — unlike Swift, Python, TypeScript, C++, C#, Java, and Objective-C, each of which has a dedicated resolver.

This lands the narrow, high-confidence slice the issue itself suggested: `self.method()` inside `impl Foo { .. }`. The receiver's type is known syntactically at the call site — no inference needed — and this alone covers the hub-method blind spot the issue measured on a real 533-file Rust tree.

## Design note: why this differs from the Kotlin/Swift resolvers

Kotlin and Swift's resolvers require a type name to resolve to exactly one node before proceeding. A literal port of that rule to Rust would have refused the issue's own motivating case: Rust routinely splits `impl Foo { .. }` across as many files as it likes, and `rust.py` mints a *separate* graph node per `(file, type name)` pair rather than merging them into one canonical type node. Requiring a single node would bail on every split impl block — exactly backwards for this issue.

Instead, every node carrying the type's bare label pools its methods together, and a call resolves only when exactly one method across the *whole* pool matches the callee name. Two impl blocks (however many files apart) defining the same method name still bail — a real ambiguity, not a false one. Verified both directions: a split impl block resolves correctly, and two unrelated structs sharing a bare name with a colliding method name correctly yield no edge.

## Test plan

- New `tests/test_rust_self_member_calls.py`: the issue's own split-impl-block shape now resolves (EXTRACTED); the pre-existing same-file case is unaffected; two differently-defined structs sharing a name and a colliding method yield no edge; a call to a genuinely undefined method yields no edge.
- Full suite: 5597 passed, 68 skipped, 2 deselected, no regressions.
- `python3 -m tools.skillgen --check`: OK.

title: Resolve Elixir alias/import/require/use targets across files
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2556.

The Elixir extractor emitted `imports` edges whose target was the bare normalized module name, while the module node it should point at was registered under a path-prefixed id. The two never match, so `build_from_json` dropped every cross-file `alias`/`import`/`require`/`use` reference. On a real 900-file Elixir/Phoenix project this silently discarded 13% of extracted edges — the entire internal module dependency graph — with no warning.

## Root cause

`graphify/extractors/elixir.py` builds a module's own node id with the defining file's stem (`_make_id(stem, module_name)`) but a reference to that module from anywhere else with just the bare name (`_make_id(module_name)`). The two ids can only ever match when a module refers to itself.

## Fix

A dedicated cross-file resolver (matching the pattern every other member-call/reference resolver in this module already uses) indexes every Elixir module node by its own id and rewrites a dangling `imports` edge's target when it matches exactly one module in the corpus. Per the issue's own testing: id-suffix matching (`application` latching onto `..._update_application`) produced wrong resolutions on a real corpus, so this matches the full id — already exact, since both sides run through the same id builder — rather than any fragment of it. A name matching zero or 2+ modules is left exactly as extracted; the existing external-reference handling turns an unresolved bare id into a leaf stub, the correct outcome for a genuinely external (stdlib/hex) name.

## Test plan

- New `tests/test_elixir_import_resolution.py`: the issue's own repro (a module aliased from another file) now resolves to a real, non-dangling node; a same-file reference (which already worked) is unaffected; two different files declaring the same bare module name correctly yield no resolution; a genuinely external module (e.g. `Logger`) stays unresolved rather than being fabricated.
- Full suite: 5597 passed, 68 skipped, 2 deselected, no regressions.
- `python3 -m tools.skillgen --check`: OK.

title: fix(imports): prefer source over built dist for workspace exports (#2849)
body:
Related issue: #2849 (the "Workspace packages resolve to ignored `dist`" row, 1,529 lost edge records in that report).

## What goes wrong

Workspace resolution is consulted and finds the right package. The defect is which file it picks. A workspace package's `exports` (or `main`) almost always names build output:

```json
"exports": { ".": { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "import": "./dist/index.js" } }
```

When the package has been built, `dist/index.js` is a real file, so `_resolve_js_import_path` returns it and `_resolve_workspace_import` stops there. But `dist/` is in `detect._SKIP_DIRS`, so no node exists for that file. The `imports_from` edge targets an id with no node and build drops it. The import is silently lost, and `affected`, `path` and `god-nodes` all inherit the gap.

#3487 fixed the case where the runtime condition points at source and only `types` points at `dist`. This is the remaining case: every condition points at `dist`, and the source tree is the only thing in the corpus.

Measured on a 19-package yarn workspace (`"workspaces": ["apps/*", "packages/*"]`, all packages built): 474 bare workspace imports in source, 52 cross-package edges in the graph. Every one of the 474 resolved to `packages/<pkg>/dist/…`.

## The fix

`_source_mirror` maps a candidate under `dist/`, `build/` or `out/` to the same relative path under `src/`, extensionless, so `_resolve_js_import_path` probes `.ts`/`.tsx`/index files as usual (`dist/testing/index.js` -> `src/testing/index`, `dist/index.d.ts` -> `src/index`). `_resolve_workspace_import` probes that mirror before the candidate itself. A package that ships only built files has no mirror on disk and keeps its current behaviour.

The three directory names are the JS build-output entries already in `_SKIP_DIRS`. `lib/` is deliberately not included: it is not pruned and is often source.

## Results

Same repo, same corpus, cache cleared between runs:

| | 0.9.62 | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| cross-package edges | 80 | 1,644 |
| `explain WalletEntrySchema` importers | 3 | 22 |
| `path wallet.ts -> facade/src/index.ts` | no path | 1 hop |

Node count is identical in both builds (10,261), so the delta is resolution only.

## Tests

Four new tests in `tests/test_js_import_resolution.py`, each failing before the change:

- root export into built `dist/` resolves to `src/index.ts`, with the symbol edge
- subpath export into built `dist/` resolves to `src/<subpath>/index.ts`
- `main` into built `dist/` (no `exports`) resolves to `src/index.ts`
- a `dist`-only package (no `src/`) keeps resolving to the `dist` file

Full suite: 5,612 passed with `--all-extras`. `ruff check` clean on both files.

title: fix: resolve workspace imports, stylesheet tokens and generic handler bindings; record what a scan excluded
body:
## The problem

Five ordinary questions about a monorepo, and what the graph answered before this change. Ground
truth built with greps over `git ls-files`, so it does not move with the tool under measurement;
corpus 9 048 files (8 570 code), one npm workspace with three apps and a shared UI package, one .NET
service, one documentation tree.

| Question | before | after | ground truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Which source files do two apps both use? | 0 | **87**, 0 extra | 87 |
| Which files does one design token reach? | 1 | **62** | 62 |
| Which handler serves this request type? | 5 pairs | **685 `handles` edges**; 3 of 3 spot-checked request→handler paths resolve end to end | 685 rows (635 request pairs + 47 notification pairs) |
| What structure do the documents have? | 0 nodes | **8 037** | — |
| Why is a file missing from the graph? | unanswerable | `graphify-out/EXCLUDED.tsv` | — |

The 14-file reproduction from the issue gives the same picture without a monorepo. Before / after,
same script, same fixture:

| check | released version | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `.css` files classified as code | 0 of 2 | **2 of 2** |
| `@demo/ui` import lands on | `packages/ui/dist/index.js` (outside the scanned corpus) | **`packages/ui/src/index.ts`** |
| css `@import` edges | 0 | **1** |
| `uses_token` edges | 0 | **6** |
| `handles` edges | none | **`GetThingQuery -> GetThingQueryHandler`** |
| `graphify-out/EXCLUDED.tsv` | absent | **4 rows** |

The right-hand column was re-measured on this branch (`uv run --frozen bash repro.sh <dir>` at
`c221e27`): `2 of 2`, `index.ts` (the `src/` twin, while `dist/index.js` is present on disk), `1`,
`6`, `GetThingQuery -> GetThingQueryHandler`, `4 rows`.

## What changed, and how to check each part

**1 · `.css` joins `CODE_EXTENSIONS`** (`graphify/detect.py`). One token in one set literal.

```bash
python -c "from pathlib import Path; from graphify.detect import classify_file; print(classify_file(Path('theme.css')))"
# before: None        after: FileType.CODE
```

**2 · `detect()` writes the exclusion register it already computes** (`graphify/detect.py`,
`graphify/extract.py`). Three kinds, one row each, tab separated: `ignored` (ignore rule or noise
dir), `unclassified` (with the extension that fell through), `skipped` (sensitive pattern). The
"partially extracted after a parse error" notice, which until now existed only as a line on stderr
during the run, becomes a fourth kind, `partial`, in the same file.

```bash
python -c "from pathlib import Path; from graphify.detect import detect; detect(Path('.'))"
head -5 graphify-out/EXCLUDED.tsv
# before: no such file
# after:  kind  path  reason
#         ignored  …/ignored.py           ignore-rule
#         ignored  …/packages/ui/dist/    noise-dir
#         unclassified  …/notes.xyz       .xyz
```

**3 · A workspace import resolves to the source, not to the build output**
(`graphify/extractors/resolution.py`, 20 lines). `development` joins `_EXPORT_CONDITION_PRIORITY`
— it was in no position in that tuple, so an exports map naming only `development` and `default`
resolved to the `default` catch-all — and
`_source_twin_of_build_output()` maps a `dist/` candidate onto its extensionless `src/` counterpart
and prefers it when that file exists — including when the build output itself is present, which a
fallback that only triggers on a missing file does not cover. In the fixture the `exports` map names
`./dist/index.d.ts` and `./dist/index.js`, the second of which exists on disk; the edge lands on
`packages/ui/src/index.ts` all the same. This is the fix that carries most of `0 → 87` in the table:
`dist/` is pruned as a noise dir, so before the change every edge into a shared package pointed
outside the corpus. The last two of those 87 files arrive through the stylesheet `@import` and
preset import edges from fixes 4 and 5. Check with the fixture — the line `'@demo/ui' import lands on`.

**4 · A CSS extractor** (new `graphify/extractors/css.py`, 78 lines). It emits the stylesheet's own
node, a node per custom property it declares, a `uses_token` edge per `var(--x)` reference, and an
`imports` edge per `@import`, resolved through the existing JS import resolver so a bare package
specifier in a stylesheet lands on a real file.

**5 · Design tokens become nodes, and references bind to them** (new
`graphify/extractors/design_tokens.py`, 112 lines; `_resolve_design_token_refs()` in
`graphify/extract.py`; `uses_token` added to `DEFAULT_AFFECTED_RELATIONS` in `graphify/affected.py`).
A reference from another file — `var(--brand)` in a component, or a Tailwind utility class whose
preset entry resolves to that variable — becomes an edge to the node that declares the token. This
is what turns the blast radius of a token change from 1 file into 62:

```bash
graphify affected "--brand" --relation uses_token --depth 1
# before: No affected nodes found.
# after (on the measured corpus, for one named color token): 61 files listed
```

**6 · A request type binds to the generic handler that handles it**
(`graphify/extractors/engine.py`, `graphify/extractors/csharp.py`, plus the relation names in
`graphify/extract.py` and query hints in `graphify/serve.py`). A small table maps a generic
interface to (type-parameter position, relation name): `IRequestHandler`/`INotificationHandler` →
`handles`, `IPipelineBehavior` → `intercepts`, `AbstractValidator` → `validates`,
`IEntityTypeConfiguration` → `configures`. The edge carries `context="type_binding"` alongside the
ordinary `references` edge, so the "this class mentions that type" signal is not lost.

**7 · The runbook feeds documents to the extractor too** (`tools/skillgen/fragments/core/*.md`, and
the generated skill artefacts). Part A collected only `detect['files']['code']`, so a Markdown file
never reached `extract()` even though a structural extractor for it exists; the semantic pass was
never meant to be the only path for those files. Part A now also walks the `document` category,
filtered to files `_get_extractor()` actually covers.

```bash
grep -c "detect.get('files', {}).get(" graphify/skill.md
# before: 1        after: 2
python -c "import json; g=json.load(open('graphify-out/graph.json')); \
print(sum(1 for n in g['nodes'] if str(n.get('source_file','')).endswith('.md') and n.get('_origin')=='ast'))"
# before: 0        after: 8037   (on the measured corpus)
```

`graphify/skill*.md` is generated: the three core fragments are the edit, `python -m tools.skillgen`
plus `--bless` regenerated the 16 skill files and their snapshots, and `gen.py` gained one predicate
so `--monolith-roundtrip` can sanction those lines. All five skillgen gates are green.

## Cost

Measured on the 9 048-file corpus (8 570 code, 464 document, ~7.7M words), full standard build:

| | |
|---|---|
| graph after | 90 004 nodes · 244 928 edges |
| added by the document category | +8 037 nodes · +10 147 edges |
| added by the token and binding relations, measured on an undirected rebuild | +12 nodes · 5 064 relation edges (`uses_token` 4 781, `validates` 239, `handles` 44, `configures` 0, `intercepts` 0) |
| net edge growth for those relations | +4 767 — 283 of the new edges replaced an existing `references` edge on the same pair, 14 replaced a `contains` edge |
| the same binding relation, built directed | `handles` 685 instead of 44 (see "choices" below) |
| added by the import fixes | +7 import edges |
| `graph.json` on disk | +1.0 % |
| full build, extraction cold, no cache reuse | 10 min 38 s (detect 258 s, extract 224 s, build/cluster/analyse 78 s) |
| rebuild before vs after the new relations | ≈11 min → 11 min 14 s |
| `graphify affected`, three warm runs | +0.1 to 0.2 s |

Source change: +397 / −7 lines across 9 files in `graphify/` (two of them new, 190 lines
together), +230 lines of tests in 8 files, +31 / −4 in `tools/skillgen/`. The remaining 32 changed
files are generated skill artefacts and their snapshots. 53 files, +754 / −43 in total
(`git diff --shortstat v8..HEAD`).

## What this does not do

- **No new CLI surface.** No flag, no command, no changed output format other than the new
  `EXCLUDED.tsv` artefact in `graphify-out/`.
- **`graphify/extractors/__init__.py` is untouched.** The CSS extractor is registered in the
  extension→extractor dispatch table in `extract.py` only, not in `LANGUAGE_EXTRACTORS`; the
  design-token module is not a language extractor at all (it exposes no `extract_*`). Where you want
  these two registered, and whether the second belongs under `extractors/`, is your call — say the
  word and I will move them and add the `MIGRATION.md` row.
- **`ARCHITECTURE.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `extractors/MIGRATION.md` and `uv.lock` are untouched.** The
  changelog convention wants an issue number per line, so those lines belong in the same commit as
  the issue reference once this has one.
- **The build-output fallback covers `dist/` only**, mapped to `src/`, for extensionless targets and
  for the `.d.ts` / `.d.mts` / `.d.cts` family. `build/`, `lib/` and `out/` are not handled.
- **The CSS extractor is CSS**, not Sass or Less, and `@import` must be a quoted string; `@import
  url(...)` is not matched.
- **Class names composed at runtime are skipped on purpose** — a `bg-${variant}` template is not
  guessed. On the measured corpus that was 2 files.
- **Nothing about undirected builds.** See the first item under "choices" — this matters.

## Choices locked in, that a reviewer should agree with or reject

- **The `handles` edge is stored request → handler**: source is the request type, target is the
  handler class. That reads backwards against the English verb, and it is deliberate, not a reversed
  edge: it makes "what runs when this request is dispatched" a forward traversal from the request,
  which is the direction users ask in. `validates`, `configures` and `intercepts` keep the natural
  direction (the validator/configuration/behaviour class is the source). If you want `handles` to
  read like the verb, it is the swap in `_resolve_csharp_type_references` and nothing else.
- **In an undirected, non-multigraph build only one edge survives per node pair.** A new
  `handles`/`validates` edge collides with the `references` edge the same generic argument already
  produced. On the measured corpus, the request→handler naming survived in 5 of 635 pairs until the
  graph was built directed; built directed it is 685 edges. The extractor is right either way — the
  loss is in the build step — but the value of this fix depends on a directed build, and that is
  worth saying out loud rather than discovering later.
- **Only `uses_token` was added to `DEFAULT_AFFECTED_RELATIONS`.** The four C# binding relations are
  not in the default traversal, so a default blast radius is unchanged unless `--relation` names
  them.
- **The binding table is a fixed map of five interface names**, matched on the bare generic name at
  type-argument position 0 with exactly one resolved reference. An unrelated library that happens to
  name an interface the same way will match. There is no configuration surface for it.
- **The Tailwind bridge keys on a file literally named `tailwind-preset.ts`.** A design system that
  does not use that convention still gets the `var(--x)` half, and nothing else.
- **`--x-rgb` companion tokens fold onto `--x`** when both are declared in the same stylesheet. On
  the measured corpus this merged 7 token nodes, and inside the declaring stylesheet 21 pairs that
  used to be `contains` ("this file declares this token") became `uses_token` ("this file uses it").
  That is a behaviour change on existing graphs, not only an addition.

## Two known limitations, not fixed here

**The two writers of `EXCLUDED.tsv` anchor differently.** `detect()` writes to `cache_root or root`,
following the convention the word-count cache already uses, so an `extract --out` run keeps it out
of the scanned corpus. The `partial` rows in `extract()` anchor to `root` instead, which for the CLI
is the scanned project (`cli.py` hands `extract()` `{"cache_root": out_root, "root": target}`). With
`--out` the two halves land in two different files, and the second one writes into the corpus being
analysed. Reproduced with `root` and `cache_root` deliberately pulled apart: the register appears
under the scan root and not under the out dir. The new test does not catch it because it passes only
`cache_root=tmp_path` with paths under it, so the two coincide. I left it as is rather than guess
which anchor you want — say which, and I will make both writers use it and pin the choice with a
second test case.

**The `extract()` writer appends.** It opens the register in append mode and writes the header only
when the file is absent, so two `extract()` runs over the same tree list the same partially
extracted file twice. A full `detect()` pass rewrites the file atomically and clears the
duplication, but a path that only re-extracts (`graphify watch`, repeated `update`) keeps growing.
Same choice as above: it becomes a rewrite the moment you say which anchor and which lifetime the
file should have, and it gets a test in the same round.

## Test plan

11 tests, in `tests/`, on the layout CI runs (`uv run --frozen pytest tests/ -q --tb=short`, Python
3.10 and 3.12):

```
tests/test_detect.py::test_classify_stylesheet
tests/test_detect.py::test_detect_writes_exclusion_register
tests/test_extract.py::test_partial_extraction_writes_exclusion_register
tests/test_js_import_resolution.py::test_workspace_subpath_export_development_outranks_default
tests/test_js_import_resolution.py::test_workspace_dist_subpath_falls_back_to_src_twin_when_dist_is_not_built
tests/test_css_extraction.py::test_css_import_resolves_to_target_file
tests/test_design_tokens.py::test_cross_file_var_reference_binds_to_its_definition
tests/test_design_tokens.py::test_uses_token_is_traversed_by_affected
tests/test_csharp_type_resolution.py::test_csharp_request_handler_generic_binds_request_to_handler
tests/test_serve.py::test_query_graph_text_type_binding_alias_resolves
tests/test_skillgen.py::test_part_a_also_walks_the_document_category
```

Each test fails when its own production change is reverted: one fix at a time, in a throwaway
worktree, with the test files left untouched — 11 of 11 go red, and the worktree was verified clean
between rounds. Two commits carry two independent halves each, and there the tests split the same
way: removing only `development` from `_EXPORT_CONDITION_PRIORITY` reddens
`…development_outranks_default` while `…falls_back_to_src_twin…` stays green, and removing only the
`_source_twin_of_build_output` call does the reverse; the same holds for the `detect()` and
`extract()` halves of the exclusion register.

Suite, same machine, same lockfile, one environment per side
(`uv run --frozen pytest tests/ -q`):

```
with these commits (c221e27):    6 failed, 5618 passed, 97 skipped
on the base commit (c7ec108):    6 failed, 5607 passed, 97 skipped
```

The six failures are identical by name on both sides and pre-existing. Four in
`tests/test_ollama_retry_cap.py` need an optional extra that a default `uv sync` does not install
(`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openai'`; CI installs with `--all-extras`, this run did
not). `test_collect_files_skips_hidden` asserts over `Path.parts` of an absolute path, so it fails
whenever the checkout itself sits under a dot-directory. `test_ts_normalizer_scales_linearly_on_large_files`
is a wall-clock ratio test (`0.0770s -> 0.2859s`, threshold 3x) that fails under machine load.
None is touched here. The difference of 11 passing tests is exactly the 11 above — checked by
collecting both sides separately (`pytest tests/ -q --collect-only`, 5717 vs 5706 items) and
diffing the node ids: 11 added, none removed, none renamed.

Also green: `ruff check --config pyproject.toml .` (both sides), `python -m tools.skillgen --check`
(`134 artifact(s) match committed output and expected/`), `--audit-coverage`, `--schema-singleton`,
`--monolith-roundtrip`, `--always-on-roundtrip`, and `graphify --help`. `bandit -r graphify -ll`
reports the same metrics block as the base commit (Low 102 · Medium 8 · High 3). `pyright` reports
`583 errors, 4 warnings` on both sides, and with paths and line numbers normalized away the two
diagnostic sets are identical — this branch adds no new one.

## A note on reviewing this

Two of the nine changed files under `graphify/` are new (`extractors/css.py`,
`extractors/design_tokens.py`). If you verify a build by hashing an installed package against its
`RECORD`, an added file produces no mismatch — only the seven modified ones show up. So the hash
diff is not the full change surface here; the file list above is.

Niets hiervan is gedraaid — de tak staat lokaal, er is geen fork, geen push, geen PR, geen release.

title: fix(python): lexical-scope-aware indirect_call resolution
body:
## Summary

- \`_emit_indirect_by_name\` (the callback-by-name resolver behind the
  Python \`indirect_call\` edge) matched the referenced identifier purely by
  bare label: first via the per-file \`label_to_nid\` map — which #3405
  deliberately excludes nested Python functions from — then via
  \`extract.py\`'s corpus-wide cross-file resolver. Neither consults lexical
  scope.
- A callback name that only exists as a **nested** function therefore fell
  straight through to the cross-file resolver, which matches by bare label
  across the whole corpus and can bind to a same-named nested function
  defined in a **sibling** function's scope — or to an unrelated
  module-level definition that the reference's own enclosing scope actually
  shadows.
- Direct \`calls\` resolution already walks the \`scope_parents\` /
  \`lexical_nids_by_scope\` chain built for #3405 (innermost enclosing scope
  first — Python's LEGB name-resolution rule, per the Python Language
  Reference's "Execution model: Resolution of names"). This PR applies the
  same walk to indirect_call resolution *before* falling back to the flat /
  cross-file maps, so a lexically-resolved name is trusted directly and is
  never re-adjudicated by the corpus-wide pass.
- No behavior for cross-file or module-level callback references changes —
  those still fall through exactly as before when no enclosing-scope
  definition exists.

## Repro

Two sibling functions each define + pass a same-named nested
\`read_then_mutate\` callback:

```python
def run_with_guard(fn):
    return fn()

def test_alpha_scope():
    def read_then_mutate():
        return "alpha"
    return run_with_guard(read_then_mutate)

def test_beta_scope():
    def read_then_mutate():
        return "beta"
    return run_with_guard(read_then_mutate)
```

Before this fix, \`graphify update . --no-cluster\` emits:

```
test_alpha_scope -> test_alpha_scope_read_then_mutate   (correct)
test_beta_scope  -> test_alpha_scope_read_then_mutate   (WRONG — sibling's def)
```

After this fix, both indirect_call edges bind to their own lexical
definition.

Originally observed in a downstream consumer repo
(ContextualWisdomLab/fast-mlsirm#1862) while auditing a graph run over two
Python test modules that each nest a `read_then_mutate` helper inside a
same-named sibling test function.

## Test plan

- [x] Added \`tests/test_issue_1862_indirect_call_lexical_scope.py\`
      (sibling same-named nested callbacks each bind to their own
      definition; a legitimate cross-file callback reference still
      resolves; an enclosing lexical scope's definition is preferred over a
      module-level same-named definition per LEGB).
- [x] \`tests/test_issue_3405_python_resolution.py\` (the related direct-call
      lexical-scope suite) still passes unchanged.
- [x] Full suite: \`pytest tests/ -q\` → 5379 passed, 26 failed, 257 skipped.
      All 26 failures are pre-existing/environmental on this checkout and
      unrelated to this change (missing optional \`tree-sitter-hcl\` extra
      cascading through \`test_terraform*.py\`, Ollama SDK retry-cap
      assumptions, a wheel-packaging test, an unrelated mtime-collision
      flake, and one markdown frontmatter test) — none touch
      \`extractors/engine.py\`'s Python call/indirect-call resolution.

title: feat(ts): free-function param/return type refs + opt-in inline-param markers
body:
## What

Two related additions to the TS/JS `references` edge model:

**1. Param/return type refs for top-level free functions.**
Top-level named callables now emit the same `parameter_type` / `return_type` / `generic_arg` `references` facts that class methods already get:

- `function f(){}` (bare or export-wrapped, incl. `export async function`)
- const-assigned `arrow_function` / `function_expression` values

The per-callable emission is extracted from `_ts_walk_class_members` into a shared `_ts_emit_callable_type_refs`, and `_js_top_level_function_nodes` feeds top-level callables into it via the shared `_js_top_level_unwrapped` traversal (#3346) — so export-wrapped `const` callables are covered too, matching the call-graph pass rather than duplicating its traversal.

**2. Opt-in `--inline-params` arity markers.**
`--inline-params` (default **off**, threaded through `extract(inline_params=…)`) designates parameters typed as anonymous object literals:

- emits a `references[inline_parameter]` self-edge (an arity marker), and
- emits the param's nested named refs as `references[field]` instead of `parameter_type`,

so `parameter_type` means "named param type" only, and a verifier can distinguish "has an inline param" from "no signature edges" instead of skipping misleadingly.

`deduplicate_entities` preserves the intentional `inline_parameter` self-loop where every other self-loop is still dropped.

## Testing

- `tests/test_js_import_resolution.py` — inline-param designation; free-function type refs covering export-wrapped const arrow / function-expression callables.
- `tests/test_dedup.py` — the `inline_parameter` marker survives dedup when other self-loops are dropped.
- `173 passed` across both files on latest `v8`.

## Notes

- Both behaviors are additive and default-off/opt-in; unflagged output is unchanged.
- Non-goal: `--same-file-refs` (a label-uniqueness same-file fallback for `references`) was explored and dropped — the subsystem-model gap-filler agent path already covers that case from source.

title: Git hooks spam ImageMagick 'import' usage on every commit (pipx polyglot shebang misdetected as interpreter)
body:
## Summary

The installed `post-commit` / `post-checkout` git hooks print ImageMagick's `import` usage dump on every commit and checkout when the `graphify` launcher uses a `#!/bin/sh` polyglot shebang (the pipx-installed layout). The graph still rebuilds correctly via the `python3` fallback, so it's cosmetic — but it spams several dozen lines of `Usage: import [options ...]` into the output of every `git commit`.

## Environment

- graphify (pip package `graphifyy`) **0.4.12**, installed via pipx
- macOS (Apple Silicon), Homebrew ImageMagick present on `PATH` (provides a binary named `import`)

## Root cause

The pipx launcher `~/.local/bin/graphify` starts with a polyglot shebang that re-execs into the venv Python:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
'''exec' "/…/pipx/venvs/graphifyy/bin/python" "$0" "$@"
' '''
import sys
from graphify.__main__ import main
```

The hook detects the interpreter by reading the launcher's first line:

```sh
_SHEBANG=$(head -1 "$GRAPHIFY_BIN" | sed 's/^#![[:space:]]*//')
```

For this launcher that yields `GRAPHIFY_PYTHON=/bin/sh`. The hook then validates it with:

```sh
if [ -n "$GRAPHIFY_PYTHON" ] && ! "$GRAPHIFY_PYTHON" -c "import graphify" 2>/dev/null; then
```

which runs **`/bin/sh -c "import graphify"`**. On any machine with ImageMagick on `PATH`, `import` is ImageMagick's screen-capture tool, so it prints its full usage text to **stdout** (the probe only redirects stderr). The check's exit code still works, so `GRAPHIFY_PYTHON` is reset and the `python3` fallback runs — the graph rebuilds fine, but the usage dump already leaked to the terminal.

`sh -x .git/hooks/post-commit` trace:

```
+ GRAPHIFY_PYTHON=/bin/sh
+ /bin/sh -c 'import graphify'
Usage: import [options ...] [ file ]
...
+ GRAPHIFY_PYTHON=
+ python3 -c 'import graphify'   # fallback, works
```

## Suggested fixes (either/both)

1. **Silence the probe's stdout too** — it's only used for its exit status:
   ```sh
   ! "$GRAPHIFY_PYTHON" -c "import graphify" >/dev/null 2>&1
   ```
   (applies to the same probe in both `post-commit` and `post-checkout`)

2. **Don't trust a `/bin/sh` shebang as the interpreter** — the launcher is a polyglot; reject shebangs whose basename isn't a `python*` before probing (or just skip straight to the `python3`/`python` fallback when it isn't).

Fix #1 alone removes the noise for any stray interpreter guess; #2 addresses the misdetection at its source.

## Workaround

Add `>/dev/null 2>&1` to the probe line in the installed `.git/hooks/post-commit` and `.git/hooks/post-checkout`, but `graphify hook install` regenerates them and reintroduces the noise.

title: fix(csharp): extract past a verbatim interpolated string ending in an escaped quote (#3376)
body:
Fixes #3376

## What

A C# file containing a verbatim interpolated string whose text ends with an interpolation hole, an escaped quote and then the terminator is now extracted in full. Before this, the bundled grammar rejected the literal and every member declared after that line was silently missing from the graph.

## Why

The spelling is valid C# — `dotnet build` accepts it — but tree-sitter-c-sharp 0.23.5 rejects it. As the issue shows, every neighbouring spelling parses; the trigger is specifically the `}` `""` `"` adjacency at the end of the literal. 0.23.5 is the newest release on PyPI and the project already allows `>=0.23,<0.25`, so there is no grammar bump to take.

The cost is silent. The file still extracts, just not all of it, and the warning names the parser's recovery line rather than the literal — the issue reports chasing an unrelated `[InlineData]` attribute because of it.

## How

`extract_csharp` now passes the source through `_normalize_csharp_verbatim_interpolation`, the same `source_override` seam `extract_js`, `extract_vue` and `extract_cpp` already use.

Only the trailing escape is overwritten, with two spaces. The rewrite is **byte-length preserving** — nothing is inserted or deleted and no line break is touched — so every offset, line and column still points at the same place in the file on disk and reported `source_location` values stay accurate (the #2876 contract that `_normalize_cpp_cli` documents). The interpolation hole itself is kept, so identifiers referenced inside it still resolve.

Two gates keep it inert everywhere else:

- a file that already parses is returned untouched, so healthy files never enter the rewrite;
- if the masked source still has parse errors the original is used, leaving today's behaviour exactly as it is.

The scanner walks the file once, skipping comments, char literals, raw strings and every other string form, so the spelling written inside a comment or another string is never mistaken for code.

## Testing

`tests/test_csharp_verbatim_interpolation.py`, 7 tests.

Before, on a class with six methods and the literal in the third:

```
warning: Config.cs (first error at line 20, 5 symbol(s) extracted)
extracted: BeforeOne()  BeforeTwo()  Offender()  Config  Config.cs  Demo
missing:   AfterOne()   AfterTwo()   AfterThree()
```

After: 10 nodes, all six methods, no warning.

Byte-level check on that same file — 783 bytes, 39 newlines:

```
same total length:   True
same newline count:  True
bytes changed:       2, at offsets 422 and 423 (both on line 20): b'"' -> b' '
every other byte:    identical
line number for every sampled offset: unchanged
```

and each member's reported location matches the line it is really on (L7, L12, L17, L24, L29, L34).

The two behavioural tests fail with the `source_override` hook removed and pass with it; the other five exercise the normalizer directly (length preservation, multi-line literals, two literals in one file, a healthy file left untouched, and the spelling appearing only inside comments).

Full suite: 16 failed, 5565 passed, 194 skipped. Those 16 are pre-existing — re-running the same ten files with this change reverted gives the identical 16 failed / 477 passed, and none of them touch C# or extraction. All 159 existing C# tests pass. `ruff check` is clean on both files.

## Scope

This does not fix the grammar, which is where the bug actually is — upstream tree-sitter-c-sharp should accept that spelling. It stops graphify silently dropping symbols while the grammar is what it is, and steps aside the moment a file parses cleanly. If you would rather wait for an upstream fix instead of carrying this, that is a fair call.

title: Resolve C++ scope-qualified static calls when the method exists only as a qualified fallback node
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2348.

A scope-qualified static call `Class::Method(...)` was not linked with a `calls` edge when the callee method node existed only in qualified form (label `Class::Method()`). This happens systematically for Unreal Engine `UCLASS()`/`GENERATED_BODY()` classes.

## Root cause

Traced this to the bundled tree-sitter-cpp grammar's own error recovery, not graphify's extraction logic. `GENERATED_BODY()` (an unknown macro invocation to the grammar) followed by `public:` and a pointer-returning method declaration produces an ambiguous parse: the grammar's recovery heuristic can successfully resync on an unambiguous token (e.g. `int FindNearest(...)`, where `int` is a `primitive_type` keyword), but for a self-referential pointer return type (`AHelper* FindNearest(...)`, where `AHelper` is just an `identifier`) the recovery mis-attributes the whole declaration as a bogus constructor-initializer chain instead — so the in-class member declaration is silently dropped, and the out-of-line `.cpp` definition has nothing to attach to. The extractor's existing behavior in that case is to fall back to a node labeled with the qualified name (`AHelper::FindNearest()`), attributed to its *file* rather than its *class*.

`_resolve_cpp_member_calls`'s `method_index` only ever indexes `defines`/`method` edge targets, so it can never find that qualified-only node — the call resolves via `Foo::bar()`'s exactly-one-type-candidate path but then has no method to land on, and the edge is silently dropped.

## Fix

A grammar-level fix (teaching the bundled tree-sitter-cpp to parse Unreal's reflection macros) is out of scope for a Python extraction layer. Instead, a second-chance lookup: when the primary `method_index` lookup for a `Foo::bar()` call comes back empty, check for a node whose label is exactly the qualified form (`"Foo::bar()"`) — still guarded by the same exactly-one-candidate rule every other resolver in this module already applies, so two unrelated classes that happen to share both a class name and a method name (and both hit the same parse failure) still correctly yield no edge.

## Test plan

- New tests in `tests/test_cpp_objc_cross_file_calls.py`: the issue's own Unreal-style repro now resolves to an EXTRACTED `calls` edge; two unrelated same-named classes both hitting the qualified-only fallback correctly yield no edge (god-node guard).
- Full suite: 5623 passed, 68 skipped, 2 deselected, no regressions.
- `python3 -m tools.skillgen --check`: OK.

title: perf(paths): memoize is_absolute_any_platform, skip Path construction on the POSIX arm
body:
## What

`is_absolute_any_platform` answers "is this stored path absolute under POSIX **or** Windows rules" — the right question for a path that travels between machines (a `source_file` in `graph.json`, a `prune_sources` entry, a cache key). It's called on the same few hundred stored paths **tens of thousands of times** — once or more per node/edge in `build`, and again per resolution pass — and each call built **two** pathlib objects (a `PurePosixPath` and a `PureWindowsPath`) just to read a flag. In one build profile it was 60,675 calls and a large share of the run's pathlib overhead (`_parse_path`, `drive`, `PurePath.__init__`).

## The change

- **Memoize** the result (`functools.lru_cache`). It's a pure function of the string (and the interpreter's pathlib rules, fixed for the process); nothing touches the filesystem, so there's no staleness to invalidate.
- **POSIX-first shortcut**: `PurePosixPath(s).is_absolute()` is exactly `s.startswith("/")`, so that arm is a bare string check, done first — a common in-repo relative path (`src/foo.py`) returns without constructing any Path, and `PureWindowsPath` is built only for the drive-letter/UNC forms the cheap check can't settle.

## Correctness

Semantics are **byte-identical** to the prior `PurePosixPath(s).is_absolute() or PureWindowsPath(s).is_absolute()`. Verified with **zero mismatches** across 12,379 generated path forms — POSIX roots, drive letters (`C:\`, `C:/`, `C:rel`, `c:`), UNC (`\server\share`, `//server/share`), mixed separators, and `None`/empty — plus a fuzz set in the test. This matters because the docstring notes these platform rules are version-sensitive and identity-critical, so the memoization deliberately preserves the exact pathlib calls rather than re-deriving them with a hand-rolled string parser.

## Measured

Microbenchmark, 10,000 calls over the repeated-path pattern the pipeline actually exhibits (best of 5):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `is_absolute_any_platform` | 14.3 ms | **0.7 ms** (~20×) |

## Tests

`tests/test_is_absolute_any_platform_memo.py` — named edge cases and a fuzz set both matched against the prior implementation; repeated calls hit the cache (1 miss / 99 hits); `None`/empty short-circuit before the cache; and the POSIX arm equals `startswith("/")`. The full suite matches a fresh `v8` (0.9.63) baseline (zero new failures).

title: `extract_corpus_parallel` misreports failed chunks as successful model omissions
body:
## Summary

When a semantic chunk raises before returning a model response, `extract_corpus_parallel()` correctly reports the chunk failure and increments `failed_chunks`, but the final reconciliation warning then describes the same file as if the model returned a successful response and omitted it.

Confirmed on v0.9.63 (`eaaec1abd99d3a7fb30301ccb49f4cc72ae34011`).

## Minimal reproduction

```python
import io
from contextlib import redirect_stderr
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from unittest.mock import patch

from graphify.llm import extract_corpus_parallel

with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    doc = Path(d) / "guide.md"
    doc.write_text("# Guide\n", encoding="utf-8")
    stderr = io.StringIO()
    with patch(
        "graphify.llm._extract_with_adaptive_retry",
        side_effect=ImportError(
            "OpenAI package not installed. pip install 'graphifyy[gemini]'."
        ),
    ), redirect_stderr(stderr):
        result = extract_corpus_parallel(
            [doc], backend="gemini", token_budget=None,
            chunk_size=1, max_concurrency=1,
        )
    print(stderr.getvalue())
    assert result["failed_chunks"] == 1
```

## Actual output

```text
[graphify] chunk 1/1 failed: OpenAI package not installed. pip install 'graphifyy[gemini]'.
[graphify] WARNING: 1/1 semantic chunk(s) failed — see errors above. Partial results returned.
[graphify] WARNING: 1/1 dispatched file(s) produced no nodes and are absent from the graph: guide.md. The model returned a response but omitted them; a re-run will retry them.
```

The final sentence contradicts the preceding failure: no model response existed.

## Cause

The dispatch/return reconciliation computes every dispatched file with no returned node as `uncovered`, but it does not retain which files belonged to chunks that raised. The single omission warning is therefore used for two distinct cases:

1. a chunk failed before returning a usable result; and
2. a chunk succeeded, but its response omitted one or more files.

## Expected

Files from failed chunks should be described as failed before returning a usable result. The existing “model returned a response but omitted them” wording should remain only for files absent from successful chunk results.

This matters for missing optional dependencies as well as provider/backend errors: the first error tells the operator what to install or fix, while the final warning currently sends them toward model-output debugging instead.

title: fix(llm): distinguish failed chunks from model omissions
body:
## Problem

When a semantic chunk raises before returning a usable result, the final reconciliation warning says the model returned a response but omitted the affected files. This contradicts the preceding chunk error and points operators toward model-output debugging instead of the dependency or provider failure that actually occurred.

## Change

Track the files assigned to failed chunks and split uncovered files into two groups:

- failed before returning a usable result; and
- omitted from a successful model response.

Each group now receives an accurate warning. The existing omission wording remains unchanged for successful responses that omit files.

Fixes #3616.

## Validation

- Added a regression test for a missing optional dependency/backend exception.
- Kept coverage for genuine model omissions and asserted the original warning remains.
- `pytest tests/ -q --tb=short`: 5,643 passed, 96 skipped.
- `ruff check graphify/llm.py tests/test_chunking.py`: passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

title: Fix: save_manifest can erase a deleted file's row before it is ever reported (#3426)
body:
## Summary
Fixes #3426. `save_manifest` could prune a manifest row for a file that no longer exists on disk *before* any caller had a chance to observe that deletion via `detect_incremental`'s `deleted_files` report — making the deletion permanently unreportable from the very next run onward, whenever a save happened without also pruning the graph (a scan only run, an interrupted pipeline).

## Root cause
The reported issue described two cases:

1. Out of scan files wrongly reported as deleted — this turned out to already be fixed by an unrelated earlier improvement (#1908), which is unmodified in this PR and already distinguishes "excluded but alive" from "genuinely deleted" on the `detect_incremental` read side via a direct `Path(f).exists()` check.
2. Genuine deletions becoming permanently unreportable after certain save patterns — this was still live on current code. `save_manifest` pruned any row whose file no longer existed on disk unconditionally and immediately, regardless of whether `detect_incremental` had run yet on that same state. A scan only run or an interrupted pipeline that calls `save_manifest` without also acting on the deletion would silently erase the evidence before anything downstream ever saw it.

## Fix
Removed the unconditional `Path(f).exists()` prune from `save_manifest`. The existing scan corpus based prune (already used to drop "excluded but alive" rows, per #1908) still cleans up a genuinely deleted row when the caller passes the full scan corpus — a deleted file always falls outside that scan, on path alone — but now this happens naturally sequenced *after* `detect_incremental` has had the chance to report the deletion on that same scan. Only a partial/subset save (no scan corpus) now leaves a dead row in place; the next full scan reconciles it.

## Test plan
- Added `test_save_manifest_subset_save_keeps_a_deleted_files_row` in `tests/test_detect.py`, reproducing the exact sequence from the issue: save, delete a file, confirm it is reported once, save again without the full scan corpus, confirm the row survives and the deletion is still reportable on the next pass.
- Confirmed the pre-existing `test_save_manifest_full_scan_still_prunes_missing_file` (scan corpus based prune) still passes unmodified.
- Full suite: `python3 -m pytest -q` — 5622 passed, 68 skipped, 2 deselected, no regressions.
