title: fix(ocaml): extract classes and their methods and instance variables
body:
### What
The OCaml extractor drops classes completely. A module made only of classes comes back with just the file node:

```ocaml
class counter = object
  val mutable count = 0
  method get = count
  method incr = count <- count + 1
end
```

Before this change that file produced **zero** definition nodes — the class, both methods, the instance variable, and any calls made inside the method bodies were all missing from the graph.

### Why
`walk()` handles `module_definition`, `value_definition`, `type_definition`, `open_module`, etc., but there was no branch for `class_definition`, so the whole subtree was silently skipped.

### The fix
Add a `class_definition` branch that:
- mints the class node (`defines` from the file, `contains` inside a module) and registers it for local call resolution,
- walks the `object … end` body — `object_expression` in a `.ml`, `class_body_type` in a `.mli` — emitting each `method`/`val` as a member of the class,
- attributes calls made inside a method body to that method (e.g. `method render = log "hi"` gives `render → log`).

Method names are intentionally **not** registered as local definitions: an OCaml method is only reachable through `obj#m`, never as a bare `m …`, so registering it would let an unrelated bare call bind to it and create a false edge. Same reasoning the existing code already applies to nested `let` bindings.

Works for both implementations (`.ml`) and interfaces (`.mli`, via `method_specification`/`instance_variable_specification`).

### Tests
Added three cases to `tests/test_ocaml.py` covering member extraction, class-scoped containment, method-body call attribution, and the `.mli` signature form. Full `tests/test_ocaml.py` is green (13 passed).

title: fix(elixir): extract defprotocol and defimpl as containers
body:
### What
`defprotocol` and `defimpl` are dropped by the Elixir extractor. Given this file:

```elixir
defprotocol Sizeable do
  def size(data)
end

defimpl Sizeable, for: List do
  def size(data), do: length(data)
end
```

the graph came back with **no** `Sizeable` node and **no** implementation node — and, worse, both `size` functions were attached to the *file* node rather than to the protocol / implementation they belong to.

### Why
`walk()` recognises `defmodule`, `def`, `defp`, and the import keywords, but there was no branch for `defprotocol`/`defimpl`. They fell through to the generic recursion, which descends with `parent_module_nid=None`, so the inner `def`s landed on the file and the containers themselves were never minted. (`defprotocol`/`defimpl` were already in the call-pass `_SKIP_KEYWORDS`, but nothing created their nodes.)

### The fix
Treat both as module-like containers:
- `defprotocol Name` → a container node (`contains` from its enclosing scope), and each callback `def` inside becomes a `method` of it.
- `defimpl Proto, for: Type` → a container node labelled `Proto (for Type)`, with an `implements` edge to the protocol and each function as a `method`.

A protocol implemented in another file simply won't emit the `implements` edge — it's caught by the existing dangling-edge guard, not left hanging.

The top-level protocol node is marked `_elixir_module` like other top-level modules so cross-file resolution can find it.

### Tests
Added two cases to `tests/test_languages.py`: one asserting the protocol/impl nodes exist, their functions are contained by them (not the file), and the `implements` link is present; and one asserting a cross-file implementation produces no dangling edges. `-k elixir` and `test_elixir_import_resolution.py` are green.

title: fix(fortran): link type-bound procedures to their derived type
body:
### What
A Fortran derived type's `contains` section binds procedures as the type's methods, but they were being dropped. For this module:

```fortran
type :: circle
  real :: radius
contains
  procedure :: area => circle_area
  procedure :: scale
end type circle
```

`circle` came out of the extractor with **no link at all** to `circle_area` or `scale` — the two procedures existed as bare module functions, disconnected from the type they belong to.

### Why
The `derived_type_definition` branch minted the type node and returned. It never looked at the `derived_type_procedures` (`contains`) block, so every type-bound procedure binding was discarded.

### The fix
While walking the type, collect each `procedure_statement`'s implementing procedure name — handling both the renaming form (`area => circle_area`, a `binding` node with a `method_name` child) and the plain form (`scale`, a bare `method_name`). After the whole tree is walked (so the module's internal procedures already have nodes), emit a `method` edge from the type to each implementing procedure.

A binding to a procedure implemented in another module resolves through the existing `ensure_named_node` helper to a **sourceless** stub — the same treatment parameter and return types already get — so the corpus-level rewire can collapse it onto the real definition and no dangling edge is left behind.

### Tests
Added two cases to `tests/test_languages.py`: one covering both binding forms linking to their type, and one covering a cross-module binding producing a sourceless (non-dangling) target. `-k fortran` is green (15 passed).

title: fix(julia): extract macro definitions and @enum types
body:
### What
Two everyday Julia constructs are invisible to the extractor:

```julia
macro sayhello(name)
    return :( helper($name) )
end

@enum Fruit apple orange banana
@enum Color begin
  red
  green
end
```

Before this change none of `@sayhello`, `Fruit`, `Color`, or any of the enum members appeared in the graph — and the helper call inside the macro body was lost with it.

### Why
`walk()` handled `module_definition`, `struct_definition`, `abstract_definition`, `function_definition`, and short-form assignments, but had no branch for:
- `macro_definition` — dropped, so every macro (a first-class, heavily used Julia definition) was missing;
- `macrocall_expression` — `@enum` lowers to one, and it was never inspected, so the enum type and all its variants vanished.

### The fix
- **Macros:** a `macro_definition` has the same `signature`/`call_expression` shape as a function, so it reuses `_func_name_from_signature`, mints a definition labelled `@name`, and has its body walked for calls. The signature child is skipped in the call pass (as functions already are) so a macro doesn't fabricate a call to itself.
- **`@enum`:** for a `macrocall_expression` whose macro is `enum`, the first identifier in the `macro_argument_list` is the enum type and the rest — including identifiers inside a `begin … end` `compound_statement` — are `contains`-ed members. Any other macro call still falls through to the generic recursion, so definitions nested inside e.g. an `@testset begin … end` are still discovered.

### Tests
Added two cases to `tests/test_languages.py`: macro extraction with body-call attribution (and no self-loop), and both `@enum` forms with members contained by their type rather than orphaned on the file. `-k julia` is green (17 passed).

title: Kotlin: annotations and primary-constructor properties are not extracted (JPA relationships lost)
body:
**Version:** graphifyy 0.9.68 (also 0.9.15)

## Problem

The tree-sitter engine harvests declaration annotations only for Java/Groovy
(`_java_annotation_names`, gated on those languages). Kotlin nests annotations
differently — `modifiers -> annotation -> user_type` for `@Entity`, or
`annotation -> constructor_invocation -> user_type` for `@OneToMany(...)` — so
nothing is emitted for Kotlin. In addition:

- primary-constructor `val`/`var` parameters (the idiomatic place for Kotlin
  entity fields) get no node, type edge, or annotation edge at all;
- class-body `property_declaration`s attach their type edge to the class, with
  no per-property node, so field-level annotations have nowhere to attach.

For Kotlin JPA/Spring code this drops essentially the whole domain model.

## Repro

```kotlin
import jakarta.persistence.*

@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
class Order(
    @Id @GeneratedValue val id: Long? = null,
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) val customer: Customer,
    @Column(nullable = false) var status: String
) {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")
    var lines: MutableList<OrderLine> = mutableListOf()

    @get:Transient
    val total: Int get() = 0
}

@Entity class Customer(@Id val id: Long)
@Entity class OrderLine(@Id val id: Long, @ManyToOne val order: Order)
```

`graphify extract . --code-only`

**Actual (0.9.68):** 4 nodes / 4 edges — three `contains` edges and
`Order -references/generic_arg-> OrderLine`.

**Expected:** class annotation edges (`Order -> Entity`, `Order -> Table`),
per-field nodes (`Order -defines/field-> .customer`, …), field type edges
(`.customer -> Customer`, `.order -> Order`), and field annotation edges
(`.customer -> ManyToOne`, `.status -> Column`, `.id -> Id`,
`.lines -> OneToMany`, `.total -> Transient`). With the patch below: 20 nodes /
27 edges, 13 of them `attribute` edges.

## Proposed fix

We've been running the attached patch in production since 0.9.15, and it's now
rebased onto 0.9.68. It adds `_kotlin_annotation_names`, `_kotlin_member_name`
and `_kotlin_param_type_node` helpers, and emits:

1. class-level annotation edges (`references`, `context="attribute"`);
2. a `.name` node per primary-constructor `val`/`var`, with type + annotation edges;
3. a `.name` node per class-body property (its type edges move from the class to
   the property; initializer call collection is unchanged);
4. function/getter annotation edges for Kotlin.

Happy to open a PR with tests if this direction is welcome. One open question:
Java annotations are now import-qualified (`jakarta.persistence.Entity`), while
this patch still emits the simple name for Kotlin. Aligning the two would be a
natural follow-up.

<details><summary>Patch against 0.9.68 (graphify/extractors/engine.py)</summary>

```diff
--- a/graphify/extractors/engine.py
+++ b/graphify/extractors/engine.py
@@ -791,6 +791,70 @@
             return c
     return None
 
+def _kotlin_annotation_names(declaration_node, source: bytes) -> list[str]:
+    """Collect annotation names from a Kotlin declaration's `modifiers` child.
+    Kotlin nests the annotated type under `annotation -> user_type` (no args,
+    e.g. `@Entity`) or `annotation -> constructor_invocation -> user_type`
+    (with args, e.g. `@OneToMany(...)`), unlike Java's flat
+    `marker_annotation`/`annotation` with a direct name field. So
+    `_java_annotation_names` finds nothing on a Kotlin node, and its call sites
+    are gated to java/groovy anyway. Mirror it for Kotlin here.
+    """
+    names: list[str] = []
+    modifiers = None
+    for child in declaration_node.children:
+        if child.type == "modifiers":
+            modifiers = child
+            break
+    if modifiers is None:
+        return names
+    for anno in modifiers.children:
+        if anno.type != "annotation":
+            continue
+        user_type_node = None
+        for c in anno.children:
+            if c.type == "user_type":
+                user_type_node = c
+                break
+            if c.type == "constructor_invocation":
+                for cc in c.children:
+                    if cc.type == "user_type":
+                        user_type_node = cc
+                        break
+                break
+        if user_type_node is None:
+            continue
+        name = _kotlin_user_type_name(user_type_node, source)
+        if name:
+            names.append(name)
+    return names
+
+def _kotlin_member_name(node, source: bytes) -> str | None:
+    """Property/param name for a Kotlin `class_parameter` (direct identifier) or
+    `property_declaration` (`variable_declaration -> identifier`)."""
+    if node.type == "class_parameter":
+        for c in node.children:
+            if c.type in ("identifier", "simple_identifier"):
+                return _read_text(c, source)
+        return None
+    for c in node.children:
+        if c.type == "variable_declaration":
+            for cc in c.children:
+                if cc.type in ("identifier", "simple_identifier"):
+                    return _read_text(cc, source)
+    return None
+
+def _kotlin_param_type_node(cp):
+    """The `user_type` node of a Kotlin `class_parameter`, unwrapping `nullable_type`."""
+    for c in cp.children:
+        if c.type == "user_type":
+            return c
+        if c.type == "nullable_type":
+            for cc in c.children:
+                if cc.type == "user_type":
+                    return cc
+    return None
+
 def _kotlin_function_return_type_node(func_node):
     """Find the return-type node of a Kotlin function_declaration (the type after `: ` post-params)."""
     saw_params = False
@@ -4097,6 +4161,54 @@
                                             target = ensure_named_node(ref_name, line)
                                             add_edge(class_nid, target, "references", line,
                                                      context="generic_arg")
+
+                # Class-level annotations (@Entity, @MappedSuperclass, @Embeddable,
+                # …). The Java harvester at the class site is gated to java/groovy,
+                # so Kotlin annotations never became edges. Emit the same
+                # references/attribute edges here.
+                for anno_name in _kotlin_annotation_names(node, source):
+                    target_nid = ensure_named_node(anno_name, line)
+                    if target_nid != class_nid:
+                        add_edge(class_nid, target_nid, "references", line,
+                                 context="attribute")
+
+                # Primary-constructor `val`/`var` params are properties with no
+                # walk-visited node of their own (class-body property_declarations
+                # are handled during recursion). Give each its own node + type +
+                # annotation edges (@Column, @Id, @ManyToOne, @OneToMany, …),
+                # parallel to class-body properties, so JPA mapping/relationship
+                # annotations are queryable per field. Path is
+                # primary_constructor -> class_parameters -> class_parameter.
+                for child in node.children:
+                    if child.type != "primary_constructor":
+                        continue
+                    for cps in child.children:
+                        if cps.type != "class_parameters":
+                            continue
+                        for cp in cps.children:
+                            if cp.type != "class_parameter":
+                                continue
+                            mline = cp.start_point[0] + 1
+                            pname = _kotlin_member_name(cp, source)
+                            pnid = class_nid
+                            if pname:
+                                pnid = _make_id(class_nid, pname)
+                                add_node(pnid, f".{pname}", mline)
+                                add_edge(class_nid, pnid, "defines", mline,
+                                         context="field")
+                            ptype = _kotlin_param_type_node(cp)
+                            if ptype is not None:
+                                prefs: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
+                                _kotlin_collect_type_refs(ptype, source, False, prefs)
+                                for ref_name, role in prefs:
+                                    ctx = "generic_arg" if role == "generic_arg" else "field"
+                                    tgt = ensure_named_node(ref_name, mline)
+                                    if tgt != pnid:
+                                        add_edge(pnid, tgt, "references", mline, context=ctx)
+                            for anno_name in _kotlin_annotation_names(cp, source):
+                                tgt = ensure_named_node(anno_name, mline)
+                                if tgt != pnid:
+                                    add_edge(pnid, tgt, "references", mline, context="attribute")
 
             # Ruby: `class Dog < Animal` puts the base class in the `superclass`
             # field (a `<` token followed by a constant or scope_resolution).
@@ -4764,16 +4876,30 @@
             # Field-type references stay class-gated: top-level properties keep
             # their pre-#2565 (no-references) behavior unchanged.
             if parent_class_nid:
+                line = node.start_point[0] + 1
+                # Give the property its own node (parallels method nodes: `.name`),
+                # so its type + annotations attach per-property rather than lumping
+                # onto the class. Falls back to the class if the name is unresolvable
+                # (e.g. destructuring `val (a, b) = ...`).
+                prop_name = _kotlin_member_name(node, source)
+                prop_nid = parent_class_nid
+                if prop_name:
+                    prop_nid = _make_id(parent_class_nid, prop_name)
+                    add_node(prop_nid, f".{prop_name}", line)
+                    add_edge(parent_class_nid, prop_nid, "defines", line, context="field")
                 type_node = _kotlin_property_type_node(node)
                 if type_node is not None:
-                    line = node.start_point[0] + 1
                     refs: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
                     _kotlin_collect_type_refs(type_node, source, False, refs)
                     for ref_name, role in refs:
                         ctx = "generic_arg" if role == "generic_arg" else "field"
                         target_nid = ensure_named_node(ref_name, line)
-                        if target_nid != parent_class_nid:
-                            add_edge(parent_class_nid, target_nid, "references", line, context=ctx)
+                        if target_nid != prop_nid:
+                            add_edge(prop_nid, target_nid, "references", line, context=ctx)
+                for anno_name in _kotlin_annotation_names(node, source):
+                    target_nid = ensure_named_node(anno_name, line)
+                    if target_nid != prop_nid:
+                        add_edge(prop_nid, target_nid, "references", line, context="attribute")
             # #2565: seed the initializer into initializer_nodes so walk_calls
             # collects its calls (`val repo = createRepo()`), which previously
             # died at the `return` below. Seeding the WHOLE expression (not just
@@ -5217,6 +5343,16 @@
                         add_edge(func_nid, target_nid, "references", line,
                                  context="attribute")
                         annotation_targets.add(target_nid)
+
+            # Kotlin function/getter annotations (e.g. @Transient on a computed
+            # property getter). Members with their own node attach here; the Java
+            # site above is java-only.
+            if config.ts_module == "tree_sitter_kotlin":
+                for anno_name in _kotlin_annotation_names(node, source):
+                    target_nid = ensure_named_node(anno_name, line)
+                    if target_nid != func_nid:
+                        add_edge(func_nid, target_nid, "references", line,
+                                 context="attribute")
 
             if config.ts_module == "tree_sitter_php":
                 params_container = None
```

title: Python: absolute imports drop all calls edges when the scan root is a subdirectory of the import root
body:
`graphifyy==0.9.68` (uv tool), Python 3.11, macOS. AST only (`--code-only --no-cluster`), no LLM.

## Summary

In a monorepo, a team often scans only its own subfolder. Python imports in that subfolder are still absolute from the repo root, so they carry a prefix that does not exist under the scan root. The `imports_from` edge then targets a dotted-name id that matches no node, the receiver is never bound to the local module, and every `mod.func()` call through it loses its `calls` edge.

The files are byte-identical in both runs below. Only the scan root changes.

## Minimal reproducer

```
Company/__init__.py                          (empty)
Company/Apps/__init__.py                     (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/__init__.py                (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/__init__.py           (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/lib/__init__.py       (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/app/__init__.py       (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/lib/delivery.py
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/app/main.py
```

```python
# Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/lib/delivery.py
def deliver(files):
    return len(files)
```

```python
# Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/app/main.py
from Company.Apps.Jobs.Team.lib import delivery


def run():
    return delivery.deliver(["a"])
```

### Scan from the import root: works

```bash
cd <root> && graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster
```

```
imports_from: company_apps_jobs_team_lib_init, company_apps_jobs_team_lib_delivery
calls:        company_apps_jobs_team_app_main_run -> company_apps_jobs_team_lib_delivery_deliver
```

### Scan from the team subfolder: no calls edge

```bash
cd <root>/Company/Apps/Jobs/Team && graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster
```

```
imports_from: company_apps_jobs_team_lib      (no node with this id)
calls:        (none)
```

### Expected

With `Team/` as the scan root, `Company.Apps.Jobs.Team.lib` should resolve to the local `lib/` package, and `run()` should get `calls -> lib_delivery_deliver`.

## Why this is not a duplicate

* #3723, fixed in 0.9.67, resolves absolute package imports within the scan root. Here the dotted name has a prefix above the scan root, so that fix never matches.
* #3272 is `from pkg import submodule` binding to `__init__.py` when the importer is outside the package tree. This repro uses a plain module, not a submodule of a package, and still fails. On the real repo both happen together: `lib/delivery/` is a package whose `__init__.py` re-exports `deliver`.
* #2447 cause A is the same family (id derived from the module name, not the path) for plain `import mod`. This one is `import_from_statement`.

## Real impact

On a private repo, scanning one team's 349-file subfolder gave 0 incoming `calls` edges for a shared helper that is called from 4 automation files. That is the impact analysis case the scope was chosen for. In the reproducer, scanning from the import root restores the edge. On the real repo that means indexing the whole monorepo, which is what the subfolder scan was avoiding.

## Suggestion

Either one would work for this layout:

1. Probe the dotted name after stripping leading components until the rest resolves under the scan root, when the stripped prefix matches the scan root's own path relative to a parent that has `__init__.py` files up the chain.
2. An explicit option, for example `--python-root <dir>` or a `.graphify` config key, that tells the resolver which directory absolute imports are relative to.

Option 2 is smaller and has no guessing.

title: security(skillgen): --watch INPUT_PATH still interpolated in the Aider/Devin monolith cores
body:
Follow-up to #3742 / #3642.

#3742 closed the Step 1 injection and #3742's follow-on closed the same class in the progressive-disclosure `--watch` reference (`tools/skillgen/fragments/references/shared/add-watch.md`), which now reads the trusted `graphify-out/.graphify_root` instead of re-substituting the raw `INPUT_PATH`.

The **identical placeholder is still live** in the two monolith cores:

- `tools/skillgen/fragments/core/aider.md` — `python3 -m graphify.watch INPUT_PATH --debounce 3`
- `tools/skillgen/fragments/core/devin.md` — same line

(and the shipped `graphify/skill-aider.md` / `graphify/skill-devin.md` monoliths).

An agent-substituted path containing `$(...)`, backticks, or `;` would execute when the `--watch` command runs. Same severity/class as #3642.

### Why it wasn't fixed in #3742
The monolith cores use a self-contained flow that does **not** write `graphify-out/.graphify_root`, so the sidecar trick used in `add-watch.md` doesn't apply directly. Editing a core also trips the skillgen monolith-roundtrip guard: any change needs a sanctioned-diff predicate in `tools/skillgen/gen.py` (`_SANCTIONED_MONOLITH_DIFFS`) or `--monolith-roundtrip` fails.

### Suggested fix
Either (a) have the core Step 1 write `.graphify_root` and reuse it in the `--watch` snippet, or (b) neutralize the path in place (single-quote / restructure so the shell never interprets it), plus the matching `gen.py` sanctioned-diff and a regenerate + `--monolith-roundtrip` pass. Add a test that runs the core's `--watch` snippet with a hostile substituted path (mirroring `tests/test_skillgen_input_path_injection.py`).

title: docs: comprehensive community health and contributor guide overhaul
body:
## What does this PR do?

This PR brings Graphify's repository documentation and GitHub issue templates up to a professional, maintainer-grade community health standard. It formalizes the engineering invariants, corrects factual drift in the architecture docs, and implements strict issue templates to defend maintainer triage time.

title: claude-cli: community labeling ignores GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL, only semantic extraction reads it
body:
`graphifyy==0.9.68` (uv tool), Python 3.11, macOS. `claude-cli` backend, no API key.

## Summary

`GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL` is read in exactly one place, `_call_claude_cli` (`llm.py:1761`), which is the structured-extraction path used for semantic entity extraction. Community labeling goes through a different function, `_call_llm` (`llm.py:2870`), whose `claude-cli` branch (`llm.py:2929`) never reads the env var and only passes `--model` to `claude -p` when an explicit `model` argument reaches it:

```python
mdl = model or _default_model_for_backend(backend)
...
if model is not None:
    cli_args.extend(["--model", mdl])
```

`label_communities` (`llm.py:3414`) and `_label_batch_with_retry` (`llm.py:3308`) both accept and thread through a `model` parameter, but nothing in that chain ever populates it from `GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL`. So `graphify cluster-only . --backend=claude-cli` or `graphify label . --backend=claude-cli` run with no `--model` at all, and `claude -p` falls back to whatever model the invoking Claude Code session defaults to.

## This is not #2861

#2861 frames the gap as "undocumented, defaults to Opus" and suggests documenting the env var next to the `label`/`cluster-only` help text. Setting the env var does not fix the problem for these two commands: it has zero effect on `_call_llm`. The fix is not documentation: `label`/`cluster-only` need the explicit `--model` flag threaded to `_call_llm`, or that function's claude-cli branch needs to read the same env var `_call_claude_cli` does.

## Reproduction

```bash
graphify extract . --code-only --no-cluster
GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL=haiku graphify cluster-only . --backend=claude-cli
```

**Expected:** community-naming calls to `claude -p` carry `--model haiku`.
**Observed:** no `--model` flag at all. On a real run this billed 8 calls to Opus 5.5 at $1.36, while the semantic-extraction pass right before it, same env var and same session, correctly used Haiku for 6 calls at $1.39. Same command, same variable, two different models, because the two calls go through different `_call_llm*` functions.

## Suggestion

Read `GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL` once at the top of `_call_llm`'s `claude-cli` branch, the same as `_call_claude_cli` already does, so `model or os.environ.get("GRAPHIFY_CLAUDE_CLI_MODEL") or _default_model_for_backend(backend)` resolves consistently for both extraction and labeling.

title: extract --out leaks graphify-out/cache/stat-index.json into the scan root on an incremental run (detect_incremental has no cache_root param)
body:
`graphifyy==0.9.68` (uv tool), Python 3.11, macOS.

## Summary

`#1747` and `#1774` fixed the fresh-run case: `extract . --out <dir>` no longer creates a stray `graphify-out/` in the corpus root. That fix is real and I confirmed it holds on a cold run. It does not hold on the second, incremental run against a destination that already has a manifest, where a stray `graphify-out/cache/stat-index.json` still lands at the scan root.

## Root cause

`cli.py`'s `extract` command branches on whether a manifest already exists at the destination (`cli.py:~3505` and `~3576`):

```python
if <manifest exists>:
    detection = _detect_incremental(
        target,
        manifest_path=str(manifest_path),
        google_workspace=google_workspace or None,
        extra_excludes=_effective_excludes or None,
        gitignore=_effective_gitignore,
    )
else:
    detection = _detect(
        target,
        google_workspace=google_workspace or None,
        extra_excludes=_effective_excludes or None,
        cache_root=out_root,
        gitignore=_effective_gitignore,
    )
```

Only the `else` (fresh-scan) branch passes `cache_root=out_root`. `detect_incremental()` (`detect.py:2450`) has no `cache_root` parameter at all, unlike `detect()`, which does and forwards it into `cached_word_count(..., cache_root=cache_root)` (`detect.py:1778`). On the incremental branch there is no parameter to receive `out_root` even if the caller wanted to pass it, so the word-count cache falls back to anchoring on `root` (the scan root), and `_ensure_stat_index` (`cache.py:329`) writes `graphify-out/cache/stat-index.json` there. The comment on the `file_hash`/`cached_word_count` call sites (`cache.py:450-454`) documents exactly this failure mode as the thing `#1774` closed, it just does not hold for this call path.

## Reproduction

```
Company/__init__.py, Company/Apps/__init__.py, Company/Apps/Jobs/__init__.py   (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/__init__.py, Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/lib/__init__.py,
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/app/__init__.py                                          (empty)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/lib/delivery.py    def deliver(files): return len(files)
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/app/main.py        from Company.Apps.Jobs.Team.lib import delivery
                                           def run(): return delivery.deliver(["a"])
Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/README.md          one line of prose
```

```bash
cd <root>
graphify extract . --code-only --out Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/graphify-root
# clean: no stray dir at <root>

graphify extract . --backend claude-cli --out Company/Apps/Jobs/Team/graphify-root
# leaks <root>/graphify-out/cache/stat-index.json
```

The first call is a fresh scan against that destination and stays clean, confirming `#1747`/`#1774` still work there. The second call finds the manifest the first call wrote, takes the incremental branch, and leaks.

## Impact

On a private monorepo, running this sequence at the repo root polluted the repo root itself with an untracked `graphify-out/` (caught by `git status` before commit, not shipped). The workaround from `#1747`, gitignoring `graphify-out/` in the corpus, does not help when the corpus is a big shared repo and the leak lands above the intended `--out` subdirectory, in a directory nobody expects graphify to touch at all.

## Suggestion

Add `cache_root: Path | None = None` to `detect_incremental()`, forward it to `cached_word_count`, and pass `cache_root=out_root` from the incremental branch in `cli.py`, matching what the fresh-scan branch already does two lines below it.

title: fix(extract): extract Kotlin annotations and primary constructor properties
body:
### Problem
Resolves #3842.

The Kotlin AST for annotations nests the annotation name inside `user_type` or `constructor_invocation -> user_type` (unlike Java's `marker_annotation`). As a result, the Kotlin extractor was completely blind to class and function annotations. Additionally, primary constructor parameters containing `val`/`var` properties (e.g., `class User(val id: Long)`) were explicitly skipped, missing field dependencies.

### Implementation
- Adds a `_kotlin_annotation_names` helper to correctly extract annotation names for Kotlin, handling raw text resolution correctly (using simple names instead of fully-qualified names to prevent dangling nodes).
- Safely skips `use_site_target` prefixes like `@field:` when extracting names.
- Correctly parses bracketed annotations with multiple targets (e.g., `@[Inject VisibleForTesting]`).
- Updates Kotlin class and function blocks to emit `references` edges with `context='attribute'` for annotations.
- Traverses `primary_constructor -> class_parameters` to extract `val`/`var` property dependencies as `context='field'` edges, along with their associated annotations.

### Verification
- Added 9 new rigorous test cases in `test_languages.py` covering all the above scenarios (regular annotations, parameterized annotations, use-site targets, multiple bracketed annotations, and primary constructor fields/annotations).
- Verified all 45 Kotlin AST parsing tests pass perfectly.
- Verified no regressions in existing Java/Groovy annotation handling.
- Verified the code passes `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run pyright` cleanly.

Co-Authored-By: Antigravity <noreply@google.com>

title: Suggested Questions: fixed ordering lets low-value items crowd out useful ones
body:
## Summary

In Graphify 0.9.68, `suggest_questions()` appends candidates by category (ambiguous edges, bridge nodes, inferred relationships, isolated nodes, then low-cohesion communities) and returns only the first seven. If early categories produce seven questions, later categories are never shown. Repeated low-value questions can therefore occupy the report indefinitely while more useful candidates are crowded out.

## Possible fixes

- Rank candidates by a relevance/confidence signal and diversify the final list across question types.
- Let users provide feedback or dismiss specific questions, while allowing new or materially changed candidates to surface.
- Make the limit configurable; this helps visibility but does not fix ordering by itself.

I’m happy to implement a fix once we agree on the right approach. Thanks for considering it.

title: Forward cache_root through the incremental extract detection path
body:
Fixes #3847.

## Summary

`extract --out <dir>` stays clean on a fresh scan against a destination outside the scan root — that branch already passes `cache_root=out_root` to `detect()`. It leaks `graphify-out/cache/stat-index.json` into the scan root on the very next incremental run against the same destination, once a manifest already exists there.

`detect_incremental()` had no `cache_root` parameter at all, so `cli.py`'s incremental branch had no way to pass it even if it wanted to, and the word-count cache (`cached_word_count` -> `_ensure_stat_index`) fell back to anchoring at the scan root instead of the requested `--out` directory.

## Fix

`detect_incremental()` now accepts `cache_root: Path | None = None` and forwards it into its own internal call to `detect()`. `cli.py`'s incremental branch now passes `cache_root=out_root`, matching what the fresh-scan branch a few lines below it already does.

## Testing

- Added `test_detect_incremental_respects_cache_root` to `tests/test_detect.py`, following the same pattern as the existing `test_detect_office_conversion_respects_cache_root` (#2787) test for `detect()` itself: asserts no `graphify-out/` is created in the scan root and the stat index file lands under `cache_root` instead.
- Confirmed against pre-fix code (temporarily restoring the prior versions of `detect.py`/`cli.py`) that the call raises `TypeError` there, since the parameter didn't exist yet.
- Full project test suite passes (only pre-existing, unrelated failures remain: four extractor test files needing optional `tree-sitter-language-pack` grammars not installed in this environment, and one pre-existing environment-specific test artifact unrelated to this change).
- `python3 -m tools.skillgen --check` passes.

title: fix(skillgen): prevent monolith watch path injection
body:
### Summary

Fixes **#3844** by preventing untrusted `INPUT_PATH` values from being interpreted as shell syntax in Graphify's generated skills, including the Aider and Devin monolith flows.

### Changes

* Persist the resolved scan root to `graphify-out/.graphify_root` through a single-quoted heredoc.
* Remove direct `INPUT_PATH` interpolation from the Aider/Devin `--watch` commands.
* Make `--watch` consume the trusted `.graphify_root` marker instead.
* Remove literal `INPUT_PATH` references from Step 1 comments to prevent newline-based substitution from escaping the quoted heredoc.
* Add narrowly scoped sanctioned-diff rules for the intentional monolith changes.
* Expand security tests to cover:

  * command substitution
  * backticks
  * `;`
  * `&&`
  * pipes
  * newline injection
* Add tests for valid paths containing spaces and nonexistent paths.
* Fix Linux/macOS portability in the path-resolution tests.
* Regenerate all affected skill artifacts and expected snapshots.

### Validation

* `python -m tools.skillgen --check` — **PASS**
* `python -m tools.skillgen --monolith-roundtrip` — **PASS**
* `pytest tests/test_skillgen_input_path_injection.py -v` — **30 passed**
* `pytest tests/test_skillgen.py -v` — **65 passed**
* `git diff --check` — **PASS**

### Security

The scan path is now passed to Python through a quoted heredoc rather than being interpreted as part of a shell command. The Aider and Devin `--watch` flows read the trusted resolved root from `graphify-out/.graphify_root`, eliminating direct shell interpolation of `INPUT_PATH`.

No unrelated changes are included.

title: fix(watch,cli): publish label sidecars atomically, labels before signatures
body:
## Problem

`_rebuild_code` publishes `graph.json` atomically, then writes three sidecars with plain `write_text`:

```python
graph_tmp.replace(existing_graph)          # atomic
report_path.write_text(report)             # not atomic
labels_file.write_text(labels_json)        # not atomic
sig_file.write_text(...)                   # not atomic
```

Each is truncated in place, so a crash, ENOSPC, or SIGKILL mid-write can publish a half-written sidecar. The staleness guard reads those signatures, so a torn `.sig` degrades label reuse to the count-based heuristic.

## Fix

- Publish both sidecars (and `GRAPH_REPORT.md`) with the existing `paths.write_text_atomic` helper — temp file in the same directory plus `os.replace`, with the symlink resolution and mode preservation the hand-rolled writes lacked.
- Apply the same fix to the parallel writer in the `graphify label` path (`cli.py:2332`), which wrote its `.sig` with a bare `Path.write_text` while writing labels atomically. That is the path that actually produces LLM labels, and it feeds the same guard.

## On write order

An earlier revision of this PR reordered the writes to put signatures first, arguing that it was the crash-safe direction. **That was wrong, and it is worth stating plainly because it inverted the bug rather than fixing it.** The guard is:

```python
stale = {cid for cid in labels if saved_sigs.get(cid) != cur_sigs.get(cid)}
```

`saved_sigs` comes from the sidecar, `cur_sigs` is recomputed from the *current* clustering — the comparison never involves the labels. So a crash after the signatures and before the labels leaves a sidecar that already describes the new clustering sitting beside the old labels: the next rebuild recomputes the same signatures, finds them equal, reports nothing stale, and silently keeps names for a clustering that no longer exists.

Reproduced against that revision — the signature advanced, the label did not, and the recovery rebuild kept `LLM-Name-0` with no `community set changed since labeling` warning.

Labels are written first, so an interruption leaves the sidecar trailing, which the guard sees as a mismatch and re-labels by hub. Both writers now use that order.

## Test

`test_rebuild_code_sidecar_writes_are_atomic_and_labels_first` tracks `os.replace`, `Path.write_text` and a writing `open()` scoped to the live output directory, so it asserts observable behaviour rather than the helper's name. Against the pre-fix code it reports both sidecars as `:non-atomic`; against the signatures-first ordering it fails with `saw ['sig', 'labels']`.

(The `open()` hook is scoped to `out/` deliberately: `backup_if_protected` copies the old sidecars into a dated backup folder via `shutil.copy2` before the rebuild advances them, which is a copy of the previous file rather than a publish of the new one.)

## Verification

`tests/test_watch.py`: 5 failed / 137 passed before, 5 failed / **138** passed after. `-k "label or cluster"`: 21 failed / 220 passed before, 21 failed / **221** passed after. The failures are identical with and without the change — missing tree-sitter language grammars in this environment — and are present on a clean `v8`. CI is the real check for those.

https://claude.ai/code/session_01RqZJxkPvMu7sNMeJLXtziE

title: TSX/JSX: components used as <Comp /> get no incoming edge
fix(extract): add calls edges for JSX component usage (#3854)
body:
Fixes #3854

JSX usages like `<Bubble />` and `<Card>...</Card>` now produce `calls` edges in .tsx and .jsx files (plain .ts is unchanged).

The two JSX element types are added to `call_types`, and in the generic `walk_calls` path the callee is read from the `name` field. Only bare identifiers are handled. Tags starting with a lowercase letter are intrinsic elements and are skipped, same rule as the JSX transform, so `<div>` never binds to a local `div()`, while `<_Row />` still counts as a component. Member tags (`<icons.Close>`, `<props.Comp>`, `<Ctx.Provider>`) are skipped: resolving them by the property name binds to unrelated local functions (plain `icons.Close()` already does this today). Namespaced tags and fragments are ignored, closing tags aren't counted.

One thing this doesn't cover: JSX at the top level of a module (e.g. `root.render(<App />)`) still gets no edge, same as a plain top-level call does today.

Tests are in `tests/test_jsx_component_usage_calls.py`. The same-file, cross-file, .jsx and `_Row` cases fail without the change; the `<div>`, `<motion.div>`, `<Theme.Provider>` and `<icons.Close>` / `<props.Comp>` ones guard against false edges.

I ran the full suite on Windows 11 before and after: 41 failed / 5835 passed before, 41 failed / 5843 passed after. It is the same 41 failing tests in both runs (Windows-specific ones: Erlang, hooks, install paths, watch); the +8 are the new tests. ruff is clean, and pyright reports the same 152 existing errors in the two touched files before and after.

title: feat(serve): add JEV two-stage semantic search, smart BFS pruning, and blast radius analysis
body:
## What does this PR do?

Adds an **optional, fail-open JEV semantic seed navigation and graph analysis layer** to `_query_graph_text` in `serve.py`.

### Problem Solved
Currently, `query_graph` relies solely on keyword/trigram matching (and jieba for Chinese). When developers query with colloquial or natural language without exact identifier names (e.g., *'where do we handle silent token refresh when login expires'* while the code is named `refresh_token_pair`), keyword matching often returns zero seed nodes or pulls in noisy, unrelated modules.

### Core Capabilities
1. **Two-Stage JEV Choice Navigation**: Community coarse filter (pruning ~85% irrelevant subgraphs) + node fine selection.
2. **Graph Topology Hub Ranking**: NetworkX degree sorting for God Node prioritization.
3. **Multi-Candidate Seed Picking**: Captures cross-community collaborative seeds using choice probability distributions.
4. **Hierarchical File Folding**: Two-stage selection (file -> function) for large communities (>35 nodes) to eliminate truncation blind spots.
5. **Fingerprinted LRU Cache**: Graph topology + query hash cache for 0ms repeated lookups.
6. **Smart BFS Subgraph Pruning**: Dynamic neighbor filtering with Jev Choice to prune irrelevant utility/logging noise and cut prompt token context by ~50%.
7. **Blast Radius Impact Analysis**: Reverse caller dependency tracing via new `analyze_blast_radius` MCP tool.

### Engineering & Safety Principles
- **Strictly Fail-open**: If `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` / `OPENCODE_API_KEY` is unset, or on timeout/network errors, silently falls back to original keyword seed picker (`_pick_seeds`).
- **Metadata Only**: Outbound payloads only contain file names and symbol signatures, never raw source code lines.
- **Stdlib Only**: Implemented with pure Python stdlib (`urllib.request` + `json`), zero heavy dependencies.
- **Native .env Auto-loader**: Supports local `.env` configuration with `.gitignore` protection and `.env.example` template.

### How was this tested?
- Added unit tests in `tests/test_jev_semantic_search.py` (7 passed).
- E2E tested on real-world multi-module codebases, reducing prompt token context by ~80% while achieving 100% precision on colloquial queries.

title: `cluster-only` on a `merge-graphs` output remaps against per-source community ids, so saved LLM labels are mostly lost on every rebuild
body:
### Summary

When `cluster-only` re-clusters, it maps the new communities onto the previous ones
(`remap_communities_to_previous`, #822/#1027) using the `community` attribute of the nodes in
the input `graph.json` (cli.py, `previous_node_community = {n["id"]: n["community"] ...}`).

In a multi-source pipeline, that input is the fresh output of `merge-graphs`, which carries
each **source's own** community ids (overlapping 0..N per source before 0.9.50, offset per
input since 0.9.50, original kept in `local_community`). It does **not** carry the previous
**merged** clustering, which is what `.graphify_labels.json` / `.graphify_labels.json.sig`
were written against. The remap therefore aligns new communities to the wrong groups, the
per-cid signature check fails for most communities, and they are renamed by their hub.

### Version

Measured on 0.9.46; code path unchanged in 0.9.69 (label-reuse branch identical by diff,
`previous_node_community` still read from the input file).

### Evidence

Pipeline: per-source `graphify update` → `graphify merge-graphs a.json b.json ... --out
merged/graphify-out/graph.json` → `cd merged && graphify cluster-only .` (labels file kept).
~15 000 nodes, ~1 700 communities, 5 sources.

| Rebuild after a small commit (a few nodes changed) | Communities renamed by hub |
|---|---|
| As above, 0.9.46 | **1 130 / 1 709** |
| Same, but the previous merged `graph.json` is saved before `merge-graphs` and its `community` value is copied back onto each node (by node id) before `cluster-only` — 0.9.69, first build after the upgrade | **128 / 1 660** |

The saved merged `graph.json` from the day before had 660 distinct `community` values
after `merge-graphs` (per-source ids) vs 1 709 in the previous merged clustering.

Offline simulation on the same graph (0.9.69 offsets, no workaround): if one early source
gains a single community, all later offsets shift and only **285 / 1 702** labels survive.

### Workaround (10 lines)

```bash
cp merged/graphify-out/graph.json merged/graphify-out/graph.previous.json
graphify merge-graphs ... --out merged/graphify-out/graph.json
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
prev = {n["id"]: n["community"] for n in json.load(open("merged/graphify-out/graph.previous.json"))["nodes"]
        if n.get("community") is not None}
g = json.load(open("merged/graphify-out/graph.json"))
for n in g["nodes"]:
    if n["id"] in prev: n["community"] = prev[n["id"]]
    else: n.pop("community", None)
json.dump(g, open("merged/graphify-out/graph.json", "w"))
PY
(cd merged && graphify cluster-only .)
```

### Related

#3014 (merge-graphs namespacing — this is the downstream effect on label reuse), #2452 (seed
`cluster()` with a previous partition), #2298 (exact-membership signature), #3334.

### Suggested fix

Either `merge-graphs` could accept `--previous <merged graph.json>` and emit the previous merged
`community` (keeping per-source ids only in `local_community`), or `cluster-only` could prefer
`graphify-out/graph.json` **already on disk** (the previous run's output) over the input's
`community` attribute when a labels sidecar exists.

title: Docs: labeling flags vs. context window, `--missing-only`, and `export html` node limit are undocumented or misleading (0.9.69)
body:
### Context

Upgrading 0.9.46 → 0.9.69 and labeling ~1 700 communities through an OpenAI-compatible local
model with an **8192-token** context. Each point below cost us a failed run or a wrong assumption.

**1. `--batch-size` vs. context window.** The README suggests `--batch-size 200` "for large
graphs", but `_LABEL_BATCH_SIZE = 100` is commented "sized for ~16k context windows". With an
8k model, batches of 100 reached **14 822 tokens**: 8 of 18 batches failed with
`ContextWindowExceededError`. `_label_batch_with_retry` only splits on JSON parse failures, so
these batches are not retried. Suggest: document the rule of thumb (≈150 tokens per community;
`--batch-size 40` fits 8k), and treat a context-window error like a parse failure (split in half).

**2. `--missing-only` is undocumented in the README** (only in `--help` and the CHANGELOG, #1481),
and does not do what its name suggests after re-clustering: it ignores the membership signatures,
so stale labels are kept, and communities renamed by their hub are saved as real labels (#3334),
so it never re-labels them. The README should state that `graphify label` (full relabel) is
currently the only way to refresh names after the community set changes.

**3. `.graphify_labels.json.sig`** decides which labels survive a re-cluster but is not
documented (#3808). One line in the README would have saved us a debugging session.

**4. `export html` ignores `GRAPHIFY_VIZ_NODE_LIMIT`** (`node_limit = 5000` hard-coded in
cli.py) while `cluster-only` honours it since 0.9.69. Users of the env var get the aggregated
view from `export html` without warning. Document `--node-limit` there, or honour the variable.

**5. Leiden is described as the clustering algorithm**, but without the `leiden` extra graphify
silently falls back to networkx Louvain. Document the fallback (and that switching later
reshuffles every community, i.e. a full relabel).

title: Add a Salam (.salam) language extractor
body:
Salam (https://github.com/SalamLang/Salam) isn't one of the supported languages, so a Salam codebase gets skipped and never shows up in the graph.

**Proposed solution:**
Add an extractor for .salam files. Salam has no tree-sitter grammar, so this would be a small token-based scanner (like the COBOL/Apex ones), no new dependency. It should handle both English and Persian keyword spellings, since Salam source can be written in either, and pull out packages, imports, functions, structs/methods, enums, interfaces, impl, switch/match, extern C functions, and layout/components, plus @en/@fa name aliases.

**Alternatives considered:**
Waiting for an official tree-sitter grammar, but Salam doesn't have one yet and the language's own compiler is small enough that a regex/token scanner covers it well.

**Area:**
Extraction or language support

title: fix(groovy): extract enum declarations and their constants
body:
### What
A Groovy `enum` is dropped entirely — the type node and every constant it declares are missing:

```groovy
enum Suit { HEARTS, SPADES, CLUBS, DIAMONDS }
```

Before this change, extracting that file produced no `Suit` node and none of its four constants, so a consumer branching on a `Suit` value had nothing in the graph to point at.

### Why
`_GROOVY_CONFIG.class_types` listed only `class_declaration` and `interface_declaration`. `enum_declaration` was absent, so the enum subtree was never treated as a type and was skipped. Even once the type is recognised, its members need emitting — Java/C#/Kotlin/Swift each already emit a node per enum member with a `case_of` edge.

### The fix
- Add `enum_declaration` to `_GROOVY_CONFIG.class_types` so the enum becomes a first-class type node.
- tree-sitter-groovy exposes the **same `enum_constant` shape** (a `name` field, optional `class_body`) that tree-sitter-java uses, so the existing `_java_extra_walk` enum-constant handler is reused for Groovy rather than duplicating it — one node per member with a `case_of` edge to the enum.

### Tests
Added a regression test asserting the enum type and all four constants are extracted and hang off the enum (not the file). `-k groovy` is green (14 passed); Java/C#/Kotlin/Swift/enum suites unaffected (95 passed). `ruff check` clean.

title: fix(sql): extract triggers and link them to their table
body:
### What
`CREATE TRIGGER` is under-extracted in two ways:

1. A trigger with a procedural body is dropped **entirely**:
   ```sql
   CREATE TRIGGER trg_after AFTER INSERT ON users
   FOR EACH ROW
   BEGIN
     UPDATE stats SET cnt = cnt + 1;
   END;
   ```
   No `trg_after` node at all.

2. Even a cleanly-parsed trigger gets a node with **no link to its table**:
   ```sql
   CREATE TRIGGER audit_ins AFTER INSERT ON users EXECUTE FUNCTION log_it();
   ```
   `audit_ins` exists but has no `triggers` edge to `users`.

### Why
- **(2)** The `create_trigger` AST branch read the subject table off `keyword_for`. But the table follows `ON` (`AFTER INSERT ON users`); `FOR EACH ROW` carries no table, so `tbl_name` stayed `None` and no edge was emitted.
- **(1)** A `FOR EACH ROW BEGIN … END` body has no grammar production, so the whole statement becomes an `ERROR` node. The only safety net is the whole-file routine-recovery scan — but its pattern (`_ROUTINE_RECOVERY_RX`) matches only `FUNCTION`/`PROCEDURE`, so triggers were never recovered.

### The fix
- Read the trigger's table after `keyword_on` instead of `keyword_for`.
- Add a dedicated `_TRIGGER_RECOVERY_RX` used in the `has_error` recovery block. It mints the trigger node (label **without** `()`, since a trigger is not callable — matching the AST path) and a `triggers` edge to the table named by the first `ON` after the trigger name (the timing clause `BEFORE INSERT` carries none). It reuses the same masked-source scan and delimited-identifier atom as the routine recovery, so commented-out / single-quoted DDL can't fabricate a trigger. TRIGGER is deliberately kept out of `_ROUTINE_RECOVERY_RX` because that path labels matches `name()`. A trigger already recovered via the AST path is skipped so no duplicate edge is produced.

### Tests
Added regression tests in `tests/test_multilang.py` for both the clean `EXECUTE FUNCTION` form (table link) and the procedural `BEGIN … END` form (full recovery, single edge, no dangling). `-k "sql or trigger"` green (37 passed). `ruff check` clean.

title: fix(r): recognise namespace-qualified class constructors (R6::R6Class)
body:
### What
An R6 class defined with the qualified `R6::R6Class(...)` form loses its entire body:

```r
Counter <- R6::R6Class("Counter",
  public = list(
    increment = function() self$count,
    report    = function() print(1)
  )
)
```

Before this change only a plain `Counter` variable node survived — `increment` and `report` were gone. The unqualified `R6Class("Counter", ...)` form worked fine, which made the gap easy to miss.

### Why
`_CLASS_CONSTRUCTORS` is `{"R6Class", "setRefClass", "ggproto"}`, but `call_parts` returns the function's full source text. For `R6::R6Class` that is the qualified string `"R6::R6Class"`, which is not in the set — so the binding fell through to the ordinary-variable branch and the class body was never scanned. `R6::R6Class` is the *recommended* way to reference the constructor without `library(R6)`, so this is the common idiom in real code. The same applies to `methods::setClass` / `methods::setRefClass`.

### The fix
Strip the namespace qualifier (`split("::")[-1]`) before the constructor membership check — in both the binding path (`scan_declarations`) and `process_call_declaration`. A qualified constructor is the same declaration as its bare form, so it is now recognised identically. Unqualified declarations are unchanged.

### Tests
Added two regression tests: `R6::R6Class` extracts the class and both methods, and `methods::setRefClass` is recognised as a class. `test_r_extractor.py` green (7 passed). `ruff check` clean.

title: fix(r): resolve R6 self$ and private$ intra-class method calls
body:
### What
Inside an R6 class, calls between methods are dropped:

```r
Counter <- R6Class("Counter",
  public = list(
    increment = function() self$report(),
    report    = function() print(1)
  ),
  private = list(
    log = function() private$fmt(),
    fmt = function() 2
  )
)
```

`increment → report` and `log → fmt` never appeared as `calls` edges, so an R6 class looked like a bag of unrelated methods.

### Why
An R6 method can only reach a sibling through `self$method()` or `private$method()` — there is no bare-name form. But `walk_calls` only handled a callee that is a plain `identifier`; a `self$report` callee is an `extract_operator`, which was ignored.

### The fix
Handle an `extract_operator` callee whose receiver is `self` or `private`: take the method name and resolve it against the enclosing class scope, which is already reachable from the caller via `scope_parent` (methods are registered under their class). `super$` is deliberately excluded — it dispatches to a parent class this single-file pass cannot see, so binding it locally would be a wrong edge.

### Tests
Added a regression test asserting both `self$` and `private$` intra-class calls resolve. `test_r_extractor.py` green (6 passed). `ruff check` clean.

title: feat(mcp): improve retrieval quality with phrase bonus, community coherence, and evidence-first truncation (#3810)
body:
## What does this PR do?

Resolves #3810 (MCP Retrieval Quality)

This PR addresses the retrieval precision issues in the MCP agent context when dealing with large graphs. It implements three targeted improvements to the retrieval and rendering pipeline to surface the most relevant structural evidence:

1. **Sub-Phrase Match Tier (`_score_query`)**: For queries with 3+ terms, it now applies a prefix match bonus for contiguous 2-gram or 3-gram subphrases found in the node label. This allows coherent multi-term identifier matches (e.g., `incidence algebra`) to correctly outrank isolated, incidental single-term matches.
2. **Community Coherence Filter (`_pick_seeds`)**: When query terms yield more seeds than `max_k`, the seed set is now truncated by prioritizing nodes that belong to the majority community among the seed pool. This prevents isolated nodes in completely unrelated semantic domains from stealing seed slots and hijacking the traversal.
3. **Evidence-First Truncation (`_subgraph_to_text`)**: Nodes lying on the inter-seed shortest path (the core structural evidence connecting queried symbols) are sorted first before other arbitrary neighbors. This guarantees they survive aggressive token-budget truncation cuts.

title: [security] Unbounded edge allocation: cross-file import resolution creates F*C*K edges from a tiny corpus
body:
## Security Finding: Unbounded edge allocation: cross-file import resolution creates F*C*K edges from a tiny corpus

**Severity**: HIGH (CVSS 7.1)
**CWE**: CWE-770
**Repository**: Graphify-Labs/graphify
**Affected**: `graphify/extract.py:2235`

### Description

extract._resolve_cross_file_imports (extract.py:2123-2253) iterates every imported name and, for each, adds an edge from EVERY local class in the importing file (lines 2235-2247). Cost is O(files x imported_names x local_classes) with no cap on edges, nodes, or edges-per-node anywhere in extract()/build(). A 5.26 MB generated corpus (401 files: one module defining 2000 classes, 400 files each defining 8 classes and importing all 2000 names) produced 6,405,600 edges and 5,601 nodes, driving peak RSS to ~2.1-2.7 GB and 6.6-21s of work. The subsequent watch rebuild and to_json/to_cypher then materialize all of it again.

### Impact

A small, easily authored source tree forces multi-gigabyte memory use and multi-million-edge graphs. Because graphify runs this rebuild automatically via the watch loop and the post-commit git hook, simply committing the crafted files triggers the exhaustion. graph.json/GRAPH_REPORT.md/observed outputs grow proportionally, exhausting disk as well.

### Remediation

Cross-file import resolution no longer emits a cartesian product of every imported name by every class in the importing file. Each class node is now mapped to the identifiers its own body references, and a `uses` edge is emitted only for classes that actually mention the imported name (or its alias), with (source, target) pairs deduplicated so repeated import statements cannot multiply edges. A hard global budget (_MAX_CROSS_FILE_EDGES = 100,000) aborts with a clear ValueError before more memory is allocated, so a small crafted corpus can no longer drive multi-gigabyte extraction/build memory or multi-million-edge graph.json artifacts.

### Affected Code

```
graphify-main/graphify/extract.py:2235
                line = node.start_point[0] + 1
                for name in imported_names:
                    tgt_nid = stem_to_entities[target_stem].get(name)

title: [security] core.hooksPath from the repository redirects `graphify hook install` to an arbitrary path
body:
## Security Finding: core.hooksPath from the repository redirects `graphify hook install` to an arbitrary path

**Severity**: HIGH (CVSS 8.5)
**CWE**: CWE-22
**Repository**: Graphify-Labs/graphify
**Affected**: `- graphify/hooks.py:64-75`

### Description

`graphify.hooks._hooks_dir()` reads the `core.hooksPath` value out of the target repository's own git configuration and treats it as a trusted destination, so `graphify hook install` can be made to drop an executable post-commit script anywhere the victim's user can write — including outside the repository entirely. The repository is the attacker's input, and its `.git/config` travels with the code when it is shipped as a tarball, zip or plain directory copy, which is the documented way the tool's own setup is delivered.

In `graphify/hooks.py:57-93` the function runs `git -C <root> config core.hooksPath` and, if the value is non-empty, resolves it relative to the repository root when it is relative and uses absolute values as-is, then calls `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` on the result. Nothing checks that the resolved directory is still inside the repository. `install()` then writes the `_HOOK_SCRIPT` payload to `<that directory>/post-commit` and sets the mode to 0755 (`graphify/hooks.py:116-117`), and `uninstall()` likewise unlinks or rewrites a file at the repository-chosen path.

Because the hook body is an executable script that git runs on every commit, a repository that sets `core.hooksPath` to a path such as an autostart directory, a shared hooks directory, or `../`-style traversal out of the tree converts a routine `graphify hook install` into persistent execution of attacker-chosen code under the victim's account. Git does not expand `~`, so the configuration must carry an expanded absolute path, but otherwise absolute paths and `..` traversal both resolve.

### Impact

An attacker-supplied repository can cause `graphify hook install` to write a mode-0755 executable script into any directory the victim can write to, achieving persistent code execution with the victim's privileges on every subsequent `git commit` — reliable local compromise and persistence on developer machines and CI, with the repository boundary providing no confinement. `uninstall()` can likewise delete or overwrite a file at a repository-chosen path.

### Remediation

1. In `_hooks_dir` (`graphify/hooks.py:57-93`), resolve the configured path and reject it unless `resolved.is_relative_to(root.resolve())` (equivalently `Path(custom).resolve().relative_to(root.resolve())`); never `mkdir` an unchecked absolute path.
2. Treat `core.hooksPath` as untrusted repository metadata: refuse to install when the resolved hooks directory falls outside the repository root or `.git` (falling back or erroring instead), and do not honor absolute values that escape the repository.
3. Require an explicit opt-in flag or interactive user confirmation before honoring a `core.hooksPath` that differs from the default, allowing only known in-repo hook managers such as `.husky`.
4. Verify the final hook file itself is inside the repository and preserve or report its mode explicitly rather than silently applying 0755.

### Affected Code

```
graphify/hooks.py:64-75
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "-C", str(root), "config", "core.hooksPath"],
            capture_output=True, text=True,
        )
        if result.returncode == 0:
            custom = result.stdout.strip()
            if custom:
                p = Path(custom)
                if not p.is_absolute():
                    p = root / p
                p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                return p
```

### Verification

Adversarially verified (GLM) — passed.

body:
## What does this PR do?

Fixes #3787, a follow-up to #3817.

**What:** a Terraform `{ name = "DB_PASSWORD", value = "hunter2" }` pair puts `hunter2` in graph.json and the MCP `query`/`get_node` output verbatim. That is the usual shape for ECS environment lists and for module inputs such as `environment = [...]`.

**Why:** `_redact_value` decides by the map KEY. Here the keys are the generic `name` and `value`, and the secret signal is the `name` literal, so nothing matched.

**Small example:**
- `environment = [{ name = "DB_PASSWORD", value = "hunter2" }, { name = "LOG_LEVEL", value = "debug" }]`

- With this fix it is stored as `[{name: DB_PASSWORD, value: [redacted]}, {name: LOG_LEVEL, value: debug}]`.

**Why the existing tests missed it:** every redaction test puts the secret word in a key (`password`, `client_secret`, `var.db_password`). None puts it in a value.

**Fix:** when a map has a `name` key whose string value matches `_SENSITIVE_KEY_RE`, redact its `value` / `valueFrom` / `value_from` too. This follows your suggestion in the issue and stays conservative:
- An ordinary pair such as `LOG_LEVEL` is untouched.

title: save_manifest(kind="ast") blanks a valid semantic_hash stamped by kind="semantic" (content unchanged)
body:
## Summary

`save_manifest(kind="ast")` blanks a **still-valid** `semantic_hash` when the previous write was `kind="semantic"` on content edited since the last AST stamp — with no content change in between.

`kind="semantic"` sets `semantic_hash = h` but carries the **old** `ast_hash` forward. The next AST-only write (`graphify update`, or any `watch.py` refresh) then compares the current hash against that stale `ast_hash`, sees a mismatch, and writes `semantic_hash = ""`. `detect_incremental(kind="semantic")` then re-queues a doc that was just extracted.

Version: `graphifyy` 0.9.43 (`graphify/detect.py`, `save_manifest`, the `else` branch of `if kind in ("semantic", "both")`, ~L1950).

## Repro

```python
import json, os
from graphify.detect import save_manifest

open("a.md", "w").write("v1\n")
f = {"document": [os.path.abspath("a.md")]}
save_manifest(f, "m.json", kind="both")        # ast_hash = semantic_hash = H1
open("a.md", "w").write("v2\n")
save_manifest(f, "m.json", kind="semantic")    # semantic_hash = H2, ast_hash still H1
save_manifest(f, "m.json", kind="ast")         # content unchanged since the semantic stamp
print(json.load(open("m.json")))               # semantic_hash == ""  <-- stamp lost
```

Expected: `semantic_hash == H2` (the content is exactly what was semantically extracted).
Actual: `semantic_hash == ""`.

## Impact

In a split pipeline (a nightly AST `graphify update` plus a separate semantic pass that stamps `kind="semantic"`), every doc edited between the two passes loses its semantic stamp on the next AST refresh. We saw a clean pass report "38 docs semantically stamped" and a freshness check read 33 of them stale two hours later.

## Proposed fix (2 lines)

Preserve the semantic stamp when the current content matches **either** the prior semantic hash or the prior AST hash:

```python
# detect.py, save_manifest, AST-only branch
prev_sem = prev.get("semantic_hash", "")
entry["semantic_hash"] = prev_sem if h in (prev_sem, prev.get("ast_hash", "")) else ""
```

Happy to open a PR with a regression test if that's welcome.
